In The Witcher 2, you play as Geralt of Rivia, a witcher (basically a badass magic ninja who kills monsters for money) who has been framed for the murder of the king of Temeria by another witcher, only this one has enough muscles to arm wrestle an elephant on steroids. Seriously, the dude is ♥♥♥♥ing ripped. Anyways, in the game you're out to clear your name, hunt down the bad witcher, deal with a lot of political crap and get up to a bit of *ahem* giggity-giggity along the way.
Overall, the game is really damn good.
PRO'S
1) The graphics are nice and crisp, and are pretty realistic. The lighting rocks, and the water looks really pretty. Grimy armour, tattered tunics, epic weapons, hulking brutes, trolls, ghouls, vegetaion, dense forests, shafts of light poking through trees- everything looks damn good, and the textures are on point.
Of course there's some minor stuff here and there, which is to be expected really, but on the whole the game looks great. Ah, but here's a word of warning: You'll need a good system to run this game. Even though it's, like, four years old, this game packs a punch.
2) The story is really engaging and keeps me wanting to know what's gonna happen next. It's all paced out really well, and the web of political intrigue is really, well, intriguing. The story keeps me wanting to know what'll happen next and is really interesting.
3) The side missions are good, and some of them have a nice bit of story to them, and in particular there was one in the second act which I really enjoyed, which I won't spoil here but involved restoring dignity to a poor soldier who♥♥♥♥♥♥his pants and consequently earned the title of "Crapper".
4) The gameplay is great, with tense swordfighting and awesome powers (known as 'signs' in-game) that really remind me of Skyrim. There's Aard a.k.a Force Push, which is basically a weaker version of Fus Ro Dah and Igni, TW2's version of the fire powers in Skyrim, and a bunch of generally badass powers, such as Axii which converts enemies to your side for a short while and Yrden, which is a magical trap that immobilises enemies, and finally Quen, which is a magical shield that protects you from damage.
Throughout the game you mostly spend your time slicing open enemy soldiers and a bunch of assorted monsters. There are two swords you can use: A steel sword for cutting open humans/elves and a silver sword for examining monster guts.
You'll also spend your time completing monster slaying contracts for orens (in-game currency) and ploughing (heh heh) through the main quest lines. You'll also spend your time playing dice poker, arm wrestling, getting into fist fights and getting it up with, ah, certain people of the opposite sex in exchange for orens.

5) The voice acting is on point: Geralt sounds like the cool, calm, and collected badass that he is, and the Scottish/Irish accents really sound good in-game.
CONS
1) My biggest problem with this game is the learning curve in the game. Even after being updated, the difficulty levels in this game are a ♥♥♥♥♥. The first few fights in the game are ♥♥♥♥ing tough and end with you dying repeatedly before making any progress. Mid way through you suddenly become a demi-god, and cutting open your enemies becomes much easier. The game is peppered with bloody hard boss fights that'll leave you cursing and frustrated a lot of the time, and there are a few encounters in the game that require several tries to get through. The Kayran boss fight, in particular, sucks hard, but the rewards aren't bad at all for that one.
2) When the sword-fighting comes together, it is utterly, mind-blowingly beautiful. You really feel like a medieaval ninja, blocking strikes, quickly countering, dodging hefty blows, striking only to be repelled, launching a blistering counter-attack with the help of signs: it is perfection. But most of the time, that just isn't the case. Geralt is slow to respond to commands, and oftentimes enemies got in cheap strikes that could have been prevented if Geralt wasn't such a slow coach. It can result in a lot of frustrating deaths, and rage quits. Those few beautiful moments, in my opinion, make it worth it though.
3) The game isn't really optimised well, and even though I more than meet the minimum requirements I met a lot of awful FPS drops. Most of the time, however, the game plays buttery smooth, in spite of occasional hiccups.
4) The game can get a bit buggy, with a few visual hiccups and stuff.
OVERALL: 8.5/10

Buy? Likely. Retrovirus is a Six Degrees of Freedom (6DOF) FPS about a world within a person's computer, where a destructive worm has infected and corrupted the system. Your task as an agent of the anti-virus program is to of course, delete this worm. Emails scattered across the system, hints to the reasoning behind the worm attack.
6DOF essentially means freedom of moment, so you're constantly flying and have to deal with threats that can occur from any angle in 3D space. RV can't escape (and possibly doesn't want to) the comparison to Descent and Forsaken/Forsaken 64 - I think the developer refereneces Descent in forums.
Mecanics are based on weaponry and technology that use a limited, but regenerative resource called cycles that are displayed on your gun. You also have a scan function to highlight enemies, a charged scan to scan a wide area of enemies and to activate marks (bullet holes) made by your weapons. These marks vary depending on the weapon, such as a small explosion with the pistol-like Dual Strike, push back with the minigun style Thrash, or creation of gravity wells with the shotgun-like Interruptor, my personal favoritte. The use of cycles essentially means unlimited ammo, but requires you to manage shooting as you can easily run out if you shoot too much and you don't have any reload canisters. This is a problem with the larger hoard fights and some boss fights as there where times I felt I couldn't deal with the threat and I felt impossible with the Corrupted Driver boss battle (until I found a level exploit). You can also upgrade your "ship" and weaponry with bytes earned from killing enemies, destroying corruption and orange byte pickups which I think are called Memories.
I LOVE the high tech "Futuristicy" art style, though I'm not sure what I think about the combination of that mixed up with destroyed stone and concrete walls thanks to the Worm. I guess the idea is that the Worm is so destructive, that it's destroying the actual physical structure of the machine (though, the system is nothing like any computer I've any seen, it's obviously an interpretation)
I found the game mostly enjoyable and I enjoy the technology puns and references - computer geeks may get a laugh out of the dialogue's sense of humor. I did get more annoyed near the latter quarter of the game where I died alot due to a couple bosses and a couple hordes. It's a shame that this game wasn't advertised well, because hardly anybody knows about it and there's never anybody available for Co-op campaign or competitive multiplayer (except for certain Days when the developer hosts game sessions).
If you're somebody that liked Descent or Forsaken, or a computer geek that likes sci-fi FPS games, this game is definitely worth checking out - it provided me with at least 12+ hrs of gameplay (admittedly, more deaths than I'd like). I must warn you that the game may require a strong gaming system, as the frame rate can drop significantly - it has 12-15fps on my Intel HD laptop and drops like crazy when I accidentaly leave Folding@Home on (though, it's CPU intensive anyways, but many players mentioned performance problems - look at the community hub) Due to the lack of community, it's probably best to wait for a sale or bundle.

The third part of the Alien Breed series, starting this third part will give a big Déjà vu of the second part. The intro and start-screen are pretty much the same but instead of green they used a orange/yellow theme. After a quick Google search i came to the conclusion that this part was released a little less than two month's after part 2.
First look into the game:
As stated before the intro and start menu look exactly the same as part 2, after starting a new single player you get to see the re-cap of what happened. Again this looks actually like part 2, even the first minute was the same as the previous part. After the cut-scene you get to start and it again looks actually like A.B 2, i am not stating this is a good or bad thing but since i didn't like the previous part this just didn't work for me.
The game:
Level design is done with a great eye for details, allot of scenic sightseeing helps to enhance the orbital atmosphere. The in-game cut-scenes are i bit short in my opinion, since they look decent and some of the character designs are to be called quite unique i would like to see them for longer than 5 seconds... The HUD's change of colour works better since it's easy to see no matter whats in the background. The music is still pretty good but after playing five minutes i noticed that they cut the alien ambient sounds. Objectives in the main campaign are mainly going from A to B and activating a switch to proceed in the level and some backtracking.
Verdict:
Controls are still mainly for the twin-sticks and using a keyboard/mouse feels awkward and still has some issues with turning around to shoot an enemy that is hitting you in the back. The multiplayer/coop aspect and survivor-mode are still the same as part 2, the overall gameplay is nice but not my thing. Also instead of tuning the game after A.B 2 they kept everything the same, this could again be a good/bad thing but they could of optimize the keyboard controls.
This game gets a rating of 6,5, mainly because the game feels like a Déjà vu from the previous part.

Why is this game free? I don't know. It's not a demo. There are no F2P gimmicks either. It's truly a labor of love.
So now that we got that out of the way, this is a great game. The gameplay, setting, and characters are deeply nostalgic for Quest for Glory, King's Quest, and old-school Sierra adventure game fans. The gameplay has actually taken a few modern design sensibilities to heart, adding more combat complexity and skill improvement notifications. The rich Norse setting is brought to life with colorful, interactive 2D backgrounds. While this game has a bit more text to pour through than the old Sierra games, I feel that most of the fully voice-acted characters have interesting personalities, and more conversation options are unlocked as you discover more of the world. The only thing I miss is QFG4's sardonic narrator making fun of you for trying to use a shovel on a tree--the text is there, but a voice would be more enjoyable.
I would have easily paid $20-30 bucks for this well-polished game, even though I am a miserly Steam-sale-only buyer. It must be the nostalgia factor. Rest assured, however, that if you liked Skyrim or Fallout, and you too Want To Be a Hero, there is also something mysterious and playful here to discover. Check out The Heroine's Quest, then to satisfy your appetite for more, check out Quests for Glory 1-4. QFG2 was remade, and you can download it for free here:

I think these games have actually gotten worse over the course of the series. To start with, this is Alien Breed 3. THREE. It's the THIRD game in the series, yet it uses the exact same engine as the first, as well as the exact same textures, exact same enemies (with a few additions), exact same guns (with 1 addition), exact same sounds, exact same level design, exact same atmosphere, exact same controls and gameplay mechanics, and exact same fetch quests. While the first one was mediocre, it's inexcusable that they didn't attempt to make ANY minor improvements by the third freakin' game.
The entirety of this game is fetch quests. Run here, activate door terminal, but oops power is out, run to power terminal, but oops there's flooding, run to flood control terminal, but oops it's blocked by fire, run to fire terminal, but oops it's blocked by debris. Run and find demolition charges, run back and blow up debris, run back and activate fire terminal, run back and activate flood control terminal, run back and activate power terminal, and finally run back and activate door terminal, all while fighting off tiny clusters of ridiculously weak enemies who serve only to nip at your heels while you try to complete objectives.
It is utterly ridiculous, entirely tedious, and completely predictable. Monsters pop out of the floor when you activate a terminal, search a container, or pick up an item (all which require you hold down a button for several seconds), but generally just one or two enemies appear at a time, which does not do anything other than require you to stop searching, kill them, and start searching again. Often multiple times.
Monsters are insanely weak, and do not pose anything remotely resembling a challenge. You can complete literally the entire game other than boss fights with the ultra-accurate pistol, which naturally has unlimited ammo. The only time that there is even a hint of a challenge is when the game throws 30 enemies at you at a time from 3 different directions, but even then, it's not challenging so much as annoying. There is literally not a single enemy in the game that you can't kill with the pistol before they get to you, and that is just sad. Is the whole point of the enemies to make it take longer to get to the next boss battle or something?
Speaking of boss battles (and slight spoiler here), you are required to "kill" the alien queen 7 times. SEVEN. Kill her once, then cutscene, then kill her again, then she escapes. Then on a later level, kill her once, then cutscene, then regular gameplay, then she returns so kill her again, then cutscene, then more regular gameplay, then she returns AGAIN so kill her again, then cutscene. Then on a LATER level, kill her, then cutscene, then kill her AGAIN, and she finally stays dead. If I hadn't been so annoyed, I would have laughed at the ridiculousness. Oh don't worry though, she's never a challenge. Ever.
Voice acting is cheesy as ever, which isn't a big deal, but the stupid disembodied cackling from the main antagonist gets INSANELY annoying, and goes on the entire game.
To be fair, I did actually manage to make it through this game (unlike the first 2), but that's only because I thought I should beat at least one in the trilogy. Now I wish I had powered through the first one, and never touched 2 or 3. I REALLY wish I'd never bought them in the first place, but whatever.
I do not recommend these to anyone. While I understand others may not hate this game as much as I do, the fact is that there are thousands of better games out there far more deserving of your time and money. Some of those better games (ahemALIENSWARMahem) don't even require money.

Alright, so I've now 35hrs in the game and I beat it only twice - it's about time to write a review.
Necropolis is a dungeon delver where you choose between two characters (Blackguard and Brute) and head into the Necropolis trying to escape it - there are 9 levels to be cleared in order to complete your run.
The game has its strenght in its randomized experience - levels are randomly generated as well as loot as enemy. You could happen to never find a particular loot or a certain type of enemy during your run, and that adds tons of replayability, since level layout is also always different from your previous run!
There is indeed a lot of variety in terms of enemies and equipment. Limited character customization is also there in that you can change the color of your alter ego.
Combat is quite nice, reminds a lot of dark souls and it is very good implemented with enemies requiring different strategies to be defeated.
Now top this with an inspired art style and humour and I feel I can definitely recommend this game!
Please ignore all the negative reviews stating that game is dead or not finished - this is absolutely not true.
I also never encountered any bug, game is very well polished and optimized.
Game is complete as it can be and an overall fun gaming experience!

You're looking at something that's almost 20 years old with about 3 to 5 CDs worth of DATA on a PC or Playstation One console.

There's other standard RPG elements, and its mostly reading text and learning with one or two easter eggs hidden. The characters are standard JRPG fair and some of us can remember when there was a sephiroth website and people worshipped him (maybe still do, idk).
There's a lot of history with older Final Fantasy titles, I think its worth giving it a go and absorbing it. Talk to people or research what the inspirations were, and see what the perspective was like.

This game has beautiful artwork and a great (if not somewhat cliché) story that was pretty well executed. The cartoonish style works very well for this in general.
It wasn't all peaches and cream however as I did have a few minor gripes about it.
Crafting: There's no labels for the materials you need to help identify what something is, and you'll often have no idea where to get several of the rare ones that are not sold by the shops or anything, leaving some of the more powerful rewards just out of reach for many.
Skill Tree: The "skill tree" is medocre at best and is gimped by its own simplicity. There's only a few things to choose from, and your highest stat cannot be more than four points higher than your lowest stat. This means that no matter what you do your charcter's traits will go up at a relatively even rate. A true RPG-style skill tree system would have served this a lot better in the long run and would've provided a bit more variety.
Combat: Combat is simple, and that is both its strength and weakness. The combos in this are a ridiculos thing to get the hang of, unless you just happen to be a genius with the controls. I usually found myself just mashing buttons with some dust storm mechanics thrown in. I think this would have been better served by a "Super Smash Bros." style of combo juggling instead of mashing certain combos of buttons to help make combat feel more immersive and engaging.
Map: The map isn't particularly very clear and the quest system really should have a marker over places on the world map to return to.
All of those complaints however are very minor in comparison to the actual gameplay. It's your standard platformer with some very mild RPG elements thrown in, and while I wouldn't call it a full Metroidvania game it's overall a heck of a lot of fun and engaged me nonetheless. The story of the game had me all the way up to the end. I would definitely play again and would recommend anyone who likes relatively simple but beautiful platformers in general to buy this. I loved it and would sincerely hope that a sequel comes about.

tl;dr:
Good for gameplay and editor, bad for lower-mid end PCs
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Now that that's out of the way, let's get into the details;
Gameplay:
Physics are good, simple, and don't break too often, but can be fickle in some cases. A few modifiers exist so that you can play differently each time if you want to (or want to ruin friendships). The means of putting are either too based on DPI or seemingly random, but whether it's one or the other seems to vary from what I've seen/heard. The stock courses are nice, simple, and provide a decent amount of challenge most of the time, but the workshop offers many more, and many cooler maps for those who are willing to experiment.
UI:
Menus are "clean" but seem like they each cover too much, or too little. The yellow/white font colour on top of the dark orange/brown is a bit meh, but it is readable. Overall, it functions. However, it's the same look wherever you go; doesn't matter that you're on the ice map(s), you get logs for your menus and scoreboards.
Editor:
Honestly, it's great. Once you work out how do get everything working, it's simple from there. It's broken down into track pieces, but has a large collection of pieces such that some of them are niche to gimmicky maps. And boy, the gimmicks you can do. Thanks to the play area piece, you can make a course anything from basic-on-the-track to interaction with the environment to a flat-out regualr golf course and beyond; alloying for what's been made so far to never be the only stufff to enjoy. My only gripes are that the controls seem a bit hard to discover, and that it doesn't seem like it's possible to turn off snapping(may be me)
Visuals:
Saved this one for last because it varies hard. If you have even a mid-grade PC, the game won't run well enough. The game looks decent enough even at minimal settings, but minimal is as bare bones as you can go; and to get any aesthetic apeal, you have to have a permanent PC that's up to date in terms of hardware. Not saying you need to spend big bucks on a custom PC, but you're not getting the full visuals without at least the significant bucks. (Seriously, Overwatch runs better than this).
Is it a fun game? Yes. Is it worth it to get (if you can run it)? Yes. Does it have some Performance issues? Yeah, but so long as you aren't on budget, you're good.

Classic "beat it perfectly to get 3 stars" kinda puzzle game - every puzzle is easy to beat, but difficult to get perfect. The core mechanic lends itself to experimentation, where you could move around the pieces until you get the perfect solution and get the satisfaction of nailing the puzzle and understanding the mechanic. Except it doesn't. A placed tile can only be replaced by undoing that action or resetting the entire puzzle. And some puzzles even dictate the order in which you have to place the tiles (and it doesn't tell you the order. It just hands you a tile). The puzzles are already difficult to keep track of in your head, and not being allowed to freely move the pieces passes the point of "difficult" into "annoying". Instead of inviting experimentation, the game is just unnecessarily restrictive and an otherwise interesting mechanic is lost in slow repetition.

So, I thought I should give this game a go, since I thought it would be quite short. Well, it wasn't. Actually took me quite a few hours to clear it, although I wanted to 100% it more or less.
I liked this game a lot, for various reasons. For one, you're taking the role of a little anti-virus software agent that is sent on a mission to rid the host computer of a malicious worm/virus, which is an incredibly interesting premise. As you float along the corridors and tubes of your beloved PC, you find e-mails scattered all over the place that will slowly but surely unveil the bigger picture behind this attack. Major sympathy points for the cheeky web browser Qat that can't be fed enough cookies. I love how the characters build up and change throughout the story, obviously affected by the virus.
Gameplay-wise, well a word of warning here: the steering takes a little getting used to, especially since the first few minutes will most certainly give you some kind of motion sickness. Once you get the hang of maneuvering your little ship though, you'll start enjoying hunting those evil corruptions. The difficulty curve stays steady throughout, bar the last fight which took some trial and error but it was at least a good challenge. Progression is really tough going though. Many passages seemed a bit too stretched and the fighting very repetitive at times - omniscan a certain area, find out where the intruders are, take them out one by one, rinse repeat. But it's fun, you do have a bit of choice with six weapons and several skills that you can tune to your liking. The music is good, could have used a bit more variety though.
All in all, this is a cute game worth playing. Especially computer nerds will definitely like wandering around the OS.

In our world, the Baby Boomers, our parents or grandparents, are responsible for the state we live in now. The destruction of the enviroment, the increasingly unstable Middle East, etc. are all our grand/parents fault. These are the people born in the 40's - 60's. Some are almost 70 while others are 45.
Miss Nancy is obviously a Baby Boomer. She is an old woman.
The most prophetic scene is when she leaves in the rocket, never to be seen again, leaving behind the waste she's created, while lamenting that she could have done more. She leaves the player's generation to deal with these problems.
This is exactly the world we live in.

This is just a simple clone of the Mahjong tile matching games with 10 layouts and 30 themes (which alter the background color and the color of the tiles). The layouts seem to be copy of those in Taipei Game by Microsoft in old version of Windows.
From my short time with this game (around 45 minutes, the rest are idle time to get the cards to drop), it seems that the tile placement is random and does not guarantee that the board is solvable. It also doesn't allow you to undo to choose a different pair, so this is probably the reason why the game gives you one shuffling chance per game. However, with the random algorithm, the single shuffling chance may not be sufficient to clear the board.
There are also two slightly annoying bug with the control:
- When you clear a pair, and the second tile you select reveals an open tile at the bottom, the tile at the bottom is sometimes automatically selected, which could be a "feature" for some people, but a bug for me.
- A tile cannot be deselected by clicking on the tile again.
Even with all the issues above fixed, I can't recommend anyone to buy this game at all, unless it's part of a cheap bundle to farm for card or achievement.
If you want to play similar game, just get Microsoft Mahjong if you are on Windows, or just look for the web version of the game on the net. There are better and more polished versions out there that doesn't cost you a cent.

If you're looking for anything associated with the game's title, do not so much as entertain the thought of purchasing this title. The words "real", "horror" and "stories" should not exist in the same sentence apart from "this so-called 'horror' game was a real nightmare; the story of its critical mauling will be more entertaining than the product being reviewed!".
So what's the issue, besides not being a video game by any definition? Essentially the 'game' consists of 17 levels, each a single screen with interactive objects. Because the game thinks you're a malfunctioning automaton which can't think for itself, you can't express your excitement for this wonderful game by clicking crazily on the whopping ~3 items on screen; instead, you have to mash the left mouse button for each interactive object, and hope that you've done it right.
The most disempowering I felt during this game was not when the game made a very weak - and predictable - attempt at a jumpscare, but when I didn't know what the Hell I was doing. Not knowing that I'd "failed" because I clicked an interactive object one too many times, or simply not understanding a puzzle because there's no context was a common issue in my experience. I had to resort to GameOre's walkthrough for around 6 of the rooms and even then they were not just vague, but completely inaccurate. Thankfully there's members of the community who had played further than I had so they could help, and for that they have my sympathies.
But that's the gameplay in a nutshell - you click on things. I love point and click games and I could talk for hours about them, and "you click on things" would be the very least I could say. However this game just doesn't offer anything else, besides the reward of a jumpscare.
So what stories are we talking about here? Urban legends? Creepypastas? Unsolved mysteries? Absolutely none of those. The game begins by discovering a haunted forest coming across past murder victims' ghosts, before that story is abandoned to tell another about our journey into Hell. It essentially goes from being a ghost story, which I found was the most terrifying part of the game, to a bad retelling of Dante's picnic in the underworld. Not only is it a bad story, or rather two stories that have absolutely no ties, it's horrendously told. No, it's not even that - there's no story being told. There's no narration, barely any text besides from the beginning, and you're just supposed to pretend that the previous level has something to do with the next.
As for the horror I have to give some credit to the creepy scenery, as well as the quite scary images used for the jump scares. However the game relies entirely on those jump scares, and while I'm OK with them in moderation, this game lacks the talent to pull them off effectively. While I was shaken up because I'm a complete wuss, I won't dignify its cheap thrills by remembering them.
All in all, this game offers absolutely nothing besides jump scares. There's no horror stories being told, and the definition of horror can be argued by people far better qualified than myself. The gameplay really is just "click on object and wait for thing", and it's a disgrace to both the point and click and horror genres. The day I forget this game exists can't come soon enough.

(Full review follows below)
is an interesting little item.  It plays as an exploratory 2D-sidescroller / action-platformer— a genre colloquially dubbed “metroidvania.”  Captivating, hand-painted artwork and a stellar soundscape merge with solid gameplay mechanics and a trope-riddled, but well-told, narrative to form the end result of a pretty enjoyable game experience.  Be aware: this game was designed to be kid-friendly, and does have an overall essence similar to what you may find on children’s Saturday morning cartoons.
The gameplay essentially boils down to 2D hack-and-slash combat and mild exploration.  The combat is fast paced, fluid, responsive, and quite fun at first.  But, to be honest, it does grow stale as the game goes on.  You have the same attack abilities by the end of the prologue that you have at the end of the game— and it isn’t that many.  You will quickly see the best strategy is to just spam a few buttons while hopping around, and that’s basically what the combat becomes.  The various difficulties spread the gamut from “for children” to “for masochists,” with some sweet spots in between.  Although, even on “Hardcore,” with some grinding you can raise your stats to a point where it becomes easy… if you have the patience.
Furthermore, there are a lot of secrets to discover and treasures to find throughout all the levels, which to me was more exciting than the combat.  You will unlock new movement abilities as the game progresses, which allows you to reach new treasures in all the levels.  This also was slightly annoying because often times throughout the game you will spot a treasure that is tantalizing you just beyond your reach; but it then becomes that much more satisfying when you return later to collect it with your shiny, new
ability.
The story is overloaded with tropes and clichés.  Right from the start: you are greeted with a main character with heroes amnesia, but a great power within; you are greeted with a cute-but-ditsy, comic-relief sidekick; and you are greeted with another sidekick who knows your destiny, but won’t just come out and say it… just to name a few.  From there, the story does develop into something more substantial and decently interesting, yet still quite cliché.  Also, as I alluded to earlier, the game has an overall identity akin to what you find in children’s cartoons.  And the characters and voice acting do not stray from this identity.  Thus, some of you may find some of the dialogue and acting to be annoying or childlike.  Although, personally, I thought the voice acting was pretty well done and enjoyed most of the scenes— but I am easily amused, and am unquestionably a child-at-heart.

The idea behind Dead Bits is pretty attractive -- it's supposed to be a short and simple arcade style game where you run through a knock-off of the Portal Test Chamber.
However, it's clear that the implementation falls short of the idea. I would have been totally fine with a short, simple and not particularly inventive game, as long as it played reasonably smoothly.
Dead Bits does not play smoothly, and most of the "challenges" felt rather unreasonable. Everything you encounter smacks of unpolished, slapped-together amateur work. I'm not talking about the low-res models or the art style; I'm talking about things like the giant cube hitboxes which don't fit the models at all, or the obnoxious visual effects which obscure the path ahead.
The game is supposed to be a platformer at heart, but the level design is frustrating and seemingly pointless. Everyting is designed to rush the player into moving ahead without looking; but the frequent holes in platforms and enemy-clogged chokepoints make it impossible to just race through in time to the music. Instead, you're forced to take every section slowly and methodically, memorising the safe path and the enemy locations.
There is nothing which saves this game, nothing which creates a hidden bit of fun to explore. It could have been an enjoyable game if only the creator had spent more effort on making sure that the levels were layed out better, that the enemies were in interesting locations and not just clogging the narrow parts of the track, and that the weapons available actually fit the challenges ahead. The effects and music show that the creator did put time into this game, and I don't want to simply disparge someone's work. However, as a game it simply doesn't deliver -- the gameplay is constantly interrupted by failings in the design and execution of the game idea.

As someone with a few hundred hours in overwatch I can't see the horrible "thievery" that people claim is taking place here. This is not an overwatch clone in any sense of the imagination. Does it have its similarities? Obviously. But overwatch has countless similarities to team fortress 2 or dota, games that came out far before overwatch, and I wouldn't in a million year call it a clone.
This game is pretty fun, and the payment model is extremely fair. I really see no reason not to give it a try at the very least as you'll probably get at least a few hours of free entertainment out of it. I don't really understand the complaints about "grinding" or "p2w" either. Yes if you don't spend the 20 dollars (incredibly cheap) to buy the pack then it will be a grind to get heroes, but if you don't spend any money on a game I don't see how it's fair to expect the experience of a full priced title. I personally haven't bought the 20 dollar pack yet, and honestly I might not because even as a f2p this game seems pretty easy to get content in, but if it continues to be fun like it has so far I think that's an extremely fair price for a product like this.
I could write a whole lot more on the pros and cons of this game, but honestly I doubt there are many people out there that will regret downloading it given how free and accessible it is. I mean it's not a very big download and it seems pretty easy to get a few hours worth of entertainment at the very least as the average player.

Delightful racing game similar to Mario Kart series. Likable characters, easy interface, nice variety of race types, etc.
The game suffers from a major flaw. It is WAY too hard for its intended audience which is children. The NPC characters are too unforgiving of mistakes and children will be frustrated. At higher difficulties and tracks, some of the races are very difficult. I am a seasoned Mario Kart player and even I have difficulty winning some races or time trials. I’m guessing it would be near impossible for younger kids, especially if they have not been brought up on keyboard only controls (see below).
99% of the races are determined by fractions of second (which makes it even odder why the developers chose to use whole second rather than hundredths), often with racers crossing the finish line at the same time.
I found the controls simple unlike many other reviewers. You basically only use A W D and the space bar with an occasional S key thrown in when you screw up and have to back up…not sure what all the fuss is. I think many Steam users are console immigrants or are not old school keyboarders (read: spoiled). The controls are fine the way they are.
While the game has cute elements and is very enjoyable, overall I cannot recommend the game as it will not appeal to its target audience.

- Not a terrible game, but not worth $1.99 USD. Buy at $0.49 USD, maybe?
It's a basic (very basic) Mahjong game, with very limited layouts (10 only), static backgrounds (themes), pleasant but repetitive music. It has Trading Cards (which have little Market Value = cheap Badge), and achievements that require 0 skill.
I love Mahjong, I have been playing traditional tabletop Mahjong since I was a child, for 47 years now. I have been playing digital Mahjong for as long as it has been available on PC. Windows 7- Mahjong Titans... free, much prettier than this game, and much more enjoyable.
I cannot in good faith give this game a recommendation. It is too basic, too shy of features, and too amateurish to be sold at any price. $0.49 USD might even be too much for what it has to offer. Sorry dev. But this is one of the worst versions of mahjong I have played, and I have played a TON of them, here on Steam, and elsewhere.
There  is no choice of tile sets. Just one. And they are flat, undimensional tiles, that are often difficult to tell what layer they are in and whether they are free or not. The only thing that changes on the tiles is the background color of the tiles, and the color often makes the problem of detecting layers and free tiles worse.
The themes are uninspired, flat, 2D, static backgrounds, likely royalty free stock images. Nothing fresh or exciting, just blah images. The music, though soothing at first, quickly becomes repetitive and boring, annoying after a while.
I have NO CLUE where the dev comes up with the "Mahjong + Solitaire" claim. There is NO Solitaire at all. The "Karma Points" have no purpose. other than as a score? A score that has no purpose. If the dev does add Steam leaderboards, they wll be quickly topped by keyboard kiddies altering game files to give them scores of 2 million Karma +. The achievements? Okay, if you like easy, quick 100% games that take no skill to unlock achievements, this game may be just what you are looking for. Open each theme. Open each level. Press the number 9 on your keyboard. Tada! all ahievements in 10 minutes. No need to even play the game, let alone win any level. Very unsatisfying. I had really hoped for actual skill based achievements. That may have made the game more enjoyable for me, and may have led to a different review, overlooking the many shortcomings of the game design, audio and appearance.
I got this game as part of a bundle, and was hoping for an enjoyable time killer, with a little challenge, like a good Mahjong game should have. The challenge here was idling long enough to get the Trading Cards before uninstalling. It was that bland and unenjoyable for me.
Just my experience with the game, Your Milage May Vary. Widely.

This game is the peak in the videogame industry, you have the best plot ever made but with some missing things that you have to guess. It contains the most known spoiler in the videogame history, and one of the most known antagonist as well...and he is not evil just because no reason, it has a very deep reason.
STORY/PLOT 10/10
The best story in a videogame. Deep plot involving:
Contamination problems, fighting a nemesis (which you don't want to kill, just make him come to reason), discovery extra things in the story, the saddest spoilerS (yeah one in the middle and one near the end, but it is better described in Crisis Core).
CHARACTERS 10/10
The best antagonist in a videogame, it's not "bad" for no reason, and over time you don't want to kill him, just understand his reasons and stop him from his main objetive.
You could think that you have more developed characters than others (I'm talking about their past) but when you do all their extra things you know you have been mistaken (even with the optional characters)
COMBAT SYSTEM 9/10
Of course the combat system is static, but imagine being the first FF having animations in the battles (attacking, preparing attacks, covering allies, etc, and the bosses as well). You can equip everyone with any materia, the only differences among them are the limits, some stats and some equipment of course. Some summons could be anoying to watch (specially Knights of the Round). Once you reach high lvls and equipment/materias there is no more challenge than Weapons (optional bosses spreaded over the map)
GRAPHICS 9/10
I know that some videogames had better graphics back then, but this was the first FF with:
a) 3d characters/enemies (with a proper appearance for your chars inbattle...no more dwarf chars against well drawn non-animated enemies)
b) 3d to 2d rendered spaces, you could think it's not good, but it gave them the opportunity to show a lot of detailed things within the places, and you don't have the same houses/buildings structures over and over in a town/city anymore.
c)being a pre rendered 2d place, you don't have popping textures which they were present in almost every game in that gen (it was normal then)
GAMEPLAY 10/10
I did split "gamplay" from "combat system" for three reasons:
First: no more party splits to solve puzzles (If you played FFVI you know how anoying it could be without no-encounters).
Second: the 3d map now looks the most alive map in a FF so far, so you really feel like you are discovering new places every time, and now you have more vehicles.
Third: a lot of minigames in the game, defending a fortress, doing sport, chocobos(very anoying if you don't have a proper chocobo), snow, motorbike, etc...
DIALOG 10/10
It has very deep conversations sometimes, everyone has something to say, maybe the only "bad" thing in this game is the translation (at least the spanish translation is known as the worst translation ever made)
MUSIC 10/10
Nobuo Uematsu made a very good job here, this soundtrack not only has a lot of memorable songs, it has the sephiroth theme, used in the next FFVII games, and (of course) KH sephiroth battle. I think I can say that there is not another song that identifies a videogame character like this song does.
CONCLUSION
The best PSX game (I know, the closests to this one are MGS and CTR). The best plot in a videogame.
OPINION ABOUT THE UPCOMING REMAKE:
I played and enjoyed this masterpiece a lot of times. I totally agree with a remake, and I would like to see a new combat system, because I have the old combat system in this game.
I want new stories within the game, new characters if they are needed or showing more content that we could have not seen before.
People think that a bad remake could destroy the game, but I don't think so, the FFVII was done and finished 20 years ago, you are not touching that game, you are making a new one, if it is a bad remake, it doesn't matter, you have the old game forever, and even better, you could be the guy who always says: "the original was better", "if I wanted to play FFVII I wouldn't play this♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, etc.

It's the good old PS1 classic from late 90's in the form of a good pc port. Many people, including me, know it as one of the best RPGs ever done or maybe the best of all time. The one that started it all. I think it was my first big RPG/JRPG I ever played, when I was 10 years old.
Simply put, it's a masterpiece. The story, characters, world, gameplay like Materia-system + turn-based combat and soundtrack are what make this game really memorable throughout the years. Nobuo Uematsu is a wizard when it comes to making game soundtracks.
Even though this is one of the older games that does not have voice acting, the fantastic music is one huge part that makes the world feel alive and give you emotions. It's still perhaps the greatest OST ever made for games imo. And it is always nice to imagine how the characters sound like when had no VA.
I still enjoy replaying it, be it for the nostalgia or something else and it's been almost 20 years since original release. FFVII is one of those timeless classics, like MGS1, that never gets old :).
Those who never had the chance to play FFVII back in the days, if you can get past the old graphics (characters look funny I know), you will find a very special experience that won't disappoint. Some cutscenes show more detailed characters. If you don't want to wait for the upcoming FFVII:Remake, give this one a try.

Running source on a potato is the life.
Content? YES
Melons? YES
Workshop? YES
Workshop that has mods with melon drones? YES
Able to be run on a potato? YES
Moddable? Do you think the game's name is for show?
Sandbox? YES
But, G-Mod review memes aside, I'm going to give this an actual review.
Gameplay: 9/10
Graphics: 7/10
Content: 10/10
Workshop: 10/10
Usability on poor machines: 9/10
Mechanics: 9/10
Playerbase: 6/10
Shooty shooty: 7/10
Ease of use: 8/10
Controls: 8/10
The gameplay itself is awesome. It's very easy to move around and shoot.
Graphics could be better, but I'm not going to complain because I have them on lowest settings.
There is a very large amount of content that will keep you playing for hours. In addition, the Workshop is great, large, and has quality weapons, tools, and maps. One of the most popular weapons mods would be the M9K mods.
I'm currently running GMod on an Acer potato (if you didn't see before), and on lowest it runs at about 30-40 FPS which is fine by me.
The mechanics are great, you can build a wide variety of contraptions using even stock tools and buildables.
I'm not a huge fan of the G-Mod playerbase, as the second ever server that I'd joined there were nothing but toxic people that kept spawn-killing eachother (Mind that this is on a sandbox server).
The shooting isn't amazing or horrible, one complaint is that the weapons could be slightly more accurate (stock).
Overall it is pretty easy to build contraptions, just spawn something in, attach like a thousand lightbulbs to it / thrusters and BOOOM you have a meme machine. The only thing is that it is a little hard to position things sometimes, but that's on  my end.
It took me a little while to figure out the controls, but eventually I figured them out and started having a fun time. Specifically, I was confused on what button to press to enter a seat/vehicle, although I quickly figured out that it was E.
Overall, on average this game is rated a solid 8.3/10. Good job, Valve!

I liked GalCiv 1&2. GalCiv 1 is what got me into space 4X in the first place. But since then, I have played better 4X games that either (like Distant Worlds or Space Empires).
That said, Galactic Civilisations 3 is inferior to GalCiv 1 and/or 2.
I thought I just sucked at the game, but I looked it up and it turned out to be an actual problem: You cannot play as a pacifist without bending game rules on how it calculates military strength (protip: It counts the attack score of your ships and ONLY that. So you can have a smaller invincible fleet and inmpenetrable defences, and be considered "weak").
The AI is stupidly aggressive. As one person put it aptly "they behave more like 5yolds when you touched thier sandcastle than world leaders".
Not to say the AI is good at waging war. It's utter♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It barely ever attacks after declaring war, it doesn't comprehend invasions. But it WILL declare war, often a few turns after you meet it.
The main reason for that is a silly number of negative multipliers: It doesn't like your idealology. You are weak. You are ripe for conqest. (Yes, those are two separate negative multipliers that mean the same thing). Alternatively they "Are concerned by your military buildup". You rejected their request for a handout. They will hate you for sharing a border. Etc, Etc.
Basically, the AI doesn't just stay neutral. It will hate you whether you have a strong military or not. They will hate you for every time you reject their begging, which comes often. They will absolutely hate you when they send a ship into YOUR territory to colonize a planet which first makes you share a border and then culture-flip. The only thing you can do to alleviate that is to shower them with gifts.
Another major issue is how barebones it is. Your economy is controlled with a triangle slider between Research, Money and Manufacturing. Then there's a slider between colony manufacturing (social) and ship building (military). That's it. You have no more control. There's no espionage either.
All in all, none of the problems make the game unplayable. Sure, you can play. You'll win. But only if you play the game in a very specific way. And for a 4X game, that's a crime.
Considering that you can get Space Empires IV Deluxe for £5.99, this game is not a good buy even on a sale. I got it for £10 and I'm not satisfied with the result.

This is quickly becoming one of my favorite turn-based 4X games!   It has a very different feel to it than most other 4X games, and that in many ways is it's strength!  However, if you're not into the tediousness that can come with managing a civilization, trading, researching, building, moving fleets of ships, determining which ships get constructed next, which buildings get built when and WHERE, etc etc, you might actually HATE this game.  I, on the other hand, find all those attributes exciting and strengths of the game!
GC3 certainly has an arguably steep learning curve. Even the tutorial is a bit unforgiving - it took me 3 tries to actually beat the tutorial!   But once you get the hang of things, it all begins to feel more natural. Each civ has their own buildings and perks and ship designs, which makes things very interesting.
One of the big perks to the creative types (people not like me) is the custom ship designer feature!  You literally get to determine where on the ship a weapon or component might be placed!  Or you can let the default location take over.  Either way, there's a lot of power in getting to customize your ships like this!
Unlike the tech trees in other games - or "trunks" as Stardock's CEO refers to them - GC3 actually has several different trees with branches that don't necessarily rely on the completion of all the other branches!  You can truly go through the game and easily not research everything in a single tree out of the 4 you have available!
Unlike games like Sid Meir's Civ where most of the tiles has something interesting on it that can be changed or you can do, GC3 has a lot of open tiles that you won't be able to do much with. However, this is open space, so it makes sense to the context of the game.  With that being said, there are still plenty of interesting things to find and occur, such as space junk, anomolies, wormholes, and even galactic events that can occur.
The game is a little heavy on system resources, but that's necessary to give the incredibly expansive maps.  If you're running a weaker video card, there's plenty of settings that can be turned down to help compensate for it.
Thus far, I've put in over 60 hours into this game, finished the tutorial, played a few stand-alone games, and played through the first of the three campaigns.  I look forward to seeing what the other two campains have to offer!  Well done Stardock!

This game has a very nice graphical style and a great sense of humor. The gameplay is fun except for one glaringly obvious problem that hurts the game dearly. The simple fact is that most players will not want to try the "normal" or "hard" modes when the first mode is already annoying and ridiculous (particularly with the boss battles). The game also makes another classic design mistake. Take the boss battle in level 2, it's actually a pair of back to back battles with no chance to heal or anything in between. Being poorly designed, its also setup so that if you die in the second battle, you have to redo the first one again...
NOTE: There is a patch in the works addressing this difficulty issue, and so I will need to re-evaluate this review when that comes out as it wouldn't be fair to the developer if I don't.
Tom vs. The Armies of Hell simply fails to understand that its easiest mode is the gateway for new players to join. It fails here by being one of those games to follow the painfully misguided "difficulty for the sake of difficulty" design style, which has ruined countless games. The difficulty levels in this game are all shifted up by at least one, especially when it comes to the boss battles. The boss battles in the easiest game mode feel like what most games would call "hard mode", which is not intelligent design... Tom vs. The Armies of Hell is just another game that couldn't figure out the basic game design fact, that turning away new players makes it very hard to build a fanbase. Worse, it curses the game to a niche existence where it is doomed to decay forever in the void of obscurity. So this design style that already makes no sense in a game design context, makes even less sense in a business context...
Video games first and foremost are about entertainment and fun, not unnecessary effort retrying poorly designed levels 400 times (like this game's boss fights) or pointlessly trying to prove something by seeing how hard of nonsense you can beat. Beating such nonsense is irrelvant in the grand scheme of things, and therefore completely pointless (not to mention a collosal waste of time). Difficulty in video games is a double-edged sword. It can make a game much better if done well, or turn players away in droves when done poorly (as in this game).
All too often, video game challenges are poorly designed (the boss fights in this game are no exception). You've no doubt seen them, the types of challenges that serve as a brick wall to artificially slow the player's progress by making the player bang his/her head on a proverbial brick wall for no good reason. Besides that, most challenges in video games (and this one) are lazy stuff thrown together in under 5 minutes through the use of one or more of three basic things: unreasonable time limits, unreasonable scoring goals, or unreasonable amounts of enemies or other hazards. Cheap BS like this is far too common in video games, and Tom vs. The Armies of Hell makes the same tired old mistakes (by putting very little thought into how its difficulty is designed).
It's unfortunate that so many developers put very little thought into game design or even bother to research it at all, as I have indeed done. It is a very important topic to know about if you're going to make games, which seems extremely obvious, and yet we still have a world with far too many examples of poor game design... And there is yet another basic rule of game design that this game breaks: the rule that when the player fails, they should feel that the failure was because they screwed up and not because the game is being cheap and unfair. Tom vs. The Armies of Hell heavily fails on this one.

I've always been fascinated by those games on Steam which cause me ponder and reflect upon real life moments outside of the game due to the thematic subject matter being addressed. And it's even more impressive to me when the game itself is a very comedic, tongue-in-cheek, & light-hearted one in nature...yet which explores & touches upon these deeper darker undertones of human nature....albeit in a way that is both highly entertaining and able to fill your room with endless laughter while enjoying it.
I now introduce to you such an indie title, whimsically called Tom vs. The Armies of Hell which was developed by Darkmire Entertainment. In this isometric action-adventure game, you play as a nerdy software-engineer named Tom who finds that his entire office complex has suddenly been sent straight to hell after an experiment goes terribly wrong. And it is your sole duty to fight off these hordes of evil minions, demons, and diabolical bosses in order to uncover exactly what happened as you valiantly try to find your way back to your normal everyday 9-to-5 job again - all while packing your shiny new "Soul Blaster x9000" gun which can both shoot as well as capture their released souls afterward, essentially using their inherent dark power directly against them as a temporary power-up for the gun itself. An interesting concept, and a rather fun one gameplay-wise I might add!
Clearly, the game itself is a metaphor in describing the inherent wickedness of the cold, uncaring, heartless, and dehumanizing aspects of the modern-day workplace...as well as our relationship to it where profits, deadlines, and greed trump all else...especially reinforced by its intro-video which distinctly highlights as much. And yet, it manages to do so in a very accessible way which we can all readily relate to since the aesthetics and tone found here are very much cartoon-style and infused with an ample quantity of humour throughout. And thus, this merger of an underlying serious subject matter to the silliest possible presentation was nothing less than ingenious to me.
Level design itself was quite varied I felt within its 6 different ones, and nowhere did I feel that any aspect of the game was becoming monotonous whatsoever. Because not only did the office/hell scenes change regularly, but the enemies themselves were also creatively inspired and varied considerably in design. And these include multiple weirdo bosses to do battle with as well. Furthermore, your character is able to quickly roll/dodge + melee in close-quarters combat situations when many enemies are ganging up on you. It was all very satisfying as far as its fast-paced gameplay goes, feeling fresh and certainly quite challenging the entire way through. All in all, it possesses (pun intended!) a wonderfully engaging campaign whose diverse cast of characters breathe life to its absurd story with their hilarious caption-based dialogue. However with that being said, I can't help but to feel that this game could have been taken to the next level of comedy if they instead all audibly spoke, with quality voice acting included. Although for an indie game, I suppose there are limits as to what can realistically be done...and perhaps this was one of the compromises. Nonetheless, the actual dialogue is still fantastic.
Another of its strengths is how it uses old-school mechanics like a health meter + health pickups, ammo pickups, plus the ability to upgrade your gun considerably. You won't be fumbling around with complicated inventory systems or any such nonsense here at all. This is decidely more geared towards the pick-up-and-play crowd who seek to immediately jump in and get going. Fortunately the controls are rebindable and very easy to understand, and it also includes full controller support which is a nice touch.
On the audio side of things, background music is wonderfully comprised of orchestral jazz selections which bestows upon it a rather unique flavour & charm. I suppose for its office type setting, this would certainly make the most sense to go with. Whereas gun/combat effects were very much punchy & solid as well, accentuating rather than distracting from the expeience. All in all, no complaints here.
And even though trading cards aren't present, it does at least sport Steam achievements...which only helps to make an already very fun game that much more of a blast to sit back & play.
Tom vs. The Armies of Hell recently came out of Early Access on Steam and feels very polished indeed, with an active dev who who clearly listened closely to the community's input and has spent a great deal of time improving it to perfection while ensuring that it feels balanced throughout. So kudos for that. And it is an adrenalin-inducing title with which you can pick up and start playing right away with no big learning curves, as the game does a stellar job in explaining exactly how you must proceed further into it as you quickly master its straight-forward goals and combat mechanics - allowing you to sit back and actually enjoy this action-packed experience to the fullest with minimal frustration...the way it should always be! There are no cheap deaths here, and if you die then it just means that you need to keep practicing as you hone your tactics. With such a pleasing graphical style with its fluid animations, entertaining storyline, and light-hearted atmosphere...I'm confident that you'll be more than eager to sink some quality time into it. Because this is a game full of soul at its very core...so now go start collecting 'em inside of it as you go head-to-head against these forces of darkness in your workplace...and perhaps soon, you'll too eventually find your way back from hell over there!

This game has not aged well - and it wasn't even released that long ago.
The combat feels very clunky, and often just does not work. Primary frustrations are that:
- Your character will frequently stop to have a lengthy think before attacking when you press 'attack' (or just won't attack at all), when the frustrated clicking that this inspires eventually does lead to some action from your character it often manifests itself in a string of uninterruptable, impotent swings against a defending target, who immediately delivers a fatal counter while your character is off balance.
- Your character will often roll for no reason in combat, but also he will often just not roll at all when you press the 'roll' button, leading to many a fatal strike from your enemies.
- The 'action' button is the same as the 'attack' button, leaving your character stupidly swinging his sword at thin air while your are trying to pick up loot or climb up ladders as long as you have your sword out, even after combat is over.
- Running around with your sword put away seems to be equally as idiotic, as it takes a very long time for your character to draw his sword once enemies are nearby again. you cannot defned yourself or dodge while your character is in the very lengthy process of getting his sword out.
Overall I would say that the combat is half way between Skyrim and Dark Souls in that it has none of the broad variety of abilities that Skyrim offers players, and none of the crisp consistency that makes Dark Souls tough battles playable through good timing and skill. Instead we have a game with a similarly limited repetoire to Dark Souls, but with the slightly goofy inconsistent hackathon mechanics of Skyrim. Hardly a match made in heaven.
Outside of the combat the game is equally as frustrating, and it just feels like it was never properly play tested. For example:
- When buying new equipment from merchant you cannot see how a new weapon or armour piece compares to what you are wearing.
- The game's response to user input is inconsistent, sometimes pressing 'esc' quits the specific window within a menu you're looking at, sometimes it closes the whole menu and goes back to the game (the worst case of this is when you view a letter in the inventory: clicking on the button in the bottom right that says 'esc: close', returns you to the inventory, whereas pressing 'esc' on the keyboard quits the whole inventory menu)
- stumbling into boss fights without taking the right potions leaves you woefully ill-prepared, meaning that you have to play up to a boss fight, learn which potions you need, then go back to an early save where you can create the potions, and play through the whole section again. The only solution I have found to this is to read ahead in walkthroughs so I can prepare appropriately beforehand. I have given up on the game, and I will be simply watching let's play videos to enjoy the rest of the story - that is of course assuming I don't continue feeling bored in all of the cutscenes.
All in all, I would not recommend. I hope the Witcher 3 greatly improves on this experience, or I shall be attempting to get my money back for the displeasure.

Generally when you put deep water in a video game the first reaction is going to be fear or at least acute discomfort. Water has a special propensity to terrify, by being vast and obscuring and a medium through which things can move very fast. While all manner of games from Ecco to Subnautica have used water to torment players, Abzu takes the opposite tack in presenting the ocean as a place of tranquility and meditation. This is the game you want if you'd rather swim with the seahorses and explore the colors of the seafloor than sweat about what might be lurking below.
ABZU opens with you floating in a seemingly endless ocean, just you and the gentle waters under a clear sky. With nothing on the horizon you dive beneath the waves and explore the strange and beautiful places that lie there, from kelp forests to coral reefs to deep trenches and beyond. Along the way you'll need to find little diving drones to help you progress, learn about the functions of the strange machines at the bottom of the sea, and encounter all kinds of friendly sea life. What story there is is told entirely through the environments and occurrences as you delve deeper, requiring some attention to details and symbolism to really get anything out of it.
As a game, ABZU is pure exploration with only a hint of puzzling. Each area is fairly open but also directs you along the path the story has laid out, so don't go in expecting an open ocean to roam. The progression of areas gives a definite sense of travelling far and deep, though, which becomes increasingly gratifying as you find stranger and stranger locales. Your explorations will be split between broad plains and plateaus and canyons where you'll need to find drones or machines to progress, and rushing currents where you'll navigate between rock formations and grand structures as the ocean sweeps you along. It's a good mix of peaceful swimming punctuated with some thrills that keep you from getting too complacent.
Every area you come across will be populated with fish and other sea life, and honestly this is the real appeal of the game for me. The bright, simplistic graphics of ABZU help the ocean come alive with scores of fish, including everything from tiny guppies to massive sunfish. There are seahorses and jellyfish bobbing around, eels and squids snaking about, manatees and dolphins to play with, and even whales to hitch rides on. We're not talking about just one or two of each, either, because ABZU revels in having schools of fish swarming about. Most areas will have hundreds of critters to watch, swim with, and even ride, which makes the areas mostly devoid of life all the more striking when you happen upon them.
There's a little more to the game than just swimming and watching the wildlife, too. Most large areas have special statues you can perch on to meditate, allowing you to observe any of the local fish from a third-person view. There are also hidden pools you can open up to introduce even more critters into the local ecosystem, often unique types like manta rays or sea turtles. Then there are the hidden shells laying about to collect that I suppose change the ending in some way? They're not particularly well-hidden but I passed up a few my first time through and decided to leave the rest for a future dive.
As I touched on before, the graphics are what really sell the peaceful world of ABZU. Rendering everything with bright, simple shapes makes them pop against the deep waters and draws attention to their excellent animations. The environments are expertly crafted to give impressive underwater vistas and impressions of scale, even when the areas are not actually that large. The sound design is certainly just as good, with fantastic ambient sounds and a soothing score that keeps you in just the right place for the journey. It's a light and fluffy game, almost with the feel of a Disneyland ride with how bright and pleasant it is aside from a few moments of darkness. If you need a game that both engages and relaxes then I can't think of anything better than this fanciful journey through a living undersea world.

The horror of Five Nights at Freddy’s 2 begins and ends with a hallway. Down its dark length lurks walking robot animals out to kill me, and I’m only armed with a goofy bear mask and a flashlight. If I light up the hallway, I’m treated to snapshots of terror: toothy jaws hanging open at weird angles, outstretched arms of patchy fur and gut-like cables, and eyes with a pinhole-sized glow staring right back at me. The hallway is a funnel of fear.
I peered down that hallway a lot during my roughly six hours playing Freddy’s 2, sole developer Scott Cawthon’s followup to his first spooky suit stalker simulator released in early August. Cawthon didn't wait long to leverage word-of-mouth popularity and YouTube celebrities’ horrified faces with a sequel that further establishes his skills at crafting a truly frightening experience.
What I wanted from a Five Nights sequel was more mind games and more uncertainty. I wanted the plodding animatronic suits to find me and rip my face off in new and interesting ways. I wanted working legs. What I got was a horror game dipping heavily into deception and subtlety, a wonderfully cruel cocktail of supernatural mystery and jolts of panicked adrenaline. Enjoying the good parts, though, comes with a cost of a frustratingly steep difficulty.
Once again, I’ve made the questionable career move of taking the overnight security shift at a children’s pizzeria for a measly pay rate. Strange Things occur among the tiled corridors and empty dining rooms at night, and staying alive entails warding off walking murderous animatronic animals by tracking their movements through grainy camera feeds.
I’m still rooted in place with no degree of movement beyond swiveling my head left or right; a slight disappointment to my hopes of freely wandering around. The first game used that restriction as an added layer of stress, and that’s effective enough the second time around, but the novelty feels a little worn now. Freddy’s world is interesting enough that I want to explore it. I wouldn’t mind poking around a corrupted version of Chuck E. Cheese’s.

I've been waiting to pick this one up for a while. Harebrained Schemes' Shadowrun games are some of my absolute favorites, so I was intrigued by the "Dark Souls rogue-like" angle this game was going for. It's unfortunate that it seems like the devs kinda... gave up. What's here is absolutely fantastic in concept, and even in practice I see pockets of greatness. The world looks gorgeous and constantly hints at a bigger story. The writing is humorous, the enemies have some flare to them.
If I could characterize this game in a simple phrase, it would be: "It does a little bit of everything, not enough of anything."
Combat is there, but it lacks the strategy of Dark Souls/Bloodborne; most battles seems to come down to smashing attack, or block/attack. Classes are there, but there are only TWO (a third was apparently supposed to be added, but nothing ever came of it). The world is there, but it lacks diversity or character; there was a snow forest biome that broke up the dungeons, but most everything else looked samey and gray. A story is also there, but it's dropped in bits and pieces, overly-cryptic, and much too infrequently.
With a friend, this game is absolutely enjoyable. (In fact a friend is probably required.) NECROPOLIS could have been so much better. Much like the setting itself, it's a lot of great things floating around each other that don't quite coalesce. For $5 on sale with a friend to play with, we were able to get a lot of fun out of the game, but $29.99 is WAY too steep for the game as-is.
---------
If the developers decide to return to this game, or even take a whack at a sequel, there are a few things I'd like to see:
1) Biome diversity needs to be ramped up. Stuff like the snowy dark forest should be the rule, not the exception.
2) Combat needs to be fine-tuned. One strategy shouldn't work for 90% of the enemies.
3) Key-bindings should be able to be reset. (Seriously, what *year* is it?!)
4) The story should have more of a presence. Dark Souls has the luxury of wedging its story into visuals, item descriptions, character actions, etc. If NECROPOLIS can't do that, there needs to be more breadcrumbs out in the world.
5) MORE CLASSES. Three classes should've been the minimum. Shipping with only one boggles the mind.
6) Make the "new game plus" element a bit more heady. Collecting codexes is fine, but I'd like to see more permanence of items/recipes/stats between deaths. I was really digging that feeling of incremental progress between delves, but it didn't pan out to be as substantial as I thought.
7) If you're say you're going to add something, add that thing. The Arcanist should have made it in before the devs called it quits. Sad to see HBS not follow through on something after how well they supported SHADOWRUN RETURNS, DRAGONFALL, and HONG KONG.

It's not very often a game gets me to feel the way I felt about this game. A beautiful story about finding out who you truely are and what you are meant to be. The story was the most amazing one I've seen in a video game in a very, very long time. Flawlessly executed with amazing gameplay, Dust: An Elysian Tail makes you think in more ways than one.
It's not a very long game, but it's not an insanely short one either. Dean Dodrill really found the sweet spot when it comes to how long a game should be.
Gameplay wise it was just a bit repetitive, but there isn't much you can do about that with a 2D game such as this one. But I feel like the point of this game wasn't to give the most spectacular game when it comes to mashing buttons, but I really did have fun breaking in my new controller, but I feel it was really about the story it had to tell.
Overall, Dust: An Elysian Tail is a beautiful game with a great atmosphere and a pleasing art style. It tried it's best in all aspects and exceeded my expectations to the fullest, even when they were set fairly high from the other reviews I'd read about this game.
If you are in the market for a new 2D adventure platformer, I cannot reccomend this game enough. And for only $15, it's worth every cent.

Barely over 2 hours longs, ABZÛ will take you into a magical journey of adventure and mystery underwater, where you'll explore and discover different locations and secrets, life and death, confinement and redemption, all encompassed within a magnificent setting under an exceptionally beautifully and fitting soundtrack.
Calling ABZÛ a walking (or in this case swimming will be more fitting) simulator is borderline insulting to the fantastic experience you will embark once you launch the game. Gameplay is fairly simple and I cannot stress enough the fact and the glaring warning that it's even on the store page of the game,
. Otherwise the mechanics are fairly simple, you control your character and you swim around bodies of water, finding various aquatic organisms and solving very simple puzzles. There are few collectibles and secrets around the different places you'll visit. The game is very linear although you can roam around a little bit around on the environment. There's a lot of interesting tidbits spread around the game, little things that enhance  ABZÛ a little bit that I'll let you find out for yourself. I found it particularly exciting to actually find out extinct marine life and actually see them swim around you.
The game is a perfect blend of relaxing and exciting at the same time and it guaranteed to stir up some emotions in the player. For me to be able to achieve this within ~2 hours of gameplay and with 0 line of dialogue with only the musical score and the visuals,
a testament to the fantastic job the developers have made with this game. If you enjoyed Journey and/or Flower, I see no reason while you shouldn't enjoy  ABZÛ as well, a little masterpiece.

Girls Like Robots is fueled by silliness and delightful writing. Despite being a logic puzzle, the world is an entirely crazy place. But the game succeeds at developing a personality without pushing the absurdity too far. It may appear like a mobile game, but it feels very solid on PC.
The game is a fairly casual puzzle, involving interactions between character pieces. Each group of levels focuses on new mechanics, introducing them smoothly and keeping the game fresh. Each group uses the story to justify rule changes, with some levels focused on getting the lowest score possible. The game stays fresh and hardly feels repetitive. Some levels did cause me trouble, mostly the five or so levels with a time limit. The music is solid and relaxing, but some songs can be repetitive. Sound effects are often hilarious, and still make me smile after playing the game to completion.
A sense of humor is needed for Girls Like Robots, as you can't take it seriously. It's a lovely game with a great personality, and strong gameplay to keep it going. It's perfect for a fan of puzzles and silly comedy. With the full price of $7 USD, I'm willing to recommend it to everyone.

It's such a simple concept. There is a rectangular grid and you're tasked with placing the various characters in the scene in such a way that everybody is happy or some other requirement is fulfilled. How happy people are is influenced by who they're next to, so girls literally like robots.
Nerds like girls, like robots and like being near the edge of the group but dislike being next to other nerds (I like to imagine it's because they disagree on the age-old Star Wars vs. Star Trek debate).
Girls don't just like robots, they also dislike nerds and tolerate other girls. Robots like girls and have no strong feelings about nerds or other robots.
These are just the first three characters, and already they have enough different interactions to have plenty of puzzle fun, but this barely scratches the surface. There are tons of other characters, each with their own likes, dislikes and quirks, but never so many that you're forced to remember all of them (and if you do forget you can always easily look up the relevant interactions, just in case you'd forgotten that fish and robots were mortal enemies).
The puzzles themselves also vary in type, with some allowing you to freely place characters while others restrict the order in which you place them.
This would already be a strong recommendation without bothering to go into the delightful story.
It starts simple enough, a school trip, a sports game, a volcano erupting, a big dance. Wait, volcano?!
Never taking itself seriously, but always sharing the joke with the player, the plot is as light-hearted as they come and animated in the same gorgeous style as the core game.
With three large Acts, each with around a dozen chapters to go through (which themselves consist of ~4-10 stages) there is plenty to do, but it doesn't outstay its welcome and the finale, while a bit long, is definitely worth the effort.
Strongly recommended, get some Girls and Robots in your life today.
