This is one of the most insane puzzle games I've ever played. The mechanics are simple: you have a grid of X by Y squares, place your pieces down in a way that everyone likes who they're seated beside (the basic rule of the game: Girls like Robots. Girls don't like Nerds. Nerds like Girls, Robots, but not other Nerds).
Except then suddenly you're learning that June actually really likes Bugs. But Bugs don't like Girls. And Ben likes June, so make sure to leave a space near June for Ben so he can ask her out, and...
The game's complexity builds slowly, and it comes through adorably quirky cutscenes. It also has 3 tiers of medal per stage, but in a twist I absolutely adore, "gold" does not mean "perfect" - it just means "the highest". This is one of those games where the designer didn't go through and mathematically 'solve' every stage and expect you to do the same, and that goes a long way for me in saying "This is the kind of game devoted to fun first, humor second, and everything else is just a bonus".
Plus, if you score enough golds and things, you unlock alternate silly modes. I'm waiting to see what Nerd Drop is.
edit: Infinite Nerd Drop is everything I wanted from the name.

Apparently, the fact that I was going to write this review today coincided with the add of trading cards (which was weird not to have seen dropped during my playthrough but well...).
Sarah Pennington received a word from her mother (we know about her father but nothing about her dear mamma) that she's near the discovery of the Flower of Life. However, apparently, the Dragon Clan is also interested in this and a familiar face returns, despite Sarah being sure of his demise. But her mother is kidnapped and Sarah must prevent the Dragon Clan to finish a serum that would allow them to control people.
While it's not necessary to play the previous games, it will provide perhaps a little more understanding on some returning characters. At least, Sunward isn't reintroducting the time travel! But the plot is perhaps a little less interesting and too fast on the Flower of Life being discovered and in the wrong hand (though Agent Walker, another game, worked in a similar fashion). There is just a little thing: the French translation keeps going from the singular you to the formal you... between mother and daughter. It would have been better to stick to one of them.
The gameplay is the standard one:use items, combine them, find them, clear hidden objects scenes of several sorts (which is kinda now the standard: list of words, shapes, actions required, etc..) and solve puzzles. As it's a Collector's Edition, special items are also hidden in each scene. The difficulty is also well-balanced. Here, the concept of having little friends to help is transformed into reusable pets (monkey or baby jaguar). The new artifact is a cube used with daggers to unlock powers: Eagle, Phoenix and Owl, to use to go forward. Each of them is about runes: the Eagle is to find the proposed rune into those hidden in the scene, the Phoenix is to find the second part of it and the Owl is to find the rune shown in three parts. However, that concept is quite underused for my liking.
The graphics are quite exotic and cyber. I mean by that that you're in the middle of a jungle, with ruins to explore but also the Dragon Clan labs, which are more modern and tending to sci-fi. The inventory was also redone. The soundtrack is also fitting.
That sixth entry in the Secret Order series is well done (though, if you've read reviews of the previous games, you'll find again an hint to a release of the first game on Steam). If anything, the game was enjoyable and keeping the series into a new direction and new surprises. I recommend it.

First impressions:
Girls Like Robots is a nice, casual logic puzzle game. It's very obvious that its a mobile port, but it doesn't actually play that bad on PC.
The game itself is very funny and completely unrealistic. Girls like robots, girls dislike nerds, nerds like edges, etc. Very simple gameplay, easy to pick up on, especially considering the game holds your hand throughout the first several levels. The art style is very quirky and colorful, along with the smooth animations.
The game does have a slight story to it, in the form of various cutscenes scattered in between levels. It's a ridiculously simple story, nothing fantastic, but it is rare to see any type of story in a puzzle game like this, so props for that. The story doesn't really make much sense logically, but neither does the game, so that's okay! The game's soundtrack is quite repetitive, however.
The puzzles were (for me) quite easy to follow. It gets progressively more difficult, but not so difficult as to prevent progression on my part. It really depends on how much thought you put into each puzzle before acting, as it is a logic puzzle game. The game has a high replayability if you're a completionist. Each level can be perfected, if you know what to do, and it would take quite some time to do so, hence the increased replayability.
Overall, Girls Like Robots is a fantastic little game. It's a pleasure to play, even on PC, although I can only see myself playing this on mobile instead of Steam in the future. The pricetag is set at $7, which may be a bit high for a game of this scale, so try to pick it up during a sale if you're interested.

Gameplay here:
Abzû is an underwater exploration game from the developer Giant Squid, whose founder, Matt Nava, is the man behind the well known game Journey. It would be easy to say that Abzû is like Journey, just underwater, but I'll try to go more in depth.
The game revolves around a diver of mysterious origin that swims around exploring the relaxing ocean and try to help bring certain dead areas back to life. This is achieved by finding large portals that you have to open to awaken the wildlife around them. This game also does a great job of showing you how small and insignificant we are compared to the vast greatness of the ocean, especially when you have to swim over waters so deep you don't see the bottom.
The visuals are what initially caught my attention and made me extremely excited for this game. The beautifully simplistic low poly style with vibrant colors and lighting effects that would make any AAA publisher jealous. This combined with the absolutely wonderful soundscape creates a warm and relaxing atmosphere that astounded me repeatedly.
The game controls very smoothly and I often found myself swimming in circles just for the fun of it. The movement controls are pretty solid and you use one button for the very little interaction that is required when solving puzzles and the like.
The only downside I can think of is how incredibly short it is, little over 2 hours. Even so the game costs only 20 bucks, so I still feel I got my money's worth.
In conclusion I'd recommend this game to anyone. This is a title I think everyone should play.

The Secret Order 6 is a well-made and fun hidden object game with great visuals and enjoyable gameplay elements, but one that is also almost completely unremarkable.
The Secret Order 6: Bloodlines is the kind of hidden object game that cannot really stand out of the crowd, yet it has no real weaknesses. The graphics are nice. On the plus side, the story is a lot more grounded in reality, with no fairies, princesses, or any sort of thing, just a simple adventure to the jungle and back. It is rather refreshing in its modesty.

I would narrowly approve of this deeply flawedgame, it is nothing groundbreaking or amazing.  Many have criticised it for not being what they were hoping it to be -- whatever that may be.  We all have our own ideas there, so best just give a verdict on what we get, not what we don't get.  What we get is "another" turn-based space game, where you have a number of things to sort out or initiate before each turn is over.  Most of my responses here are positives: good graphics, good layout, good loghistics.  The downside is that there is so much to do once the game gets more complex it can be a little confusing and you have to keep your eye on so many things at once.  There's no point over-complicating a game if this is seen as a negatgive feature. Some features, like "sentry" which is supposed to warn you of enemy ships in the sensor area, palpably don't work. There is a handy little window that tells you if a ship is idle, if a shipyard needs instructions, or anything else that you missed during your turn. The tuorial, whilst partly interactive, does also partly just rely on showing example screens, rather than steering you through various gameplay moves.  When there's so much to be taken in at one time, a tutorial sticks better in your head of you can perform the actiuon several times over, experimentally, until you are happy with it-- before moving on to the next topic.  So for that, a poor tutorial.  However once the basics have been grasped, the rest comes with exponential quickness, and saving frequently between turns will allow change-of-mind if you miss something important or make a silly mistake, or get a colony wiped out because you just "weren't looking everywhere at once"..
For some odd reason, despite showing the cloud symbol, this game does not appear to keep game saves on  the steam server for use on any computer i choose to play it on.  Thusly...good points, bad points, bugs and disappointments.  But it passes time.

So, #6 in the Secret Order series.
The cons: Continuity with previous "issues" in this series was little more than a hand-wave.  The plot line was pretty much muddled as usual.  The puzzles were mostly quite easy (but see the pros, next). First-timers might find some of the puzzles tricky, but they're the same puzzles as before.
The pros: There's a lot! I liked this Artifex Mundi release! Many props to the creative talent at Sunward!
The music was quite good.  Tense at the right time, soft at the right time, never detracting, never boring.
The graphics were very very good.  Even though the plot line was thin between scenes, the scenes themselves were so beautifully rendered I didn't care.  Each scene transported me to a new environment, and all were interesting with lots of detail.
It felt like there was a lot less "post-art/post-game" clean-up on this release.  It came together much better.
Most of all: the "featured-puzzles" (sort of like boss-puzzles) actually made me think a bit.  They are the kind of puzzle where you have to figure out what the puzzle is before you can formulate a plan for solving it.
Did I mention the artwork is really top-notch?  Thanks Sunward!
I can only give it one thumbs up, sorry, it deserves more.
If you look at my recent reviews, I've been very critical of Artifex Mundi releases.  This one is much better -- a step in the right direction (for my tastes, at least).  I really enjoyed it.
Edit: "Runa" is not an English word.  You might want to check on that.  Did I mention the graphics are amazing?

Excellent game with a few rough edges that the modding community are busy sorting out.  If you are new to Paradox games then prepare yourself for a learning curve that, while not as steep by any means as the likes of Eu4, isn't a simple bump in the road.  You will need some patience, especially in the mid game when things appear to slow to a crawl.  Be assured however that there is a crap ton of stuff going on under the hood and you will eventually learn to identify and deal with it.  The depth of Stellaris is unmatched and there are little stories going on all over the place as well as the big picture.
A new race to the stars popped up nearby having got themselves off terrafirma and were pretty terrified of it all, especially as their first contact was a powerful empire of space arachnids.  Through diplomacy they found that actually the spiders were not that bad.  I offered them protectorate status and they eagerly accepted.  Shortly after a beligerent empire came along and attacked them, obviously not realising the consequences, which they soon learned as their homeworld came face to face with a spider invasion.  They are now my vassels.  They don't like it but that's just tough for them because I don't like bullies who hit my little friends.
I am over 130 hours into the game so I have had my monies worth and then some.  Unfortunately the game is struggling to come up with an answer as to what it wants to be.  During development I raised a concern that attempting to create a hybrid between grand strategy and 4x was, in my opinion, foolish as Paradox were trying to appeal to two distinctly different types of gamers and it turns out that I was right, although I take no pleasure in it.  With the recent Clarke patch the game has lurched more towards 4x in the early stages and it was heavy 4x early on to start with.  People complained about the Ai being too passive so Paradox, in typical developer fashion, have rammed the lever too far in the opposite direction.  Now you can end up with a scenario ( which I had in a recent game ) where an empire will declare all out war on you simply because it can.  Now, that would be fine for xenophobic empires as it would be like an arachnaphobic striking out violently against the spider that got too close, but the empire that declared war on me for no good reason were not even close to being xenophobic, and in fact had an oppinion of me of +72.  I beat them after a shortish war and 16 years later they were at it again.
My point here is that the old 4x meme of 'I'm bigger than you so I want your stuff' has almost become front and centre.  At release Stellaris felt like an early paradox game but if Clarke is anything to go by the grand strategy players may as well throw the game onto the dusty shelf while the 4x players enjoy the experience until mid game when it slows to a crawl and fails completely to take them with it on it's faltering journey into the non-existant diplomacy of what should be a deep and interesting experience, and misses the mark by a wide margin.
Certainly Clarke made some improvments to various systems like sector Ai but most of those improvments were in response to the loud voices of the 4x players that were unsatisfied with the game.  The second patch 'Asimov' has a lot to do and will be make or break for Stellaris.  If it doesn't redress the balance then the traditional Paradox gamer will simply head on over to HOI4 or back to Eu4 while the game tries to keep it's new 4x players ( not gonna happen ) with a number of other promising 4x titles just over the next hill poised ready to take it's crown.
As it stands I will still give the game a thumbs up but that will change if Asimov doesn't deliver the goods.  Mixing genres rarely ends well and Stellaris is on the brink.

Im really REALLY trying hard to like this game. And maybe this game will turn itself around into act II which im now in but to be honest im struggling. The countless positive reviews will point to why this game is 'great', here are some of the reasons I think it isnt:
1) The auto save system is REALLY bad. And you cant save when you like, meaning you will at times have to redo entire sections if you didnt hit F5 at that critical moment. Infuriating. Oh and you cant overwrite a save meaning I now have about 50 and counting.
2) I found the game pretty much on rails, it was not open world at all. You cant really 'do' much. You cant really 'craft' that much but oddly you can loot and collect countless items, even take objects from houses in front of their owners (hello, isnt this an RPG?), a lot that you collect is just plain junk. Its feels like the developers left something out, like there is a section to the crafting system that appears missing.
3) The game is HARD, but not in a good way. Sometimes you just repeat the same 2 spells or attacks to overwhelm an unfairly powerful enemy. And the fighting system, although more developed than Skyrim is still pretty boring.
4) The running here and there is TEDIOUS. You cant jump to any locations. Yes its pretty but its just boring after a while.
5) I found the narrative and stories EXCELLENT, ive never felt so immersed in a gameworld (apart from perhaps Bioshock series) but the gameplay didnt lend itself to the narrative at all.
6) Combat is usually hit, roll, QUERN - and repeat. Skyrim had loads of different spells, long & short range weapons. Nothing like that here.
I will revisit this review while I continue the game if i feel it has redeems itself...

Ok so if you read my review of 'The Witcher: Enhanced Edition', you'd know that I was in two minds about skipping that game and going straight onto this one.
I ended up being overwhelmingly surprised at how engaging, memorable and unique that game was, in many ways, saying it was superior to Skyrim (I know, controversial).
So when I finally completed the first game and it came time to move onto 'The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings', suffice to say I was very excited, and for the most part, that excitement was justified.
Firstly, 'The Witcher 2' is VERY different to the first game, in both good and bad ways (but don't worry, theyre mostly good).
Graphically, the game is astounding. On a relatively powerful rig like mine the game looked fantastic. If somebody told me it released last year I wouldnt bat an eye. Honestly it looks that good.
The gameplay here is the biggest change. Rather than the odd choice of rythmic mouse clicks that denoted atacks in the first game, with blocking and parrying "sometimes" performed automatically, the combat now is done in real time. There are buttons for light and heavy attacks, parrying and magical signs, and now there are traps and bombs to think about using too.
Yes, the combat is more traditional, engaging and all around more exciting, but with this comes an incredibly steep difficulty curve early on that, if not youre not persistant, can put some off the game entirely. After a five or so hours you should pretty much have the combat down, but it certainly requires a certain degree of patience.
Another great addition is in the fact that you can now meditate anywhere. In the previous game, this could only be done at very select places, such as campfires and in rented rooms.
The production values are all around much higher this time around too. Aside from the obvious graphical fidelity, everything just feels much more polished now. It's truly great to see a fantastic company such as CD Projekt RED be given more of a budget to build a better game world, with better textures, character models, lighting, effects and creature types.
All this being said, there were actually a few things about 'The Witcher 2' that to me, were actually not as great and stand out as they were in the previous entry.
The biggest disappointent to me was in the game's choice of locations. Although the first game was limited from a technical standpoint, there were a lot of memorable locations that all stood out from each other. There were country villages, cities, swamps, sewers, graveyards, fields and marshes. Everyhere felt unique and individual.
In 'The Witcher 2' however you spend a VERY large portion of the game in 3 locations; A small village with a nearby forest, an army camp on a battlefield and a war-torn stronghold. Now, these locations in their design are well executed, however they are boring locations to say the least. Unlike the first game where there was a lot of backwards and forwards between locations, this one actually sets you on a much more linear path, and as a result there is no breathing room between the locations. Act II of the game makes up the crux of the runtime, and this is where you are situated in a bog-standard army camp out on a battlefield. It's boring, and a bit of a letdown considering the high production values and the set designs of some of the other places in the game. Some might not even notice or care about this, but to me personally, the world of 'The Witcher 2' was just a little boring compared to that of 'The Witcher'.
The other noticable disappointment comes in the lack of memorable characters. There were TONS of memorable characters from the first game, some i'd recognise and be able to place on name alone. But with the focus on politcal sabotage and betrayl in this game, this is less a fantasy game and more a playable mystery.], with only a handful of pretty fogetable characters to really interact with. Geralt's awesome band of misfits from the first game (especially Zoltan the Dwarf and Dandelion the Bard) return here, as well as your optional romantic interest Triss Merigold, an although they themselves are given much bigger parts, the new characters arent particulary exciting or memorable, and since the game gives you two optional paths to follow after a big decision is made in the first act, your'e actually given even less characters to intereact with.
The only other TINY disappointment is int he game's soundtrack. It's not bad in any sense, but just isnt as beautifully orchestrated and sweeping as that of it's predecessor.
It is still a beautiful, well realised and enjoyable RPG that in many ways brings something to the table other games in the genre fail to do. There is lots more customization in terms of weapons, armour, character etc in this game, and the game AS A GAME feels a lot more refined.
Many people dub this game FAR FAR superior to the first, but to me the first had some great little charms that were omissed from this entry. TO me they are as good as each other. Which is no poor reflection on either game AT ALL.
For everything that 'The Witcher 2' VASTLY improves upon from the first game, it also lacks the same charm the first one had. in some areas.
But in summary calling this game no more fantastic than the first is still calling it fantastic. Which it ABSOLUTELY is.

Puzzle games normally don't hold my attention for very long, but Girls Like Robots was a complex story about love, rejection, and being unable to make everyone happy. It's not a game for everyone, but I was surprised to find out that it was a game for me.
Some things about the game might seem tedious, but they sort of break away if you overcome the difficulty curve and truly learn how to play. It also helps to get into the mind of every character and understand what they like and dislike, rather than memorize a series of patterns.
The soundtrack is very folksy, and I happen to love folk music. I don't think everyone else can appreciate that, but that is a factor to consider before getting this game as a gift for a friend or loved one. Also, I appreciated how it was Safe For Work and at times amusing.

The game is insanely fun to play, and has high replay value due to the different difficulty levels, although it will never be as engaging as the first playthrough.
All in all, I am very glad to have purchased Dust: An Elysian Tail for the $3.00 i got it for, although now that I have played it, I would have payed a lot more.
I hope that Dust is not the first and last chapter of Falana, and am very anxious to hear some sort of information on a sequel. Even if this journey is all there is, I have no regrets in taking it.

I play this game so much and so often that it might as well count as an addiction. Here's why.
When you're playing a rhythm game, the music is an essential component. Thankfully, Necrodancer doesn't disappoint in this area. The soundtrack is fantastic, enough that I don't find myself switching to custom songs, though the option is there should one want it. One of the nicest touches is how when you switch characters, the soundtrack shifts subtly to a different style of the same song. (Personal favorite would be Bard's "Synthwave Cuts" soundtrack.) This is one of the few games where I absolutely recommend buying the bundle that comes with the OST.
Graphics have that comforting retro feel and the character designs are fun, which is always a plus, and the rougelike elements make sure that your game is always a little different each time you take a crack at it. The controls are simplistic and easy to master, which is a nice counterbalance to the difficulty of the game. The learning curve can definitely be a steep one; I'm not saying it's the Dark Souls of rhythm games, but it definitely makes you work at it. And with enough modes and character variations, you won't find yourself wanting for a challenge.
If I have any gripes, it's that I do get the rare crash on occasion, but it's maybe one out of fifty times I play it, so I'd hardly call it a deal breaker. Still, it's worth pointing out for those who worry about these things. (I've noticed it happens more often in full screen mode if that's any help!)
All in all, 10/10 game with very high replayability and a soundtrack that you'll be humming for days.

With the sale at the same $10-$15 GET IT NOW.  If you likes GalCiv 2 then you'll like GalCiv3.  Not much has changed other than the graphics which are massively updated, the map size is now mind bogglingly huge and the modding is fantastic.  Building on planets is far more tactical now as adjacency matters big time.  The battles however fall short of the huge ones youre used to in GalCiv2, and the AI seems dumb as hell sometimes.  Make sure you turn off conquest as a victory condition otherwise every game seems to be a rush to invade and ignore all the other techs.  Military starbases seem utterly useless as all they do is slow enemy travel unless they decide to attack it directly.  Economic starbases are the way forward with the ability to put 5 or 6 per planet for HUGE boosts in industry.
Get it on sale, as I paid nearly $75 for it plus all the DLC and I dont think it's worth that price.  But overall I would recommend if you enjoyed GalCiv2.

A decent puzzle game with a cute presentation, but some annoyances as well. Under the hood it's all math: each of your square figures has a like/dislike relationship with every other one, and score is kept based on which faces are in contact at any given time. This is only explained briefly, once, though there's a button to show current relationships on a colour scale instead.
Things become more complicated when you're forced to place tiles in a specific order. Things become annoying when, doing one of these puzzles, you realize that in order to correct a mistake made a dozen turns ago, you have to undo all twelve moves. Tile swapping puzzles present a similar challenge in that you're only given a certain number of moves, and a similar annoyance in having to restart if you realize that you've fouled things up royally.
Unfortunately, the developers decided to throw timed minigames into the mix, and make them part of the scoring/unlocking scheme for the bonus puzzle levels. They're skippable, but again, they're tied into the system that unlocks bonus levels. This kind of thing baffles me-- these games are supposed to be brain teasers, not repetitive, fast-paced drills.

Filled with the same kind of niggling game design problems as its prequels.
The visual design is highly polished, but it feels like they never had anyone who understands game design sit down and play through the nearly-finished game for the first time. All of my problems with it are extremely minor and can be overcome, but the list is very long -- here's a sample:
Anomalies provide an odd incentive to change to your most expensive technology and improvement at the beginning of each turn.
Tooltips about improvements provide inadequate or straight up misleading information, the buy tooltip shows your treasury if you have enough to buy something, but not if you don't.
A guarded anomaly gives you an option not to attack if your ship has weapons, but there is no indication that this option will not be available if you do not have weapons until you try it.
Improvement layout is incredibly important, but all the planets in the campaign have terrible layouts.
I still can't figure out the logic for cancelling starbase improvements -- at one point it cancelled everything _except_ the one I had selected.
Running out of cash auto-sets your government to max economic. This often brings in less money than the setting it was on before you ran out of cash and essentially results in a game over as you have no ability to pick the government setting that would bring your cash back to the positive -- I suppose this is a decent metaphor for austerity though.
These and things like them make the fun option and the optimal option often quite different and take away from the enjoyment of the game.
This doesn't make Galactic Civilisations III worse than its predecessors (on the whole, it has improved a little in this regard), but given the huge budget and fanfare I had much higher expectattions.

Stellaris is a 4X space strategy game made by Paradox Interactive, a company famous for empire management and war games with vast strategic depth, high replayability and Asperger level attention given to detail. As a brainchild of a respected company that has standards set higher than all other game studios, the release of Stellaris was waited with extremely high expectations.
And, at first, it seemed to me like it met them. The race customization system seemed remarkably balanced, there were quests and events that helped me get to know the universe and my chosen form of society better, I expanded my empire, build a massive fleet, enslaved xenos, fell in love with the randomized research system that promised more diversity, appreciated the automated governors system and reduced micromanagement, jumped up gleefully when I first saw the diplomacy screen and thought someone finally got it right, waited with dread and anticipating for my first end game crisis...
But the more I played the more the reality sinked in... It's all superficial. Most of the features that Paradox added to the game that seemed cool initially actually have very little in-game effect and some even affect gameplay adversely.
The quests and events get repetitive quickly and mostly have boring, generic rewards, usually XP or few research points, neither of which has much impact especially later in the game. Leveling your scientists doesn't actually yield you anything aside from faster surveys and decreased risk when analyzing anomalies. You don't get to choose skills for them and assign them grant bonuses to your units. The concept of leveling 'hero' characters and questing seems unfinished and its full potential unrealized.
The demesne system familar from EU and CK forces the player to form Sectors and give excess planets to AI controlled sector governors or face penalties. The idea probably was that it decreases micromanagement, and creates entertainment in the form of court intrigue as the sector leaders may rise in rebellion against you. In reality the only thing the sector leaders do is waste resources and bungle up the management of their planets, while you still have to perform every crucial task manually. They are unlikely to rebel and you have plenty of tools to ensure that they can't. There's no risk or challenge involved, just waste of resources.
Because the resource gain/spending system isn't adjusted properly every empire should produce resources in abundance. This means that trading between races is not required. Not that the AI would accept any deal anyway unless they are madly in love with you and want to have your star children. You could join an alliance to protect yourself from militaristic imperialists but since the AI is highly pacifistic and rarely ever declares war (and is terrible if it does) you really don't have to worry about it.
The war system is needlessly restricted and battles becomes increasingly tedious and frustrating as the game progresses. Wars generally drag on for ages and are unenjoyable cat and mouse games where decisive battles can easily be avoided. Even if you do manage to destroy a fleet they are build so rapidly that another one is already ready to join the fray. However, the greatest problem in the war system is that there really is no incentive to fight. You have all the resources you could ever desire. Expanding your empire simply means more mind-numbing micromanagement and more production that goes to waste.
The semi-random research system that seemed so innovative at first glance does a terrible job at informing you when a technology is better than what you've researched before. Worse still, majority of the technologies feel like fillers that only give you a tiny percentual increase in performance and nothing else. I guess that's how the game is dragged out longer than it needs to be.
And that really is the main issue with the game. It lasts longer than there is content. After you've expanded as far as you can and there are no new systems to survey the only thing left to do is stare at your screen, hoping a fly would land on it so there's something to look at.
It has no end state. It has no actual victory. It has no narrative or meaningful interaction between races. It's a sandbox game where *you* make the story.
And *still* I recommend Stellaris because I want to believe Paradox will fix the issues. Their games are known to be unfinished on release. I have hope. And even if they don't fix it Stellaris still manages to provide many hours of entertainment for those with imagination, and offers a stable platform for multiplayer galaxy conquest, which ignores most of the inherent flaws of the game.
Tl;dr: If you are expecting a single player master piece with depth akin to Europa Universalis and Crusader Kings, prepare for disappointment because Stellaris is not even close. Or perhaps I should say: it's lightyears away.

After playing 11 hours now, to me this is closest to Sins of a Solar Empire except with a lowered initial stress/panic level that too many things are happening at once in realtime.  This combines the realtime aspect, the more real 3d effect missing from others like Galactic Civ and Distant Words, but it has far more gradual 4x feel to it and I think hits a really quite perfect mix.
So I would say it's
40% Sins, (realtime 3D, very little automation)
20% Distant Worlds, (It does have a live feel to it, that the universe is alive, and it's HUGE, and freedom to go wherever, not on a path)
20% standard 4X, (alot of exploration, alot of setting up cities, planets, mining, juggleing stuff)
20% Galactiv Civ genre. (Only in in the basic premise really, and the managing of planets)
Overall I'd rate it so far as 85%
However, there are things that bug me a bit.
I don't like the separation of the solar system view and then jump to galaxy. When in a solar systems, I'd like to have a better visual sense of the galaxy around me as opposed to feeling like I'm in a closed room. A smoother transition between the two, or a seamless transition would make this game feel much much more immersive.
Doesn't seem like anything can be automated as far as scouting ships, fighting things, etc. This is good and bad, and so far has been good, but I can see where it might get out of hand as it gets much larger (and it will)
Hard to tell what to research next, as far as I can tell there's no "This leads to..." type explanation of new tech.
When jumping into a solar system, the amount of icons can be overwhelming to quickly see what is happening.
There's no "easy" mode, just normal, hard and insane. I was quickly surround in a normal game by systems and races I simply could not overcome so my game just sort of ended because I couldn't expland or jump or explore new systems.
Visually it would have been nice for the planets to revolve around the sun. Again, to just bring a little more life to the whole thing instead of feeling like a static board game.

Wow I never thought I would be simultaneously on the edge of my seat and bored out of my mind when playing a game, Dead Bits surprised me though and accomplished just that.
Dead Bits is a pretty straight forward fps that has you plopped in mario style to level after level where you have to reach an objective on a linear path, usually shooting your way through hordes of enemies.
The world the game takes place in is similar to the void of the Xen border world from Half-Life, you make your way across floating platforms in a pastel expanse of nothing.
Visually the game is minimalistic. Everything is square, rectangular, box and cube shaped with single faces being made up mainly of one color. When enemies die they fall apart into short lived physics based giblets.
For the majority of the time I was playing I felt bored out of my mind by the repetitive combat punctuated only by the admittedly satisfying death physics of the enemies "dead bits."
Fighting the enemies in this game is grinding in its purest form.
HOWEVER! There is one type of level this game offered where the first person platforming style felt fully realized, and that section is the only reason I am recommending this game.
In some of the levels you will have one large ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a lot of health chasing you from the beginning of the level to the very end. In those levels I found myself at the edge of my seat, fully focused on making the jumps from platform to platform as a mother♥♥♥♥ing bipedal tank barrels down on you, the controls are reasonably responsive so when you die in those sections it usually feels fair and you can't wait to restart the level to outsmart the big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ barrelling down you.
Other than that though this game feels soulless and empty, buy it if you're interested in mining the trading cards but beyond that, unless they do a major overhaul to the focus of the gameplay, Dead Bits ain't worth is friend.

The beginning is great with exploration and little story missions scattered around. Upgrading your starting planet and first few colonies is fun and discovering unknown aliens is exciting.
And then the UI strikes. When you get over 5 planets you have to put any over that into an AI controlled sector. The AI does what AIs usually do. Strange things. Buggy things. And you can't intervene. You can build star ports in a sector but they don't show up in the overview UI so you have to click through each (of soon dozens of planets) to build ships.
Strategic ressources in a sector? You can't access them. A primitive civilisation in a sector? Can't control your empires behaviour towards them. Even though in the official Stellaris stream a month ago that was classified as a bug, its still in the live version of the game.
Want to find a good colony target? Click through each solar system as there is no planet overview.
Want to wage war? Hover over every enemy fleet icon as there is no difference shown between an enemy doomstack and a harmless enemy science ship. Speaking of doomstacks: The bigger fleet wins. Best strategy: Place all your warships in one single fleet and immediatly go for the enemy homeworld. A single battle usually decides a war.
If there is war. Most of the time the AI does nothing. They'll form huge federations and alliances and then do nothing. The mid-game consists of waiting as there is nothing happening unless you initiate a war yourself.
And the (spoiler alert) vaunted end game crisis? There are 3 of them. All 3 function very similar and one of them is bugged so you can never win anyway.
Worst of all is that most mechanics either have UI issues (horrible to control) or are implemented poorly (sectors) even though there aren't that many features in it. Its a very light weight 4x (2 victory conditions, conquest or control a certain amount of planets) and the famous grand strategy aspect of Paradox games never appears.
After one play through you've seen everything there is and each subsequent game plays mostly the same.
And lastly, the options menu of the game is a joke. There are (almost) no graphic options, no gameplay options (can't even change the scrolling speed which is too fast when zoomed out) and almost no options to customize yout starting galaxy.
Maybe it will improve with patches, currently I wouldn't recommend it. It feels rushed and has a serious lack of polish.

Great game. I haven't played many other grand strategy games to compare it to, but I think you could visualise this game conceptually: Start with Sins of a Solar Empire and visualise its galaxy, with stars, jump lanes, space combat, trading, etc. Now take one of those super-complicated, empire-managing grand strategy games you love, rotate it 90 degrees, and intersect it with the Sins of a Solar empire galaxy. That's Stellaris. Horizontally, it's Sins of a Solar Empire, and vertically, it's one of those crazy empire management games that I've never played. Despite that sounding a bit like a beautiful mess, Stellaris is well-designed and streamlined in a few places to keep things interesting and deep without getting totally bogged down in complexity.
The complexity really overwhelmed me at first, so to give you some perspective, I'll go over a healthy sampling of all the little things you can control in the game. You create your own race, with traits, lifespans, preferred climates, religion, philosophy, government, diplomacy, politics, military, etc. Colonised planets have "tiles" where you can build buildings for resource output -- a fully populated planet can be total resource powerhouse.
You assign "leaders" to command fleets, govern planets, and lead research efforts. Those leaders have traits that give bonuses to certain aspects. You scout star systems for resources and anomalies, which can produce special research projects for your scientists to perform. These lead to quest lines which provide extremely powerful rewards, but take dedication to complete. Leaders level up, grow old and (probably) die. You participate in elections (if you're democratic), keep your population happy (or don't), and appease or suppress sub-factions that appear in your political system. Factions have certain political leanings, so you can embrace them to permanently adjust your faction's political leanings that you chose at the start of the game, meaning you always have avenues for adaptation in that regard.
You research new technologies and upgrades, then apply those upgrades to your buildings and units. You can create ship designs specialised for certain combat scenarios, build and upgrade spaceports to buff your planet, or its defences, or its ship build speed. There are three methods of getting between stars, each of which have distinct tactical applications. You can enslave or subjugate other species you encounter, or be egalitarian, or something more fine-tuned. You can farm them like cattle or commit genocide, and most people won't like you very much after that. You can vassalise other empires, or replace their government to reform them in your image.
Despite all that, certain systems are very streamlined, which helps keep things focused since the game has so many moving parts. Combat has straightforward rules -- once you're in a fight, you either fight to the death or retreat. There's no micromanagement -- it's all AI. The interesting part is that fleets are given combat ratings, so you know who's going to win a battle before it starts. That leads to a lot of juking and hunting for stragglers to weaken your enemy -- choosing your battles is critical. The economy is also conceptually very simple. Energy pays for upkeep, minerals pay for new units, food grows your population, influence pays for diplomatic actions, unity unlocks empire-wide perks, science speeds up your research. Despite the complexities earlier, that's the *entire* resource system. It's only as complicated as it really needs to be.
What I think I'm getting at here is that to me, an ex-SoaSE player, Stellaris initially looked *absurdly* complicated. Like, impenetrable. But, as I played it, I realised that it's only as complicated as it needs to be to be an interesting game. The game is a constant feedback loop of optimisation problems, where you're constantly trying to squeeze more blood from the stone that is your empire. It's really fun actually, and with the huge amount of variation there can be between games, you always feel like there's a few more interesting things to try.
So yeah I'd recommend this game. If you liked Sins of a Solar Empire, this is worth the full $40. Just be sure to tackle the complexity head-first until you've got a foothold in the game, and you'll start to see where I'm coming from.

For a mobile port, its pretty good. Graphics arent bad, especially for a mobile port. Textures and animations are pretty simplistic though. Considering its origins, I think that is to be expected. Where this game shines however, is the audio. The sound track is amazing and perfectly fits the tone of the game.
Exploring is kind of fun. Its a relaxing break inbetween fights which allows you to collect gems (by clicking them) which unlocks the boss fight, challenges, story, as well as lets you upgrade your abilities, such as your shield or your energy regeneration. There is also a nice button to allow you to get the "birds eye view", which lets you see the entire map you are currently on which can help if you still need to collect your gems.
As far as abilities go, you can only claw and shield. Clawing only works when you can see your enemies eyes, and you use it by making a "slash" with your mouse. Shield works by drawing a circle. To use abilities though, you need to have the energy to do them. The controls are fairly responsive which was very nice to see from a mobile port.
The story is fairly simple as well (which you can sort of expect since you play as a bird). Basically, you are a crow that met a dark spirit that gave you some powers and wants you to use them to destroy things. While you are progressing, you start to have a second/good voice that encourages you to forgive instead of destroy. Which voice you follow determines which end path you get set on.
The only real downside to this game (for me) is the length and lack of depth. The game can easily be completed in an hour or two, which doesnt leave much room to expand on the world of the game. Id have loved to know more about the "ancients" and the baron in the third act. The game lets you have a quick peak into what could very easily be an immersive, fantasy world, but they dont have the time to expand on it, so you get to fight a couple ancients with little backstory (why do they exist? what do they do?), and fight a baron who was trying to enslave an ancient (we learn why in game and I dont want to spoil, but what gave him the idea to do it? what is the history behind him?).
Overall though, I do recommend this game, especially if you see it on sale. Even if the story is a bit shallow, its a nice quick little adventure with a very nice soundtrack, decent graphics, that plays pretty well.

The Witcher 2 is everything the original was, but distilled into a more potent experience. From beginning to end, you'll be engaged with an incredibly well built and incredibly detailed world. The choices and paths you can take will impact your game a thousand times more than the first Witcher game. While I felt that the game was a little shorter than the original, the third and fourth chapters are effectively two diffent stories depending on your choice in the first. Overall 8/10, would recommend.
Pros:
-Importing your decisions from the first Witcher game is a great way to reward fans.
-A greater variety of decisions that have more immediate and meaningful changes.
-There's so much story being told regarding Geralt, the mages, the non humans, the kingdoms, the empire... it can be overwheling in a good way, like Game of Thrones.
-The combat and character development system in this one is vastly improved over the original. More playstyles, more meaningful choices.
-Despite being a "dark" and "gritty" setting, they pack a lot of humor into it as well. I chuckled aloud a few times at some of funnier moments.
Cons:
-With all the major plot going on, it's hard to feel like a Witcher. There aren't many monster contracts to claim and fewer sidequests.
-The inventory and crafting system is a bit of a clusterf***. By the end of the game I had hundreds of useless mundain crafting materials in my storage and no reason to use them. Sadly I often overburdened myself looting dungeons and punishingly walked back to town in slow motion before realizing how little I needed anything that could be crafted.
-The level cap of 35 is a bit punishing to players who complete sidequests. I was max level by the end of chapter 2 and basically wasted all the exp I could have gained doing quests in chapter 3.
Runs on any old computer and good simple fun.. Love the graphics and style.

Very fun, little, casual puzzle game.  The art style is playful and vibrant with a wonderful attention to detail, especially in the backgrounds.  The animations were smooth and fun to watch, as a feature the game also allows the player to skip the cutscenes or even watch the cutscenes again in the level viewer.  The story was surprisingly well done as well. Normally, I would not expect a story in a puzzle game like this, however there was a story, and it was quite easy to follow.  Though the adventures were wacky and didn't make any logical sense, it fit the overall tone of the game perfectly.  I must also applaud the creators of the game for adding little references from other media and of course geek culture.  The soundtrack of this game was great, however it got very repetitive as the game progressed, for my ears got tired of hearing the same banjo tune strummed over and over again.  The best way to remedy this problems is to take a break once in a while to let your ears rest.  However this little problem did not and will not dull the rest of the gaming experience in anyway.
The game was easy to pickup and play, however don't get me wrong, some of the puzzles will take a little bit of thinking to figure it out, especially if you are a completionist.  Bonus content allows for some replayability which adds to the value of the game itself and in no ways detracts from the main game itself.  The system of unlocking bonus content is well done, as even an intermediate skilled player will be able to "buy" the content (The main game will provide more than enough "happy" points to unlock them).  The achievements brings nothing new to the table, but it fairly awards those who are willing to spend some time in the game.
Overall this is a solid game with little to no faults to describe.  It is a must own for people who like puzzle games, and for people who don't, this is a good game to pick up, because of its ease of play.  The game's content to value ratio is good, however don't expect to sink hundreds of hours into this game.  9/10

Gameplay here:
Abzû is an underwater exploration game from the developer Giant Squid, whose founder, Matt Nava, is the man behind the well known game Journey. It would be easy to say that Abzû is like Journey, just underwater, but I'll try to go more in depth.
The game revolves around a diver of mysterious origin that swims around exploring the relaxing ocean and try to help bring certain dead areas back to life. This is achieved by finding large portals that you have to open to awaken the wildlife around them. This game also does a great job of showing you how small and insignificant we are compared to the vast greatness of the ocean, especially when you have to swim over waters so deep you don't see the bottom.
The visuals are what initially caught my attention and made me extremely excited for this game. The beautifully simplistic low poly style with vibrant colors and lighting effects that would make any AAA publisher jealous. This combined with the absolutely wonderful soundscape creates a warm and relaxing atmosphere that astounded me repeatedly.
The game controls very smoothly and I often found myself swimming in circles just for the fun of it. The movement controls are pretty solid and you use one button for the very little interaction that is required when solving puzzles and the like.
The only downside I can think of is how incredibly short it is, little over 2 hours. Even so the game costs only 20 bucks, so I still feel I got my money's worth.
In conclusion I'd recommend this game to anyone. This is a title I think everyone should play.

An excellent game that provided me hours of fun (adult). This game has pleasant aesthetics, does not suffer from major bugs, and provides a little bit of challenge to complete the races.
The controls are slippery, but not the bad kind of slippery; it is part of the game to be able to master it (which only takes 2-3 races).
Here are some bugs I've noticed:
- AI only moves forward, so sometimes they get trapped and you need to bump into them so that they can go back to the race.
- AI doesn't usually take the shortcuts (only when forced, by bumping into them), but they should on expert difficulty.
- The middle of the city stage has a problem on the rank system, so even if you are half a lap in front of everybody you will keep changing positions with everybody until you are out of the buggy zone.
- Twice I was racing (I think it was on the last stage) and one of the enemies got stuck out of stage (one of these times I was smashed, and the one who smashed me ran over me and ended up outside of stage). They wouldn't come back.
Improvement points:
- Add online multiplayer
- Add manual drift
- Add more stages; it gets boring to play the same thing over and over.
- I'd always avoid the milk bottles, as they are almost always a problem than a solution; when you hit someone you smash them, but you usually get thrown somewhere else, or even flip over, making every other player pass you. Maybe they should be removed or improved somehow?
Anyway, awesome game, and I'm looking forward to the Teddy Floppy Ear - The Race 2.
Note: Put the Diddy Kong Racing OST on the background and have fun.

I do like a good 4Xing from time to time, and when I do, Galactic Civilisations 3 (GC3) fills that hole for me. This is important because I have the following options to satiate my need for space empiring: Endless Space, Sins of a Solar Empire: Revellion and Homeworld. If I had to choose between the 3, I would choose GC3, followed by Endless Space.
My main gripe with GC3 is the lack of species to choose from. I feel like the devs spent this time on developing and integrating modding tools into the game to allow anyone to create their own civs very easily. Creating your own civ involves having some artwork, selecting/creating some ship designs, writing some fiction and ultimately filling in survey with a lot of tickboxes to determine the AI's behaviour and the advantages of the species - and perhaps because of how easy they've made it, I find it irritating that they couldn't have added many many more species. There are around 5 species in the vanilla version. I think the mercenaries DLC adds two species.
The range of ships also suffers from a lack of content but not to the same level - I am less upset about this however as the ship editor is excellent and there are some modders who have created impressive forgeries of licensed ships such as Star Wars, Star Trek, Games Workshop and BattleStar Galactica. Civilisations from these licenses are also available but this content is far less impressive and none of it comes close to the quality of vanilla content.
Galactic Civilizations 3 is pretty good as far as 4X space games go. However it's more akin to games like Civilization 5, Age of Wonders and Endless Legend then it is to other space 4X games like Endless Space and Space Empires. This is not necessarily a bad thing however, and as the quality of what is there is so high I end up playing GC3 over it's competitors anyway.
Overall I would recommend the game at 20 NZD which is ~ 30 USD.

Cute small cart racer for beginners.
There are 6 well-designed tracks (some have a night mode, most have a shortcut), some racing modes (single race with 4 difficulties, time trial, cone collecting, and two different tournament modes, respectively), no performance tuning, street features such as speedup arrows, a slow sand patch and a wet patch that wets your tires so that your next turn is harder to control. There are also a bunch of power-ups that speed you up or the others down (no weapons more violent than a box of thumbtacks, though). There's no story. All in all it's fairly varied.
You get two keyboard setups and you can also use one Xbox controller, which unfortunately is also all you get for split-screen. I'm calling this a beginners game because the AI and the difficulty of the challenges are no match for more experienced players once you've gotten the hang of the game (do have a look at the help before you start).  Physics are a bit strange in that you get rubber on the road long before you can hear a tire squeal, and I turned the music off after a while, but all in all it handles predictably enough for cart game physics.
I'm approximately halfway through the game, and to me it feels casual and I'm happy I didn't spend any money on it. But given the variety of race modes and tracks, it'd be a good game for a budding racing gamer - and that's precisely who it's aimed at. Recommended.

I purchase Gal Civ III because it seemed like it would fufill my desire for a interstellar 4X game. However, I was very dissappointed with this game. It starts out decently enough, requiring you to explore for habitable worlds for you to colonize and resources to exploit. You also have a tech web with several types of tech to research. Planets you colonize have tiles on which you can build buildings to increase yields of food and science, etc, etc, etc. The early game is fairly eventful as you try to build up your empire and meet the other empires. However, the pace stalls out in mid to late game. At that point, all you can really do is build up your colonized planets, continue grinding research, and attacking our defending against other empires. Also at this point, micromanaging becomes a massive problem. On the larger maps, you'll usually have a butt ton of planets under your countries. As far as I know there is no way to automate your planets. Late game turns usually consist of going through your planets to fill out their construction queues. This makes the late game tedious and un-fun.
Please save your money and don't give it to this sub-par game. If you really want a space 4X, buy Stellaris.

===
Necropolis is a roguelike procedurallly generated dungeon crawler, that can be played either in single player or up to 4 players co-op online. Brave groups of adventurers keep trying their luck in finding what lies at the end of the Necropolis, the dark and unforgiving reign of a poweful entity known as the Brazen Head. This devilish dungeon master creates perilious floors, different for each group and filled with enemies, traps, vendors and treasures. Oh and secrets, aswell.
Necropolis is a challenging and brutal game, in some ways similar to the Souls series, and in some other ways different. You can think of it as a low-end graphics, procedural co-op, "light" version of Dark Souls, that is a good analogy.
===
+ Good combat system based on timing and dodging, similar to the one seen in the Souls series (but less complex), with challenging enemies, very diversified weapon classes, and well done mechanics.
+ Decent variety of enemies to encounter
+ Crafting system with recipes for a wide variety of consumables
+ Good variety of weapons, accessories, armors, especially unique / named ones with specific bonuses and effects
+ Passive skills unlockable with Tokens earned at the end of every run, to upgrade your character and get better in the next one. This is the only form of lasting progression in this game.
+ The design, although minimalistic, has its charm, at times.
===
- Balance in the late game stages (Levels 7-8-9) is not really well thought as you find very good gear and have lots of materials to craft Healing items and poweful potions... in short words, late stages are too easy.
- The final boss is easy, laughable and anticlimatic, it is little more than a normal enemy with a giant health pool. And is the only boss. Mediocre.
- Late game stages (7-8) are generated to be considerably larger than the others, this means players have to mow down rooms upon rooms of the same enemies over and over, and it becomes very boring once you know what they drop and already have the best stuff at that point.
- Enemies may be varied but Archetypes are not, meaning there are many variations of one enemy but the core type of said enemy is only one, so there are not many archetypes overall, many enemies are just reskins of previously encountered ones, only stronger.
- Netcode can be sometimes unstable and lead to desync and crashes, rare but happens. More frequent with more players, 2 players is mostly fine but 3-4 can be worse.
- The absence of a map in larger levels is very annoying.
- Once beaten and seen all stages, this game has really not much on replayability even if you might think the opposite. This because most enemies and places will be the same over and over again, and while this game leaves a very good and fresh impression at the start, after not many hours everything will have that "already seen already done" feeling that really will dumb down the playability.
- Ranged weapons, especially Handcannons and Grenade Launchers are absurdly overpowered and can mow down hordes of enemies with no effort while at safe distance. Youc an literally kite 30 enemies and then have your friend Grenade Launcher them all down in a jiffy. Miserable.
===
Necropolis has a very good concept but falls short on replayability, content and features. At a first look this game might seem huge and really replayable, but in truth it is not. Not impressive technically or graphically, it features a simplified version of the famous Souls-like combat style, which works pretty good anyway. There is, at the end, a lot of repetitive content, and even procedural generation cannot save it from being so.
At a great discount, pick it up and play with a friend or two, it can be fun for some runs, but dont expect a long and replayable game here, because it is not, nor is worth the full price.

They are able to get a lot of planets right out of the gate, which means they get a big boost to every stat.  Looking at the graphs, all of mine have very little growth and theirs sky rocket.

The Witcher 2 is everything the original was, but distilled into a more potent experience. From beginning to end, you'll be engaged with an incredibly well built and incredibly detailed world. The choices and paths you can take will impact your game a thousand times more than the first Witcher game. While I felt that the game was a little shorter than the original, the third and fourth chapters are effectively two diffent stories depending on your choice in the first. Overall 8/10, would recommend.
Pros:
-Importing your decisions from the first Witcher game is a great way to reward fans.
-A greater variety of decisions that have more immediate and meaningful changes.
-There's so much story being told regarding Geralt, the mages, the non humans, the kingdoms, the empire... it can be overwheling in a good way, like Game of Thrones.
-The combat and character development system in this one is vastly improved over the original. More playstyles, more meaningful choices.
-Despite being a "dark" and "gritty" setting, they pack a lot of humor into it as well. I chuckled aloud a few times at some of funnier moments.
Cons:
-With all the major plot going on, it's hard to feel like a Witcher. There aren't many monster contracts to claim and fewer sidequests.
-The inventory and crafting system is a bit of a clusterf***. By the end of the game I had hundreds of useless mundain crafting materials in my storage and no reason to use them. Sadly I often overburdened myself looting dungeons and punishingly walked back to town in slow motion before realizing how little I needed anything that could be crafted.
-The level cap of 35 is a bit punishing to players who complete sidequests. I was max level by the end of chapter 2 and basically wasted all the exp I could have gained doing quests in chapter 3.

In Crow you play as the titular bird and, after a chance meeting with a dark spirit, you're imbued with special powers and set on a path of revenge: it's up to you wether you want to follow the dark spirit's voice or listen to a new one soon appearing in your head, a voice of forgiveness. You'll be exploring small maps flying around and trying to uncover hidden trinkets (to earn skill points) or point of interest: once you're done the actual fight starts and this section plays somewhat similarly to an on-rail shooter.
Crow is a mobile port and, despite an upgrade for the Steam release, it shows in its simple gameplay: the concept and story are intriguing though and are original enough to make it worth a shot if you're interested.
-the graphics are decent and pretty, considering it was originally a mobile game
-the soundtrack is quite nice and has a dark, epic feel to it
-while you can't expect the depth of an RPG the story is quite interesting and pretty original
-the fight section gameplay is nice and controls well
-good level and boss variety
-the fact you can choose to take revenge or spare bosses adds a nice touch and justifies a second playthrough for those interested in seeing what happens
-one of the two paths is noticeably easier, but you won't know that until you follow it
-some graphical elements stand up as noticeably simpler due to its mobile origin, some textures don't hold up well when you fly nearby and human enemy models are very simple both in looks and animations
-the exploration gameplay section feels a bit slow and dull as you fly around somewhat aimlessly trying to uncover what you need
-the ending is delivered through credits and feels quite lacking
-pretty short,expect about an hour and a half
Crow is a simple game with an equally simple gameplay, as long as you know that and are ok with it its story and narrative are good enough to keep you interested with their mix of dark magic, myths and nature spirits. It's a bit sad that said story is only told through text whenever you reach a point of interest, a few more cutscenes'd have been appreciated for sure.
The actual gameplay is ok,as mentioned above the world exploration is honestly "meh" at best and felt like filler while the on-rail fights were actually quite fun despite their simplicity: you'll also be able to unlock and upgrade a few skills whenever you gather enough points and this very light RPG element adds some depth to the game.
All things considered I think Crow was a satisfying experience and it'd be the same for you if you like this kind of game and/ or love crows: the price is honestly way too much for what it has to offer though. Thankfully Crow has been often put in bundles, or you can wait for a deep sale on it.

Crow is an excellent example of an interesting game badly ported from mobile devices to pc. True: I've not gotten far into it, and only scratched the surface of the story after half an hour. To make matters a lot worse: this is probably the first game ever which got me motion-sick. I've played thousands upon thousands of hours in first-person shooters, some of them very fast moving ones, and never got this feeling before. But I can tell you: it's horrible to feel and it makes me really sick. I guess it's because of the fact that the entire screen wobbles while flying, looking upon the crow in third-person view from over the shoulder (and pretty far of). There's no fixed point left, no horizon, and apparently I can't have that.
So although the idea is interesting, I can't recommend this game because I can't play it. If better ported, maybe the motion sickness wouldn't kick in that bad, I don't know. Truth is: it never feels like a pc game at all.

I bought this game as a fan of turn based strategy games looking for something different.  I've played through a few games and overall I think I got bored of it pretty quickly.
I think this is one of those games where if you want to put 100 hours into a round and customize your ships to the nth degree, it could be fun.  But for those without all day long to spend micro designing your fleets, it's quite a grind.
Here's my major gripes:
1) The culture aspect is super unbalanced.  You can win the whole game by just playing super defensive and focus heavily on spreading your culture.  You can turn planets to your own side by doing nothing.
2) Some aspects of the game just aren't useful for anything.  I.E., military starbases.  They're purely defensive, and they don't even get involved in a battle unless the enemy specifically attacks them.  It would make way more sense if they provided defensive coverage in a "zone".
3) They spent time creating some visuals for space battles.  You see them in the screenshots for the game.  They add absolutely nothing to the overall content of the game.  Yeah its kind of fun to watch it like twice, but then you just end up turning all of it off because it takes a long time for the game to have a "space battle" that had an outcome calculated before the battle started.  Should have spent that dev time adding other cool things.
4) Diplomacy AI is weak.  To be fair, almost no game gets this right.

GalCiv2 was what everyone needed after a long time had passed since MOO2. Obviously, based on that success, fans were expecting another home run with GalCiv3. And what they got was a single.
There's not much new. If anything, it feels "streamlined" and has less overall "stuff" than GalCiv2 did. That could just be my perspective but I'm certainly feeling less involved this time around. I have mixed feelings about the AI as sometimes it was incredibly smart if not too smart and other times I shook my head in embarassment for them. It just doesn't seem consistent at the mid-to-high difficulty levels.
Visually, which is usually not a 4X game strong point, it's pretty but it's not mind blowing. The game has held my attention for 4 or 5 moderately long sessions so far. I'll play it through a few times but if you're expecting something above and beyond GalCiv2, I just don't feel that it's here.
That said, this is WAY better than the MOO reboot in Early Access. Yikes, that thing is a mess.

Endless Space feels more like "real" galaxy exploration instead of moving tokens on a gameboard. The discoveries and events feel more story-like, wheras in GalCiv3 they just feel like excuses to click through and get resources. The graphics in Endless Space are far more beautiful, and the music is far better.
The truth is, for me Endless Space IS GalCiv3. And GalCiv3 is... well, it's GalCiv2 Remastered. I've gone back to playing Endless Space, and I'm looking forward to the sequel.

There have been many Space 4X games that are currently out there. Some good, some not so good. Stellaris, the latest Space 4x game, is one for the record books in my opinion. Most 4x games I have played, other than Sins of a Solar Empire, have been turned based in some way for form. Whether combat, or on a galactic scale or even both. Stellaris really holds a unique story with every playthrough. I’ve played over half a dozen matches with various friends online and we all love it!
Overall, Stellaris is complete RTS, no turn based in any way for form. The UI is great, with information on almost everything you hover over just in case you weren’t sure what something was. There is a pretty in-depth tutorial as well, but gets quite annoying on each play through so I usually just turn it off. Did I mention this game has Steam Workshop Support? Well it does, and that can only mean limitless playtime in the future with user generated content.
You start as a single planet, branching out to your solar system, then eventually to nearby systems, eventually colonizing those systems forming your empire. Eventually forming massive fleets from Corvettes all the way to battleships. With that said, you can eventually form an alliance with other empires you come across, and eventually federations as well. Or you can try to dominate everyone either by diplomacy, or by military might. Games “Will” last for hours on end with almost no end in sight. In fact, me and a group of 3 friends started a match not too long ago currently over 6 hours gameplay in that save game. We are now at the stages of wars with other empires and alliances/federations.
Every story and every play through will be a different story whether you are solo, or play with friends. The game offers a great “hot” seat mechanic which is essentially drop in/drop out gameplay. Research is definitely a game changer as research is completely randomized. One play through you can advance in ship shielding first, effectively giving yourself a tactical advantage over some others. Or may not end up search that type of technology for hours of gameplay.
The graphics of the game are great, not super fancy fantastic like the latest AAA games come with today, but the gameplay is solid enough, and there is still enough eye candy to keep you coming back for more. The sound of the game is phenomenal. Though can be very repetitive after hours of gameplay, I can always find myself drawn to the ambient music of the game. The Penetrator is the most visceral gun I've ever seen in a manshooter (even more in slow-mo). On that topic, FEAR is a great SP manshooter and it plays just right. There's only just enough interaction, and it doesn't interfere with the action. The UI doesn't get in the way, melee is fun, slow-mo is fun, and it's unabashedly gory. It's questionably horror-like though, and the game never finds a good way to combine manshooter with horror. The standard mode in NightSky is a beautiful and relaxed experienced, with very little to trouble or annoy you as you're playing. I will no doubt go back and replay this mode again in the future.
The advanced mode, in comparison, takes the same levels and turns them into something that takes a little more precision and a lot more patience, subtly tweaking mechanics and layouts to add that extra level of challenge and frustration.
Nothing in the advanced mode was beyond my ability, but some of the levels required passing through tricky sections to get to the fiendishly difficult sections, many of which you only got one attempt at before failing miserably and going back to the start of the level and having to go through the tricky section again before being allowed to attempt the fiendish part again. This makes it very difficult to play around with the mechanics of the level to work out the solution to the puzzle and can get quite frustrating after a dozen or so attempts.
After completing both modes, finding all the stars, and finishing off the final levels, I can heartily recommend this game for either people wanting a peaceful experince for a few hours or for those wishing to atone for some major sins in a past life.

Simple, fun, and unusual sums this game up quite well.  Though it has to be said that even getting it at half price I still felt I didn't get too much bang for my buck with the whole game being easily complete-able in well under 2 hours.  But I still feel this is worth recommending.
The game consists of essentially 2 game modes.  One where you are free to explore as you steer your crow around a small open area, finding collectables (or "trinkets") and unearthing further nuggets of story.  And the story missions which functions quite like a semi-on-the-rails shooter (or slasher) as you fly about, collecting gems to allow upgrades, deploying shields to fend off incoming missles, and attacking enemies.
Deploying shields and issuing slash attacks is quite nicely implemented, as you have to press an action key and then draw the appropriate symbol onscreen with your mouse.
The game does not hide it's phone origins with its focus on drawing symbols and easy difficulty, but it offers a suitably unique experience that is worth having.  It marginally increases its difficulty over the course of the two hours but it's still on the easy side, with the end boss being the only real challenge which resulted in a couple of repeats.
There is a choice element at the end of each chapter, a simple binary good/evil choice, which I assume has an effect on the ending cinematic, an assumption based on the ending I saw.
There are also some optional challenge missions that function very similarly to the scripted story missions only they are repeatable, but weren't enticing enough to have me coming back for any more.
I'm looking forward to seeing what else this developer puts out.
