Nightsky is a casual physics platformer puzzle game with exceptional sounds and graphics. Although, despite sounding and looking amazing, it’s gameplay can be repetitive, I can still recommend this and here’s why.
Pros:
♦ Great Atmospheric Graphics (It’s simple art style but it all fits together and looks amazing)
♦ Relaxing Eargasmic Sound (Relaxing and calming sounds that just fit together and make playing the game so much better)
♦ Relaxing/chill gameplay (Gameplay isn’t 100% but if you want a game you can easily pick up and put down in your spare time or want something to relax to, then this hits the nail on the head)
♦ Nice number of easy achievements (You can get all the achievements just by completing the game)
♦ Reasonable price considering the amount of work that has gone into the Graphics and Sound (Though if you are buying it for the gameplay, I’d say buy it on sale for a couple of bucks)
♦ Controls that just work (They just work)
♦ Interesting Vehicle Concept (I won’t spoil it, but vehicle concept is very interesting and fun)
♦ Interactive Credit Concept (This was a nice little way to do the credits and made reading them that little bit more enjoyable)
Cons:
♦ Really Repetitive (I say this as I was happily playing and then all of a sudden when I expected the game to almost be finished, it tells me there are more levels but to progress I have to redo the old levels and find a “Hidden Star” which it never told me about. This concept is so annoying, as having to redo levels you’ve already completed to find a hidden object just to progress the main storyline seems really redundant and stupid)
♦ Really Easy (For 90% of the game all I had to do was hold down the left or right arrow and roll to the next screen/part of the level. This is kind of silly for a puzzle game to be this easy)
♦ Non-Existent Puzzles (I say this as I mentioned above I could hold left or right and progress easily. Also the only puzzles I seemingly found were timing jumps or rolling balls into the correct spot at the correct time, which I imagine a 5 or 6 year old could figure out easily)
♦ No Steam Trading Cards (Would be a nice addition as the graphics of the game are amazing and I imagine they could create some really stunning backgrounds, emotes and badges).
♦ No way to tell how far you have progressed in a level or how many are left (There is no level numbers and I could only seemingly tell how far I had progressed via exciting and selecting the level I was on. Then again it still didn’t tell me how much of that level I had left and how many more levels were left. The only way I could tell how many levels were left was via the Achievements. This concept is annoying as they should show each level and part of level as locked, not hidden, to make it easier to know how far you have left).
♦ No real storyline (Tried to implement some kind of Storyline but never executed it well enough to make any sense or significant impact on the game)
♦ Wasn’t aware some levels had hidden objects that I needed to collect to progress later in game (Not being aware of this until I needed these hidden objects to progress is really annoying as I would have searched and collected them on my first run through to save me having to repeat the levels again just to find one hidden object)
On a Side Note:
♦ I haven’t finished the game as much as I wanted to because even though I had only played 2-3 hours of it, it was already getting on my nerves. I say this because it was repetitive and never really offered anything new in the terms of its puzzles per level and every time I progressed, I felt like I was just playing to get the next achievement. Then when I got to the point where it said I had to go back to levels I had already complete and find hidden Stars to progress… it just ruined the whole game for me and I closed it. I ultimately wanted something new, not having to go back and search old levels for something I missed on the first run.
Overall, even though there are a lot of cons, I never finished the game and probably won’t and the gameplay is repetitive, I can still recommend this. I recommend this if you want something easy and relaxing that has great graphics and eargasmic sounds. Therefore, I recommend you pick it up for that reason. However, if you are buying it solely for the gameplay, I’d recommend buying it on sale at the cheapest possible price due to lack of actual puzzles and how repetitive it is as mentioned in my side note and cons.

By far the largest, most immersive, and complex strategy game available.  Beautiful graphics up to 4K resolution and possibly higher.
The size of the largest maps put to shame every predecessor.  I mean, these things actually resemble small galaxies in scope.  I think the one I'm playing on has over a thousand solar systems, and I'm not quite sure if I picked the largest size available.
You might infer from the previous information that, despite streamlining and concerted efforts to fight excessive micromanagement that was rampant in the previous game (and, really, any game of this type), playing on the larger maps will still require lots of time per turn, excellent memory, and a sharp eye for enemy actions.  I've probably put.....20 hours or more into my current match, and I would consider it to still be in the early-mid-game stage.
The ship designer is back, retaining all of its former glory and with even more features.  The funky variable-hardpoint system of the previous game has been reevaluated, so that parts artificially labeled as 'small', 'medium', etc. generally have the same number of spots now, cleaning things up a bit.  The tech tree feels a bit less expansive than before, but still outclasses most competing games.
Anyways, back to playing GC3 - and back to enjoying brilliant explosions, highly detailed planets and planetesimals, and of course some damn good gameplay.
Edit: Oh, I forgot to mention - the AI that shamed Deep Blue is back to put you in your place again, though some others playing have mentioned that it might not be quite as cunning anymore.

SUMMARY:
Being abandoned by it's developers, it makes it hard to suggest to anyone.  That being said, Necropolis is the solid foundations of a game which provides you with a unique art style, good music and entertaining gameplay.  The combat is slower and clunkier than many other games, but with careful timing, it can be used to your advantage, rather than be a nuisance. However, I felt the monochrome environment lacked enough sustance to fully grasp my attention.  That being said, I did play seven hours in one sitting whilst watching YouTube and TV shows.  It was a great TimeKiller.
COMBAT:
This is not a soulslike.  Anyone looking for a soulslike, go elsewhere, you will be dissapointed with this game. That being said, if you are looking for a fun, non punishing but difficult perma-death roguelike, than look no further. Combat has some extremely slow wind ups, but with timing, you can strike and dash away with ease.  Later on, getting a wand in the off hand or a gun, enables you to thin the crowds with range before charging in with your sword. Being able to craft bombs, scrolls and potions to paralyse, freeze, slow, and command your enemies adds some extremely fun details to combat, and also the stress of not waisting your valuable resources. However, that being said, the lock on system is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥  It swaps to whoever is closest or the direction in which you happen to bump your mouse whilst attacking, causing you to miss your attacks all together.  It is certainly not useful for groups.  That being said, it is imperative to use for ranged combat, as well as being good for solo fights.
CRAFTING:
Crafting seems quite robost.  You gather resources from killing enemies or looting small chests and the like. It's nothing special, but also not really lacking.  It simply works well to support your gameplay.  That being said, you loose all your reciepies upon death, so you have to choose what you think will help you most with what jems you have.
MUSIC:
Good.  I wouldn't listen to it outside of the game, but it does support the overal feel of it, without really getting repetative or annoying.
SIDE NOTES:
One aspect to which I was quite frustraited with at first, but came to love later on, was the slowly and constantly diminishing stamina bar.  As you fight, and especially with power attacks or secondary weapons, your total stamina bar depletes, causing you to enter different stanges of exhaustion.  What once was an easy four hit combo encounter, now has to be a careful hit and run, cause you don't have enough stamina.  Eating food doesn't seem to replenish your health too much, but it does restore a fair portion of your max stamina.  This led me to be much more willing to use power attacks and use up my stamina frequently, and just restore it with food, rather than saving my food for my health, as you health can be saved with tactical use of your stamina in the first place.  It was a very fun addition to the game.
MULTIPLAYER:
I haven't yet had the opportunity to try the game multiplayer, though I certainly aim to.  I think all that I have mentioned above would be ten times better with a best friend to run around with, changing combat tactics and resource management.  It seems like it would be a blast, but I have not idea how well executed it is nor any concept of potential connection bugs.
BUGS:
As the game has been abandoned by the developers, it does have bugs.  I cannot deny this.  However, the comments below mention a desease ridden host of bugs, which I did not experience.  In seven hours, I only encountered one bug. I had saved and exited the game to grab dinner, and when I reloaded the game, I clipped through the floor, landed, clipped again, then was teleported back to the beginning of the dungeon.  It was a brief and annoying setback, as I had to make my way back to where I was, but all the enemies were dead, so it was not a big issue.  Since then, I have quit and reloaded four times without a glitch.  All in all, the bugs are there, it is undeniable.  However, I have not found them to be game breaking as some comments suggest.
CONCLUSION:
Not worth $30.  However, a cheap pick up on steam sale, Definitally worth it.  I've had a lot of fun, and I expect to have several more hours of entertainment from it, especially once I find someone to co-op with.  Aditionally to that, I've already got 3 times the amount hours of entertainment from it than I would have gotten going to the cinema.

Forewarning: This game is part 1 of a 2 part series that will in all likelihood never be finished. It is a bit of a Kickstarter flop that was eventually sold to another company to fulfill KS backers' and promptly tossed on a shelf due to inhouse reasons.
Red Hood Diaries is a gothic Victorian retelling of Little Red Riding Hood. It's an action platformer game (or at least, it claims to be) about searching for the murderer of Red's father.
That's about the last thing that ends up making sense about this game.
The gothic asethetic is done decently, and the music is alright. The presentation is sort of there, but animations are stiff and unnatural feeling, which isn't bad when half your cast is robots, but stands out noticeably on Red, the Pied Piper, and on Woolfe himself. The level design is about as varied as you could get for a retelling of the Red Riding Hood story, in that there's a town level, a sewer level, a harbor level, a mystic forest level and a burning forest chase level. If you noticed a distinct change there at the end, that's because the game takes about a 180 degree tonal shift in its second half, completely destroying what narrative what originally there. The game transforms from a murder mystery to a game where the woods outside the city has transformed into mystical floating platforms (this is never elaborated on) Red has unexplained magical powers and the abiltiy to slow time (this is never elaborated on), Granny is a sorceress with curse powers and wolf claw magic (this is never elaborated on), and Woolfe himself is a lightning calling, wolf summoning shadow sorceror himself after being presented as a corporate Victorian businessman, and also possibly a werewolf. (you guessed it, this is never elaborated on). Considering the game literally ends after this revelation with a black screen that says "TO BE CONTINUED", well.... yeah.
Red herself makes for a decent enough narrator - but the rhyming gimmick is done inconsistently, and sometimes without any sort of meter. While it's not always as forced as, say Child of Light, there are some occasions where you can tell they were definitely reaching to get the rhyme down. Unfortunately towards the end Red is about as in the know about the story as we are, making her narration to the audience unhelpful at best, but still somewhat immersive. The game has unlcokable diary entries that help fill in the background story about the characters, but nothing even comes close to explaining what happens in the last half of the game at all, and really only serves to reinforce what the players already know: Red's family is great, Granny is nice and a teacher, and Woolfe murdered her father and kidnapped her mother. We knew all this from the outset, Red tells us explicitly.
The controls are mediocre, both in play and response. Attacking is clunky at best, and you're generally best served by mashing the light attack button or using the AoE smash magic attack. All other options are inferior unless you're smashing rats with the vertical attack. Normal enemies can and will kill you in groups of two, and there is nothing in the way of progression in the game save auto-learning new magical attacks for what appears to be no reason at all. Most of them are useless except the AoE ground smash. Platforming is dicey, with only specific highlighted ledges able to be grabbed, and a lack of 'stickiness' making even acceptable ledges hard to see sometimes. The camera angle is fixed, creating often more of a 2.5D field rather than a true 3d environment, but there's often just enoguh depth to throw off your perception of a jump you need to make, and since nearly every fall and every field obstacle is an instant kill without fail, you will tire of the platforming very, very quickly.
The game spikes in difficulty combat wise in the Harbor, being very minor platforming with hectic, difficult comba,t then does the exact opposite in the next level, expecting frequent pinpoint double jumps in 3d on spinning moving platforms in the mystic forest. The game even seems cognizant of this decision, due to there being achievements for these levels specifically for beating them on hard, and for speedrunning it. Not a good decision, IMO, and it brings down the flow of the game.
I absolutely cannot recommend this game on any level. It doesn't matter that the game is only two hours long. You know what other story based narrative platform light puzzle game is about two hours long?
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons. Now THERE'S a game worth playing, instead of this one. Pass on this.

I worked my way through a lot of this game and just ultimately couldn't be bothered to finish it. The world is beautiful. The art is great. The platforming is fine, albeit a little uninspired for a 3d platformer, and buggy as hell. The mechanics are awful. There just seemed to be no clear cut idea of what the game wanted its mechanical hooks to be. It tried for a lot of different things (stealth, combat, puzzle platforming) and managed to excel at none of them, and only just barely accomplish the later two of those three. The writing is some of the worst I have seen. It's possible to overlook considering how richly layered the visuals of the levels are and how wonderful (if thin) the world-building is. They've got a great backdrop, but that's all most of it is. There's practically nothing to interact with in the world despite it being so beautiful that you can't not want to interact with it. There's also practically no cast despite the world being filled with characters that have complicated, interwoven back stories, but you learn about most of them in cut scene soliloquies and bonus text content revealed as easter eggs. The game drops hints about all the wrong things, and seems to resolve buggy geometries by insta-killing your character should she get stuck somewhere. That's ultimately what made me put it down and uninstall it uncompleted. For the 7th time in a span of about 20 minutes I was insta-killed in the same boss fight when I wasn't taking damage, was doing things correctly, and just happened to hit the scenery wrong on a jump. I hadn't been enjoying anything but the visuals and considering all the best cutscenes were laiden with some of the most poorly crafted and paced writing I'd ever had to listen to in a game, they weren't even that enjoyable to watch on the whole.
Learning about the story of the original devs, clearly they couldn't get the game finished. Whatever the reason, they sold off what they had and its being distributed in a half-baked form. Maybe with a lot of testing, a more cohesive development process, and a lot more money this could've been something great. Right now, it's just a source of frustration, both in bad mechanics, and in a game, world, and main character that all could've been much better than it was.

Sometimes, a game is so good, nothing really needs to be said. Dust is one of those. It's absolutely amazingly well made, from beginning to end, with wonderful characters, a truly awesome storyline, and a breathtaking art style. I'm usually not a fan of platformers, but this one is just amazing. The 10.4 hours I have on record are me beating the game on the lowest difficulty setting. I can only assume that those looking for a more challenging experience would get it on the higher difficulties. For myself, I was only interested in the storyline, and it was worth every penny of admission.
As far as mechanics go, the fighting is absolutely spot on, and the combo system is an absolute blast to learn and use. There are tons of different enemies that require lots of different techniques to destroy, and there is even some puzzle solving. These moments were not overly difficult, and, to me at least, added to the enjoyability and immersion.
The crafting system is unique and interesting, and it was fun running around trying to find the various parts I needed for a new set of armor or a new upgrade to my weapon. On that topic, there is only one weapon in the game, but the number of combos that are available to use with it make up for this, I think.
The musical score is absolutely phenominal. I actually paused the game at some points, just to listen to the music. It's gorgeous, and fits perfectly with each level.
I cannot recommend this game enough. For the storyline alone, it's worth the price. When you include the music, the puzzles, the rock-solid combat, and the multitude of spectacularly well-realized levels, the price is right whether it's on sale or not.

It is one of the best metroidvania titles available on PC. Fully worth it even at the full price, but if/when you can snatch it at a discount it is an absolute must-have.
Everything about this game is swell, especially if you realize that only one guy made the whole thing. It our day and age, when some games require multiple huge studios to be developed, and then they still don't work, it's great to see a title that defies the industry "standard." The art is gorgeous, the platforming and combat is spot-on (even on a keyboard, which is a huge plus for me). Exploration harkens back to the days of Metroid and Castlevania: SOTN. My only gripe is the boss fights. They are challenging (especially at the higher difficulties), but they could be a more spectacular.
The voice-acting is great as well. Some people (*cough*TB*cough*) complained about the side-kick being annoying, but I had no problem with her. The FMV sequences offer a welcomed break from the usual way the characters interact. The only thing that left me wanting a bit more is the fidelity of character portraits in cut-scenes. In comparison to the crisp in-game graphics, the characters just seemed a bit blurry to me.
Finally, Dust runs well even on my humble 650M laptop. I was running a solid 60fps with no dips even during sequences heavy on effects and characters.
Buy this game, especially when it's on sale. Even on full price, it comes highly recommended.
PS: I maintain that this game is highly playable using mouse & keyboard combo. However, as with most action platformers and metroidvanias, having a gamepad will make some platforming sections much easier for you (especially those involving wall-jumps).

I try to be fair in any review that isn't a joke, so I'll endeavor to do the same here.
We'll start with what most people notice about the game, which is the visuals. The models are cute and the textures quilt-like, which is very pleasing to the eye, and the animal sounds are pretty good. For Shelter 1 & 2, this definitely made it pop. Now that we are on at least 4 different games (or interactive media) that all have the same visual style, their visual unity is all the more apparent. It's also for this reason that it's not breath-taking in its own right anymore; birds fly, fish swim, Might and Delight make cute, nice-looking animal games. Like all of their titles, the soundtrack is quite pleasing when it wants to be and makes some nice use of simple instrumentals. It's nothing ground-breaking, but I think it does the job reasonably well for the communication of tense or calm moments.
The biggest issue you'll likely have playing this game is the controls and camera. The controls are slippery, temperamental, and can get you killed if you are in any part of the game that requires precision or timing, like when a fox comes by. It's extremely difficult to get the lynx to jump where it's supposed to, and there are points where you will find yourself unable to jump up a ledge because the bear suddenly stops being registered as something to jump on by the game. There isn't much to tell you what the buttons do, either, which wasn't a huge issue for my own playthrough but seems to have lead to a number of new players getting confused. All of this is exacerbated by being unable to zoom and move the camera very well; it's always quite close-up and tends to get stuck in things. All of this is enough to make it difficult for me to play it for very long stretches, and losing out on a collectible simply because the bear stopped dancing and won't let you land on its back anymore for some reason gets wearying.
As I consider the gameplay and usability of a game to be the most important aspects before building anything on top of that, and that Paws is not really trying to be a piece of art wherein every aspect plays a pivotal role, we can try stripping away the purely visual aspects and see what we're left with. A simple story with endearing little animals that gets let down by janky controls and an annoying camera. It's more solid than a lot of other titles and digital toys out there and it has a well-defined beginning and end(s), but the gameplay just isn't as enjoyable as it could be and most of the challenge comes from the controls of the game rather than the game itself or any conscious gameplay design choices. If you're a diehard fan of the Shelter series, you may enjoy it or you may be let down by how different this one pilots. If you're new to Shelter, this game's tone fits well but may give you a somewhat-inaccurate view of the series. Hence I will give Paws: A Shelter Game a hesitant 6/10, which is still "above average" but has room for improvement.

I'm just going to come out and say it; I love this type of game and keel-haul it all it's nice to discover one in this extremely niche genre. If you're like me, there's a good chance you'll buy this game just because there's so little variety on the market. Fire Emblem, Tactics Ogre, FFT...this game pays homage and stays true to what we cherish in those games.
So why the not recommended? Well, because I believe that just because you find an miracle oasis in the desert, you shouldn't neglect to put up a sign warning other travelers that there's Ebola in the water. Here's three points that I think you, the reader, will need to come to terms with before this is worth buying. Beware, there are light spoilers, but it's mostly things you'll discover in the first fifteen minutes of play.
1) This does not have a lot of difficulty, and it will get increasingly easier as you go along.
At first, I did not think this was going to be an issue. I really didn't. This game starts off pretty solid, with not a 'lot' of difficulty, but enough that it keeps you on your toes while teaching you the ropes. The problem that began to happen though, was that as my army grew, the opposing army lost a major part of it's bite. Knocking people into the water with shove was hella cool at first, but it became downright overpowered fairly quickly. Making roadblocks and creating ice paths was awesome, but again quickly threw the game's balance out of whack. Healing is quick and spammable; a well-maintenenced army isn't going to go down under normal circumstances. The enemy WILL get you by cheaply shoving you off a cliff though.
Most fights are going to become obstacle control fights; it's less about your gear and level, and more about shoving and bottling hallways so your mages can aoe the living hell out of them. This is really fun sometimes, but you as the reader need to understand that your army's going to be either a snail's pace fortress, or you're restarting when your cute archer 5 panels away gets kinectly shoved off a cliff for an auto-kill. Speaking of cute archers, here's the second glaring issue...
2) 90% of your army is female, and the 10% that are male will suffocate from the estrogen in the air.
You're laughing now reader, but I'm dead serious. There is so many f'ing girls in my army, I'm almost certain that the girls on the isles are genetically born to battle.  The main character, Emma, is a stereotypical 'I'm an independant (non-black) woman who needs no man', and is like a crude, not-cute version of Xena, Warrior Princess..that's a lesbian. Her (female) sister accompanies her as she travels the isles, making Team Rocket-level traps and pitfalls. Along for the merry ride is; A   (female) archer, a (female) lumberjack, a (female) cleric, a (female)crossbow(wo)man, a (female) knight, a (female) demon, a (female) mage, a (female) engineer, a (female) shadowling, a (female) mage, a (female) lancer, a (female) lizard, and many, many more (females)! Also starring for literally one scene, one male scummy thief, and one male mage.
I asked the female mantis knight about her mantis, and how long she had known him; she got snippy at me for assuming only male mantis can be armored harbingers of war. Remember that folks, female mantis can be knights too.
3) This is honestly a minor thing, but Yawah help me if I can't pick between my units. You obviously can't bring half your army into battle, but I've never had so much trouble picking units before. In tactics ogre, I have trouble deciding between subbing one or two, but here it's like I'm benching half the units I 'want' to use, but can't. Emma and her sister have to be there, and that's two of the same generic warrior class. Hell, I'd rather take Team Rocket girl over Emma, at least badly-hidden traps are a fun mechanic to watch ppl fall into. You're bringing an archer-unless you enjoy being one shot by a pyromancer. A cleric has to be there, and they're basically a healbot. Then there's one or two push-pullers...and now you have your army basically set.
But wait!; There is so many cool classes out there. The issue that shows up is how outclassed they are, or that there is never enough room. I love my lumberjack girl, but I'm gimping myself if I bring her over a lizard...who already I don't have room for. I like my bow archer, but I'm not going to deny I get way better mileage out of my crossbow user. And Ms. Mantis is only around cause she's riding a F'ING MANTIS, she's outclassed in every regard by my robot...
So there you have it. Those are the three things that going into this game, you need to accept and embrace. Is this game fun? Yes, yes it can really be a blast. But these things hold it back, and can repel you from really getting into it. If these don't bother you, buy it. If they do...watch a let's play first and see. Especially if the second one bothers you, because I'll admit the story and mob of females really drive me off of really getting immersed. But even then...there is something oh so satisfying about pushing that heavy knight of a cliff with psyenergy. Happy gaming!

So before this game was dropped, I played a marathon amount of DW:U just to ready myself. I played enough of DW:U to see right away, once I started Stellaris, that these games are apples and oranges. I'll keep playing Stellaris because there are things about it I just don't have in DW:U. If nothing else, it looks pretty, even if after playing so much DW:U it seems wierd looking at a static (if pretty) solar system. I miss seeing my sims, I mean private sector npc's, going back and forth between my worlds, but I remind myself this is a different game.
One example of how this game differs from DW:U is expantion. In DW:U you need to expand as quickly as you can. It'll punish you a bit if you expand faster than you are capable of defending, but ultimately if you don't expand rapidly you'll end up boxed in by other races. Your outlying planets will suffer frequent pirate raids and will glrow slowly and have trouble but it's doable. In stellaris, you simply can't expand too far or too fast without inflicting severe consequences on yourself. The bonus to this is neither can any other faction. Eventualy you'll come accross technologies that allow for larger empires to be managed, but it takes quite some time. You have to be much more selective about the worlds you grab and make sure that grip is fairly firm before moving on.
This is just one of the differences. The way I look at it, each provides a unique challenge and is enjoyable in it's own way.

Then I played Vanguards.
Vanguards fixes literally every issue I have with MOBAs. The genre has been stripped to the essentials of what makes it fun: use your powers to kill enemies and destroy their base. No creeps or minions. No items or levels. 3 unique heroes instead of a million. Games take less than 10 minutes.
I thought I'd be bored after a game or two, but there's something addictive about Vanguards. Being so streamlined means I can focus on tactics and mastering my powers. I wish it was easier to find games with real players, but the bots are actually fun and challenging by themselves.
The game does have rough edges: I hope they'll add a few more menu options and clean up some of the graphics. It also runs a bit choppy. But knowing it's a student project and costs zero dollars helps me overlook the issues.
So don't like MOBAs? Try Vanguards. Like MOBAs but wish you could play a game in 10 minutes? Try Vanguards. I don't think you'll be disappointed, but if you are, the game was free anyway!

Ah, physics, where would we be without it? Well, we wouldn't have this little ball beauty for a start! Or gravity. Or molecules. Or ukuleles. Or underpants. Or hotdogs. Or gangrene. Or police pension funds being suspiciously syphoned off into untraceable dummy accounts. Sorry, where was I?... Oh yeah, NightSky!...
NightSky is a physics, balling, roll-'em-up puzzler of sorts where you have to guide a ball through a wide selection of varied obstacle courses. This is primarily done by simply moving around with the arrow keys and adjusting your ball momentum and timing accordingly, as well as speeding up, slowing down or braking on the stages where it's allowed. But as it goes on, further elements are added, like parts of the environment that can be manipulated or inverting gravity or any number of marvellous contraptions that can be guided around while housing your ball. It really is amazing just how creative the game manages to consistently be through so many different areas and that it rarely ever feels repetitive despite the generous number of stages, which include an "alternative set", essentially a remixed version of every stage you've already completed, but this time ramping up the hardness on your ball.
The difficulty is judged nicely as well. It teaches you each element perfectly whilst at the same time testing you fairly with every mechanic you learn. As should always be the case in any game, if you fail here, it doesn't feel like the game's fault, and each "death" isn't a punishment on your ball, but rather a lesson to learn as you further refine your strategy and ball technique. If there is any frustration to be had it's when you get to the end of a tricky stage, have your ball suddenly drop or get your ball stuck somewhere, then have to go all the way back to the start and drag your ball the whole way through again. But between the quick restarts and well designed stages, this shouldn't be too much of a problem for anyone with any patience, and when you finally achieve success, that euphoric feeling should be ample reward enough for your struggling ball.
The look and sound of the game deserve some attention, too, as the solid black foreground of most stages set against the beautiful night-time backdrops help keep your blood pressure down during even the most difficult of ball manoeuvers. This is further reinforced by the sedate music and charming little dings and thuds of any moving parts around you. I can imagine it could have been tempting to try ramping up the tension and sense of urgency on your ball by adding more energetic music to push you forward, but I think they judged it perfectly here and are real enablers of that "one more go!" mentality you want to have in your ball games.
So for a slightly different breed of puzzler with fun, fair, challenging and yet relaxing ball play, you really need look no further than NightSky... now with 87.8% more ball jokes.

Vanguards is an entry-level free to play MOBA style game that focuses on individual short, action-packed matches.  Every match will last between about 5-10 minutes on average, with the longest matches lasting about 15.  This is a game you can pick up and play for a couple of minutes just to have some fun without feeling the need to put in a lot of time or effort into it.
The game has three character types that you can choose before you begin a match.  Each character type focuses on a different style of gameplay.  The Lightning Knight is very good at pushing the objectives and transporting the "ghost" to sap the power out of the other team's shrine.  He focuses on quick movement and sacrifices power and crowd control in return.  The Flame Knight has abilities that disrupt the other team and help push and defend your position.  The Ice Knight mainly deals massive damage.
Gameplay-wise the game is fairly simple by MOBA standards.  Each character has 4 basic abilities used with QWER with cooldown times.  Unlike other MOBA's on the market, there is no complicated leveling system or itemization so you never feel like you can't come back from a bad play.  Every character is equal to another of the same type strength-wise no matter what point of the game you're in.
The only downside to this game, at the point of this day one review, is that the game still needs a few optimization patches before it can be called complete.  I do not forsee any new characters being added to the game, but a patch or two to help with the frame rate in game will help people with regular computers or bad internet connections appreciate the game more easily.
I recommend this game as it can only get better from here.  Once you learn the abilities and understand how to play it starts to get really fun.

Vanguards is an interesting concept to me. It is a moba game stripped down to its most simple state. There are no minions, no towers, and relatively small teams. There are three heroes that support different playstyles and there is some interesting interplay between them. I personally suck with the lightning knight, but I quite enjoy playing the other two.
The mechanics of the game itself ensure short games and make for some interesting decision points, like whether it is better to charge a shrine by yourself in an effort to get the ghost to stop munching on your own shrine, or whether to wait for teammates.
All in all given it is a student project I think it has been very well done. It is not overambitious and the game that is there has a respectable amount of depth to it without being overwhelming to newcomers with experience in the genre.

This is a well executed game, which harkens back to its Fire Emblem inspirations If you're a fan of tactical games, then pick this up.
Pros:
1. Great 2D art. It's clean, well animated, and beautifully colored. Again, very close to its FE roots. Some people might compare it to RPGmaker, but they'd be dead wrong. The art direction could use a bit of help on the intro screen, but overall, it's crisp and pleasing to the eye when playing
2. Tactical Depth. If you haven't read his take on RNG vs. deterministic play then check out his blog. Regardless, this is a game that punishes bad tactics, has RNG elements in the right places, and gives you the tools to beat levels in different play styles.
3. Great encounter design with varied maps. From my understanding, there are a variety of maps that are procedurally (sp?) generated, but most are hand crafted encounters. and it's easy to tell. The difficulty is ramped up as you find yourself normally outnumbered, so positioning, movement, and tactics are key to try and beat the enemy
Cons:
1. No in-game save. The battles are tough and long and having this missing is the biggest weakness of the game. My understanding is that the dev is working on it, but it's still a big eyesore in an otherwise nice gem.
Overall, I'd recommend anyone who is a fan of Fire Emblem, Final Fantasy Tactics, or X-Com to pick this up. If the lack of in-game save is an issue with you, then I'd still pick it up but would shelve it for a month or two. It's worth it, If you have enough time where saving is not an issue, then pick this up immediately. Highly recommended.

I've played many fantasy sword games like Brave Fencer Musashiden, Musashi Samurai Legend, Zelda Series, etc. But suprisingly, this one is just as amazing and enjoyable. The story line is very well put together, keeping your character in the dark of who he really is and slowly bringing his memories back along with many shocking revelations of his past. Also, many tearful moments and cutscenes. The main character's sidekick is perfect for comic relief and she has her moments. I also enjoyed the level design and artwork for the characters (Great voice acting I might add). The music they made for the game is at some moments calm and peaceful and others just have you wanting more adventure! I've played this game at least twice through (once on normal and then Hardcore. Four different modes to play btw including Casual, Normal, Tough, and Hardcore. If you feel the difficulty is too easy, try the harder modes it makes for much more of a challenge as spikes and bosses tend take either half your health or one shot you, but with proper spec, gear, etc you'll be able to beat it.) The gameplay is a 2-D hack and slash game where you can perform combos, get new abilities that assist find hidden rooms with treasures, use projectiles to attack enemies, farm gold from enemies which is used to buy materials to make gear or buy food items to restore health (not to mention revival stones in case you die) and has a leveling system where you can spend points on stats. Bottom line, if you enjoy a one player fantasy/action/adventure game, this is the game to buy and play! :)

Not being able to recommend this game is one of the hardest things I've ever done.  Full disclosure - I bought into the closed beta, I love games like Fire Emblem, Advance Wars, and Disgaea, and so on.  And don't get me wrong.  The gameplay itself is phenominal.  I honestly don't think I've found a game that I've played that has a combat system I've enjoyed more.  This game scratches an itch that fans of the genre don't really get much of nowadays.  Combat is complex and offers much more tactical depth than most other games I've played, and it was built from the ground up to support custom content.  The soundtrack is pretty good, and while the graphics aren't, I'm more than willing to look past that for gameplay of such high caliber.  But there is one thing that, no matter how much I tried, I couldn't get past.
This is a 2D, turn-based game.  Please explain to me why it runs so poorly on my computer?  Seriously, I'm getting 15 fps when other, more graphically rich games get a full 60?  This has to be one of the most poorly optimized games I've ever played.  And it really is a damn shame, too, because for a fan of turn-based strategy like myself, it's a great game, if a bit ugly.
There really is no excuse for this, Mr. Stern.  I was so hopeful that this game would be good, and I wasn't wrong from a gameplay perspective.  It's a shame I won't be able to play this turn-based, 2D, very lo-def game without buying a gaming super-rig.
I'll be trying again every few patches to see if it gets any better.  If it does, you'd better believe I'd recommend it without a second thought.
tl;dr: 2D, turn-based game runs like♥♥♥♥♥  If you have a super-computer, buy it in a heartbeat.  Otherwise, you won't hardly be able to play it anyways.

So in my second game, I created a race of religious extremist fungus people with my leader as their holy ayatollah, looking to bring the Word of the Mold throughout the galaxy. Growing was slow at first -- our industrial output was pitiful compared to the cost of a single colony ship. But inspired by the divine wisdom of our holiest leader, Psilocybin, the shroomfolk colonized a couple of nearby worlds, kept the science ships scouting, and ran into our first leaders. The badger people, the boar people. Heretics one and all who would be purged in due time. Even without yet engaging in interstellar war, our Righteous Navies of the Lord kept busy blasting crystalline monsters and the like.
We also encountered some pre-FTL races, quickly setting up observation posts to see if this rabble might someday be receptive to the Word, quietly observing both an early-space-age race and an industrial-age planet. We later encountered a third race, some sort of bird-like creatures called the Juvan in a steam-powered era, just as His Holiness had decreed it was time to expand once more. A quick summary of these creatures revealed they were both spiritualist and fanatic pacifists -- they would find their spiritual guidance in the mines and fields. There are options to co-opt pre-FTL races -- granting them technology in exchange for their servitude; supplanting their leadership with dopplegangers to take over the world from within.
But these routes take time and money, and the Lord of the fungus people is an impatient one. So instead, the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Assault Armies of the Lord were directed to embark on their crusade ships immediately, destination: the planet of the Juvan.
Oh, what a day that must have been for the Juvan and their primitive armies, to be blessed with the Word in such a fashion! Without warning, the skies opened up and legions of space fungus-people descended upon them, supported by orbital bombardment from the Righteous Navy. A pity they did not realize how fortunate they were to be allowed to serve His Holiness Psilocybin! So we quickly clapped the irons on them to relieve them the burden of self-determination. They, their children and their children's children would forever serve the Lord, one way or the other. Our borders expanded once more, our scout ship crews pushed further into the void, their hyphae filled with the joy that only comes with serving the Lord of the Mold.

I have fond memories of games like Fire Emblem, Ogre Battle, Shining Force, Final Fantasy Tactics. What I loved about those games is that you had to play smart. Telepath Tactics captures that in oodles. This isn't a game you can run into willy-nilly and win. You must carefully command your troops across the battlefield. Using their unique abilites, strengths, weaknesses. All the while countering the enemies movements. With plenty of classes, abilities, and environmental hazards. Telepath Tactics brings plenty to the table. The combat itself is based on positioning and stat based damage. Keenly placing units to flank enemies and do devastating damage is required to win this game. Sadly Telepath Tactics is a very unappealing looking game. The terrain is flat and lifeless, the pixel characters lack personality. The combat animations are underwhelming. The only good thing about the art style are the Fire Emblem-esque avatars. While this isn't necessarily anything to break the game. The battles can take anywhere from 30 to 60 minutes. It would've been nice to have had something pleasant to look at. Also a save and quit feature would've been great too. The game for the most part is designed well. With minor bugs that don't really affect gameplay all too much. With the map editor you've got plenty of replay value. If you find yourself really enjoying the game and want to get more out of it. In all the game is a great homage to TRPG's and Fire Emblem.
If you don't mind the graphics and are looking for a deep strategy game. Telepath Tactics is a good choice.

I'm still playing through the campaign, but I think I've played enough to write a mostly complete review. I haven't played any multiplayer games, nor modded it at all, so I won't be reviewing those aspects of the game.
Summary:
Telepath Tactics is a strategic turn-based RPG, with many ways to complete each mission. The game has no random chances* (e.g. critical hits, varying damage/damage reduction), and so the only unknown variable in the game is pure strategy. With a variety of different classes, weapons, armour, and items, you have to out-think, and out-fight the enemy AI. Once you learn more about the AI through fighting them, you can start building new strategies to combat the AI more effectively. But the enemies get more tricks up their sleeve as they go, so it's up to you to do your best and keep your troops alive and fighting effectively through superior and adaptive strategy.
*Technically there is one random element; psy attacks have a 50% chance of inflicting their respective status effect (see below)
Pros:
+ Through the varying classes, equipment, and items, almost any strategy you can think of is possible to defeat the enemy:
· Destroying bridges, or making your own bridges, or barricades to direct the enemy to where you want them to go
· Weapons of varying lengths/ranges allowing multiple characters to attack the same enemy from a line formation
· Psy abilities causing varying statuses (50% chance of effect) based on their element (as well as their base damage) (Light = Blindness, Dark = Softness/Slowness, Ice = Freeze, Fire = Burning) which can be taken advantage of to great effect if planned well.
· Creating a completely defensive position with healers and ranged units protected by strong melee units in front or surrounding them.
· Using flying characters and/or high mobility characters, you can rush the enemy and try to defeat small groups before they have a chance to gather against you.
· Using Emma Strider's Motivate or Inspire abilities grants other units a second turn, which can be, and usually is one of the best abilities in the game, allowing for many more strategic capabilities.
· And so much more can be accomplished with what's available to you.
+ The campaign's story is straightforward and quick to the point, and is much more down-to-Earth than most game's stories (where the starting characters discover some inner hidden talent and end up being key to the world's survival against hordes of enemies in an endless war). This story is simply about two sisters escaping from the slaving Shadowlings, and trying to return one day to save their father from captivity.
+ The music is very nice, with Classical and Medieval tunes to fit the game very well.
+ Lots of replayability; if the mission didn't turn out the way you would have liked, you can restart, and try out other strategies and see what works. And once you've learned more about the AI, you might decide to start another new campaign and see how much better you'll do now.
+ The Sinister Design forums for the game (
) allow you to interact closely with the game's development, to report bugs, and suggestions which all get looked over closely and/or implemented if they look good.
Neutral points:
= The art of the character portraits is hit-and-miss; some are done fairly well, but for some (e.g. the golems, the art looks very messy)
= A number of small (and some not so small) bugs. However, the creator, Craig Stern keeps close tabs with his forums and address and fixes all bugs and issues very quickly.
= No in-mission saves; the only saves are just before events and missions. While not good or bad in of itself, it should still be noted. I believe the game is best like this, otherwise a player could save and reload once they know what will happen.
= There is no wandering in towns, or random encounters. The game simply goes from mission to event to mission.
Cons:
- Some persistent bugs, such as an equipment-swapping bug, and animation slow-downs over long missions can cause some inconvenience.
- Sometimes a bug may cause your game to crash, losing your progress of the mission. It's not the end of the world if it happens though, just press 'L' to produce a log, and make a bug report on the steam forums or the Sinister Design forums, and Craig will fix it as soon as possible.
- The fact that there are no in-mission saves means that if the game crashes, or you decide a mission is taking too long and you want to finish it another day, you aren't able to keep that mission's progress.
**Overall I would currently rate this game a 9/10**
While this game does have some kinks to work out, Telepath Tactics is an exciting, mentally-challenging constant struggle against the AI. I personally love how this game has turned out and how unique it is, in that all damage is static.
For people who don't like a tough challenge but still like the game's concept, the Casual difficulty is strongly recommended, where killed characters don't die permanently, but lose some permanent maximum health instead.
For those who like a good challenge, and who like to think tactically and outsmart their opponent in various cunning ways- this game is definitely for you.
~Thaecrasis

ABZÛ reminds me of thatgamecompany’s Journey, having the same art director probably contributed to that feeling. As I was exploring the wonderful environments, it was hard not to keep thinking about Journey during some of the sequences. I was having flashbacks of another game while playing this one. ABZÛ does enough to set itself apart with its underwater setting and some game mechanics, but despite having some good moments, I think it still falls short when compared to the big J.
One of the strongest points of this game is how the environments are put together. The graphical fidelity is there in spades. How they used colors for the various environments also played a gigantic part in creating underwater places of wonder. At times, I felt as if I were swimming around in a forest populated by fish and other marine life which seemed surreal. When it comes to art direction, ABZÛ understands how to make it magical. You’ll explore more than just beautiful kelp forests too.
The story is a wordless affair. You’ll glean parts of the plot through the environment when swimming through ruins or looking at the strange hieroglyphics. The views are absolutely gorgeous when you reach that section of the game. Some parts of it are vague, but I suppose it does the job well enough. I wasn’t exactly impressed with the tale it told.
What I was impressed with was all the different kinds of animals they managed to stuff in this game. You’ll see regular fish, some deep sea weirdos, and the biggest of the big. You can even grab onto some of the bigger sea creatures and ride them around. There are also meditation statues to find that let you just sit back and meditate on top of them while watching the sea critters swim around or interact with each other, usually with their mouths. Their names will also pop up while meditating which I found useful because I spent some time looking up the very exotic ones.
Journey did something to me. I fell in love with the game to the point of playing it seven times in a very short time span. It left its mark on me which only those few special games can do. The score was perfectly created to make those powerful moments even more impactful. ABZÛ failed to match or exceed Journey’s excellence, despite having some wonderful moments of its own involving whales or riding a current through pristine ruins. The experience as a whole just didn’t affect me in the same way. Maybe the music just wasn’t grand or uplifting enough when it needed to be. Or maybe it was how the controls just seemed slightly irritating enough to cause me to make unwanted turns and loops. Or how the performance would just nosedive in certain areas and cause the framerate to drop to 30fps.
That doesn’t mean ABZÛ is a failure of a game, just that it could’ve been a better experience. What it can offer is a nice time exploring beautiful, colorful underwater environments. Do not expect a deep narrative or anything more than simple game mechanics.

Pretty good mix of roguelite and third person action RPG.
Design is minimalistic and doesn't hurt your eyes on hours-in.
Game is easy to learn. Mind there are little to no item/monster guides so it's one of those games where you need to prepare a pencil and a notebook to document your discoveries to help you later on. Including figuring out monster weaknesses by finding weapons that clash with their lore or figuring what elemental damage each weapon has. Lots of differently designed levels, "rooms", items and monsters. Will be finding new stuff even on your 3rd playthrough.
Combat is simple but in a good kind of way. You have your dodge, block, bash, light-fast and heavy-slow attacks. There are super-moves too but you cannot perform them without making some sacrifices.
Every combat action drains your permanent stamina pool and so you are forced to seek/craft yourself food in order to be able to fight back. Food management becomes a chore after a while but it's a necessary element that adds balancing between two hero classes and also prevents players from using OP moves too much because those cost more stamina to perform.
Each and every monster have different stats, strengths, weaknesses and moves. You won't be able to get through this game by simply left-clicking everything to death. Requires patience, timing and thinking.
After each death you lose your characters possessions. Description of consumable items gets erazed and their icons get swapped simulating you losing your knowledge and forcing you to discover all of them anew. Dungeon itself also shifts itself after each death.
What strikes the most is that at very beginning dungeon splits into two paths. Those paths can cross somewhere later but might never cross again. And even those two paths can split onto other paths that can also split or cross with each other. Keep in mind that players are not forced to always be on the same floor and on the same path with each other. This actually justifies splitting your party for once to cover more ground and collect more useful items faster.
However, this game does have about three striking problems.
You only have a single save slot. It means that in order to start co-op with someone else in their game you will have to eraze your own progression in yours.
Playerbase is pretty small. Too small. Game haven't been marketed well and many people fail to see the difference between something like very hard hallway action RPG like Darksouls and roguelite. Thus treating it as Dark Souls rip-off without realizing that those games aren't even in the same genre.
Developers seemed to cease the game development and the third planned class will probably never see the light of day.
Aside from that this is a very good game that is worth its money. I highly recommend it for hardcore action fans for a solo playthrough. Or for a group of people who would like to test their skills in a cooperative roguelite with "permadeath" scenario.

Like its predecessor Journey, ABZU is a delight on the eyes. A short game that can be done in less than 90 minutes, it is nevertheless one of the most memorable experiences and beautiful games you can play.
The art style reminded me of Disney films, specifically from the Renaissance era. The way the colours explode at you and are so vibrant is nothing short of gorgeous and there were times I simply had to stop and take it all in. Combined with the music, it made the game even more of an experience and one I refused to take a break from, beating it all in one sitting.
Its a fairly linear game, having you go from one place to another, there's no markers or anything to show your way but its easy enough to figure out your next destination. Yeah there's a HUD but the only times it shows up is to show a control or when you're meditating. Combat is also non-existent, this game is all about exploration.
There's a story but not unlike Dark Souls, it's told through the game itself via cave paintings that detail the history of the world and how its current state came to be.
If you can put aside how short this game is and have 2 hours or so to kill, then I can't not recommend this game, it's just so beautiful.
So Steam Awards 2017 is coming soon so I'll just nominate this one for "Suspension of Disbelief" because I still have no idea what I'm doing when I play it but it's ridiculously fun.

Nightsky is an odd mix between a puzzler and a 2D platformer. On paper, it sounds like the two would muddle up, but it's actually quite simple: you're a glass sphere that rolls around, and obstacles and physics ensue. It's a simple concept, but it starts to get naturally more complex and interesting as the levels go on. Timing, precision, focus, and manipulation of the game's physics are all gradually introduced, giving the game a natural progression of complexity. Overall, it's fun to play.
It has its hiccups though. For one thing, the mechanic of holding certain keys to change the ball's traction and speed through various "modes" is never referenced or formally taught to the player, but is nearly essential in many of the game's levels. It has its fair share of frustrating levels as well.
The story was a bit dissapointing. Much of my motivation for playing though the game was from the single sliver of story teased at the beginning, but any hint of a plot is never brought up again. It's not a huge loss, especially since a narrative would demand regulation of the game's fantastical and often unrelated settings.
I was NOT expecting this much atmosphere from a such a simple game. The best way to describe it is pure, unadultered Zen. Ambience such as wind, trees rustling, and the humming of caves provide a constant backdrop for the laid-back soundtrack and the soft "clinks" of the glass ball as it rolls about. The visuals compliment the sounds perfectly, resulting in a game that's extremely relaxing if nothing else.
Difficulty is bizzarely estatic; one level could take ages, whlie the next takes a single attempt. This could be seen as postive in many ways, but nevertheless, it's notably peculiar.
The best game I have played in recent memory. I highly and emphatically recommend.

This game is great! And also terrible to learn. I needed a big number of games to learn how to go ahead.
I tried to limit the problem playing with humans only. Map Small. One opponent, Beginner level. This is a must. You will lose even against a beginner opponent at first. But this is the way to learn. After a good number of games, I started to win. I specialized on Technological and Diplomatic victories. Mainly because I let to research and build warships later so I could use the effort instead to develop my planets and the other sides of research. So mainly I research top and bottom of the four main research options, the social/research and diplomatic/money options.
I start each planet with a factory, a farm, a research building. Every planet. Then I go developing them as I need. On a small map, I have one planet for manufacture, another for research and a third for money. I try to use to the most the advantages that each planet have. In the end, each planet will have three food buildings (when going into the three top difficult levels I need more of them). With the game advancing, I will stop building extra manufacture and money (then more ahead also research) buildings besides the three initial on each planet, and focuses the planets on Influence/Benevolence/Tourism. On bigger maps I tend to not specialize planets on only one area (but it depending on how it goes), instead I try to more or less balance each planet on all three areas (since the stations will push them on all three areas), only specializing the ones with clear advantages for some area. On the very big maps like Insane its necessary to divide your planets in clusters around Shipyards, since the distances are too big to keep sending ships from one side to the other. Actually, its always a good idea to keep just the closer planets sponsoring the Shipyards.
I choose only Benevolent options, and on Benevolent Ideology screen, get first the research advantage, then the one that gives a colony ship, then more research. From there it depends on the situation, but the second tier, the one that gives Moral advantages, is important, since developing it will prevent the necessity of too much moral (happiness) buildings on the planets and save the space for other buildings. And Research. And the one getting more planets, etc. At some point I get the Missionary (third tier) building so I can improve my Influence, and all new planet, and old ones with space, will get the Missionary building (usually close to the 'castle' icon, having side by side with a Consulate, Embassy and the... forgot the name, the one for Tourism, all together). (Earth is always focused on Research, and I build the Research Capital there, plus the Essence building if there is space, to boost research to maximum.)
Another fundamental aspect are the space stations. I make a point of making early Economic stations, in a way so every planet is under the influence of one of them. Or two (that tends to be difficult to do on the first half of the game, but the result is amazing). And develop the Research, Manufacture, Money and Moral options on the station as soon as available. This will boost immensely the planets.
Also, mining space stations are important, of course. And depending on the situation, you can build some Cultural ones to push frontiers and take planets using culture (they flip to your side if the culture pressure is high enough). I usually dont colonize the low end planets (level 5 or 6), making sure they are on my area. Opponents will colonize them and soon they will flip and become mine. Really cheap (:
Dealing with the opponents: some will want to be your friends, others not. But if your diplomatic level is high enough, you will have all being friendly, and making Alliance with all of them will mean Victory. So if you see an opponent going to red fast, develop Diplomacy quicker.
After winning consistently on level Beginner, I made some games on Huge or Immense maps, just to get the feel. It becames really difficult to keep track of all planets and stations, and the increased number of opponents, but its really fun!
Then I moved to the next difficulty level, Small map... and won at first! Same on big maps. Same again on Normal level... same on next level... Only on the last but two level I started to have problems. Winning depended on which races I got (I leave them on random). If I had to develop the militar side it hurt my research advance, so I wasnt #1 on research all the time anymore (check your position on Diplomacy screen only, its more realistic), had to build more food buildings on the planets, had to deal with smarter opponents searching the map faster than me, getting the really good planets first... so there is where I am now!
Now I want to try approaches using Pragmatic and Malevolent postures. And mixing them. And start trying the other races to see what happens.
One thing that bothers me on the game is how fragile the stations are. They are too expensive to be so fragile! Well, of course this was planned to be so, but  I'm tempted to change this on the .ini files!! (:
Anyway, I have already 170 hours on GC3 and surely will keep playing it for many more to come!

There isn't much I can say about Half-Life 2: lost Coast that hasn't been said already. It's a short mission cut from the campaign of HL2 that also serves to showcase the high dynamic range Lighting added to the Source engine a bit after the release of the game. This is pretty much a fancy way of saying "improved lighting anf draw distance", and it certainly shows.
Going in, I knew Lost Coast was gonna be pretty short, but I had no idea it was gonna be only 20 minutes long -- in fact, I spent around half as much time fiddling with the options as I did playing through the game for the first time. If you want an idea of how short Lost Coast is, I'll list literally everything that happens:
1. Gordon wakes up on a beach with a crud ton of weapons
2. Some old fisherman tells Gordon to destroy a Headcrab Shell launcher
3. Gordon ascends a mountain and shoots some Combine soliders
4. Gordon comes across a monestary and (most likely) tries in vain to open all the locked doors
5. Gordon enters the church where the launcher is and jams it with a random object
6. Gordon is assaulted by more soldiers and takes them out
7. Gordon takes on a helicopter with a rocket launcher
8. Gordon takes an elivator back down to the beach
9. THE END
While this demo may be only half as long as I expected, the few enemy encounters are all enjoyable, and the brevity serves the game's replay value. If you're like me, you'll want to play it again several times so you can explore every nook and cranny of the coast. In fact, it's even possible to reach the city of St. Olga! Read the guide below to get a step by step tutorial of how to reach the island:
One of the things you'll notice when you begin the mission is the beautiful sight of an oceanside town in the distance, which would have been concealed by a cloud of "fog" in the original HL2. HDRL would've have made the coast of Highway 17 look so much better that I almost wish HL2 would've been further delayed so the feature could be implemented. Combine that with incredibly detailed environment, and even over a deccade later, Lost Coast looks stunning.
Aside from its brevity, my only issues with HL2: Lost Coast are its lack of enemy variety (you only come across soldiers, poison Headcrabs, and a chopper) and the scarcity of Kelly Bailey's pulse-pounding techno soundtrack.
If you've already purchased Half-Life 2, you'll be able to install Lost Coast for free, and the fun you'll have more than justifies adding this title to your library.

An improvement over the first game, although not in all areas.
The game's story and characters are a continuation and improvement of the great work from the first game. Geralt's circle of friends have even more of a role to play this time around and join him more often. The game also goes into a lot more detail about The Wild Hunt and Geralt's past. In terms of quests, it does feel like there are a lot less but the ones that are there are more interesting and more involved. The final monster contract, though, features some incredibly dumb puzzle-solving and there are a few quests that you cannot complete unless you keep objects from earlier chapters, such as getting stuck with a dumb tattoo. Pro-tip: if you get the tattoo and don't like it, immediately get the stuff required to remove it.
In terms of graphics, it's obviously an improvement. Characters and the voice acting are much more unique and diverse; no more reusing the same handful of models/voices over and over (although a little of that remains, usually with people you can't really talk to). The lighting is appaling though. I spent most of the first chapter fidling with the brightness controls because, either, every dungeon or night was clear as day (who needs Cat?!) or every day time scene or interior was overly dark (brunette Triss). The world also feels much smaller then the first game (although obviously more detailed), and ridiculously small compared to something like Skyrim (or even DAI). This seems to be the the trade-off for prettier graphics.
The interface is horrible, at least for someone using the 360 controller. You have to access the main menu to get to things like your journal, level up, map, etc, and then it spits you back into the game world afterwards. Annoying if you want to keep accessing those pages. For example, a common one is looking up info on a monster. For some unknown bloody reason it's split into two areas, there is (a little) info on the bestiary page of the journal and also (the important info) hidden on the "knowledge" page hidden within the "attributes" page hidden within the character development screen! Inventory management is also a pain due to unnecessary difficulty of trying to figure out what you currently have selected. Button prompts are missing on certain screens (most noticeably on the poker screen - it's Y to select dice, you're welcome). The quick menu/radial wheel also leaves something to be desired. You can tell it's the devs first time creating something with controller support. Although it's hard to forgive the fact they haven't addressed these problems in the years since release. The game also creates a new save each time you save, leaving you with literally hundreds of saves and slowing down the game! Also, the game constantly updates quest info, character bios, etc. with interesting writings by Dandelion, yet it is an absolute chore to constantly go back into the menu and scan every entry, slowly scrolling down to the bottom, to see if the last thing entered is something new. It's interesting writing that feels like it goes to waste. Perhaps an option to press a button, say the "BACK" button, to quickly jump to the new bit of info would be nice. And, finally, for those using a controller you are forced to take everything when looting. Which leads to a lot of unneccesary inventory management.
The combat is improved, you do feel (at times) like a badass swordsman. But it does often feel like you're just substituting the silly combos of the first game for silly combat rolls and waiting for counters (unlockable "Ripostes"). Once again it feels like certain areas of the game aren't worth the effort. Traps didn't seem particularly useful, since enemies either avoid them or interupt your placement just as often as they take damage from one. Bombs and daggers often seem to do less than you'd expect and are easy to miss with. Generally, they're there to spam if groups threaten to overwhelm you. I found the signs to be disappointing as well. I barely used anything besides Quen (and that barely survives a hit). Ignii seemed to do very little damage. Aard was good for little more than blowing down brick walls. Yrden did help a lot early on, chiefly in a boss fight and with some big, tough, charging enemies but I barely used it past the first chapter. I think part of this has do with the way character development is handled. You have 3 main branches: 1 for swords, 1 for signs, 1 for alchemy. and I think this split is unnecessary and annoying. You are given so few perks in the game you'll only be able to master one branch (which leaves almost nothing for the others). This leaves a rather one note Geralt (who is supposed to be a well-rounded master Witcher). I think it'd be better to have mixed branches with perks from all the Witcher disciplines (sword/sign/alchemy). Maybe name/design them around the three Witcher schools: Wolf, Viper, Griffon. Then no matter where you go you'll have to chance to be well-rounded and dabble in all areas, yet still have a ton of choice.
So, despite its flaws (which I hope are addressed in the third game), I recommend the game. It's a great story with great characters and has a lot of interesting choices for you to make, just expect the odd frustration or disappointment.

I have real mixed feelings on Telepath Tactics. I was super excited leading up to its release. The game is basically a PC Fire Emblem, with features (for better or worse) from that series like weapon durability and unique characters with perma-death.
The thing that led me to trying Telepath Tactics was the trailer that showed a lot of pushing and pulling enemy units around and also building features like traps and bridges. All of those things are, in fact, really neat! I have waited a long time for a good grid based game with knocking enemies around like fourth edition dungeons and dragons.
The battles themselves have an impressive degree of tactics and strategy to them. One major difference between Fire Emblem and Telepath Tactics is there is no weapon triangle rock-paper-scissors mechanic where one attack type beats another. On one hand, this makes it so you don't get the instantaneous little thrill of easily dispatching an enemy because you "did the right thing". On the other, it makes you look a bit deeper for the tactics you have to use to win each battle.
Battles are largely won through zoning and facing.  You lead a quite large force into each battle. The game has facing rules with backstab damage so the large amount of units are very helpful to cover the backside of your troops. It is important to figure out exactly where each enemy can move to and attack and plan accordingly. Thankfully, you can highlight each enemy's movement range and closing with enemies is generally done by staying just out of reach. You will want to limit your exposure to enemies and can do with by guarding your backside with other units, luring enemies into traps to cancel their actions (very satisfying), tactical withdrawals and front line cycling which you can pretty much  ignore in other tactics games, bumping enemies into lakes or off ledges so they are no longer a problem, etc.
Also, battles are largely deterministic. There are no critical hits, as far as I can tell. And there are no misses on regular attacks. So you will never get screwed over by dice rolls where an enemy crits you out of nowhere and perma-kills a party member or you whiff all your attacks and get steamrolled because luck wasn't on your side. Special moves that are super far range have a chance to miss and certain status afflictions that are bonuses to attacks can also miss. I like this a lot. It makes me feel like my choices matter a whole lot more.
This description might sound a little bland but I assure you the combat is involving, mostly because the rules for it are so well thought out and balanced. Each encounter feels like a little puzzle. As you click your units around, you will start to notice opportunities for moving in really precise ways and absolutely maximizing the actions of your units. Setting up escape routes, shuffling people around in ways that get you extra backstabs, etc. There are a lot of advantageous circumstances that will arise constantly from the rules and they feel real satisfying to exploit.
Now for the flaws.
Some bugs, mostly performance issues. The developer is actually real good at fixing these so they are less of a problem now.
The game can be brutally unforgiving on regular difficulty. One small oversight will cause you to permenantly lose a character and by "permanently lose a character", I mean "loudly curse and restart the battle because there is no way in hell you are going to lose that character." The theory behind perma-death in these games is that it should make every battle feel high stakes. Instead, it makes every battle feel rage inducing.
The reason why this is so frustrating is because many of the battles can be utterly massive in scale and take about an hour to play through. There are no interim saves. No. Interim. Saves, So when you lose your one and only healer on the home stretch of a map you have just lost a huge amount of time you have invested. Not like 5-1o minutes. Like 50 minutes. Do this a couple of times and you will ragequit and put the game away for a few days before coming back to it.
I honestly don't know what would fix this problem or make it more fun for me. Perma-death is a pretty ingrained part of the game's design and everything is balanced around it.
There is a Casual difficulty where if characters die you get them back after the battle but the game isnt balanced for it at all. I mean, it is pretty easy to win each battle, it can just be difficult to do it without losing a character or completing the bonus objectives like getting far off treasure chests. So this kind of feels like cheating and doesn't feel terribly rewarding because you are prettymuch going to win every map with it.
I am going to tenatively recommend this game and see if my opinion changes over time.
