The game is an intense labor of love by the developer and it shows.  He's basically build a greatly improved version of the SRPG maker program (cousin to RPGmaker that was discontinued long ago) that uses XML and thus become very friendly for anyone to try making their own thing.  Be it moves, classes, or stories.
His resource library included in the game holds dozens of classes with very distinct abilities, including exemplary Heroes within those classes; 20~ songs, sprites for everything and guides for making your own sprites, an Engine for dynamic terrain being a major part of the battle; eploration mode maps to function like towns or puzzle dungeons, and robust multiplayer modes.
If you wanted to you could use the map editor like a virtual tabletop for Role playing games with grid combat.
Added in, the default campaign, serves as a tutorial for all the mechanics the system supports yet without feeling like a naked tutorial.  Hours of play, challenging battles, Fire Emblem style personalities in the cast.  Even if you don't want to go nuts with the creative mode, you'll still get a good game for the price.  You can even use the tools provided to tweak the main game?  Don't like weapon breaking, you can take it out.  Want to modify your character's development you could do that too.  You can even toggle permadeath or friendly space blocking easily in the options menu.

Long time Paradox fan. Review of the initial release.
Stellaris is an attempt at fusing the Galactic Civilizations / Masters of Orion games with Europa Universalis. As such, it is fairly successful as a proof of concept. The game has a wide amount of content and great writing. Sadly, under the veneer it is extremely shallow. Basically the game needed another year of development to flesh out. Knowing Paradox, that will actually occur over time and players will be forced to pay for that continued development if they want to play a finished product. This explains and justifies the lower initial price of the game.
I cannot recommend the game in the state that it is in, but I suspect this will change in perhaps 6 months time.
Specific gripes
- Diplomacy system is excessively shallow. Think 1\3 of the depth of Civ5.
- Domestic AI (sectors) are an attempt at reducing micro for large empires and simulating the challenges of a sprawling star empire. They end up being both annoying (unable to micro stuff that needs to be microed even when you want to) and downright infuriating (the ai makes suboptimal choices that limit growth).
- Allied AIs simply blob up and follow your main fleet instead of doing any thinking at all.
- Ship designs organization is rudimentary. Probably the most glaring issue. You cannot upgrade ships to different classes; you can only upgrade existing classes. This leads to hair pulling for players used to microing their builds ala Galactic Civilizations.
- Game UI needs a lot of work.

Like its predecessor Journey, ABZU is a delight on the eyes. A short game that can be done in less than 90 minutes, it is nevertheless one of the most memorable experiences and beautiful games you can play.
The art style reminded me of Disney films, specifically from the Renaissance era. The way the colours explode at you and are so vibrant is nothing short of gorgeous and there were times I simply had to stop and take it all in. Combined with the music, it made the game even more of an experience and one I refused to take a break from, beating it all in one sitting.
Its a fairly linear game, having you go from one place to another, there's no markers or anything to show your way but its easy enough to figure out your next destination. Yeah there's a HUD but the only times it shows up is to show a control or when you're meditating. Combat is also non-existent, this game is all about exploration.
There's a story but not unlike Dark Souls, it's told through the game itself via cave paintings that detail the history of the world and how its current state came to be.
If you can put aside how short this game is and have 2 hours or so to kill, then I can't not recommend this game, it's just so beautiful.

This game doesn't look like much, but once you start playing it, the game really grows on you.  A friend of mine saw this game on sale a while back and purchased it.  He then gifted it to me.  At first glance, I thought it looked dumb and didn't really expect to play it much.  Once I had it downloaded (didn't take long its a small game) we played it in co-op mode.  Now, my Internet is horrendous and I know some kid in Africa has better Internet service than me, so I had to let my friend host.  Besides a few times I had lag spikes (whicn don't get you killed by the way) it was pretty stable.
What I liked:
1. The art:  At first it seems kind of bleh, but grows on you and is pretty fitting for the game.
2. Humor: Anything from what the Illuminati head guy says to the the writings on the wall or the actuall equipment descriptions can be pretty darn funny.  However, you own't get some of the humor unless you understand some things are just have the intelligence to appriciate it.
3. Decent variety of weapons: There are many types of weapons, and some have special effects and funny descriptions.
4. Crafting: It is a faily simple crafting system, but it adds something to the game and allows you to make some interesting items.
5. Exploration:  If you like exploring in games, well... this one is for you!  There are supposedly over 200 tile sets you can get at random and the maps are of a decent size, with multiple branching paths.
6. Simplicity: This game is not super complex.  It is very straight forward and anyone can pick it up and start playing it.
7. The game is small:  Only a few GB.
9: Supports Co-Op: Play with friends.... or strangers if you really want to.  Anyone on your Steam list with the game really...
10. Can save at any time and start playing again when you want.
11. Keyboard and Controller support:  You can use either one!
The Bad
1. Price: IMO not worth $30.  I am not even sure I would pay  $20 for it.  My buddy got it when it was on sale and gifted it to me.  The sale price of $10 seems about right, but $15 wouldn't be unreasonable either.
2. Difficulty:  This game gets crazy hard and when you die you lose your stuff and have to start from scratch.  Some groups of enemies will straight up, kick your butt.  If you aren't careful, you can get auto-killed.
3. Enemies will respawn at times in areas you have already cleared as soon as you get a certain distance from the room or hallway, which makes it a bit harder and annoying when you hit a dead-end and have to go back.
Conclusion:
The game isn't bad.  Buy it when it is on sale.  Play it solo or with friends.  I prefer Co-Op, but i don't mind solo play either.  It is a good game you can just pick up and mess around with or you can sit there for hours trying to get lucky enough to get through the game (9 floors though technically 10 apparently.)  You can easily spend hours playing this.

Edit: I've changed my review to positive as the easy alliance victory has been patched. It is now no longer possible to get most of the AI civs to sign an alliance after researching a few diplomacy techs. The fact that relations with the AI is now based more on your actions and the galaxy situation instead of your diplomacy skill bonus is a fantastic improvement. This is enough to tip the balance to a positive recommendation. My original review is below, I will update it when I have time.
I can't currently recommend Galactic Civilizations 3 for full price. While the game is certainly improving with patches it is still has a long way to go. I describe some of the major issues below.
There's a lot of micromanagement of planets. You need to adjust the global slider for research, social manufacturing and income. Then there's a separate global slider for social and military manufacturing, because buildings and military units have separate production queues. On top of that, each planet has its own individual focus for manufacturing, research and income. You're going to need to make lots of adjustments so that production and research are more efficient for each building and military unit you construct. Production times are quite quick, and you're going to have a lot of planets, so a good portion of each turn is spent on this. The time spent micromanaging isn't helped by the fact that the "military subsidies" project which is used to build ships has a bug that causes your accrued production overflow to be lost in certain circumstances. You'll want to try to micromanage to minimise the lost production that occurs as a result of this bug.
Galactic Civ 3 has limited documentation in game which doesn't provide much information about how the mechanics work. The tutorial only touches on the most basic concepts. You're going to spend a lot of time alt-tabbing to look up game concepts in your browser. The documentation in game that does exist describes your research technologies, ideology options and random events. Unfortunately, this documentation often incorrectly describes the gameplay effects, for example many researchable technologies provide bonuses completely different to the bonus described in the written description for the tech. The research tree also describes bonuses that don't seem to apply. For example, none of the techs that claim to give bonuses to military manufacturing actually make any difference at present.
Some research technologies give you an option of specialization. You can only pick one choice per technology. Some of the choices are seriously unbalanced. For example, one of the specialization techs has a choice between 10% extra research or a 10% reduction in the maintenance of research labs. Research labs only cost about 1 credit per turn to maintain, so the maintenance reduction is a negligible bonus. Since you're stuck with your choice for the rest of the game, it's a clear choice in favor of the research increase. Stardock is likely to improve these unbalanced specializations in later patches.
Diplomacy is pretty broken at present. It is very easy to make an alliance with most other civilizations in the game and win an alliance victory after researching a few diplomacy techs. This is because the diplomacy techs provide a large diplomacy boost. Just a few of these techs can make an AI that would otherwise be neutral willing to pay through the nose to sign an alliance with you. There is also an issue with tech trading where civilizations can trade tech when they don’t have the prerequisite for it. Imagine having a game of Civilization where you can give another civilization “flight” when they haven’t discovered “the wheel”. Apart from the obvious lack of realism, it makes tech trading unnecessarily confusing due to the sheer number of techs that show up to trade. It also has the potential to allow civilizations to skip techs giving them a huge leg up the tech tree. You really shouldn't be able to give a civilization a tech unless they have the prerequisite first.
Sometimes, another civilization will make you an offer in exchange for a tech. Since the tech tree is complicated, you may have no idea whether it's a good trade or not. They might even be offering you poor specialization tech that will lock you out of better choices. Unfortunately, you can't check the in game tech tree without first declining or accepting the offer. This makes it difficult to properly assess any offers made by the AI.
The AI is not very intelligent. It will do things like build massive fleets of tiny vessels which have a very short range. It will then declare war on me because it thinks it has a stronger military, without realising that its ships can't even reach my planets. I've never seen the AI move a planetary invasion transport away from the shipyard in which it was built, even when there are undefended enemy planets nearby. This means that even if the AI could reach me with its other military ships, it can't actually invade my planets. Since the AI is incapable of invading my planets, I have no need to defend them. Even worse, some AIs don't build any military ships whatsoever, even late in the game. These AI are defeatable by sending unescorted troop transports directly to their planets. To top things off, I've even had these shipless AI declare war on me or try to extract tribute from me in the face of my overwhelming military power.
I find the back stories to the alien races to be quite interesting. It makes playing the game a richer experience, as you know why the races play the way they do. The only downside to the story is that there is a lot of use good and evil concepts. For example, your ideology stretches the range from "benevolent" to "malevolent". Basically, you decide whether your civilization is "good" or "evil". Several of the alien races are "evil" while others are "good". Malevolent alien races don't hide the fact they are "evil" and seem proud of it. It’s like something off Fox News or CNN, with humans as the good guys.
Overall, I'd say Galactic Civilizations 3 is an OK game, but Endless Legend, Civilization 4 & 5 are better. If you're bored with the other 4X games and have time on your hands then it’s worth a look. The longer you play, the more issues and bugs you will notice, and the more it will detract from your enjoyment of the game. As it stands, the game feels like it should be in early access, which is a shame given it has been out for around a year now. Stardock do update this game so it will improve over time, and it's slowly approaching a level of polish that I would expect of a game at release. The game definitely has huge potential which I hope will eventually be realised.

Over-all, this is a decent game.
The gameplay is rather simple. You buy stuff with in game currency, you burn said stuff, and get money from burning it to buy more stuff. Each item, however, will react differently to the flame. There is a plot involved, but that's not where the game shines.
The game's biggest selling point is the creativity with each item. Many items have special effects when burned, and some will interact with each other.

Once you've beaten the game, once you've unlocked all of the items, and once you've accomplished all of the combos (or get bored of trying to figure them out), you're likely done with this game forever. There isn't any modding support to add new items, they don't come out with new item packs every now and then, and watching the same things burn over and over again, no matter how creative they are, gets tiring.
Again, overall this is a decent game. However, it is a game you will only play once or twice.

This game is beautiful and wonderful. Just from the beginning, you can tell that Might and Delight put lots of work into the designs and patterns in the forest. I say that this game is adorable and takes you on a little lynx's journey throughout her first steps.
Get ready for a rollarcoaster:
SPOILERS: TURN BACK NOW IF YOU WANT TO!
You start out as a little lynx, snuggled up with her siblings at her mother's lap. Then, the mother takes them out for the first time. You get to play games, tackle your brothers and sisters, and eat your first prey. Then, your mother takes you to the river, where you play and run. Then, it overflows. Squealing at the top of your lungs, you are carried across the river by your mother. But then, another kitten squeaks for help. The mother trips and loses you. You yowl for help, and the mother turns around and sees you being carried away. She yowls back, racing desprately to reach you. But a huge wave crashes on top of both you and your mother, and you are carried away as your mother continues to yowl and run after you.
You wash up on a creek bed. You open your eyes and explore. Mean swans thrust you about and you get scared from all the big birds. You are trampled from a deer herd, and you try hard to sniff out the trail to your mother. You sniff, following the scent. Sometimes you can see the outlines of you mother, her and your littermates calling your name. They are searching for you, like you are for them. Soon, weary and tired, you come to a clearing in the forest. There, sleeping in the middle, is a lost, little bear cub.
You hunt for the bear. The bear cub eats three finches before it walks around with you. Maybe he could help you find your mother...

I would recommend this game, but only just. The early game is fantastic but I find it falls short in the mid game and for late I game I simply can't comment as I haven't gotten that far yet.
Why I Love the Early Game:
You start out with just a few ships and a vast galaxy full of mysteries, you go out exploring, finding interesting resources, and uncovering anomolies with pretty interesting dialouge and even quest lines. It's all very exciting and engaging to be finding all these new things. So many different empires and worlds you constantly keep discovering, it really keeps you engaged.
Why I Feel the Mid-Game Falls Short:
Once you reach the mid-game you've explored everything, or almost everything and you no longer have this really interesting story being told. You're all of a sudden trapped in a stalemate with others, you begin politicing and readying for more and more war. This sounds great in theory, but this game lacks much depth to this section of the game, there's no trade to manage, no espionage, nothing other than establishing embassies, managing sectors, and designing ships to keep you engaged. You end up with a lot of down time, where you are just kinda sitting around waiting for things to get done. Waiting for your fleet to upgrade, waiting for someone's opinion to reach a certain level, waiting for a tech to finish. Where in the early game this was all fine because you had anomolies to discover and learn more about, now it just becomes a time where I pull up a YouTube video and wait until my stuff is all done.
With all this being said I still think it's a fantastic game, and I would recommend it to people whom are fans of Paradox's other strategy games, I would still give a note of warning, that the game is lacking in a few areas and it will undoubtedly get better as they continue support for it and release some expansnions, but until then, this is a tentative recommendation.

Turn-based strategy games with permadeath can be a painful experience for a newer player, or a thrilling experience for a combat veteran. Telepath Tactics is a game that walks this line perfectly, by offering a casual mode that will revive your fallen after combat with a reduced health total. As someone who put over 600 hours into the GBA version of Final Fantasy Tactics, as well as smashing my fair share of Fire Emblem games I was certain this game would be a cakewalk. This is simply not the case. Your strategy most be on point. It’s important to take advantage of flanking and backstabs for your melee fighters, as well as using higher terrain to power up your archer’s attacks. Find that a characters is a bit out of range? Use a skill or spell to push/pull them to a more convenient position. It takes a conventional formula and seems determined to improve upon it. Will it push its way to the top? Or will flaws pull it into obscurity? Let’s find out as we take a deeper look at Telepath Tactics.
There are skirmish battles which can be set up, but the true glory of Telepath Tactics lies in the campaign mode. The story starts out in a fairly generic fashion, with two girls escaping from a slaver camp to find their father. Along the way, many interesting characters will join your force and before long you will be mixing and matching your favorite classes to decimate your foes in the manner of your choice. Combat is extremely gratifying, and victory or decimation is almost always based on your tactical wits. You will often recruit new members from cutscenes, or by talking to allied troops during a battle. These extra reinforcements are great for filling in the gaps that might be left by people lost via permadeath, which is how I chose to play. Far more characters were recruited than died in my play of the campaign, but I can imagine the situation becoming quickly sticky for a novice player left with nothing but revived, weakened heroes. There is a level up system as well which can make your main fighting force an absolute wrecking ball, but newer recruits and heroes that manage to die enough on casual mode will eventually be left in the dust.
The music is another pointedly enjoyable factor of this game. The pulsing beat of a battle march captures the pounding of my heart as I sit for 10 minutes deciding how my next move will lead into the one after, and what my enemy might do to thwart me. Some campaigns have a different objective than simply slaying your opponent. From rescue missions to capture the flag, Telepath Tactics offers an array of ideas into a genre that is generally pretty straightforward. Telepath Tactics also has the ability to create and share custom campaigns, so the possibilities are as endless as you care to make them. User-created content is one of the most exciting advances in this new generation of content, and although the game only features local hotseat multiplayer currently, you can still smash your overseas friends’ egos by creating the most sadistic map possible and challenging them to complete it. I feel I should mention you can do much more than just shove people into water. You can freeze the water to create a path, blow up terrain, and even build your own bridges! The possibilities are amazing, and even if I don’t find the graphics particularly enjoyable, I think the game itself has more than passed my expectations.
Telepath Tactics isn’t without its flaws. The controls don’t seem extremely intuitive, the graphics displease me, and as everyone knows: local hotseat multiplayer is only for people with friends outside the internet. I also found the sound FX a bit repetitive after a long battle, there is no voiceover work and LOTS of text, and while the spellcasting sounds aren’t great, the score is slightly redeemed by things like the golem punches, which are actually quite impressive. Overall Telepath Tactics is an extremely fun and deep game with a campaign that is sure to pull you in with its lore, and gameplay that will keep you coming back for more. Kickstarter seems to have a better track record that Greenlight for allowing new developers to flourish. I am pleased to say $15 is a bargain for this game. There are hundreds of hours of gameplay here for slightly more than the cost of a movie ticket. With online multiplayer and a big of graphical polishing, I think these developers are headed for something huge. Thanks so much to Sinister Design for letting IGB put this beauty through its paces. We hope to see more soon!

The art style is a bit awkward and mismatched, the interface is a bit clunky, the game is pretty buggy (usually not gamebreaking), and while I understand permadeath the fact that I can't even save in the middle of the battle if I have to turn the game off and return later is very annoying--you can lose an hour of playtime if you have to leave for some reason. I can't tell if it's a bug or not but there seem to be features missing (there's talk of classes being promoted to prestige classes and a number of weapons that can only be used by these expert classes but I never came across a way to actually promote my soldiers. Maybe I just missed it, but the general bugginess of the game makes me suspicious some script just didn't trigger). And my final gripe is that there is no workshop support so downloading custom campaigns is a pain (not that there are many available as of 4/25/2015 on the developer's website).
So...why do I recommend you buy it if I have so many complaints? First, it's an indy game made *nearly* entirely by one guy. Some slack is cut for that. But more importantly because the game is FUN. The creator really understands strategy and it is legitimately difficult and entertaining in a way I haven't felt since I played Fire Emblem. I love that the different classes actually have powers which dramatically affect strategy options like Engineers which can build barricades (Fire Emblem should take note!)--leveling up your little soldiers is very fun and the fact that they usually have personalities and a role in the plot is great too. You don't notice the hours going past because making the many little strategy decisions in evolving battels is so engaging. Basically, if you want to scratch that tactical RPG itch this is for sure your game. I was sad when the main campaign ended and given the riduculous backlog of games I still need to play it should tell you something when I say I played this and only this for several days straight. The story was charming. Not amazing, but I enjoyed it. Oh, and the music was pretty good.
In sum, you should pick it up! I don't regret my purchase. Once some of the...bugs get squashed and some costum campaigns appear (awkwardly on a random forum page? Which I don't have time to visit regularly? Workshop support please...) then I look forward to returning to Telepath Tactics again.

This game had a LOT of potential.  I loved the premise of a twisted take on the Red Riding Hood tale and I did get that.  What I got, also, was an entirely too short button masher.  Highly disappointing to say the least.
The graphics are absolutely beautiful.  Such utterly gorgeous scenery really gives immersion into the world.  The bgm helped that immersion along.  The voice over of Red speaking in rhyme fit as well and, while it likely will annoy some, I found it rather charming and clever on the part of the script writers.  My only complaint for the female voice actress was that she seemed to be trying too hard to adopt a sultry tone which caused her voice to be too 'breathy' in some parts of the dialog.
I really, really wanted this game to be worth the $10 I threw at the developers.  I wanted to love this game with every bit of my gamer heart.  I absolutely loved the little details such as seeing Red's perfect reflection in the mirror of the first room when you start the game.
Now, I don't normally have any problems with button mashing.  Some button mashing is expected as you work to figure out combos with the basic attacks, picking up the rhythm of the game to be most effective.  The drawback here was that Woolfe has no actual combos.  You get a basic attack and a hard attack that you have to spam like crazy to progress.  That's it.
The fixed camera angles will get you killed in a certain segment.  I invented a whole new series of vulgar verbal combinations because of the camera.  It has to be the worst one I've dealt with in any platformer game.
I beat this game, start to finish, in two hours and three minutes.  For $10, I expected a bit more for my hard-earned money.  Beautiful graphics and bgm do not make a game worth five bucks per hour.
I cannot, in good conscience, recommend this game to anyone at the $10 price tag.  Sadly, with how it disappoints in the end, it's not even worth half that.  If you want to get the game, wait until it's at least -70% so you don't feel cheated.
If you get this game on sale, I'd say it's worth it.

TLDR: Fleet combat system ruins the fun and several aspects of the game.
At writing the 13.4 hours represent my second game, my first game (~6 hours) was at a friends, and I loved it.
The research/tech system is one that most
fans will like, the game has 3 research/tech categories. You will be presented a choice in all categories [number of options varies]. When you've completed a research the choices in that category get randomized, meaning you get to pick only between a few of the available research topics. It works well, for making new games different. However there is a problem:
Combat currently consists of your fleets getting "locked" in combat, and you are no longer able to control the ships. So for my second game, when I had focused on long range, large, fast moving ships [no armor and/or shield]. I got completely destroyed, even though I had 185% the range and 130% engine speed.
So if you don't mind that there is a [definitive] right way to play this game, and that you might get the wrong research options repeatedly: you'll have a great time.

The first thing you need to know is that Telepath Tactics is a good game with a lot of potential. That said there are a lot of missed opportunities like the lack of online multiplayer, even an email multiplayer system, that works well in turn based games like chess, would have made this a much more enjoyable experience. Online multiplayer is the most obvious useful feature in turn based tactics/strategy games & its absence is keenly felt. Additionally I'd have liked to have a free roam system across a world map with random encounters but we can't have everything.
What is here is a decently written & lengthy campaign that very much reminds me of fire emblem even if the characters all felt a bit samey particularly in their speech paterns. The game is very challenging but more in the vein of a complex puzzle that semi randomly rearranges itself. Trying to keep all your characters alive in normal mode greatly increases the length of the game & adds to the fun. The developer has chosen to eschew the element of chance found in most similar games in favor of fixed damage dealt & attack chances rarely straying from all but certain hits.; this makes the game more deterministic which is something some will like & some will hate. The potential to change this exists with a robust system of modding which is the key feature of the game with the potential to relatively easily mod in your own classes, maps & campaigns which is very exciting. Steam workshop isn't currently added & we all hope it will be soon.
There are plenty of bugs the most painful of which being massive slow downs as a long battle progresses & another which involved a slain prison guard not dropping his keys on his death if you choose to attack rather than make a grab for the keys.
Overall I very much enjoyed Telepath Tactics & while it has some obvious flaws it is very much the best game I've played in quite some time. If you love Fire Emblem, Xcom or just about any other game with tactics in its name then you'll love Telepath Tactics. If you haven't played those games, go buy them & become addicted to sRPG's & turn based tactics/strategy for the rest of your days. If you have played these games & didn't enjoy them then I cannot help you. Seek psychological council immediately, something has gone horribly, horribly wrong with you. You should buy this game, you may lament as I have the lack of multiplayer, however you will have a great time of it & it is well worth your money.

Not a single JRPG can match the perfection of final fantasy 7. Although the visuals are definetly dated nothing else of the game is. This game poses an ageless soundtrack that is always spot on and a flawless battle system youll never get sick of. Wether you are on the hunt for Sepiroth or grinding for XP the game never gets dull and maintanse a perfect pace the whole time. The writeing is also  perfect, both the main plot conversations and side conversations felt like they had an equal amount of thought put into them.
The visuals are probably the most common complaint over the game but honestly they still hold up in some ways. The hand drawn backgrounds do clash with the polygon monsters that are the characters, but the cutcenes have aged well and same to most of the hand drawn backdrops.
Also I sould not shy away to the fact that the controls in this port arent very good butt arent horrific. Most of the time the bad controls arent too obvious but they do become a pain during mini-games (most obviously during the submarine game, and chocobo raceing).
Although this port has a few problems with controls it keeps the rest of the game in tact and adds both anti-aliasing  and 1080p, two improvements that help the enjoyment of the game.
So the verdict: Final Fantasy 7 hasn't aged well in the visual department but has aged like  fine whine when it comes to game play and the soundtrack. Also, the sound mixing, editing, and writeing have aged equally as well as the gameplay and soundtrack. This all sermounts to the best JRPG ever created, and the best ps1 game ever. So look past badly aged visuals and abnoxious controls and see to it that you give yourself the pleasure of owning and completeing this game.

I fished a quarter out of a wishing well and ran as fast as I could to the farm.  I asked my adopted father if I could have the money from his Mastercard if I gave him the same amount in cold, hard cash, and when he said no, I just took his credit card and bought it anyway. Ladies and gentlemen, today is the day I start my Let's Play career, and when the money I get from videos from this game starts rolling in, I'll finally be able to buy Minecraft and start making millions.
Ladies and gentlemen...you're looking at the next PewDiePie.

A very good game with a few flaws. I really enjoy playing this game, and it has some very good features. These include and are not limited to extraordinary graphics and a built-in ship designer that is second to none, as well as faction creation that is excellent. There is also a very nice feature that allows play on smaller maps if you have a lower powered computer, so that you aren't locked out of the game just because you don't have a top of the line gaming machine.
There are a few big flaws: first, there needs to be a reset to defaults button, badly. After playing a number of games, your galaxy setup will probably be way off from the start, and this can be a problem if your games have been going in the wrong direction and you want to backtrack without losing customized ship designs and the like. Second, there needs to be more options for the type of galaxy in a meaningful way. Although there are multiple galaxy types, in reality the planetary and star distribution don't have signifcant differences except in two cases, especially in smaller maps.
On the whole, I would recommend this game to anybody looking for creative ship design, a generally good play experiece, beautiful graphics, and the patience to work around the flaws.

Fantastic story telling, beautiful game.  The game is worth it for the story and the looks.
However be prepared for a less detailed leveling system vs the first game and the worst combat system in a 3rd person rpg (at least that I have played).  You may have thought the combat system in the first game is bad, but at least it pulls together after leveling up some skills.  The combat system in Witcher 2 reaks of console clunkyness, topped with unresponsive actions.  Not to forget bad hit detection, and classic rail roaded boss fights where only a certain tactic can be used (reminescent of Star Wars for Game Cube where you had to defeat AT-ATs only by roping their legs, instead of using the x-wing you had parked out back to blast them apart).
Be amazed as the Witcher stands there and drools after you tell him to evade, attack, or parry.  Perhaps he only turns his back to get back stabbed rather than doing the evade you told him to do.
Be amazed as you lose 3/4s of your health from the wake a golem leaves as he charges right past you 4 feet away.
Be amazed as you have to reload the game over and over and over again because you died to the disfunctional combat system not responding to your inputs, or its poorly thought out design.
Be amazed that the witcher can not effectively fight groups of foes anymore as he must resort to exploitative tactics such as agroing one foe at a time, or having to keep dying and reloading until he gets a few lucky stuns or knockdowns for an instant kill.
One you get that lucky stun or knockdown, be amazed as the game switches cameras for a spectacular finisher to instant kill a stunned opponent only to be attacked with impunity by other enemies while the cut scene runs, let alone be blind to the movements of the other enemies as they go behind you.
And last but not least: be amazed as the game continues the same antics as the first game where after a cut scene it will spawn you nose to nose with an enemy with your weapon sheathed and always have a free hit against you to start no mater what you try.  Also be amazed that when you re load and enter into those fights with your weapon drawn, that the game conveniently sheathes your weapon for you, so you can't even parry the initial freebee attack on you.
Absolutely terrible combat system, but worth the story.  Luckily it seems to be a relatively short game compared to the first one, or other AAA RPG titles such as Dragon Age, Skyrim, or Fallout 3.

This game is similar to American Mcgee's Alice in terms of sinister take on a fairytale. However overall quality of the game is much lower.
is a mixture of 2D/3D platformer with some combat and climbing mechanics.  With 2-3 Hours of sub par gameplay and unresolved story it is less than satisfying experience. It is not like the game is completely broken but we only got 50% of the desired length and 70% of the desired polish.
The first thing you will notice are beautifully crafted levels, backgrounds, and attention to small details in the environment. Even the game menu got notably stylized. You can still tell that some parts of the game did not get as much attention but that is the least of your worries. Although I really like the art style, developers still sold the unfinished game for more than it was worth. As it stands it is worth $2-3 if you just want to look at few well-animated stages and few short segments of good platforming.
Gameplay can be described as Crash Bandicoot meets Assassin's Creed. Like what is with all the wall climbing. I am not sure if that was the right design for the game, it feels a little weird with the camera constantly chasing you. If they just did the third person it would probably be easier on them and on players. (the game has some platforming depth problems due to the format)
Combat is very limited.You get some new moves along the way but for the most part, you just spam your attack and hoping that enemy won't hit you back. It just seems that developers were not really sure what they wanted to do with the combat system. There are basic moves that would imply complexity but mechanics do not back it up. Like it would be better if the combat was more simple or more complex.
When I started playing it was running at 5 frames. For some reason, I have to ALT-TAB in and out from the game to make it run properly. I never figured out for to fix it reliably but try running the game as administrator, allow all features to run and maybe forcing it to use the video card (or maybe if you lucky you won't have that problem at all)
I don't want to be too critical because I think developers had an awesome idea but for whatever reason could not execute it. Not sure if it was funding or lack of experience (maybe both) It reminds me games like Crash Bandicoot because of mixed 2D/3D gameplay with running away segments and I appreciate what they were trying to do.
There is a glimpse of a good game but this is not a finished product. Although it is a half of a game I did mildly enjoy it and I hope to see more of it. The art design and decent platforming gameplay are enough to justify buying it on a good sale.

All in All a decent game. Especially if you donn't mind the story, but like a good atmosphere I would really recommend it.

Before early access was available, there was the demo.  And that demo was good.  Sure it limited you to a single small multilayer map against an AI opponent, but that was enough.  Using the (then temporarily free and heavily incomplete) map editor that had been posted to the forums, I got to start playing around with everything, and I got hooked.  Before the manual contained anything with information as to how to mod the game, you could change it if you knew where to look.  But now it's easy.
The modding support for Telepath Tactics is incredible.  Not only can you add new content to the game, but you can change almost anything you can think of.  Don't like your lizardmen green?  Just open them up in a photo-editor, make them pink, and throw the file back in.  Main campaign too hard?  Make all of your characters invincible with just a few keystrokes!  If you want to do it, Telepath Tactics will let you.  Want to play chess with game characters?  Go right ahead; the scripting for it is all there just waiting to be put together.  A square version of Hex?  Go ahead and write it.
If you're looking to write your own stories or create your own game, look no further than Telepath Tactics.

Haven't gotten too far into the story yet, however, I can say that the battle system is excellent and quite rewarding. Be warned that the battles in this game are tough! Carfeul thought and planning are required to defeat your enemies, not blindly charging in. I also like the fact that they include a casual mode where characters defeated on the battle map are not permanently dead. This removes the frustration of repeating levels to ensure that all your characters survive.
I really like the artstyle of this game. Don't let the simple graphics fool you, there is quite a lot of charm and detail to the characters, especially when attacking. If you are a fan of Fire Emblem, as I am, then this is defintely worth the purchase.
If there is one thing that annoyed me somewhat - though this is an entirely personal preference issue - it's that you get rushed from one battle to the next. I like the pacing of Fire Emblem games more, where you have a chance to catch your breath, equip and talk to your party members between battles. So far, I've only come across two instances where that happens. Then again, this is most probably a design choice by the developers.
Pros:

+ Levels that are tough but fair. A good plan will see you through.
+ Very nice graphics and art style.
+ Good story so far.
+ All this in merely 200 MB, which is fantastic!
Cons:
- Some slowdowns on larger battlefields with lots of effects.
- No saving. The game automatically saves between battles. If the battle ends with a victory, but you're not satisfied, you can't go back and replay it (I think).

This game has almost no redeeming qualities when put up against literally any other action RPG *or* roguelite that I can think of.
The controls are like playing Dark Souls with your character's feet stuck in glue, the enemy design and distribution is just set up to annoy you (either with massive damage sponge enemies or like 17 small skeletons you have to kite for 5 minutes), there is no sense of progression (you're never told what makes a new weapon better and very little carries over after death), and the procedural generation is at times completely absurd. At one point I got stuck because the only way I could go on was so far down, any reasonable person would've seen it as certain death, and going back up where I came from was impossible too. I never got the sense that I was moving towards a goal in any of the areas I played, just simply walking around some big blocky rooms with a bunch of stuff in them.
On a complete surface level, the game looks good, but that vanishes as soon as you experience the choppy, slow, stilted animations. Any sense of wonder or mystery about the world is also completely sabotaged by how almost literally every single line of text has a joke in it, often even jokes about the very idea of being interested in its lore. Which is absurd, when the game clearly HAS lore and it HAS potentially interesting characters. I've never seen a game go to such lengths to make sure you don't care about its world.
I didn't play Necropolis for very long, but I did not have a single second of fun while I did. Whether you're looking for a good action RPG, Souls-like, or roguelite, you're better off looking just about anywhere else.

Ultimately, If you are new to the franchise, and are a strategy games fan, I recommend picking this up. But if you already played galactic Civilizations II, think about if you want the finer points of game play and strategy over again. Yes, there is a huge graphical improvement, but this like comparing Sid Meir's Civilization 5 to Civilization 4: one is graphically superior, but both are equal in the quality of its game play, even though they are vastly different. If you know you can go from one entry in a strategy game series to the next without trouble, I would recommend picking it up. But if still play Civilization 4 more than Civilization 5, this is probably an unwise purchase.

It lives up to the standard of Paradox grand strategy games, and is one of the few that I would not mind paying for DLC. My only real gripes are that diplomacy seems fairly mechanistic and impersonal. I was really excited when my militant theocratic fox empire came into contact with a materialist plutocratic oligarchy, but nothing really came out of dialogue options. There's also not really that much variability, they could have done more with the species, and it's rather annoying having to mod name lists in when it would have been easy to just let you create a custom list. More CK-ish features such as dynamic portraits would have been awesome rather than just making all characters look the same besides minor differences. Like I said, it's one of the few games that I hope there will be DLC for, especially because of that reason.

I see the price has been moaned about quite a bit on here as the game is relatively short, however I think the price is just right, if the game is played properly you will get much more out of it, the aim (FOR ME) is not just to get to the end by rushing through it (there are two endings) also 'memories' to collect as you progress through, personally I think these should have been a necessary part of completing the game, also giving you the freedom of revisiting past locations and perhaps offering a much more open world (just a suggestion)
To a point I understand why the developers have made it so you can just race through it not actually needing to collect anything, it's very hard to please everyone and I can see a good few people on here that would just give up on the basis of not being able to find a certain memory, plus some people don't appear to like backtracking.
This game has a lot to offer, the challenges are there should you choose to take them on, most of us older gamers were sat playing happily for hours on a commodore 64 when we were younger, accepting the simplest and hardest of challenges, and believe me one short game could take hours when setting challenges for yourself, my point being at the risk of sounding old - some of todays gamers don't like challenge because 'it's to hard' or 'time-consuming' do the achievements here to get the most out of the game, there's definitely a few extra hours of playtime to be had.
Also, I would like to point out that In Shelter 1 and 2 food is a must! but in this game it really doesn't appear to matter if you eat or not, you never seem to get tired, weak or hungry but seeing as there is plenty of food about anyway this statement is slightly irrelevant but it would have added a little more challenge to the game should you have needed to feed at certain points throughout your journey.
As I said there is plenty of food around coupled with some achievements (if you catch the required amount of whatever meal) so again if you take some time to do a little hunting eventually you will be rewarded with an achievement, this is another reason to replay or to spend some extra time on your first run though.

In modern parlance Paladins would be described as a free-to-play "hero shooter" - that is to say, an objective based, co-op only, first-person shooter where, rather than your avatar being largely defined by the gun you pick or the items and abilities you equip, they're already fully formed characters with their own unique, pre-defined abilities and specific roles.
There are several modes to play, but the main thrust of the game is Siege mode, which sees two teams of five charge to the centre of a map and try to hold an objective zone. While there's a lot of nuance to the mechanics and conditions of play, the fundamentals are this - capturing an objective zone to spawn a payload earns your team one point; escorting the payload to the enemy base earns you another point; but if the opposing team manages to successfully prevent the payload from reaching their base within a set time, then they earn the point. First to four points wins the match.
Characters, or "champions", technically fall into one of four different roles - front line; "tanks" made to take punishment and hold the objective - damage; made to dish out said punishment - support; primarily focused on healing - and flank; who are all about being sneaky-sneaky and harassing the enemy from behind. I say "technically", because, even though that's how they're labelled in-game, most champions can bleed into a couple of roles to varying degrees.
One important thing to note is you can't change champions once the match has started. So if you're part of a terrible group of players who wouldn't know how to create a decent team composition to save their life, then you're kinda screwed and more or less have to endure a horribly unbalanced game where a team lacks any real cohesion and synergy. But to help with this to some degree are loadouts and items.
Every champion has a deck of sixteen cards that are unique to them, and during your time outside of matches, you can construct your own loadout based on five of these cards which boosts the effectiveness of their abilities. Items are like temporary versions of cards that can be acquired mid game but are only applied for the duration of the match and bought with credits earned during play. And finally, there are Legendary cards, with each champion having three of these but needing to commit to one for the whole match. These are cards which apply a massive bonus to one of your abilities and can make your champ highly specialised in one aspect of performance or another. But this is where you have to be really careful, as choosing the wrong cards or items could make or break how a match goes.
This is actually one of the most ingenious features of the game, I think, as it allows for a lot of strategy and means the player with the best aim or reflexes won't necessarily be the victor. In fact, one of the things I love so much about the game is how accessible it is to so many different skill levels and styles of play. If you just want to do the shooty pew-pew thing, there's plenty of characters that'll have you covered there. Maybe your aim isn't so good but you have a keen sense of timing and situational awareness, in which case healer might be the role for you. Or maybe you just like being a stonkin' great big tank throwing your weight around at the centre of it all. There's a little something for just about everyone.
But the real star of the show here is the ever increasing cast of colourful, creative characters that somehow manage to all play massively differently from one another. Both the design and artwork really shines through, and is topped off with great animation and largely top-notch voice acting. There's an abundance of detail in every aspect of them, whether it's some little nicks and scuffs on the side of a firearm, or even the motions as they actually fire and are reloaded, or just the way a character moves around and performs each of their abilities, or even how they idle. There's a real sense of love and attention that's very clear to see, and that extends to every aspect of the presentation both throughout the UI and within each of the many maps as well. And, if anything, this only seems to be getting better as more and more interesting and creative content is being released with admirable and impressive regularity.
As well as all the artwork (I don't think enough credit goes to the card art in particular, while I'm at it) I think special mention has to go to the audio as well. Sound is very important in this game as every single champion has their own noises, from the sounds of their abilities being activated, to their main weapon being fired, to the stomps of their feet. If you listen out to what's going on around you then there's an awful lot of information to be found just by keeping your ears open. At any given moment you'll likely be able to tell exactly who's firing, roughly what direction they're in, and probably even how far away they are. A lot of players probably aren't even consciously aware of it, but it's always there and making a huge difference, more so than just about any other game I can immediately think of.
It's not all roses, though, as the game does have its fair share of problems. Personally, I think the damage feedback is desperately in need of improvement. Having the very outer edge of the screen momentarily turn a faint red hardly seems adequate in the heat of combat, and at this point I've lost track of the number of times I've died without even knowing I was being attacked in the first place. But a bigger issue than that is the matchmaking.
I wouldn't go so far as to say it's broken, but I'm only a few more bad games away from calling it that. It feels like it's becoming increasingly hard to get games with consistantly matched players of equal skill, and 4-0 stomps are becoming more of a thing lately - which are never fun, no matter what side of them you're on. The rating system, on the other hand, I think at this point I can call broken. In Competitive mode, both your individual champions and your overall account ratings are awarded or docked points based on whether you win or lose, and then (presumably) used to calculate further matchmaking as it attempts to queue you up with players of equal skill. The trouble with this system is, it seems so focused on the bottom line win or lose result and has little bearing on personal preformance. As a result, you could play the best game of your life, but if you were teamed up with bad players, or someone on your team was disconnected or there were heavy lag issues, the game doesn't really care and will still deduct you for it. It's really not fun when you feel as though you're being punished regardless of your own ability or contribution, and as it stands right now, my own personal rating for both my account and many of my champions are in the toilet despite my consistant above average performances. And the worse thing is, that effect only seems to be confounded with time, as it takes multiple wins to make up the points for a single loss.
Also, due to recent changes, the grind for new players seems a little rough going. Cards need to be unlocked through a random loot chest system or bought with "essense" from duplicate cards, which could take a while and doesn't exactly encourage new player experimentation. Although, to its credit, it's nowhere near being pay-to-win, and I think Hi-Rez are generally pretty reasonable, and maybe even generous, with its current financial model.

Little biased as I'm a Kickstarter backer, but very happy with the game.
It's extremely similar to Fire Emblem (and somewhat related games, Ogre Battle, Final Fantasy Tactics, Advance Wars, etc). You move your squad through the map, defeating enemies along the way and reaching the objective. It plays a bit like chess, and you need to protect certain units that can die extremely easily. Even the tanky units die in a few hits so you need to make walls or use terrain to avoid ways in which the enemy can hit you. Most of the difficulty comes from the fact that units die forever if they are killed in battle, though you can play on easy mode without permadeath.
Telepath Tactics takes advantages of a lot of the small but interesting mechanics in Fire Emblem and expands on some of them, for example: being able to talk to enemies and neutral characters to convert them to your side during battle and destroying/pushing/pulling environmental objects strategically.
It also adds a lot of different skills and abilities - magic users have a variety of spells and healing while regular units can have skills such as sprint or motivate. There are also some interesting items (so far I bought the grappling hook, which lets you pull enemies towards you). Overall it feels like a game made with a lot of love and a lot of different things to explore.

Telepath Tactics has a lot more to fofer than a first glance suggests. If you have played Fire Emblem, you can consider this a PC tribute to the series that is well executed and has extra features too. If you haven't played Fire Emblem, here are the basic selling points:
- It is a turn based strategy RPG
- Combat is tricky. You will need to think out your moves. If you are too reckless, you'll lose characters and suffer later on.
- Your warband evolves with you throughout the game, from battle to battle. Each unit has their own abilities and they will level up through combat to grow stronger, earn new abilities and spells, and eventually evolve into elite units. However, if they die... they're gone for good, which can lead to tricky decision making. (You can play on casual mode to disable permadeath)
- Each battle will have several things drawing you off to explore - distant treasure chests, neutral units to talk to and recruit, potential allies to save, items to loot etc.
- You can interact with the environment. Characters can smash down doors, or learn abilities to lay traps, push, pull enemies etc.
- There is an ongoing storyline between battles and your actions in battle can influence future events (like whether or not you saved a character will affect whether they join you after the battle, and they may be able to have special interactions later).
ONE BIG POINT: The graphics interface looks quite quaint and basic, but don't let this turn you off. There is fun to be had and more functionality than it suggests. Have fun!

If you want to read just another rant on how the devs didn't deliver everything one could imagine from a few promo frames, go somewhere else.
25 hours in and I happily admit defeat. I didn't beat the game but got close enough on a few runs and had a lot of fun with it. The problem (like with most roguelikes) is that you have to start over and over from the same weak position and work yourself through the rank only to perish from some random mistake. The early maps always get old.
That in turn makes it even more gratifying if you manage to advance.
What does the game offer?
Roughly 5 locales, 2 of which look rather similar. Temples, Tombs, Snowfields, Factories, Swamps and something Hellish
An excellent random map generator. Each locale has a large number of different rooms that get combined into rather interesting levels. There are branching paths, circular paths and even some one-way passages (which the game is fair enough to always package with a second one-way return trip, just a different one)
How ever you will see a lot of the initial temple on account of dying repeatedly.
An adequate supply of different enemies. Sure there are some stock troops that you see more often than not but once you get a kill quest for a certain enemy you realize how rare they can be.
Quests for upgrade tokens. Upgrade tokens are your persistent progress from one run to the next, you use them to buy skill books that give your toon some advantage like not being knocked over, jumping higher or eating less. However the quests are a mixed blessing. Kill 8 Spiders! I'd love to, but if the dungeon just doesn't contain any spiders to kill, tough luck.
Stylish visuals. The minimalist visuals work for me me. I wouldn't mind more fancy visuals but like this you have little distraction from the core of the game and something you don't see every day. Still it occasionally feels like it should run on a pc from 1999.
A pretty large armory. Lots of stuff to pick up and hit enemies with. One repeated criticism is how cryptic the descriptions of the weapons and their effects are. You have to pay attention to how hits it takes to kill an enemy and judge your new toy from there.
The game is very focued on experience. Not the experience you get in drops from enemies and use to level up your toon in any other game but the experience you as a player accumulate. Which weapon for which enemy? Dodge or Block? What does that cryptic scroll description actually mean?
It is a game of discovery.
Why am I putting it down without beating it? I had hours of fun with it. My last run got me 90% through the game and took over 4 hours. Thats fair enough for me

This game calls itself Real Horror Stories.
And I believe it. In real life, I find myself poking things until they make a *slightly* different noise than before, and I get a jump-scare, usually in the form of police. Yep, that's Biggles' good ol' day-to-day.
The problem, you could say then, is that this game is TOO real. I don't want to be reminded of that time I played Simon Says to unlock a spooky door, or that time I hung out with a crucified Pope. Those were rough days!
Oh, or how about that time I could only progress by lighting an arbitrary pattern of candles? That Slayer concert didn't go well at ALL.
You see, this game, much like life, is a sequence of poorly-photoshopped flitered .png files. Occasionally, by which I mean literally twice, it does present a challenge with some logic and reasoning that you can sorta see if you squint hard enough and tilt your head and hold your breath nearly long enough to pass out. Too often though, the solution is simply to poke a random object MORE TIMES. While this happens more often in life than you'd think (ask your parents, kids), it's not exactly fun.
So, let's move onto word #2 of the title.
"Horror". Horror, according to my handy pocket dictionary, means "an intense feeling of fear, shock, or disgust". Wow. I was disgusted pretty intensely when I learned the corner shop near my abode sells those awesome lollipops with the bubble gum inside for $0.25, the price I paid for this game. Those were a crucial part of my childhood, and a big part of why I'm a blubbery bear today. And I could have had that nostalgia trip instead of this game. Consider me horrified.
Word #3: Stories
As far as I can tell, this game's overall branching narrative was to throw some dude my girlfriend affectionately called "YARRRLL" based on the noise he makes down a well. I don't know what the devs have against YARRRLL, but he seemed like a cool guy to me.
Word #4: Ultimate
This sure was as ultimate as a game about clicking things in the hopes they'll throw me some progress if I promise to stop is ever gonna be.
Word #5: Edition
Yep, this was an edition of the aforementioned game.
So that's 2/5 categories in which I was satisfied. Not good enough in today's cutthroat gaming industry.
For my $0.25-
You know what?
My heart's not in this anymore.
It's just not good, as you all already expected.
Go home.
Leave Biggles to his sadness. Could've had that blubber pop.
*sigh*

Stellaris is exactly what I wanted in a space game, and it does an excellent job of meshing 4X with Grand Strategy.
What I love most, and expect many love most about the game, is the create your own species which allows you to choose your traits, FTL type (Warp, Hyperlanes and Wormholes), ship look, government type, species ethics, appearance even ship prefix. It will alter your entire game and your playstyle for that game. It's probably what makes Stellaris great to be honest.
After having set up your species and started the game, that initial burst of exploration and expansion is executed almost perfectly. Sending out your science ship to survey and explore other systems isn't just some mindless task of clicking from one system to the next as anomalies and research projects pop up in your situation log. This leads it to be far more immersive than any other 4X space game I know of at the moment, leading to weird and sometimes exciting events such as a brand of ultra-reactionary religious quacks breaking off from your empire to take a stand against your purging policy. Or your scientists finding a ceramic pot drifting around a sun that they just.. Can't explain. All this means that exploration isn't just "oh. a planet to colonise, great. NEXT SYSTEM."
The land grab stage is also done incredibly well as you aim to cut off your opponents in a desperate grab for planets and minerals. Establishing frontier outposts and desperately trying to build colony ships in order to expand your borders. But make no mistake, there is no need for you to grab as much as you can. I've been three times the size of the AI and they've STILL had superior tech and equivelant fleet power/capacity to me. It's possible to build not just wide, but tall and that's done so well in the this game, in comparison to other games such as Sins of a Solar Empire where it's alllllll about the wide.
Colonising is a relatively simple affair of sending your colony ship to X habitable planet, then settling there, waiting a year or two for it to be established and then bam, you have your colony; planets however aren't just things that set down borders, they'll be your main income for science/minerals/energy if you min/max one or the other. Every planet has a planet surface tab, which is divided into multiple squares consisting of as little as 5 up to 25 and this is where it starts to look a bit like Civ. Each tile has a natural resource within it which can either be exploited or ignored and built over to provide a different resource, in order to harvest said resource the tile requires an active pop be living on it; which are grown through the amount of food you have (Currently there is no point to having a surplus of food on a fully popped planet). Pops can be resettled between different planets within your core sector allowing you to keep your eithical bloodline pure.
Now, many 4X games descend into tedious micro-management of -every- planet and system that you own, which obviously a lot of people aren't all that in to. Some like spreadsheets, some don't. Stellaris attempts to alleviate this with something I've not seen in other space games as of yet, it allows you to break up your empire into "sectors", the number of sectors allowed is based on your population and planets owned. This sector is essentially an AI which will manage and govern the area you portion out to it. You can choose to assign each sector a governor who will convey specific bonuses to the entire sector. The sector doesn't just micromanage the planets though; you can allow it to redevelopment tiles on planets, and set it a specific function; such as military, minerals, research or credits. The sector AI will then attempt to do it's utmost best to supply as much of the chosen function as possible, except for military sector AI who will build military stations and strengthen their borders with space-station defenses, defending armies, etc. A lot of people have moaned that the sector AI seems woefully incompetent and doesn't really seem able to balance itself out; now this is incorrect, at the start you may notice that it is minus on energy credits for a while, this is because it doesn't have it's planets infrastructures built yet; simply pour minerals and energy into it and you'll see it even out, and eventually it'll even surpass itself. I've been provided with up to 400+ minerals by my sectors alone at times. They really do become incredibly good.
As time goes by it starts to morph into a GSG more than a 4X game, with an emphasis on war and diplomacy. They're not as fleshed out as a lot of people were hoping for. I was expecting what we got since I read all the DD's and didn't expect anything more. War is a very set in stone thing. You declare war for specific wargoals such as cede X planet, and liberate X planets. Then it's simply a march to your wargoal (gained through winning batles, capturing planets, etc). 90% of the time the AI will surrender and hand it over to you should you be utterly stomping them. If they're winning however, they will go on winning unless you surrender and give them your systems. This is a rather brutal AI in that respect. Many however have complained that the AI seems overly passive, and while this can be the case it's more luck of the draw and power than anything. They'll only go to war with someone they're superior over, which is just basic sense really isn't it.. And they're less/more likely to go to war based on their ethics and government aswell.
Diplomacy does need some work as it's rather basic right now, reminds me a lot of Sins of a Solar Empire with how basic it is, but I expect expansions and future content to change this. It's a relatively simple affair of alliance, rivalry, star charts. Trading is simply energy credits or minerals in an instant transfer or monthly. It's lacking basically, but it's more than sufficient for the game at current. Alliance blocks can turn into federations, with one nation that leads them which switches out every 5-10 years to a different nation.
Research and tech. Boy, did they outdo themselves with this one. This deck-of-cards research system is simply amazing. I've found tech in some games I didn't know existed, only to never see it ever again in any other game. Basically it's split into three categories; physics, society and engineering. And within each category you'll get 3 techs to choose from, you pick one, research it, and when you go back to picking 3 again, it'll have shuffled and present all new options. Some are weighted to appear simply so you can advance in the game, such as colony ships, and spaceport upgrades, which makes sense otherwise you could get shafted hard. If your science ship surveys debris and finds certain tech then it will appear as a permanent tech option, below the normal three, that you can pick regardless of how many different techs you research.
Overall, this is the game I've been waiting years for. It's exactly what I wanted in a Space 4X game, and it's growth into a GSG over time is well executed as it turns more to war/diplomacy. I want to note that this game isn't missing any features, it's just not fleshed out certain ones enough. Such as diplomacy, trade and managing factions. All of which are pretty basic right now, but that's to be expected when you think of the sheer scale this game has gone for. I'm all too happy to pay PDS money for DLC since I know that when they bring out expansion, it's actually an expansion for the game. I'm confident they'll continue to polish and add to this game for years and years to come just as they have for all their other titles/series: Victoria, Crusader Kings, Europa Universalis'
Sorry if I missed anything, the games just got so many features and so much content, I'm sure I did miss something but hell, there's almost too much to write about! xD

One step forward, two steps back!
A buggy mess even at this late date!
Little things add up in a game that lasts for hours on a playthrough  . . .  And when you're hankering to conquer the universe you have to be prepared to spend multiple hours getting the job done.  So when lots of little things keep popping up, those little niggling things become major annoyances. Like having to click twice on a button or object  to select it or get the button to register the button press, or watching an icon over a planet vibrate like it's unstable until what apparently is a text refreshing and stablizing?  I dunno, it's weird.
I've had AI's declare war when I've never met them.  I have then had the Peacekeepers wipe out my entire Scout and Survey force because, since I've never met the opponent I was at war with, I could not seek a peaceful solution.  I have researched every-god-damned Diplomacy tech and offered every planet in my empire (except the homeworld) and still couldn't get the Iconians to accept peace.  Broken Diplomacy = bad game.

This may be a design choice, but it seems more like a bug to me:  When I play on larger maps, the game scales in such a weird way that 90 percent of my time I am looking at the ugly icons for my ships instead of the supposedly updated graphics.
And god forbid you actually watch a fight.  Not only is it difficult to follow the action, clicking on a unit just highlights how fundamentally 2008 these graphics are.  The battle consists of the units flying at each other.  Then turning in circles, endlessly.
Minor races threaten me endlessly even though it is clear that they have the one planet and two or three ships.  What gives with that?
Documentation is horsesheet.  If I hadn't played all the other Gal Civs in the past, I couldn't begin to guess what some of these things do.  Even with my past experience, half the time I am not certain what a particular stat does.   Like what does a leveled up basic factory do?  I shouldn't have to experiment to find out, and neither should Joe New User.  Here is another one:  Raw Production.  What is that and why does that matter when I have a level 3 Mega Factory?  Or food.  It's not clear to me what a farm actually does in terms of population cap of a planet (which apparently is different then the planet's quality number).
Bad things happened in the evolution of this game.  The quasi-RPG aspect of the ships gaining experience and getting better?  Gone.  There is absolutely no incentive to rename my ships anymore.  I have to gain a tech to tweak my spending on individual worlds, or have COERCION as a trait.  What's up with that?
There are lots of other niggling things that make me regret investing the 100 dollars that I did.
While it's not unplayable, this game is a chore and the fun quickly drains away.
Play Gal Civ II Gold.  It's a better product (even without the expansions).
Edit:
I have attempted, since I wrote this review, to really try and get into this game.  I cannot.  Despite all the work they've done, this game is broken.  All the updates, the DLC, etcetera, just cannot put a soul into this game.  Following the Elemental disaster, and now this, it's clear that I cannot, nor ever will, purchase another game from Stardock.
