Ah... Great game for many reasons listed in all the positive reviews stated here. Let me start off by saying that I agree with most of them.
However, I have to give this game a negative review and NOT recommended it. This is why this game didn't work for me, and if you can relate, may not work for you, even though there are a lot of positives, the two following reasons are why you should save your money:
THE FIRST REASON IS THE TECH TREE: The tech tree is not a tech tree per say where you can plan your empire's technology by following a strategic path determined by you, like in other similar games we are accustomed to. The tech tree in this game is like a deck of cards, where each cards represent a technology, divided into three different stacks. Each turn you get to choose from three different options within these three stacks. Sometimes you get rare cards (rare techs), and the deck is "stacked" in the sense that for example, at the begining of the game, the likelyhood of you getting critical required techs is much higher, so that you do not start at a disadvantage. The logic behind this from the developer is to have every game feel like a different one, since you can not choose your techs, but must work from the random draw of cards. The reality is that makes the game less fun. Let's say you want to play your empire a certain way, for the sake of this example, you want to play it as an economic pacifist nation. You need to improve your hydroponic farms to improve food output in your colonies. In previous type games with a regular tech tree, you would research the path that leads to the technology strategically required for your empire. With this system, imagine you keep getting military related technologies in the draw. You are therefore OBLIGED to research military technologies. You can't improve what you strategically had planned for your empire, therefore you are forced to adjust and end up not being able to play your empire the way you wanted to. The whole point of a game like this is to be able to create something you want, and to have success doing it. If you plan a strategy, but the game doesn't give you the techs that go with that strategy, you must change it. Bottom line is that you end up playing a way you didn't want to, and that's no fun. At least it wasn't for me. There are other ways to create a challenge, I feel that not letting you go the direction you want to (which does indeed create a challenge, but an artificial one) is not the way to do so. It’s like creating a challenge in Mario Bros where Mario sometimes doesn’t jump the way you want him to. Yes the game is harder, but is it fun? I certainly don’t think so. I like to roleplay my empire, and I like to decide which way it goes, not have the game do it for me.
THE SECOND REASON IS YOU ARE FORCED TO RELEGATE CONTROL OF YOUR COLONIES TO THE AI: Yes you read that right. You can only control a certain number of colonies (4 or 5!!!!) and the rest have to be put into sectors, and given to the AI to control! Yes you can give general direction to the AI, but you can NOT micromanage your empire if you wish to do so! You MUST relinquish those colonies. In other games the options is there as a convenience, when your empire gets too big and you wish to focus on your fronts. Then you the player, can decide if you want to or not. In this game, this is forced on to you, which is a very strange decision that I do not understand. I don’t see how in a strategy game this is something the player would want.
These two factors, which are both things that remove choice from the player, are game breakers for me. It means that my empire is not truly mine to control, and all the other great features just makes these two annoyances even worst, because I realise what a great game this could be, if only the game would let me rule my empire the way I intend to.
Hope this helps.

I've played enough by now to know that this is a solid and good game.  It has some interesting things to say about the 4x model and correctly approaches the many pitfalls that other games just like it have failed at.  In the end it also has a good price-point, which talks to me about the thought put into addressing it's audience.
O.K.  The good, the bad and the ugly:
Good: It has intricate depth to almost all aspects of the game.  Once you think you have figured something out, you quickly find out that there is much much more.  The sound track is REALLY good.  The AI does not simply focus on KILL KILL KILL. They act appropriate to their civ traits and tech levels (shocker).  It's really a very pretty game.
Bad:  The AI that "auto-designs" your space fleet is ♥♥♥♥ing terrible and, until I figured out what was going on, I lost like 4 or 5 games to crazy inferior civs because of it.  The UI needs some tweeking (for example: there are moons that you need to click on sometimes that are so small that you have to barely adjust your mouse this way or that in order to click it... very dumb).  The tutorial for the game does a farely decent job at addressing the basics like what one interface or another is for, but does nothing for others.  Additionally, there are entire aspects of the game that could use SOME sort of information, but has none to offer.  In some way this lends to an atmosphere of mystery, but some people would just call this poor game design.
The inbetween:  The tech tree is non-existant.  In lue of this basic 4x concept the game uses a new and interesting mechanic that the game designers call a sort of semi-random lottery.  You draw 3 random techs from the pool of possible techs every time you start a new game or finish researching a technology.  It's really interesting to be sure, but semi-frustrating because I have no idea what the technologies are that are possible.  My initial frustration was that I couldn't make a plan... like in CIV 5 for example.  In Civ 5 I look at the tech tree and look at what resources are available and make a plan that involves my ersearch path and the units I build to take advantage of available materials around my cities.  After playin about 15 games now I can tell you that I really like the way Stellaris does this.  I'm sure that the developers looked at this and called it a risk, but in the end I think it's something unique... a risk in game design that has payed off.
The ugly:  Fleet battles in Stellaris are sure pretty, but unlike a game like Sins of a Solar Empire that absolutely hit the concept of "Fleet Battles" out of the ♥♥♥♥ing park home-run style... Stellaris really just failed.  Once a battle begins you have NO ♥♥♥♥ing control over it what-so-♥♥♥♥ing-ever.  You can't, for example, force a singular ship that is being focused by the other fleet to retreat.  There is only one ♥♥♥♥ing thing you can ♥♥♥♥-all do once combat begins: force the entire fleet to retreat... and oddly enough there is a random trait that fleet leaders can develop after retreating that disable even that small piece of control. SO. ♥♥♥♥ING. FRUSTRATING.
So all that said I think that if you like games like CIV 5, Gal Civ, Sins or any 4x like that, then you should certainly check this game out.  I'm still having a lot of fun with it.

While I certainly won't say I necessarily agree with the price of this game (especially since I got it from a humble bundle pretty cheap), I will say that this is a very nice, relaxing game that's definitely worth a playthrough.
It's a very simple game, so don't expect any super in-depth challenging gameplay out of this, however there are a few moments that will require you to think a little more critically. Generally, the game remains pretty easy and just as relaxing all the way through. Definitely a good thing to do if you need to clear your mind and if you're stressed out.
The forefront visuals are very basic and unfortunately there isn't much support for high resolutions at all, so fullscreen will have you super zoomed in sadly, but for what it's worth, the backgrounds are very nice looking and are probably the strongest point of the visuals. The sound is also really nice. Not very much sound as far as what you do, but the very, very calming soundtrack that's more or less just ambience really helps add to the relaxing mood of the game.
All and all, I'll say I recommend it. Even though it's another indie puzzle game, this one has always stood out for me as one of the best designed.

If you are already familiar with the franchise and enjoyed it, in particular
, then you will be pleased to know that this game is very similar. It follows the same story line as its predecessor, but differs in that it now allows gamers to experience life through the lens of a young cub. Ultimately, this is a game that will pull at your heartstrings as fast as it will mend them. This is the game that introduces us to Inna.

I read about this game's development and its rocky history. After reading the heartbroken blog post of the original developer and the new company's dedication to fulfilling pledge rewards, I felt compelled to give this game a try.
Unfortunately, even though I had the best intentions in mind, this is a game I couldn't even consider keeping. The screenshots and videos on the page absolutely do not represent the actual product.
In-game animations are extremely low-budget, to the point where they feel unfinished entirely. Hitboxes are iffy, models look unpolished and the enemy AI's only possible redeeming quality is that it sort of works, even though the behaviour itself is pitiful.
Combat is incredibly janky, platforming is far too floaty, cutscenes are so borderline unfinished that I cannot take them seriously.
Some people have pointed out that the actress for Red Hood is hammy but I actually didn't find her all that bad. The true issue was the writing. The rhyming script was a good idea, but it strays from that stylistic choice far too often so it feels inconsistent. It's hard to shake the feeling that the writer just couldn't think of a way to rhyme for some pieces of the script, so he or she decided just not to bother. I'm sure this isn't the case, but that's definitely not the impression the script should be giving me.
The game does not run well on my mid-end laptop, but it certainly should. I play more demanding things on it.
To conclude, just no. Just don't bother. If you're like me and you've being compelled to try it out because of the sad story and because of the alluring screenshots and promotional material, just trust me on this and stay away. The original developer's long gone anyway, so it's not like buying this now will help it get any better.
The art direction was in the right mindset, for the still images. The finished game couldn't be further away from what is advertised.
I'm truly sorry, I am infamously known for playing devil's advocate, but I can't possibly defend this. If I called Woolfe an utter mess, I would be being nice.

I originally did not recommend this game. But seeing it recently got only 40% recommendation, I think it's time to balance it out, because I think the game should definitely score higher than 4 out of 10.
I got the game on sale for, if I remember it correctly, 5$. And for 5 $, this game is worth it. For 10$, this game is not worth it, as it is an unfinished product.
The studio that originally developed the game went bankrupt, so there is no sequel, no further support. The good news is that at the time I have finished the game (which is a long time after I purchased and originally played it and gave up due to a glitch), there are only few twerks and bugs left (well, not really bugs, just poor coding/physics collision). Therefore, the game is definitely playable at this time.
The best thing of this game is its art style and interesting diaries. BUT THAT'S IT.
The majority content of this game is mediocore--the story (had a lot of potential, but since the studio went bankrupt...), the voice acting, no hints on most of the levels (sometimes could be really annoying), and so on.
The core combat system is pretty lacking in the game, it feels like it is from a game that came out pre-21st century, in which you can only do light/heavy attack and four magic attacks. No combos, no fancy stuff.
The lacking of the combat system is related to the lacking of enemy types, there are only three types of normal enemies, with two bosses. So later on in the game, fighting these minions can be very boredom.
The 2.5D design is another down point for the game, especially later on in the game where you have to jump a lot, 2.5D doesn't give the player the best sense of distance and space, and because of that, I have fell down many, many , many times. It would be so much better if it were a 3D platformer.
All in all, I'd give this game 5 out of 10, and for the sympathy of the dev, 6 out of 10.

Real Horror Stories Ultimate Edition is disappointing, at best.
The
behind the game wasn't bad - walking through the various horrors, real or fictional - but the execution left much to be desired.
A. The gameplay was overly simply, and very un-intuitive. The point and click mechanics would have been fine, if you had a visible reaction when you clicked. The game left me clicking on everything, unsure of what to do next, while giving no real hint as to the next move. Each move should naturally flow to the next, and in this the game failed completely. You shouldn't have to click repeatedly to make something happen, without any indication that you are clicking the proper things att he proper time. It is annoying and frustrating when you aren't sure just what the hell you
be doing, and the game is giving you nothing to go on.
B. The "scares" in this game were nothing more than cheap "jump in your face" shock value type scares, which leave nothing to the imagination, and definitely doesn't leave you wating more. Quite the opposite, in fact. After the 3rd level, I was already bored, and by the 8th, I was done,
Seriously, nine candles and nothing else to clue you in on what you should do? Really? Of course you light them. And when nothing happens, then what? Spend all day lighting candles in various configurations until something happens? Not here. Give me a clue when I light a key candle, and I'll keep at it. Leave me staring at a monotonous screen with nothing but those candles happening, and I'm outta here.
Frankly, this game was a waste of $0.29. I wouldn't recommend this to anyone.

Ah... Great game for many reasons listed in all the positive reviews stated here. Let me start off by saying that I agree with most of them.
However, I have to give this game a negative review and NOT recommended it. This is why this game didn't work for me, and if you can relate, may not work for you, even though there are a lot of positives, the two following reasons are why you should save your money:
THE FIRST REASON IS THE TECH TREE: The tech tree is not a tech tree per say where you can plan your empire's technology by following a strategic path determined by you, like in other similar games we are accustomed to. The tech tree in this game is like a deck of cards, where each cards represent a technology, divided into three different stacks. Each turn you get to choose from three different options within these three stacks. Sometimes you get rare cards (rare techs), and the deck is "stacked" in the sense that for example, at the begining of the game, the likelyhood of you getting critical required techs is much higher, so that you do not start at a disadvantage. The logic behind this from the developer is to have every game feel like a different one, since you can not choose your techs, but must work from the random draw of cards. The reality is that makes the game less fun. Let's say you want to play your empire a certain way, for the sake of this example, you want to play it as an economic pacifist nation. You need to improve your hydroponic farms to improve food output in your colonies. In previous type games with a regular tech tree, you would research the path that leads to the technology strategically required for your empire. With this system, imagine you keep getting military related technologies in the draw. You are therefore OBLIGED to research military technologies. You can't improve what you strategically had planned for your empire, therefore you are forced to adjust and end up not being able to play your empire the way you wanted to. The whole point of a game like this is to be able to create something you want, and to have success doing it. If you plan a strategy, but the game doesn't give you the techs that go with that strategy, you must change it. Bottom line is that you end up playing a way you didn't want to, and that's no fun. At least it wasn't for me. There are other ways to create a challenge, I feel that not letting you go the direction you want to (which does indeed create a challenge, but an artificial one) is not the way to do so. It’s like creating a challenge in Mario Bros where Mario sometimes doesn’t jump the way you want him to. Yes the game is harder, but is it fun? I certainly don’t think so. I like to roleplay my empire, and I like to decide which way it goes, not have the game do it for me.
THE SECOND REASON IS YOU ARE FORCED TO RELEGATE CONTROL OF YOUR COLONIES TO THE AI: Yes you read that right. You can only control a certain number of colonies (4 or 5!!!!) and the rest have to be put into sectors, and given to the AI to control! Yes you can give general direction to the AI, but you can NOT micromanage your empire if you wish to do so! You MUST relinquish those colonies. In other games the options is there as a convenience, when your empire gets too big and you wish to focus on your fronts. Then you the player, can decide if you want to or not. In this game, this is forced on to you, which is a very strange decision that I do not understand. I don’t see how in a strategy game this is something the player would want.
These two factors, which are both things that remove choice from the player, are game breakers for me. It means that my empire is not truly mine to control, and all the other great features just makes these two annoyances even worst, because I realise what a great game this could be, if only the game would let me rule my empire the way I intend to.
Hope this helps.

I've played enough by now to know that this is a solid and good game.  It has some interesting things to say about the 4x model and correctly approaches the many pitfalls that other games just like it have failed at.  In the end it also has a good price-point, which talks to me about the thought put into addressing it's audience.
O.K.  The good, the bad and the ugly:
Good: It has intricate depth to almost all aspects of the game.  Once you think you have figured something out, you quickly find out that there is much much more.  The sound track is REALLY good.  The AI does not simply focus on KILL KILL KILL. They act appropriate to their civ traits and tech levels (shocker).  It's really a very pretty game.
Bad:  The AI that "auto-designs" your space fleet is ♥♥♥♥ing terrible and, until I figured out what was going on, I lost like 4 or 5 games to crazy inferior civs because of it.  The UI needs some tweeking (for example: there are moons that you need to click on sometimes that are so small that you have to barely adjust your mouse this way or that in order to click it... very dumb).  The tutorial for the game does a farely decent job at addressing the basics like what one interface or another is for, but does nothing for others.  Additionally, there are entire aspects of the game that could use SOME sort of information, but has none to offer.  In some way this lends to an atmosphere of mystery, but some people would just call this poor game design.
The inbetween:  The tech tree is non-existant.  In lue of this basic 4x concept the game uses a new and interesting mechanic that the game designers call a sort of semi-random lottery.  You draw 3 random techs from the pool of possible techs every time you start a new game or finish researching a technology.  It's really interesting to be sure, but semi-frustrating because I have no idea what the technologies are that are possible.  My initial frustration was that I couldn't make a plan... like in CIV 5 for example.  In Civ 5 I look at the tech tree and look at what resources are available and make a plan that involves my ersearch path and the units I build to take advantage of available materials around my cities.  After playin about 15 games now I can tell you that I really like the way Stellaris does this.  I'm sure that the developers looked at this and called it a risk, but in the end I think it's something unique... a risk in game design that has payed off.
The ugly:  Fleet battles in Stellaris are sure pretty, but unlike a game like Sins of a Solar Empire that absolutely hit the concept of "Fleet Battles" out of the ♥♥♥♥ing park home-run style... Stellaris really just failed.  Once a battle begins you have NO ♥♥♥♥ing control over it what-so-♥♥♥♥ing-ever.  You can't, for example, force a singular ship that is being focused by the other fleet to retreat.  There is only one ♥♥♥♥ing thing you can ♥♥♥♥-all do once combat begins: force the entire fleet to retreat... and oddly enough there is a random trait that fleet leaders can develop after retreating that disable even that small piece of control. SO. ♥♥♥♥ING. FRUSTRATING.
So all that said I think that if you like games like CIV 5, Gal Civ, Sins or any 4x like that, then you should certainly check this game out.  I'm still having a lot of fun with it.

A bit slow to get going, with a few rather unintuitive issues with the controls, character progression, map, and exploration here and there, this game is a little difficult to get into.
Compared to more open-world games, Witcher 2 can sometimes feel narratively and physically claustrophobic at the start, as it alternates between leading you by the nose, and abandoning you to the minimal and often unintuitive UI to figure out the next steps yourself. Invisible walls abound, and interactive objects often blend right into the environment. Most games avoid this through flashy UI, or by leading you through an overbearing and extremely artificial tutorial sequence, but the Witcher 2 largely prefer to immerse you directly in the world. Patience through this slow period is ultimately rewarding, however,
Once you make it through the first town, and uncover the many tacit rules for how you play the game, the scope of the story and the importance of your decisions seem to open up, and the story becomes rich and intelligent, the characters nuanced and realistic, and the gameplay enjoyable. All gamers out there who have some kind of access to gaming media have most probably heard of a videogame that stormed 2015 year of videogames and is argued to be the best rpg ever: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. What most people probably haven't heard of is its predecessor; which is, while incomparably smaller in scale, brings about atmosphere, plot, storytelling, intrigue and gameplay as good as its sequel if not better; The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings. While this brilliant game conveys much less emotion than its much-renowned sequel, it weaves together brilliantly crafted pieces to form a great scenario, where every element of the main story and so much of the sidequests will bring about critical questions to your mind and that (blessful in gaming) feeling that you can't comprehend what will happen next, but you can recognise the paths leading up to them. Gameplaywise; while the combat feels initially awkward and even outright clunky, after a bit of getting used to it feels just perfect for a witcher; while it is less dynamic than Witcher 3 you feel much more in control and more powerful, the way a witcher should be. The atmosphere is less ambitious but brilliantly designed in Witcher 2; you won't find nearly as much captivating scenery as you do in Witcher 3 but this game was designed to be more dark, gritty and political and it conveys the dark, gritty and political so well, with a refreshing touch of deep emotion here and there. Overall; while this game obviously lacks the scale, ambition and power of its sequel, it is doubtlessly of highest quality and I consider it to be one of the best rpg games to be made hands down.

I've played about an hour so far.
You're a deep-sea diver in a green and pink undersea world. Everything around you is flowing. Your path suggests itself to you, and you follow it at your own pace. Maybe you call out to a nearby school of fish, and swim with them for a while. Or maybe you take hold of a passing dolphin and let it choose the way. Sometimes the current catches you and pulls you along into a new place.
I'm not really sure where this game is going yet. It's not particularly important. Yeah, the controls can feel a bit clunky, but you don't really need to be precise. You may drift off-course a bit. It's no big thing. You adjust your flow.
The coral is waving. The light is slanting.
There's a story by Walter Jon Williams in which humans have learned to translate the language of of the massive whales that inhabit the deep oceans of a distant planet. Because the whales live suspended in a liquid medium, they communicate without reference to fixed points. And because they experience being as holistic and interconnected, they tend to speak communally, emphasizing interrelationships over identity, describing what is shared instead of what is individual. They wouldn't say "I'm coming to you"; they would say "we are in a condition of becoming close to each other."
This game is sort of like that. If you're into that kind of thing.
I'm looking forward to the rest of this experience.

"Wait... Really? That was it? WTF!" That's pretty much the reaction you'll have at the end of the game. The story isn't very engaging and by the time you get any sort of meat to sink your teeth into, it ends. You get a few solid plot nuggets throughout the game which ultimately go unresolved leaving you unsatisfied and wondering what the point of it all was in the first place. Honestly, it feels as though they had unfinished 3 plot concepts squished them together and hoped for the best.
Well, at least it was a challenge and fun to play right? Nope... It encapsulates one of the most reviled characteristics of the classic point and click adventure games. In order to progress through an obvious puzzle you first have to interact with something 10 screens away so that the option then becomes available. The constant backtracking, the inability to collect stuff without you'll obviously need before interacting with something unnecessary and the occasional pixel hunt make the game play nearly insufferable.
The sad thing is, despite the game having a largely unfinished feel... Actually, I think it's safe to say it is unfinished. The art work is actually pretty good. Some of the sub plots are fairly dark and interesting, even though most of the story is just hinted at, and no real plot is there. This game could have really had potential but it is ultimately doomed by a clear disinterest in actually finishing it.

A fun "like Dark Souls but" game for a short time, but there's really not enough there.
Yeah it's really stylish, and yeah it's fun to adapt to the randomized situations that you get out of it being proc-gen, and it's got a really fun melee fighting system. Once I found out enemies can hurt each other, trying to coax them into accidentally hitting each other with their attacks became a really fun way to try and manage and deal with multiple enemies. But the game gets old and repetitive too quickly. Also, co-op is pretty broken.
The fact that it's procedurally generated is more of a weakness in the end. Rooms are just slapped together at random, as are the majority of enemies that populate them. You can be wandering through an ancient temple, then a winter wonderland, then a prison, then a swamp, all in the space of about 500m-1km. They're put together in a way that clearly shows no one even tried to make it make any sense, and it makes no attempt to hide this. If you stand at the edge of the level you can quite clearly see the future rooms just floating in the air where they've been awkwardly stuck together. It's kind of cool to explore alternate paths and see them wind back in on each other, but even then it doesn't happen in any meaningful way.
I assume they were going for some kind of impossible 'eldritch' world, that's creepy because it makes no sense. But in practice that's just the norm. It isn't weird when that's what it all is. You just get used to it because you've seen all the tricks it has in the first 30-45 minutes of gameplay, and then all it means is your progression through a campaign happens with much less actually visible progression. There was no adventure in an ancient tomb, or through a zombified village, or a decomissioned prison haunted by ghosts, or a super villain's secret north pole lair or whatever. It's just a series of random rooms picked from a hat, none of them holding any significance other than being the start or end of a level. They'd be forgettable if it weren't for how out of place they all seem next to each other.
There's not much overarching lore tying it all together from what I can tell either. It just seems to be this strange world that's built in impossible ways, with some overlord watching you the whole way and setting you pointless tasks to complete. There's some bits of history that are interesting, and explain a few of the enemies who you'll come across. But without any real narrative, purpose or characters, that's all just extras. These snippets of history give the pyramid overlord opportunities to say something irreverent more than it actually adds to the world you're walking around. Maybe I missed something though, because it's all given through snippets like item descriptions. ("like Dark Souls but") But in the end they just don't seem to add up to anything that gives the game or your journey through it any purpose or motivation.
I'm not really that into video game stories, and I don't expect a masterpiece or anything. But I think a willful disregard of story and world has been genuinely detrimental. Even a very simple story of a journey is a great way to give a campaign a sense of progression. And I do think Necropolis suffers because it lacks that. The only progression you'll see is a few new room types appearing on later floors, as well as more difficult enemies, and that's it.
I don't think this game should have the 'co-op' tag. The multiplayer is hilariously broken in my experience as I went entire floors in coop being ignored by every single enemy, while the game host had the attention of everything. I just walked around behind everything and slashed away while they all ignored me. It's certainly not in a state that you can justify buying the game for it. Which is sad because the more I play this game, the more I feel like it was meant to be played in co-op instead of single-player.
On the subject of co-op, the GOG version is completely lacking in co-op, and the devs don't seem to have any intention of changing that. That may not mean much about the Steam version of the game, but I think it says something important about the developers and their willingness to abandon the game before it's finished. In the case of the GOG version, it's very demonstrably unfinished.
I may come back to this game at some point in the future, to see if a wiser and more mature me can find anything else that may redeem it. But it would have to be something absolutely incredible for me to turn that 'No' to a 'Yes' on this review. My experience with it has certainly been conclusive enough that I'll be steering friends away from it from now on.

During some points of the dialog, you can literally hear the actors beginnning to smack their lips in order to start the sentence. Similarily, the plot is virtually non-existent, and you spend the entire game searching for one specific piece of plot. There is no character development whatsoever, with all of the characters being static. Finally, the actual gameplay elements of this point-and-click "adventure" game are lacking. Specifically, there are specific actions that you cannot perform unless you examine a particular object before hand, causing you to backtrack in a very linear manner. The bottom line: view some of the screenshots people have posted in order to get a feel for the aesthetics, but don't buy the game.

Dangenronpa 2 is a great game plagued by several minor issues.
You play some lame japanese kid who's a nice guy but also prone to worrying, stuck on some deserted island with only several quirky characters and a psychopathic bear for company. One thing leads to another and you find yourself trying to find which one of your 'friends' killed the person you kind of liked. You gather evidence, usually while you, as the player, formulate your own theories about what happened and once you have every neccessary piece a class trial is initiated (which is essentially you and your buddies acting as jurors). For actual real life detectives, it might be disappointing to discover the game doesn't allow you to find the murderer alone, but for the rest of us plebiens the trial is spent slowly but surely piecing together the killer's identity using your own logic and contributions from the class.
While you aren't alone, you are always the key character in solving the mystery. Most of the actual deduction is performed during class discussions and one on one 'rebuttal duels' with other students. Unfortunately, the game has several additional minigames you need to pass to solve the mystery.
The most broken of these is 'Hangman's gambit' where you have to play a minigame about putting together letters forming a phrase which is key to the discussion (and therefore mystery) at hand. The gameplay itself is fine, but it has one glaring problem. It only accepts one specific phrase. This is, I believe, a problem resulting from the japanese translation, because in japanese there is probably no synonyms for the object or action. Problem is in English, when you try to enter something like (for example) 'water bottle', it doesn't work, and the game turns into a trial and error game where you enter an extremely confused state as you realise what you thought is wrong and the entire investigation has shifted oh my god. Then after ten minutes of fiddling around, you find that the word you were supposed to enter is actually 'drink bottle'.
This is a broken minigame, and you do it about least twice every trial.
Another problem is a weird rhythm minigame which resulted from the developers not knowing why people play the game (hint: it's not for the sick beats and autotuned phrases). It's out of place, and slightly annoying but it wouldn't be such a problem if the tutorials weren't so thoroughly ♥♥♥♥ed.
The tutorials are entirely text based. This isn't too bad, except when the translators perfectly copied what is in japanese (which isn't too much of a problem in character interactions) and you don't know what the ♥♥♥♥ they're talking about, especially seeing as you have no pictures to reference. It turns the first time playing a minigame into another trial and error piece of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥e, but after you're done with all of them, you're usually alright.
Another problem (which is actually pretty subjective) is that between deaths and trials you spend your time faffing about with the other kids. It's alright, but not super interesting. The game also spends a lot of effort trying to set you up with 94M3R waifu, which is annoying but not obtrusive. While it is neccesary for the sake of the trial to look at the locations before the murder, its boring and the game kind of forces you to do it.
But that's not nearly as bad as I'm making it out to be.
Why do I play the game? I really, really enjoy the convoluted mysteries and the slow edging towards the killer. It's well done, and unless you are actually some sort of uber detective or have fourth wall technology, you only have an incomplete picture of how the killing was carried out (due to the fact you are piecing it together as your collect evidence). Ironically, it's only during the class trials, the only time where you play from 3rd person, that you truly feel like you are in the game. It's not because the main character's♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's because the mysteries are just so engaging, and the game usually does a great job of making you feel like you are actually solving it.
These are easily the best parts of the game, despite all the issues I have with them. The feeling of being some sort of beta-male uber detective is just too good. You're not dodging bullets, or saving princesses, you are using your head, engaging with the world of the game and solving crimes. That's fun.
For those worrying that the game gets too anime, don't worry. It does, but only with a few characters and moments which are infrequently spaced, and you kind of zone it out after a while. Don't let that stop you from playing this game.
EDIT: It does get pretty anime.
Also don't watch the 3rd series anime because I'm 99 percent sure they lose sight of the themes and just focus on plot.

As a veteran with several thousand hours across CK2, EUIV and the Paradox grand strategy games, I'll admit to some bias. But still, Stellaris is just as amazing a game as these.
The difficulty curve isn't quite so harsh as the infamous steep curve of EUIV/CK2, with helpful (but not too intrusive) info pop-ups explaining the various components of the game, and a helpful starter tutorial to get you into the swing of things. The mechanisms of the game are probably fairly familiar to people who've played games like Galactic Civilisations, but with enough originality, depth and fluidity to keep you satisifed.
It's not perfect; still some early glitches and bugs to be rooted out, but two hotfixes have already been pushed out and more patches are yet to come. Diplomacy could probably use a bit of refinement, and I'd certainly welcome a peace negotiation system closer to EUIV's. Still, even as it is it's more than worth the cost. 100% recommended.

Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair is a story about Hope and Despair, but one with a far different take. Instead of a hero that is relentlessly optimistic, we have a protagonist who is grounded in reality, virtually normal in all ways, but still intelligent and sharp, and his way of solving murders and talking to friends is different than Makoto Naegi.
The gameplay is more refined, although some minigames could stand to be a little more polished. The non-stop debates are back, and they're as fun as ever. Like usual, you have to use the evidence to find holes and twists, and this time, you don't just say people are wrong. You agree with them, back up their statements, reinforce points.
The cast of characters is just wonderfully entertaining. There are bound to be favorites. I know I've chosen my favorite waifu(s), and it makes it all the more painful when you see them become a victim or become a blackened.
The story kept me heavily invested and I was on the edge of my seat wondering what evidence and whose testimony would change the course of the trials. The many moral dilemmas that each characters face made me consider what I would do in a similar situation.
There is also a good chunk of post-story content that'll keep you coming back for more. Minigames are fun, but the main attraction here is the dating sim. Now you can date your favorite character! What's not to like?
Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair is a story that invests a lot into its story, its characters, and its presentation. It takes what made the first game good and makes it better, exceeding the first game in almost every way. I give this game a 9/10.

A bit slow to get going, with a few rather unintuitive issues with the controls, character progression, map, and exploration here and there, this game is a little difficult to get into.
Compared to more open-world games, Witcher 2 can sometimes feel narratively and physically claustrophobic at the start, as it alternates between leading you by the nose, and abandoning you to the minimal and often unintuitive UI to figure out the next steps yourself. Invisible walls abound, and interactive objects often blend right into the environment. Most games avoid this through flashy UI, or by leading you through an overbearing and extremely artificial tutorial sequence, but the Witcher 2 largely prefer to immerse you directly in the world. Patience through this slow period is ultimately rewarding, however,
Once you make it through the first town, and uncover the many tacit rules for how you play the game, the scope of the story and the importance of your decisions seem to open up, and the story becomes rich and intelligent, the characters nuanced and realistic, and the gameplay enjoyable. Unlike certain other RPGs, there are no obvious good or evil choices to be made here, and yet every bit of the story feels like your decisions have meaning.
Strongly recommended. The Witcher 2 is well worth the challenge to discover the rich world awaiting you.

TL;DR: If you want this game, get it on sale. But be aware that it is short and also has a terrible camera and clunky controls. Also if you often get motion sickness from games, this might cause problems for you.
Longer version:
This game is cute. I really really wanted to really enjoy it, even knowing that it was just going to be a short romp.
Unfortunately trying to play with mouse and keyboard was an absolute nightmare. The controls are.. meh. I don't know. It felt like even with the sensitivity turned down trying to move around would often result in me having to zig zag around, making my motion sickness worse. It's weirdly difficult to get back to moving in a straight line.
I'm sure, with a lot of fiddling around, I could have the controls and camera be actually manageable, but who even knows about the motion sickness. It's a real deal breaker for me, though I'm sure I'll try playing again anyway. It's still something you should keep in mind if you also get motion sickness from games.

All gamers out there who have some kind of access to gaming media have most probably heard of a videogame that stormed 2015 year of videogames and is argued to be the best rpg ever: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. What most people probably haven't heard of is its predecessor; which is, while incomparably smaller in scale, brings about atmosphere, plot, storytelling, intrigue and gameplay as good as its sequel if not better; The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings. While this brilliant game conveys much less emotion than its much-renowned sequel, it weaves together brilliantly crafted pieces to form a great scenario, where every element of the main story and so much of the sidequests will bring about critical questions to your mind and that (blessful in gaming) feeling that you can't comprehend what will happen next, but you can recognise the paths leading up to them. Gameplaywise; while the combat feels initially awkward and even outright clunky, after a bit of getting used to it feels just perfect for a witcher; while it is less dynamic than Witcher 3 you feel much more in control and more powerful, the way a witcher should be. The atmosphere is less ambitious but brilliantly designed in Witcher 2; you won't find nearly as much captivating scenery as you do in Witcher 3 but this game was designed to be more dark, gritty and political and it conveys the dark, gritty and political so well, with a refreshing touch of deep emotion here and there. Overall; while this game obviously lacks the scale, ambition and power of its sequel, it is doubtlessly of highest quality and I consider it to be one of the best rpg games to be made hands down.

While I didn't manage to complete Witcher 1 (after ~17hrs of gameplay) due to issues I have with the combat system, Witcher 2 is on a completely different level. Even though it was released in 2011, the revamped Enhanced Edition puts the game's graphics on par with current games. As I stepped into the beautiful fantasy world, I was quickly drawn to the lovable characters (with reappearances from W1) and interesting story that at multiple turns forces you to make decisions that have drastic consequences on following events.
One of the most important choices you have to make is towards the end of Chapter 1, thereby splitting the game into 2 major fractions each with its own development. Therefore, I highly recommend playing W2 twice. Doing so will allow you to earn steam achievements from both fractions and also to make more informed choices when making the gamesave transfer (/quick decision recap if you lose the gamesaves) for The Witcher 3 (HYYPPPPEEEEEE!!!!!). My first playthrough was 20 hrs, and a second should be much shorter with the option to skip most cutscenes prior to that decision.
While there are many positives about the game such as its beautiful graphics, good voice-acting, a larger variety of character models (much needed upgrade from W1) etc, there are some things I didn't like too. For example, I felt that the door/ area transition is pretty clunky, especially when fighting around an opened door and your character moves to the next room when he gets too close. Also, there is a significant lag time after an enemy/ monster is defeated and issuing the next action, such as picking up loot, opening doors, or climbing cliffs.
Other than the above-mentioned negatives, which are actually quite reminiscent of old RPGs, the game is really good and a must-play before Witcher 3. I would recommend skipping W1 and start with this title instead.

Red Hood Diaries is, in my opinion, a very underrated game. With a fantastic soundtrack, terrific graphics, and an interesting twist to the old Red Ridinghood fairy tale, this game certainly doesn't deserve the mixed reviews it has. While not a perfect game, it makes the most of what it gives and made for an overall enjoyable experiance.

Fantastic graphics - bright and sharp contrasting colors fit the fantasy genre of the game
Exellent lighting - the game effectively created a surreal mood, very fitting for a fairy tale
Fun platforming - many people complianed about the 3D platforming being annoying, but I rather enjoyed it. While it was sometimes difficult to see what was a platform and what was the background, I saw this as an extra challege that promtes a little exploration and taking a leap of faith

Cons:
there are only 2 voice-acted characters - just a minor gripe, but I believe some other characters should have been voice-acted as well
length - this is a rather short game, and I didn't feel it was challenging enough to make up for the short story
combat - very simplistic hack & slash, while not broken, it feels out of place in a flowing fantasy land
In closing, I thoroughly enjoyed this game, but was a little dissapointed by it's length. If it's on sale, I recommend picking it up for a weekend playthrough.

tldr:  Game is ok, consider if interested in art and on sale.
Woolfe speaks to me of a team with tallent, but no experience.  The art is absolutly gorgeous, I could just drink in the visuals all day.  Level design is less great.  Most of the time it's clear where to go, but when it isn't, it really shows.  Jumps that you can ALMOST make, and invisible walls where you'd like to go abound.  The game very much loves instant kills, and you will hit spikes that blend with level terrain  dozens of times.  This becomes very clear on bosses, who have more instant kills than regular attacks, making them a trial and error fight.  A running sequence towards the end of the game has a major issue with having two branching paths, one of which will randomly kill you.  Go back and start from checkpoint.
Story wise, the game suffers from being very angsty.  Red is so wrapped up in suffering that it becomes hard to take her seriously.  This is not helped by the fact that most of the game's  writing is poetry, which becomes cringe worthy fast.  Oddly, about 30% of the lines aren't rhyming though, so it becomes even more jarring  than it would normally.  The pacing of the story feels seriously off, with a forced climax coming out of nowhere and leading into a badly handled sequel hook.  The game is also only 2 hours long, which might contribute to this awkward pacing.
Mechanically, the game is servicible but mediocre.  Platforming is floaty, with a fixed camera sometimes making it difficult to tell where to go.  Combat is very awkward, mainly consisting of mashing light attack.  It gives you some magic attacks a short ways into the game, but these prove to deal very little damage, and have a slo-mo effect that makes them hard to use.  The combat in general feels poorly though out and in need of polish.
At the end of the day, I paid 5 dollars for the game, and got a decent amount of fun out of it.  But although it pains me to give a game that evidences some solid tallent a thumbs down, I can't recomend it at full price.  If the art interests you, consider getting it on sale.

this is another example of the point and click adventure games' resurgence that has been happening lately.
the best part of the game is undoubtedly its art style. backgrounds are nicely prerendered/drawn, locations do feel different, yet appropriate and both backgrounds and charactess have the same art style. animation of characters could be better at times but is definitely passable (or even surprisingly good for a budget game). 3d characters on prerendered/drawn backgrounds is a decidedly oldschool way of doing things and the developer has chosen to fully accept the limitations apparently without seriously considering mitigating these. it is not all bad as you might think, fixed resolution inherently means that the visuals do fit together incredibly well.
a bit on the technical aspects - i want to say visuals are great in general but unfortunately these remain within the confines of the technical capabilities of the game (or the engine). resolution is limited to 1024x768 and aspect ratio setting only changes the ratio leaving resolution the same - the ar correction setting (that has been mostly misunderstood in forum conversations) is aimed at displays not able to preserve the aspect ratio by themselves. looking at the other settings - without antialiasing the characters are horribly aliased thanks to the low resolution but fortunately enabling it incurs only a very minor performance hit.
story is about a near-future dystopia-ish society with a decidedly eastern- or middle-european take on the sci-fi genre. it is focused on the society and people with sci-fi technology remaining essentially just a backdrop. as customary for this, story does not wrap up too nicely and does not reveal all the details. story progression is slow and calm but not overly so.
story follows richard, a man who in a world of  big corporations and oppressive state (more hinted than shown) gets fired from one of the all-powerful corporations of the future and whose future prospects with that go from bleak to worse. standard fare of resistance, conspiracies, family history etc. ensues.
point and click works as well as expected from such a game today. there are not too many interactive objects and these can be hinted at to prevent pixelhunting. puzzles are very logical (but not always easy), the only annoyance is some degree of having to move over 4-5 screens and back for some puzzles. this is not critical though thanks to double-click acting like a quick-move (run to the object when double-clicking on one and practically immediately get to the next screen when clicked on screen transition).
finishing the game took me around 5 hours. definitely recommended for an adventure game fan (who does not dislike sci-fi setting) - it contains several hours of very good fun.

A fun "like Dark Souls but" game for a short time, but there's really not enough there.
Yeah it's really stylish, and yeah it's fun to adapt to the randomized situations that you get out of it being proc-gen, and it's got a really fun melee fighting system. Once I found out enemies can hurt each other, trying to coax them into accidentally hitting each other with their attacks became a really fun way to try and manage and deal with multiple enemies. But the game gets old and repetitive too quickly. Also, co-op is pretty broken.
The fact that it's procedurally generated is more of a weakness in the end. Rooms are just slapped together at random, as are the majority of enemies that populate them. You can be wandering through an ancient temple, then a winter wonderland, then a prison, then a swamp, all in the space of about 500m-1km. They're put together in a way that clearly shows no one even tried to make it make any sense, and it makes no attempt to hide this. If you stand at the edge of the level you can quite clearly see the future rooms just floating in the air where they've been awkwardly stuck together. It's kind of cool to explore alternate paths and see them wind back in on each other, but even then it doesn't happen in any meaningful way.
I assume they were going for some kind of impossible 'eldritch' world, that's creepy because it makes no sense. But in practice that's just the norm. It isn't weird when that's what it all is. You just get used to it because you've seen all the tricks it has in the first 30-45 minutes of gameplay, and then all it means is your progression through a campaign happens with much less actually visible progression. There was no adventure in an ancient tomb, or through a zombified village, or a decomissioned prison haunted by ghosts, or a super villain's secret north pole lair or whatever. It's just a series of random rooms picked from a hat, none of them holding any significance other than being the start or end of a level. They'd be forgettable if it weren't for how out of place they all seem next to each other.
There's not much overarching lore tying it all together from what I can tell either. It just seems to be this strange world that's built in impossible ways, with some overlord watching you the whole way and setting you pointless tasks to complete. There's some bits of history that are interesting, and explain a few of the enemies who you'll come across. But without any real narrative, purpose or characters, that's all just extras. These snippets of history give the pyramid overlord opportunities to say something irreverent more than it actually adds to the world you're walking around. Maybe I missed something though, because it's all given through snippets like item descriptions. ("like Dark Souls but") But in the end they just don't seem to add up to anything that gives the game or your journey through it any purpose or motivation.
I'm not really that into video game stories, and I don't expect a masterpiece or anything. But I think a willful disregard of story and world has been genuinely detrimental. Even a very simple story of a journey is a great way to give a campaign a sense of progression. And I do think Necropolis suffers because it lacks that. The only progression you'll see is a few new room types appearing on later floors, as well as more difficult enemies, and that's it.
I don't think this game should have the 'co-op' tag. The multiplayer is hilariously broken in my experience as I went entire floors in coop being ignored by every single enemy, while the game host had the attention of everything. I just walked around behind everything and slashed away while they all ignored me. It's certainly not in a state that you can justify buying the game for it. Which is sad because the more I play this game, the more I feel like it was meant to be played in co-op instead of single-player.
On the subject of co-op, the GOG version is completely lacking in co-op, and the devs don't seem to have any intention of changing that. That may not mean much about the Steam version of the game, but I think it says something important about the developers and their willingness to abandon the game before it's finished. In the case of the GOG version, it's very demonstrably unfinished.
I may come back to this game at some point in the future, to see if a wiser and more mature me can find anything else that may redeem it. But it would have to be something absolutely incredible for me to turn that 'No' to a 'Yes' on this review. My experience with it has certainly been conclusive enough that I'll be steering friends away from it from now on.

I've played about an hour so far.
You're a deep-sea diver in a green and pink undersea world. Everything around you is flowing. Your path suggests itself to you, and you follow it at your own pace. Maybe you call out to a nearby school of fish, and swim with them for a while. Or maybe you take hold of a passing dolphin and let it choose the way. Sometimes the current catches you and pulls you along into a new place.
I'm not really sure where this game is going yet. It's not particularly important. Yeah, the controls can feel a bit clunky, but you don't really need to be precise. You may drift off-course a bit. It's no big thing. You adjust your flow.
The coral is waving. The light is slanting.
There's a story by Walter Jon Williams in which humans have learned to translate the language of of the massive whales that inhabit the deep oceans of a distant planet. Because the whales live suspended in a liquid medium, they communicate without reference to fixed points. And because they experience being as holistic and interconnected, they tend to speak communally, emphasizing interrelationships over identity, describing what is shared instead of what is individual. They wouldn't say "I'm coming to you"; they would say "we are in a condition of becoming close to each other."
This game is sort of like that. If you're into that kind of thing.
I'm looking forward to the rest of this experience.

Necropolis is a three-dimensional action role-playing game with rogue-like elements from Harebrained Schemes, of recent Shadowrun fame.
In Necropolis, you play an adventurer of one of two character classes -- Brute or Blackguard -- entering the great Necropolis in search of fame and treasure. You are greeted as you enter by the ancient keeper of the Necropolis and all-round nice 'guy'. It offers you hints and tips, as well as quests to complete for its favour, which you can then use to advance your character's abilities. It also makes various sarcastic comments when you die.
The graphics in Necropolis have a unique and consistent feel to them. There are some large polygons and sharp edges, but also some great dynamic lighting effects and nice cartoonish textures. Together they combine to give a nice, moody, dark comic type of atmosphere.
The appeal is reduced somewhat by the rather impersonal character choices; even with only two classes to choose from, they could have allowed more customisation than some colour changes. Similarly, animations are a bit of a letdown, seeming a bit wooden and not well combined. The environments, too, which look quite nice and atmospheric when you first see them, quickly become bland and repetitive, with very little variation.
The user interface is simple, but a little lacking. It all works, but just looks and feels a bit clunky, especially with the bugs. For example, looking at empty slots on your inventory tab will show descriptions of items 'beneath' them in your crafting tab.
There are plenty of graphics options to play around with if you experience performance issues with everything turned up to maximum, but there aren't any useful descriptions or tooltips for any of them, and not all of them are self-explanatory. I've noticed, too, that when playing in full screen in Windows 10 with the Windows taskbar locked, the taskbar will appear on top of the game. It's not game breaking, but it is annoying.
Music is great, with a broody, minimalistic sort of instrumental theme that drips atmosphere; it's absolutely perfect for the game. Sound effects are pretty good, too, but player characters should make a bit more noise when they get attacked; sometimes it's hard to tell when an enemy has hit you.
There are no real voices, but there are some sections with gibberish speech and subtitles. These work quite well.
Necropolis is a three-dimensional action role-playing game (ARPG), viewed from a floating third-person camera. On your quest through the strange environment of the necropolis, you'll collect items and gems (the game's currency) and destroy countless enemies. It's a format that's pretty common and beyond the rogue-like elements, Necropolis doesn't really break any new ground.
The basic gameplay is hack-and-slash, with a little bit of simple platforming in some parts as well. You have control over your left hand (shield) and right hand (weapon), and each has a primary and secondary use: your shield can block and shield bash, and your weapon can do a light and a heavy attack. You can also hold down the attack buttons to charge up a 'power attack'; use this with caution as it depletes your stamina very quickly. Other than that you have a small inventory and you can collect food, potions, scrolls, and that's about it. Oh, yes, there's a basic crafting system, too, which works quite well, but you have to find recipes first.
The first thing you'll notice if you try to play the game with keyboard and mouse is that the controls are shocking, and can't be remapped. It's almost unforgivable to not allow control reconfiguration in a game like this. Thank Abraxis, then, that the game has full controller support and it works pretty well.
The next thing you may notice is that there's no map: no full-screen map or minimap. What were they thinking!? The procedural level generation works pretty well and creates some interesting levels and rooms, but when you have five doors with long corridors all leading away from one room and doubling back on each other, and ... well, let's just say that not having a map of any kind is rather frustrating. On some levels I probably spent more time wandering around trying to remember how to get to the already-found exit than I did actually playing the level.
After that, I hate to say, the list of disappointments grew. There's not enough in-game information on what some things do. For example, what does "Son of Erebo" mean, other than that you have clothes of a different colour? The game is still very buggy, too, with some serious enemy pathfinding issues, and it's been eight months since its last update. And there are only two classes! Two!? Even the pre-release information for the game mentioned three, and some information you can find out there suggests four.
Along with the unique graphical style, the rogue-like elements in Necropolis are where it really shines, and they're part of its core gameplay: permadeath; procedural generation of levels; and Nethack-style unidentified potions and scrolls, each with unpredictable results until you've tried them in game. The rogue-like elements are well integrated into the game and increase its appeal immensely.
Character progression in game largely amounts to equipment and item finding and crafting, as well as unlocking favour points with the keeper of the Necropolis. These can be spent at the start of each level after the first on a special item chest, or from the start on 'codexes': books that give your character (and all future characters who equip them) special perks. I was quite excited by these until I tried to equip two at once on a new character, and found that the game would only let me have one active at a time.
The game's lore also seems fairly interesting, and generally I like that sort of information being introduced while playing, but Necropolis gets it a bit wrong. It's fine to have the lore, too, but the actual game effects of items and 'codexes' need to be given, too, even if only in tooltips or something, and the coloured robes ... I still don't know whether all they do is change your outfit colour.
Necropolis also supports multiplayer, but I couldn't work out the very minimalist user interface used. From what I can see from the Steam Discussions and Guides for the game, you can only play with Steam friends and there's no server browser or anything like that, which seems like yet another huge oversight. In any case, watching a few videos of multiplayer shows me that gameplay isn't any different to singleplayer, but I imagine if you have friends to play with, it could be a fair bit of fun in spite of everything else I've mentioned.
Finally, indications in the Steam Discussions are that the developers have no further updates planned for Necropolis. In other words, what you see is what you get. This is really a shame. With more content and love this could have been a much better game.
Pros:
+ Unique and attractive graphical style
+ Great integration of classic rogue-like elements
+ Controller combat can actually be quite fun, in spite of its simplicity
+ Good sense of humour
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Only two character classes
- Combat is rather simple, with only occasional potions and scrolls to break up the monotony
- No map
- Bad keyboard controls with no reconfiguration available
- No pause (even in singleplayer)
- Buggy
- Can only play multiplayer with Steam friends
I'm a huge fan of Harebrained Schemes and love their other titles. Given my expectations, I'm rather disappointed in Necropolis. It's not a bad game, exactly; it's just very far from the game it could have been.

Before I start my review, let's paint some perspective. I have been looking to finally play a Final Fantasy game from all the posititive things said about the series. Then I saw this on sale in the 2015 Summer Sale. Somehow I missed the actual release of this game. I brought it as fast as I could and here I am.
Presentation:
Everyone says that the graphics of FFVII are♥♥♥♥♥♥and to be honest they are kind of. However, FFVII does some cool things with its graphics. When it's playing a animated cutscene, sometimes you will be able to move around while its playing it. A really good example of this that I have found in the game is when Cloud has to use a lift type platform. When it goes down and up, it starts a cutscene however you can still move Cloud while its playing. I don't know why but I found this really cool. Overall in my opinion I think the graphics are okay. They are not that bad but they are not good either.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is in a a&b format. You wait for your action gauge/time to fill up and then you can attack. However there are some things that make this battle system really fun to play. It uses my favorite system for the magic in any RPG right now. Basically, you equip materia and different materia have different magic spells. You could get a materia with Fire, Ice or Bolt as well as others but those are the 3 main elemental damage materias. You can also get more interesting materia, my favorite being the Enemy Skill materia. This allows you to copy enemies attacks and use them on your own. Very good to use early on so you have a OP move from a boss that you are not meant to have. You can also level up these materia to do better in battle. Leveling up Fire to Fire3 gives a massive damage boost but will make you consume more mana when using it. The gameplay in this game is perfect in my opinion.
Story:
To be honest, at the time of writing this I have not beaten the game. However I am very very close. I think i'm almost on the final boss. The story is really good though. Every character has their own problems that they have to try and clear up as the story progresses. I really want to say some examples of this shown in the game but spoiling JRPGs is no good. I guess I can talk about Cloud though. Cloud is the protagonist of FFVII. Cloud is a former member of SOLDIER and has now joined AVALANCHE. An rebellion organization that wants to stop Shinra Inc from absorbing the Mako energy, the only natural resources of the planet. The story is really good and made me want to play to the end.
Final Fantasy VII was a great entry to Final Fantasy for me. I finally understand all the positive things that are said about this game. While playing this, I started to play Final Fantasy X Remastered on the PS Vita and thats a great game too. I don't think it's as good as VII but its still really good. This game is almost perfect and if you are looking to start getting into the Final Fantasy series this is a great entry point. However I must say, Square Enix's DRM is on here. You need to make a Square account to actually get on the game. Even worst is that when I first got this, Square's servers were down so I could not play. If you don't mind the DRM then get the game. It is brilliant.

This was my very first RPG back in 1997 on the PS1. I fell in Love with RPGs after this game and, well, have played and beaten every possible version/port/sequel/prequel (Excluding the cell phone game that never made it to the US) associated with FF7. When I found out there was a PC version back in 2003 I jumped on it immediately. Despite the Chocobo racing bug, despite the horrible midi music, and despite everyone aside from the main playable characters unable to close their mouths I still loved the PC version. Then the Graphic mods came out. Needless to say I was playing this game non-stop again. I was a bit confused when Steam said they had a version with extra features cause I thought it was just the PC port with maybe the bugs fixed. I was glad to see achievements added and better then the one that came directly from SE's re-release.
FF7 redefined RPGs and did a fantastic job at setting the bar. The story is very in depth and the twists you encounter are fantastic. SE (then Squaresoft) made very risky and Bold decisions while making this game. The story aside the gameplay is amazing. The Materia system makes for easy customization of characters and skills while still limiting the amount of skills you can use, but completely interchangeable. FF7 was probably the first FInal Fantasy game that really required inventory management and strategy on how you customized your characters. Do you go with the super powerful weapon with 2 non-linked materia slots or do you go with the okay weapon with 8 linked materia slots? Do you equip the added effect materia with bio on your weapon to add poison to your attack or your armor to protect you from poison?  DO you use the ALL materia with your Cure or your Fire? DO I use this weapon that give me more slots but no materia exp or not? Choices that really effect HOW you play.
The mini games are fun as well and not just 1 time events. The Gold Saucer lets you go back and replay any mini game you have already done at least once in the main story. Take Road Rash, Cool Boarders, underwater submarine battles, and "Horseback Racing" (Done on Chocobos) and put them into FF7 and you can spend countless hours just messing around.
FF7 is challenging and very rewarding with tons of side-quests that give you a good payoff but also enrich the story and characters. Not to mention multiple optional bosses, secret gear, hidden/optional characters. There is so much to be done in FF7 you wont be disappointed.
Thankfully the things I don't like about this port you don't have to do or use.
The Character booster is a bit of a let down. Instead of just maxing out your level it only increases your HP, MP and Gil to the "max" and dummies down the enemy's stats. I would have rather just seen it increase my character's level to 99. Using it early on in the game makes limit breaks impossible to ever obtain and just eliminates the "getting to know how to play" stage where you developed strategy. Plus once you use it there is NO going back. So if you are stuck on a boss and just wanna get a quick boost to beat it then go back to playing normally you can't you are stuck with the weaker enemies and constant leveling that just becomes un-important. I would have rather seen a character editor then a booster. But luckily you don't have to use it, so it's a moot point.
The only other thing I would haveliked to see would be a New Game+ option.
In all FF7 is still a FANTASTIC rpg and although the graphics are.... well... blocky... the game has aged very very well.

TL;DR: It's an awesome RPG that every RPG fan should play at least once because it's choices have real consequences to the point that you have a different 2nd and 3rd act depending on what choices you make. The side quests come to very interesting conclusions. You will want to do them all. Some of them can be hard to find though. This game will not hold your hand. You actually have to find your objectives by listening to what people tell you. you aren't going to just be walking from quest marker to quest marker.
Highly recommended. A must play by all RPG lovers. If you like RPGs then you will love this game. I love this game although in some ways I prefer the original non-enhanced version better. Seeing as this is the only version available on Steam I am reviewing this version. Don't let my Steam playtime fool you. I've played this games extensively. Most of my playtime is on the original version of The Witcher 2 when it first came out, before it was available on Steam. Which I played through four times(twice for each side of the story). The Witcher 2 wasn't on Steam until a year after it released and the original version is still not available on Steam unfortunately. We are stuck with the (noob friendly) "Enhanced edition" that coincided with the 360 release of the game which I played through twice. With the enhanced edition they did add "Dark" mode though which is awesome to play and has it's own armor sets and weapoons that are exclusive to dark mode.
The Witcher 2 has anything that anyone could possibly want from a singleplayer RPG. If you name the reason you play RPGs I guarantee that this has it (and The Witcher 3 has it x100).You play as a Witcher which is sort of like a Jedi monster hunter. It has the most interesting side quests of any RPG besides the other 2 games in the series. If you play this game, actually coming into it with an open mind, and actually taking the time to understand it then it will probably be amoung your top 3 RPGs easily. It's sequel will be tied for the top spot with whatever your favorite is right now if you are only picking one game per series.
The choices in this game have real consequences and all the choices you make are grey. There is no right or wrong in The Witcher 2 only consequences. Often times you will make a choice thinking you did the right thing but you will later find out that your choice had consequences beyond what you could immediately see and it turns out that you actually harmed someone that you were trying to help. The choices all have interesting outcomes. None of them are boring or meaningless. The biggest choice you make changes the entire second and third act of the game.
Now I'll list some negatives. The first negative is that the only version available is the enhanced edition which is far easier then the original version of the game. The enhanced editions hard mode is equivalent to the originals normal mode. The enhanced editions normal mode is a new easier difficulty they made for the enhanced edition. They did add Dark Mode though so this is kind of balanced out. The third act is also far too short. Geralt can also be a little tough to control too when trying to pick up some items too. You mgith even miss whole side quests if you don't make sure to explore enough and talk to everyone.

What a spectacularly bad game. Everything in this game seems like it could be passable with just a little work, but none of it actually is. The story is almost non-existant and ends with a cliffhanger after a mere 2 hours of gameplay. One which will of course never be resolved with GriN shutting their doors. The acting is flat, with boring dialogue. The combat is as bare bones you can get, but in a frustrating way. Enemies will maul you repeatedly with no invincibility frames or way to block attacks, even though they can block attacks. Level design makes little to no sense with poor flow and construction. The game is also divided into basically 3 major sections: a free roaming combat heavy first area in Ulrica and it's sewers, a platform heavy forest area, and a foot race against a carriage. All three have major issues with their design.
In Ulrica there are several enemies that can flat out oneshot you with little indication of this capability, and the combat is not good enough to focus an entire first part of the game around it. Once you get to the forest area you realize how hilariously awful the games platform detection is. One spot in particular shows you a lower floor you need to jump around spikes to land on, but it would be easier to just drop down. LIttle Inferno is not a game; or, better saying, is not just a game. Of course it's funny, and will consume a couple of hour (about five) to finish. But that is not what is most important here. This is a gaming experience that intendes to discuss game experience itself, and postmodern life, and global warming, and nihilism... It's a complexe and vast critical material about life and human behavior.
If you are not interested in the concept of the game, or thinking about deep things, you can still buy it (as it's fun to burn things and find combos); but, in this case, the game price is a little high, and you should wait a promotion to aquire it.
----------------
Little Inferno não é um jogo; ou, melhor dizendo, não é só um jogo. É claro que é divertido, e irá consumir algumas horas (por volta de cinco) jogar até o final. Mas isso não é o mais importante aqui. Little Inferno é uma experiência que pretende discutir a própria indústria de videogames, e a vida pós-moderna, e o aquecimento global, e o niilismo... É uma crítica complexa e extensa sobre a vida e o comportamento humano.
Se você não está interessado no conceito do jogo, ou não quer pensar sobre temas profundos, você ainda pode comprar o jogo (ainda é extremamente divertido queimar coisas e descobrir combos); mas, nesse caso, o preço do jogo está alto, e vale a pena esperar uma promoção.
