If you just want to know whether you should buy this game, all you need to read is the next sentence:
If you're up for a relatively light-hearted and "cute" fantasy hack-and-slash, BUY THIS GAME. BUY THIS, BUY THIS, BUY THIS.
If you're not convinced and need details, well, okay. I avoided buying this game for a long time because it's definitely not the kind of game I usually go for, but I kept hearing about how good it is - in really nonspecific terms. So I bought it in the most recent summer sale and it's blown me away. Dust: An Elysian Tail is really good, but the thing is, it's really good because of reasons that are difficult to put into words. Now I know why everybody was so vague about why it's good.
The closest I think I can say is "Every individual part of the game - the sound design, the art, the combat mechanics, and so on - are 'okay' to 'very good,' but they work together so well that the game taken as a whole is more than the sum of its parts."
That's not to say it's perfect. The voice acting in particular keeps getting my attention, and not in a positive way. Meanwhile, the dodging and parrying combat mechanics are slightly clunky - or at least, poorly explained. But seriously, the rest of the game more than makes up for these faults. The story, the art and sound, and, yes, even the "furry" character designs pull me into the earnest and innocent fantasy world that serves as a refreshing counterpoint to the "big-headed child loses their innocence in a big, dark world" indie RPG/adventure games that are so common these days.

So, after about 40 hours each, my friend and I decided to start a Multiplayer game, and the game really shines here.
There are some issues though, for example the Technologies you get to research is randomised each time, which is frustrating as in twenty years my friend have UV Lasers and Level 3 Shields, whilst all my fleet had was Level 3 Thrusters, Sensors, and a Level 2 Hyperdrive (He had a military strength of around 1500, I had a mil strength of 450). So if we could get a more conventional Tech Tree, or at least the choice to have a Tech Tree, that would be great.
All in all, the game is very good, with some more features it could be great, it just needs a bit more polish, some Trade (Outside of minerals for energy, or info etc.,) such as Trade Lanes that provide a net boost to Credits, more in-depth Diplomacy, a bit more control over the sectors (I have a few hundred energy and they often have thousands), and a bit more balance over the Military, and it should be great.
Still worth a buy right now, it is very enjoyable, it just has potential to be even greater.

The combat is a lot better than the first Witcher, but still can feel rather clunky and awkward.
The Tiny Inventory that was annoyingly small in The first game is improved in the 2nd by being more spacious and has a weight system instead, I can explore and loot for quite a while before I have to go sell or store. Despite being more spacious the inventory still feels flawed, it's a higgledy piggledy ugly mess of a list. The perfect inventory system would be a much larger grid system, sort of like what the first Witcher had but 4 times as spacious.
While the inventory has improved, alchemy has gone backwards. Only being able to drink potions during meditation is annoying. You can't drink potions during battle, so you have to guess what you may need before a fight which can be wasteful or go in blind see what happens and figure what you need and reload a previous save. Rather time consuming. The first witcher's alchemy system was better it let you drink potions in battle and I prefer being able to drink potions in battle. A really stupid decision to change it.
Moving around the world feels restrictive, with only certain spots you can climb or descend with no ability to jump over obstacles, movement is rather linear and so is exploration.
Map is flawed, especially bad for me since I have a bad sense of direction. The map seems to expect you to memorise where everything is, nothing is labelled, I had to find Phillipa's house and it did not mark or label it on the map, so I spent ages entering each house trying to find hers which is rather frustrating and time wasting
The game has way too many long cutscenes making it feel more like a interactive movie than a game. I want to play a game, not watch a movie.
Boss battles feel like a movie script as well, you have to pay attention to when to rapidly click your mouse at certain points.You fight a boss only to  have the battle interrupted by cut scenes such Geralt moving around on a tentacle or to be distracted by a falling bridge cutscene after each time you chop off a tentacle.
I find it annoying, I want to fight a boss and not continually have the battle be interupted by a cutscene. I really dislike the Quick Time Events, it ruins any immersion for me.
The world of Witcher 2 is dark in an over done way, it's not even all that terribly original - it's your generic "Dark and Gritty Fantasy" setting, set in wretched, crappy world where all the people are ignorant, filthy and full of extreme hatred.
Sure the 2nd Witcher has better graphics and inventory but overall I just feel the first Witcher was much better, in every way, quests, mini games were done better, alchemy and so was the story. Witcher 2 the story is too political and I find a heavy emphasis on political stuff rather boring.
Though I reccomend playing both paths as it gives you slightly different access to each area, different quests, information, characters and choices.
I played Iorveth's path first and then Roche's and I enjoyed playing through Roche's path much more, I found it more interesting.
But overall I'd class this as a shallow action game that wants to be a movie as well, that pretends to be deep, but fails and falls short. This is a overhyped game that does not deserve the praise it gets.
I guess I've been spoiled by the massive epic exploration Skyrim offers and The Witcher 2 isn't even half that, just 3 towns to explore. *yawn
At least I know now that Witcher isn't very good for what I want in an RPG. Sure some may love it, but it's not my cup of tea. And from watching gameplay of Witcher 3 I can see it's more of the same or worse. With lengthy cutscenes and Geralt's character model now looks very ugly.
I prefer RPG's like The Elder Scrolls and Fallout, which has a lot of depth, choice, exploration and you can be whoever you can imagine.
This game is more for those who like a light action oriented RPG with a limited set character, than those who like a deep, open RPG with more freedom, seemingly endless choices and character builds that can vary a lot.
It's hard for me to decide if this game is worth reccomending, I'd class it as sort of ok and to me sort of ok, doesn't deserve reccomending.

For $3.75, I wasn't hoping for much. I was impressed at the beginning but as the game progressed, the lousy respawn points really spoilt my impression of the game. There are only 2 voice actors in the whole game, Red and her grandmother. Other characters like B.B. Wolfe and the Pied Piper just say nothing.
PROS
1. Storytelling Style
The narrative is told by Little Red Riding Hood in a rhyming fashion. It's pretty good when it rhymes but horrible at all the other times.
2. Background Foreground Interaction
I love the way you can move back and forth from the foreground to the background. It's unintuitive to do with keyboard controls but I found a way around it.
CONS
1. Bugs
Lots of them, I took the screenshots and uploaded them to Steam.
2. Controls
They didn't port it over properly. I couldn't see my health and mana bars at all.
3. Game Time
It's so short and I played it on Hard mode. It took only 2 hours. This was crap.
4. Respawn Points
If you die, the respawn points can take you all the way back to the beginning. Chapters cannot start from mid way, they must start from the beginning.
5. The Combos
You only use the Wolf Claw at the very last stage against Wolfe and that's where you get the last combo. You only use it for 1 battle and it's not even necessary to win.

Just based on the "To be Continued" ending, I am most disappointed. The story is meant to go on with Red saving Ulrica. and you using all the combos. You might even find out that Red is somehow related to B.B. Wolfe even. It is hinted that her mother was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥before being put in the mines.

/!\ Long and detailed review. /!\
Woolfe - The Red Hood Diaries is a very beautiful game.
→ I was amazed by the maps and the visual effects of the game: like the slow motion when using special moves, which is very cool. There's many details: the reflect on water, mirors, or even when Red is near a rock, her leg doesn't go through the rock but is posed on the rock. The sun's rays are here as well.
Links of the screenshots:
;
→ The soundtracks are very pleasant as well and well chosed, they totaly fit the situations.
→ The writing is very beautiful and poetic. There's rhymes, plays on the sound of the words, and is full of imageries. Red's voice is also very nice and the woman behind her voice articulates very well and the intonations are pleasant to hear. There's few puns as well, which I found nice. "Thanks for the ride, you rock" (when lifted by a rock), for instance.
The controls are simple yet convenient either you have a controllor or just your keyboard.
→ However you'll have to change the controls if playing on keyboard (as I did, because somehow my controllor didn't work), choosing inputs that best fit for you.
→ If you're interested in mine, then I chose: 4/8/6/5 (left, up, right, down) for the camera ; ←↑→↓ (keyboard arrows for the character's moves) ; A (or Q for QWERTY keyboards) to sprint ; Z and E (or W and E for QWERTY keyboards) for basic hits) ; R for the Magic ; space to jump ; D to roll ; F to sneak ; and ENTER for the interactions.
→ The automatic camera is nice, the moves of your camera is okay. You don't really need to move it a lot, just sometimes to the sides to see what there's next, or to the bottom to see wheter there's a platform or not.
The gameplay is amusing, the difficulty however is maybe too easy.
→ The character's gameplay is convenient and easy to understand. There's the basic hits, with four possible combinations for special moves. The jumps, double jumps, and grips (when escalading) can be alternated very smoothly. → Howevery even in the highest difficulty, I found the game pretty easy. I have been lost only two times because of my own mistakes (I didn't pay enough attention to some things around me), and even so I wasn't lost for long. The maps are amusing (especially the forest) however they're not very puzzle-like. There's also only two time trials, which is really unfortunate because I totally enjoyed them, though they were short and with not many obstacles. If they were made harder, it would have been really nice.
→ The bosses are not hard to beat either and there's only two. The first one can be hard unless you understand the tips. When understood, it's really easy. It doesn't have many HP either, and it follows the same pattern. Thus, I beated him in only two rounds (it gives a possibility to hit the boss only after "a round" (let's say that) and I could beat it in the second chance it gave, which is very fast because it's impossible to beat it in only one round because you don't have enough time). The second and last boss is easy as well. It has more HP but still is easy if you avoid its very strong spells and take some distances (don't go total meelee). It also follows an obvious pattern and is finished too fast.
However it's (almost) compensated by the boss' strengh. A hit can one shot or mid-life you. But as said earlier, if you know the tips, they won't even be able to lay a hand on you (or almost not).
The story is okay.
→ I really haven't been into it in the begining. I wasn't surprised by the first "surprising" event because we didn't know enough about the concerned character of the event. The story went by very quickly, I had the feeling that they burnt many steps.
→ However, even if I first found the pattern of the story simple, at the end of the game it became interesting and I thought "maybe it's more complicated than what I thought".
The game is however very short.
→ I finished it in 5 hours, knowing that I really took my time to discover the maps because they were really beautiful. I took many screenshots as well as showing them to my sister and friends, like "hey this game is really beautiful, look at that".
→ It's supposed to have a second episode because it ends with "To be continued". It ended at the most interesting part, though.
In the end !

I can recommend this game on so many high points. Let's start with first impressions.
The game is so visually appealing. It even feels good on the eyes, like a gentle massage for your retinas.
The sound effects and music combine to create a relaxed atmosphere that immediately soaks into you as the player. It's a calm, mellow and relaxed game that passes on those feelings to you.
There is so much hidden depth in this game. Even by the end of it, many mysteries are simply left unsolved, or left to the player to interpret as you see fit.
There is so much content. I know this joke was old and worn out when it first started, but there is more content here than in No Man's Sky. If you ever went through a phase of being obsessed with marine biology, as I have, you will have a blast just identifying all the different species represented here.
The art style is beautiful. It comes across as simplistic, but it works and makes everything feel clean, fresh and gorgeous. Plus it leaves plenty of room for the imagination to work.
There is a plot here. I'll try to go over it as spoiler-free as possible, but if you don't want to take a risk, avert your eyes now.
The story is told purely through exploration and a few murals found throughout the game, as well as simply through the game mechanics themselves.
In spite of this being a non-combat game, the developers managed to work an antagonist into this story... and it's not who you might think!
The story, thread-bare as it may seem, has an incredible level of depth attached to it, and is left entirely up to the player's imagination to fill in the gaps. Without a single line of dialogue, this game delivers depth and emotion to characters who's only backstory is told through cryptic murals found in ruins.
Alright, end potential spoilers section.

Developed by GriN Multimedia for the PC and soon to be released on the PlayStation 4, Woolfe – The Red Hood Diaries is a modern reimagining of Little Red Riding Hood that is quite a dark and twisted story of this classic fairy tale. The game for me also has some parallels to American McGee’s Alice due to the two protagonists in the story who are not afraid to get their hands dirty and also share some similar gameplay parallels.
So its core, Woolfe – The Red Hood Diaries allows the gamer to control the protagonist Red who is investigating her father’s death at Mr. Woolfe’s factory and also wants revenge. Red was also raised by her grandmother who taught her a few things about fighting and magic. So with your axe by side, magic in the other, Red commences her journey through this dark and twisted world looking for clues, answers and blood.
In terms of gameplay, Woolfe – The Red Hood Diaries is basically a 3D arcade game with a strong emphasis on 2D platforming mechanics which looks glorious on a PC with full detail. The world of Woolfe is rich, diverse and even though it is quite dark can be very colourful at certain times. Apart from killing enemies and fighting bosses, Red must also use stealth to sneak around the environment.
To complement the engaging story about Red, there’s some great voice acting that goes hand in hand with the gameplay and the fantasy inspired musical score. However there are a couple of bugs here and there in the gaming world but developers GriN Multimedia are thankfully addressing these issues which is more so with the timing mechanics. Another issue was jumping between different platforming levels that at times had me dying quite a number of times.
Although the game supports a keyboard/mouse combination, to play the game as it should be played is via a PC controller which transforms the game into a FULL HD arcade console experience. As you defeat enemies, solve puzzles and explore the world, all the clues are right in front of the player but at times, the puzzles which require timing can be quite a challenge. Overall, the experience is just over 2 1/2 hours but there’s plenty of arcade enjoyment to be found in Woolfe – The Red Hood Diaries.
Final Thoughts?
Although this is only part one of Woolfe – The Red Hood Diaries, developers GriN Multimedia should be commended on creating a rather engaging arcade experience on the PC that harkens back to American McGee’s Alice with its twisted storytelling and gameplay.
The game looks beautiful on a PC with some exceptional detail and sturdy gameplay mechanics that for the most part work well. Reiterating again, the game needs to be played with a controller because it does make the experience considerably easier and even though there are a few flaws, it’s definitely a game for those wanting a fun arcade fix.

Little Inferno, in three words: Fun, Simple, Anti-Climatic
Without ruining the story for too many people-
Little Inferno is a game, about burning objects. That's it! That is to say: it's not a point that can be counted against it.
So many games fail to balance story, with gameplay elements. In my experience- Little Inferno leans just a little bit more towards the 'story' aspect; but that is only true because the gameplay lacks variety, save for the objects in which you burn.
What I liked:
> Burning things! It's simple, and fun to play with.
> The overall story arc, and the not-so-deep meaning to the game.
What I disliked:
> Lack of variety when it came to objects, a lot of objects were either an upgraded version of a previous object- or a 'mix and match' of effects.
Little Inferno is a basic set-things-on-fire sandbox, for the pyromaniac in all of us. If you're willing to spend the money: you too could own your very own, special, spectacular, Little Inferno Entertainment Fireplace.
Just don't expect it to have much replay value. I've played it twice, and I'm likely not going to hazard a third time.

Play an older Gal Civ title, play Sid Meier’s Civ VI/V.
The logical progression in Galactic Civilizations series.
$69.99 (Preorder /w Beta)
I played Galactic Civilizations II in the past and was looking forward to a sequel. Sure enough one came, and even added multiplayer to it.
4X games aren’t overly popular due to the fact you take turns. In the case you are playing multiplayer, this could mean you will probably have the chance to go and make coffee before their turn is over.
Action is certainly not a descriptor for games like these. If you have played Sid Meier’s Civilizations VI or V, you should feel right at home. There are quite a few similarities between the two titles, but there are the differences.
Right off the bat, the tech tree in Gal Civ is much, much, much larger. Trading technology has its advantages, as trade does in general.
The difference in scale is also very apparent. Setting a requirement of a 64-bit operating system to handle the much larger maps/universes was viewed to be a necessity by many (including myself). Those without Windows XP will find themselves unable to play as well because of the Direct X 10 requirement. There is supposedly a reverse engineered version of DirectX 10 floating around for Windows XP, but it’s hit and miss and also uses the CPU to do the effects.
Ideology makes gameplay interesting, with the three having their own bonuses associated with them (as well as cons). Plant colonization tends to bring these up more often than by chance.
Diplomacy can also rock the boat as well, so don’t think pushing for a military victory will always work in your favor.
I find that technology victories are the easiest to achieve, as some of the AI can be quite brutal – even on normal difficulty. Reason being is that the AI learns player’s gameplay strategies and updates itself through the internet.
Seeing the game in beta, and at its final stage, it has come a long way. Resources make the game interesting as well as the ascension route you can take to victory.
As I warned before, a game can take quite sometime. My recommendation is to have a LAN Party with a few friends, as it can end up being like a game of Risk.

Welcome to the wild and wacky world of "Real Horror Stories Ultimate Edition", AKA "Cheap And Nasty Jump Scares And Insanely Illogical Puzzles: The Game".
It's cheap...ooh, it's cheap. And it actually does manage to scare, if you turn off all the lights, put on some headphones, turn the volume up real loud and don't tire too easily of some spooky face zooming suddenly up at you from the middle of the screen approximately every 2.5 minutes of gameplay (something which does admittedly seem to work on yours truly again and again and again, but then again, I honestly do believe one of the scariest moments in cinema history is that shot in the Exorcist of the guy with the painted face suddenly bursting onto screen...so I may be somewhat biased here).
And the puzzles...oh, the puzzles...I especially loved the one where you have to write "Belial" in the tiled letters of a floor...everyone knows who Belial is, right? I personally just thought it was the ugly little round thing from Basket Case, but apparently he's also a world-famous demon...I really do need to read my bible more, apparently...
Which brings me to the next, er, curious point about this game. If you read the Steam Store page, you'll be under the impression this is a game about "urban myths", and it does manage to keep up that particular thematic, more-or-less, for at least the first quarter or so of "gameplay" (note the inverted commas; they're not entirely accidental). But by the end we're seeing Popes on crosses in fiery barren landscapes, coaxing blood through lines carved into ancient Egyptian doors, and stabbing babies on altars just to see where the blood dribbles down to so we can solve the next puzzle. All "urban myths", apparently. I don't know about you, but nothing cries out "urban" more loudly to me than Egyptian tombs and desert landscapes.
In all seriousness, this is probably a rival for the "worst" game I've ever played. Having said that, I still managed to enjoy it much, much more than many other games which are undeniably more aesthetically accomplished, not least of all on account of its stupidly short playing time and the generosity of the game-makers themselves in including a "hints" section which all but tells you exactly what to do. AND it only cost me twenty cents, on super-sale.
If it ever gets down to that low, low price ever again, I'd actually recommend you buy it. It does have some really nice imagery, which you can make some pretty groovy screenshots out of. The only downside to this is, in order to get said screenshots, you may actually have to play the game.
Verdict: 4/10 (for the pretty pictures and spooky sounds).

It failed to give a better gameplay experience than Gal Civ 2. They didn't improve much from Gal Civ 2 except better graphics, which are inferior to other games released today, they improved custom races and ship design and that's where it stops. Everything else got worst, including the removal of over 40+ options that controled various aspects of graphics, battles, general gameplay options.  This game as a successor was made to cash in on the reputation of Gal Civ II Dreadlords.
I believed in Stardock ability to make an awesome game worth every penny,  before this P.O.S., now I have been so repulsed by its quality, effort, general development, or I should say complete lack of.
They decided to take the road of making money from DLC's and a new expansion over fixing memory leaks, general game stability, or improving the UI of the game itself.  Most of which are very small details that can make the game considerably better like the abilitly to move production Q's to the top of the list or the usage of waypoints.
I came up with over 14 total failures form Gal Civ II to this version that they made worst. I only mentioned 3 here.  Dreadlords may have set the bar high for this genre, but they didn't even try with this game.
Here's a few specific examples of what was removed from the game as far as UI goes.
1. Custom waypoints, there is no way to place a waypoint for your ships to goto anywhere on the map like in Gal Civ 2. On Gal Civ 2, there was a button you clicked to create waypoints on maps, very handy since docking and undocking fleets from planets/starbases is a bit of a hassel. YOu would avoid doing so to keep the fleets together.
2. Ability view which planets have undeveloped land plots via the governor screen. On Gal Civ 2 there was (1) under planet class column showing there's 1 undeveloped land plot.
3. Ability to select specialization via the governor screen, on Dreadlords you could change all planets to military, social, or wealth production by clicking the top of the column, you then had the option to go through changing individual ones or even turning it off on the govenor screen.
4. Planetary indicators showing if the planet has no production, open land plots, mainly if ships are in orbit.  This leaves you to never seeing ships in orbit around planets and can easily forget about them, thus becoming nothing more than a drain on your budget. All these icons have been removed.
5. Ability to group select fleets on the map, a simple point and drag on the map to select everything in an area and give them the same move orders. Not used often, but once in awhile it came in handy.

A quite unique 'hack and slash' roguelike (perma death) game which offers up to 4 player co-op.
The game has a very unique look graphics wise, very minimal, all hard angles and gradients, now this style isn't for everyone, I'll admit that, but to me it gives this game a look very much of its own.
Sound wise it is passable, there's not much music wise and sound effects are good and communicate what needs to be communicated.
Gameplay wise the controls need some getting used to, this isn't a mouse button mashing hack and slash game where pressing a button results in an immediate swing, this is more of a Dark Souls type of hack and slash where you need to pick your battles and need to be aware that your weapons need time to swing before connecting to the enemy (and each weapon will feel different enough), all before they can interrupt you with a swing and hit of their own.
On top of that, using special abilites or heavy swings of weapons will deplete your stamina quickly and lower the maximum stamina cap, which fortunately can be restored with various items you find or craft yourself.
Dieing results in starting over and loosing all your items and weapons, with the exception of books that give certain abilites that can be unlocked throughout your play through and can be equipped again once you start over, albeit being able to use only one.
Dieing also means you get a brand new dungeon (as the areas, room layouts, lighting, color grading and enemy placements are randomized), this might sometimes work in your advantage and sometimes not so much (running into corrupted/crystal enemies at the first door your enter.)
There's sometimes some finicky player collisions (especially on the crystal like structeres, and especially the ones at the boss area, which when getting stuck can result in death, which can be very frustrating, especially when you got that far in.)
Overall a very good game, but, the forced roguelike permadeath might (rightfully) turn some people of, so if you can't handle that, I'd suggest to avoid it, otherwise, this game is well worth the money.

I was told the witcher 2 is where the witcher series gets good.  Unfortunately that is not true.  While in most ways it is a massive improvement over the witcher 1, which was one of the worst games I have ever played, minor improvements on a terrible product do not make a good product.
Some of the more glaring issues I have ran into during play.
-Extremely crash prone, particularily when rapidly rotating the camera or moving through doors.
-Terrible boss fights.  Bosses have thus far come in two varieties, terrible god of war ripoffs with illogical ways of resolving the fight (a monster described as having indestructably thick skin is killed by dropping a hand grenade on it for instance) or fights against humans who are more capable than they have any reason to be (superhuman ability needs to be explained in the story!).   The fights all share serious issues as well, such as the bosses starting to attack you while the introductory cutscene fades into gameplay and before you can control, meaning you start most bossfights dead or with large chunks of HP missing.
-Dissapointing story.  As with the witcher 1, there is a good story here, but it is delivered in such a terrible way.  As an example one of your NPC comrades is supposed to be so deep and angsty.  Reason for his angst?  Doesnt like being called names.  Or the time when the guy who has framed you for murdering a king asks you, without a hint of sarcasm, why you are chasing him.  Not quite as offensively badly delivered as the witcher 1 however.
-Terrible character progression.  You can choose between three progression trees, Mage, Swordsman and Alchemist.  There is no point going down the mage tree as the 1 usefull spell is given to you at the start, is not improved by progressing down the tree and you are punished for using it if you do try to build for magic.  The swordman tree is reasonable but overshadowed by the alchemy tree and the alchemy tree is simply overpowered.
-Terrible combat.  The movement is, to put it nicely, janky as all hell.  On top of that attacks have more or less range than they appear to (both Geralt's and the enemies) and you are stuck in animations for obscene times.  This is made worse by wierd enemy behaviour (for example, enemies have set zones where they are active for example, if you move from the zone while trying to fight them they teleport away and then you have to do a little dance on top of thier spawning point to get them to come out.)  And woe be anyone who runs into a ranged unit, they are 100% accurate and if you are within LOS when they decide to begin thier attack animation you will be hit no matter what you put between you and them.
-Generally bad game design in many ways such as quests which are partially broken if you do not complete them in the right way, or having to follow NPCs from point to point in order to progress but those NPCs having incredibly terrible pathfinding, often adding several hundred percent to the time a journey should take (ie a 1:30 journey becomes 8:30), or being given choices of dialogue but only one of those choices being right and the rest being instant gameovers (and instant gameovers which make no sense in the game as well which is the worst part).  And as the icing on the cake they intersperse the game with sections where you play as other characters.  While playing as these characters you have the same base stats as your Geralt, but you lose Geralts abilities.  In some fights the lost abilities are only your magic signs, which is somewhat bearable, but in others you lose your signs, your ability to dodge, your ability to move towards targets while attacking, your ability to use items (etc.), its really goddamn terrible...
It looks nice, a beautiful game no doubt, but that is prettymuch its only good point and it doesnt outweigh the rest.   I recommend avoiding this as well as the witcher 1 and just going straight into 3.  3 is the only good witcher game.

If you just want to know whether you should buy this game, all you need to read is the next sentence:
If you're up for a relatively light-hearted and "cute" fantasy hack-and-slash, BUY THIS GAME. BUY THIS, BUY THIS, BUY THIS.
If you're not convinced and need details, well, okay. I avoided buying this game for a long time because it's definitely not the kind of game I usually go for, but I kept hearing about how good it is - in really nonspecific terms. So I bought it in the most recent summer sale and it's blown me away. Dust: An Elysian Tail is really good, but the thing is, it's really good because of reasons that are difficult to put into words. Now I know why everybody was so vague about why it's good.
The closest I think I can say is "Every individual part of the game - the sound design, the art, the combat mechanics, and so on - are 'okay' to 'very good,' but they work together so well that the game taken as a whole is more than the sum of its parts."
That's not to say it's perfect. The voice acting in particular keeps getting my attention, and not in a positive way. Meanwhile, the dodging and parrying combat mechanics are slightly clunky - or at least, poorly explained. But seriously, the rest of the game more than makes up for these faults. The story, the art and sound, and, yes, even the "furry" character designs pull me into the earnest and innocent fantasy world that serves as a refreshing counterpoint to the "big-headed child loses their innocence in a big, dark world" indie RPG/adventure games that are so common these days.

NOTE: Please realise this game is not meant to be like the two Shelter games. It is not an animal survival game, but a story driven game about exploration. I see too many people saying it is bad because it is not like the Shelter games. But it is not supposed to be like them.
On to my review then:
Paws.. there is a lot to say. I know you will be seeing me saying to not buy this game, even though I admit: I love it.
This game was great. Storytelling, music, gameplay, the emotions and how Might & Delight have a really good sense for telling stories from an animals perspective.
But then there are the cons. This game is short. Hellishly short. And it saddens me, because I feel like there could have been so much more dangers happening and more bonding between the Lynx cub and her new found friend, the Bear cub.
Despite it being claimed as a puzzle-platformer, there was not very much of either. You do jump a lot and there are some areas that are freakishly well hidden, but it all sums up to not really being in that genre in the long run. If I had to put it anywhere, it's a lot like an explorable storybook, which would be okay if it was longer.
All in All: I am a hardcore (as hardcore as it gets) fan of Shelter 2. But even I can not really recommend this game entirely. It's beautiful, it's stunning and has a lot of exploration to offer, but it falls short on its length and on the platforming, as well as the connection between Lynx and Bear.  Perhaps there will be DLC to iron its issue out, but as it stands right now, you are better off sticking to Shelter 2.

Might and Delight have certainly gone above and beyond with creating the worlds seen in their Shelter games. Paws: A Shelter 2 Game is a standalone expansion on Shelter 2. The music is absolutely beautiful as usual, and the patchwork style graphics take art seen in gaming to a new level.
Taking the role of a baby lynx learning the basics of survival in the wilderness, you follow your siblings and mother around, eating butterflies and other such critters.
Paws: A Shelter 2 Game weaves a beautiful yet heart-breaking story of a baby lynx who finds itself swept away from it's family by a freak wave. During your time in the wild, you put your recently learned skills to the test and follow the footsteps of your mother. Along the way you come across a friend who helps you get through the rough and unforgiving forest that has become your temporary home.
Will the baby lynx ever find it's mother again? Take a look at our
, then head on over to Steam and get downloading!
What prompted you to take Shelter 2 in the opposite direction by putting the player in the paws of one of the baby lynxes?
It seemed a natural progression. A fact echoed by a vocal majority of our fans and supporters, who had made it clear they really wanted the chance to assume control of one of the younglings in a Shelter game. They told us what they wanted, we listened and et voila.
The Shelter series is very much focused on motherhood. Is there a particular reason for you shining the spotlight on mothers?
The theme is largely underrepresented in games. Not just motherhood, but parenthood as a whole and the wave of emotions that comes with the responsibility of taking care of young ones. Also, when trying to come up with the original Shelter concept, members of the team were either parents or making their first inroads into parenthood. That played a big part in the games theme.
Where did you initially get the inspiration for the patchwork graphics seen in each Shelter game?
It’s easy to assume both Shelter 1 and Shelter 2 have the same visual style, but they are born from two separate sources of inspiration. The first games visual style was heavily inspired by Japanese Kamon, which is a form of emblems used to uniquely identify a family or person - not unlike a coat of arms. Whilst the second Shelter was inspired by Russian embroidery ornament patterns.
Why did you decide to release Paws as a standalone game rather than as DLC for Shelter 2?
We felt since the gameplay and story explored different themes to the Shelter series, it warranted a spin-off. If it proves popular we would be open to developing the Paws concept further.
A lot of people seem to be interested in co-op being implemented in Paws. Do you have plans to make this a reality?
We try to listen to feedback from our fans and if there is genuine interest in another Shelter game or co-op then we would be silly to completely ignore it.
Seeing as Shelter 2 has you playing as the mother lynx, and Paws has you controlling one of the babies, will you ever make a standalone game based on Shelter 1 where you play as a baby badger?
Never say never.
What can gamers expect to see from Might and Delight in the future?
We also released what we call a living book along with Paws called The Lonesome Fog. It’s an opportunity to explore other ways of conveying narrative we’re excited about. Apart from that stay tuned for more announcements from us in the coming weeks.

Long time Paradox fan but this new entrant does not (in my opinion) match up to the hype.
There is a lot of new and shiny to grab the attention initially, but it is all very shallow.
1. Combat:  This is just a "bigger number wins" with very little player input.
2. Diplomacy is basically non-existent. As AI is notoriously difficult to programme well in a fluid negotiating system Paradox have gone for the easier route of "The only deal the AI is going to agree to is massively one-sided in their favour". Irrespective of supposed species/cultural preferences. This means they can avoid the AI making stupid deals by forcing the payer to make them instead.
3. Planet development/ Empire Development: Build stuff, research new stuff, build that. Very little so far to make each planet feel unique after the intial clearance/settlement. Some minor balancing of resource generation.....
4. War/Conquest: There seem to be a lot of artificial barriers to carrying out a war of conquest. You can only capture X number of planets before the war finishes, no war after that for Z years with same faction, integration very slow etc etc. Some of these may be realistic but I have the terrible suspicion that they were put there to prevent a good player (not me) from steamrolling and winning too quickly.
All in all I found myself too often playing on "Fast" or "Fastest" waiting for the next bit of research, planet development.
Conclusion: Shallow 4x light that is disappointing given its creators. However your enjoyment may differ and hopefully patches will add some depth!

Crypt is a rhythm-based roguelike where you have to move to a hot beat while you slay and slay and slay. Compared to other roguelikes, there is a huge focus on positioning and tactics. If you take the time to identify the behaviors of each enemy, you will be rewarded with fast, smooth domination to a sick beat.
The pixel art is charming, and a lot of care has been put into making a world that lives and dies to music. You want to fight a giant octopus where each leg makes up part of an orchestra? Done, and each leg you kill knocks out a component of the accompanying song. You want to battle a skeleton necromancer to death metal? Done, and Death Metal is his name too.
Loads of content to unlock, loads of progression. Each failed run brings an opportunity to hire staff for your home base, to buy upgrades for yourself, or to unlock new items and characters. I appreciate the effort taken to making the other characters unique to play; many of them play with remixed versions of the soundtrack, and some of them fight different final bosses.
There is a TREMENDOUS skill component. You may initially -think- that RNG can stuff a run, but there are people out there who regularly, flawlessly win runs with the starting weapon. This game truly tests your ability to read a situation quickly and respond accurately. You like that? Great.
If you can't maintain a rhythm, Crypt probably isn't for you. If you don't particularly enjoy music (!?), same.
GET IT. You'll easily know if you like Crypt before the two hour refund mark hits.
Well worth $5, so captivating and intriguing - music is beautiful, and the whole dystopian aesthetic is just awesome. Tugs on all the right heart strings.

Danganronpa 2 has some small quality of life improvements over the first game and the story gets a good bit more interesting toward the end, but on the whole, it doesn't match up to its predecessor.
The single worst offender is that just like the first, Danganronpa 2 gleefully wastes your time as it pads out the game. By breaking the story into discrete days and nights, it forces you to sit through an announcement at night, a dream sequence immediately thereafter, an announcement in the morning, and breakfast after that. You basically have player agency taken away from you for 5-10 minutes of IRL time every damn day in the game. One would've hoped the sequel would drop this practice.
But while even the first game padded itself out like that, Danganronpa 2 distinguishes itself with flatter characters that are a lot harder to care about. While a large-cast visual novel is rarely going to have deep characterization, here we have one-note disappointments like "Screaming man who yells about bowel movements a lot," and "Christ, we get it; you're meek and accident prone," and "Excessively rude girl." When one character dies, the game insists over and over that she was the heart of the group and had an unwavering force of personality to cover up for the fact that the game does nothing to characterize this bland, blank slate.
This is on top of cases that just don't match up to the first game's. While the murders are more complex, key details come up during the trial rather than the investigation, which makes many of them beyond the reach of your deduction. Instead you just sit there and play some minigames to hammer out convoluted details that the writers couldn't figure out how to get the character to realize by way of the evidence.
And the minigames. My god the minigames. They're bigger, more intrusive, and so much more tedious than in the previous game.
Where I said of the first game that its mysteries were so fun that players might look past the padding and tedium, the math just doesn't add up this time around. With weaker mysteries and a LOT more baggage, Danganronpa 2 never really gets off the ground like its predecessor did.
This, of course, will be lost in the sea of positive reviews, because anime-likers are the worst people.

Solve murders, discover secrets about the island, and learn the truth about what Monokuma is planning this time around (and yes, this plan is full of despair). But that's not all! The story about the Danganronpa universe in this game picks up from where the last game left off, throwing in various elements, old and new. (I won't say anymore about it, as it's best to go into this game knowing as little as humanly possible).
So in conclusion, I thoroughly enjoyed this game. The murders were engrossing, the characters were detailed and well thought out, and the story was AMAZING. This is a worthy edition of the Danganronpa series, in more ways than one (But I won't spoil!).

GALACTIC CIVILIZATIONS III
Turn-based, customizable 4X goodness . . .  IN SPACE.   :-)
Graphics - "Perdy"
Learning Curve - Easy enough to start playing, with tutorial
- At times, higher end gameplay mechanics felt like they could be more plainly explained, if at all
(currently - I had to go look up on online forums for clarifications with some of this)
- Planet invasion and ship battles seemed to lack some depth,
though, for how often these tend to happen,
after a while I was glad that the focus seems to be more on my empire as a whole,
Music - Nicely done epic sounding orchastral soundtrack
Tutorial - Did help get  me started well enough
Length of Play - CAN be set to rather small, yet easily turns into a marathon of fun.
Be sure to save and take breaks.  :-)
In-game customizability - The ship designer tool has a great many parts to choose from.
It takes no time at all to slap parts on a premade hull.
Though, from the time it took to make the custom ships I wanted,
it almost feels like a mini-game in itself  :-)
Combine that with being able to name your ships and planets,
along with the ability to make exceedingly potent "hero" ships using special limited resources,
and I found this a rather gratifying experience.
Side-note - the way this game plays reminds me much of Sid Myer's "Civilization" games
IN SPACE
I count that as a good thing.
Conclusion - Although there were a few places where the features felt lacking depth,
everything combines together for an epic turn-based 4X space game
that I find highly enjoyable.
Also, the mulitplayer function is greatly welcome indeed.  :-)
RECOMMENDED

There is a lot to unpack about this game, and most of it is spoilers, so I apologize if this review comes off somewhat vague. Few tagged spoilers notwithstanding.
I really really enjoyed playing this. The design idea was AWESOME, and I enjoyed every minute of it. When I started, I was worried that kind of extreme minimalist contrast would lead to problems, and it never did. The way the camera shifts angles was also a great idea. The atmosphere worked, the design for the ghosts was awesome, and the placement of the matches/lights kept me on edge without ever feeling unfair. Overall, as a visual and gamePLAYING experience, it was top notch.
However... for me, and especially in a game like this, I am really looking for a story that knocks it out of the park, and while there were a lot of interesting plot choices that kept me intrigued throughout, it just kind of fizzled at the end. It wasn't a bad ending, but it wasn't good either. Almost a lacklustre finish to a great game. So, if you're an extremely story-oriented person, you might not enjoy this one as much as you would have.
Maybe another ending option, maybe harder to get, where
would have felt more satisfying, what with the themes I took from the game's plot.
. But the ending as it is,
So yes, if you like creative and neat aesthetics in your game and solid gameplay, I'd get this. It was a lot of fun and VERY spooky. But if a big portion of your grading system is story, you might want to skip it. Not definitely, it is a very interesting game throughout, but if you're the type who rants about a movie ending for years to come for not delivering (as I often am), consider picking something else.

was released with middling fanfare and mediocre reviews. It was presented as a procedurally generated 4-player cooperative dungeon crawler in the same vein as Dark Souls, with unforgiving combat and challenging enemies, which in principle sounds excellent. Needless to say, there were some very valid reasons for criticism.
The simple geometric aesthetic inexplicably causes overheating on some machines. More than once an enemy started drowning in the floor or got stuck on a ledge. Once the player finds a ranged weapon, most enemies no longer posed a threat. It's entirely possible to move from one randomly generated room into an exact copy. Worst of all, in spite of these flaws the developers have supposedly abandoned all hope on this project and moved onto greener pastures, so these issues with the game will most likely remain.
In spite of all this, I love this game. And you might, too.
distinguishes itself in terms of aesthetic and mood. You are one stray soul summoned by the Brazen Head, a caretaker of sorts, to clean out some pesky monsters in Necropolis. Each character sent in to clean out the riff-raff ends up dead, which your guide will regularly remind you. The nihilism is offset by an aura of the absurd, from the scribblings left behind on the walls of abandoned temples to the descriptions of items you pick up.
Which is endearing, though can be frustrating; don't expect to look at any items and have a clue whether your fiery axe is any better than your glowing red broadsword. Each weapon and item has a rank that gives a general idea of how useful it might be, but beyond that there's no way to effectively gauge your items.
Players can juggle not only weapons but shields, spells, potions, and food. After looting corpses or finding hidden staches, players can craft consumable items to fend of their inevitable demise for a little longer. Players have access to few recipes at the start, but can acquire more over the course of each game. Just bear in mind that while you're crafting or in your menu, your opponents will not be sitting idle.
Most enemies follow particular predictable patterns that you can observe and counter in small engagements. The trick is when you stumble into a mob of knife-wielding fiends supported by ranged enemies. It can get a little hectic, though so long as there is a place to run, most enemies can't catch up to you. Even if they could, your nameless protagonist seems to be the only soul gifted with potential for vertical exploration; feel free to sit on top of a rock and recover while the enemies below putter around like idiots.
In the event you don't manage to scale that rock in time, you'll be cast back to the beginning of the game after being ranked and rewarded tokens that can be used to purchase different color schemes for your doomed heroes or Codexes, which can be purchased for a permanent bonus. Only one codex can be equipped at a time, however, so purchase with care.
With the right codexes and a little luck, it's more than possible to complete the game in under six hours. Players can go back to acquire all the different codexes and colors, though there may not be enough replay value to justify paying full price. It may be worth going back and playing again with different groups of adventurers in co-op, though my experience was limited to exploring alone.
It isn't a perfect game. It has a few bugs, optimization issues, and maybe doesn't feel quite complete. If you like the art, enjoy a challenge, and can catch this game at a discount, it may not astound you but you just might enjoy it.

The Witcher 2 is a single-player fantasy role-playing game by CD Projekt RED, starring Geralt, the hero from the first game released in 2007. Geralt is a witcher, a ghost-haired mutant that can wield swords and magical powers to dispatch foes. Expect a large cast of characters to interact with, plenty of ways to upgrade and customize Geralt to suit your play style, and at least one boss fight against a giant tentacle beast.
From what's been said about the game so far, The Witcher 2 is enormous. The official word is 38 hours long, though it's unclear how much that may vary if you decide to take part in all the side quests and minigames. Like in the first game, your actions while playing affect what happens later. In the sequel, this may mean you'll miss entire towns (as well as the associated storylines and side quests) on your first playthrough. According to the game's official site there'll be four different beginnings and 16 possible endings.
Combat has also received a significant overhaul. Gone is the restrictive timing-based system used in the original, replaced by a more free-form system that should be more familiar to those who play third-person action games. You'll be able to equip lots of different armor pieces this time, as well use weapons, spells and alchemical components to kill your enemies.
It's best to use Geralt's steel blade against humanoids and the silver one for monsters. Geralt's active target is painted with an icon, letting you know who you'll strike with an attack.
The most important thing to be mindful of in combat is your command wheel, which can be brought up by holding the Ctrl key. Bringing this up slows time and allows you to select one of Geralt's magical signs, as well as switch between combat items. Using the magical signs is a must. Even before they're powered up through leveling, these abilities can set enemies on fire (Igni), stun and root them in place (opportunity to perform finishing kill), knock them down and a temporarily dampen incoming damage (Aard), shield (Quen), trap to immobilize enemies (Yrden) and triggers a hex that causes an enemy to fight alongside with us (Axii).  Axii is my favorite sign while fighting with group opponent. Hexing them to fight along your side will reduce their enforcement pressure towards us when they are tightening their fight.
The Witcher 2 looks great. Only hours in you'll be treated to stunning views of enormous, sweeping vistas from the side of a castle under siege. Nearly every scene is populated with plenty of characters; the animations are more realistic than the first Witcher game during conversations and combat. Contrast lighting and warm color tone really brings up Witcher 2 among the best-looking games in existence - only the facial animation is imperfect. Background music and sound effect suit the atmosphere so much plus good voice acting supports a charismatic script really brings up Witcher 2 as a whole fantastic game.
Approaching a sequel to a dense role-playing game can be daunting. If you never played the first, The Witcher 2 stars an established character you may know nothing about and is set in a detailed fictional world you're likely not familiar. Why bother playing if you're not already invested in the story and characters?
So far, a number of reasons The Witcher 2 feels like a older style of role-playing epic: a rich, detailed experience packed with curiosities, creative and flexible quest designs, powerful reasons to explore and deep gameplay mechanics. And, as a bonus, it's much prettier than its predecessor.
Witcher fans that played all the way through the first game are definitely getting something extra here. For you there's an existing emotional bond with some of the characters. When Triss and Geralt walk across the screen and reference past events and the names of lands and cities, there's an added layer of meaning.
If you didn't play The Witcher you'll be missing out on context, but it won't be long until you're caught up in the pressing drama of the sequel. I certainly wouldn't say you should wait to play The Witcher 2 until you've completed the first game. Due to a number of changes, mostly for convenience's sake, The Witcher 2 for now appears to be the better game. There's a definite learning curve when it comes to things like combat, managing the numerous menus and brewing and using potions, but it doesn't take long for it to make sense.
Some role-playing games present choice and consequence in very clear terms. Sometimes you're given points for being good and evil. Your overall moral standing is displayed as a giant glowing meter on your character statistics page. All your decisions are distilled into one numerical value. Sometimes your appearance changes and characters react differently to your presence. The aim of all this is the make your decisions feel like they're having an impact in the world, that the virtual people you're helping or terrorizing remember your actions and, as a result, feel a little bit more human.
In The Witcher 2, there's no meter for good and evil. Instead, Geralt operates outside the reach of a persistent morality rating. During a quest Geralt can choose to help out or tell people to get lost in blunt, explicit terms. The results aren't as simple as unlocking a few extra dialogue options. Instead, there are significant changes to the direction of the quests.
In The Witcher 2, choice is not an illusion. At no point has this been more obvious than how the story develops toward the end of the first Chapter. A decision needs to be made about how to proceed forward, and the impact will radically change how things evolve. It determines the next city you visit, the cast of characters you follow and the quests made available. It changes your entire perspective on the main events of the game.
Though the core sword-slashing combat of The Witcher 2 might strike you as straightforward – time mouse clicks to string together slices – there are a lot of ways to modify Geralt's effectiveness in battle. One of the best ways to secure upgrades is through crafting. Most of everything that can be used and equipped in The Witcher 2 can be crafted. You can make traps, steel and silver swords, armor and even crafting components. When you have the appropriate Diagram, usually purchased from vendors, you need to go talk to crafter NPCs standing around in town. By interacting with them a crafting menu can be called up that displays all your Diagrams as well as whether or not you have the proper components. If you do, then after a simple button press the item is generated. There's no percentage chance to fail and there's no associated mini-game.
The value and function of potions in The Witcher 2 differs from fantasy role-playing game standards. You can't consume health restoration potions mid-battle in this game. Instead, you need to drink them before a fight begins, which gives Geralt temporary boosts to things like damage and health regeneration. It's a great system because it means you can't run into a conflict without thinking.
Making potions is similar to crafting gear. Vendors sell Formulas for potions, and by combining the appropriate plants special brews are created. The actual process of creation isn't handled by a vendor, but instead accessible through Geralt's mediation menu. Here you'll find listed all your Formulas for potions, bombs and oils. If the proper ingredients are in your inventory, the product can be outputted with a keystroke. Simple enough.
Of course, if you have dozens of times. The Witcher 2 has four different beginnings and 16 possible endings. Enjoy !

In the gaming climate as of late, two things are regarded as near constants. The first is that indie games have small development teams, while the second is that any game which has a longer-than-usual development cycle never turns out to live up to expectations (we're looking at you, Timeshift and Duke Nukem Forever).
Dust: An Elysian Tail basically takes the cake on both counts.
With the exception of the voice acting and the music design, everything in Dust: AET was done by a single person. Dean Dodrill took the artwork, animation, coding, storyline and even the creation of a PC version he deemed worthy of release and spent nearly half a decade getting the job done.
And it definitely shows, but not how you'd expect. Dust: AET is, indie job or no, one of the most well-polished and complete 2D MetroidVania-style games to grace the PC. To find something "better" for our trusty desktops/laptops, you technically have to break the law and go trawling for roms.
While the anthropomorphic/"furry" aesthetic may be something of a turn-off for some, the artistic style of the characters in this game is like the sprite-based graphics of Terraria, a choice made by the developer (and the singular is actually correct in this instance) and nothing more.
Scratch beneath it and you get the usual trappings of the MetroidVania world; a gradual widening of the protagonist's repertoire, the need to backtrack and revisit locations to satisfy the needs of the completionist and so on, all wrapped up with an RPG-esque level-up and equipment system and garnished with over-the-top (at least on Dust's part) combat that wouldn't look out of place in the love-child of Devil May Cry and Streets of Rage.
At the end of the day, Dust: AET is an absolute blast to play and, even at its full price, I'd say it's worth it.

The one thing NightSky gets right is being a soothing game to play. The silhouetted visuals, color palette full of blues and violets, and ambient / new age soundtrack combined with its gentle pace make this physics-based puzzle game a relaxing ride.
Unfortunately, that's about all I can praise here. Given the near-universal acclaim of other reviewers, I'll probably be shouted down as in the minority here - but this game just didn't do it for me and I can list a number of reasons why.
The plot is a complete throwaway. There are a few screens trying to explain the origin of the ball players roll around, but that explanation never goes anywhere. It's the kind of tactic that screams "indie game trying too hard to be important."
The core mechanic ("roll a ball to the end in a side-scrolling maze") isn't revolutionary and is mostly well-implemented, but it has some issues. The "wall riding" and "air control" mechanics in particular are awkward (as in one must continue to hold down the direction the ball was originally traveling to continue rolling, no matter which way it is going - but be sure to switch directions mid-air once it falls off). There is no native gamepad support - an analog stick would have been desirable for this reason.
While there is a good bit of variety with fun contraptions and game mechanic modifications that are used in some scenes, the problem with these scenes is that they are often easier than the standard "control the marble directly" levels - which are already pretty easy.
And that's probably the biggest issue with the game. This game's normal mode is way too easy. There are way too many scenes that only require the player to hold the right arrow to complete. There is an advanced mode, but since it contains no prompts at all (including what the controls are), players will likely need to play through most of the normal mode to learn the game's mechanics before tackling that mode. Personally, I had no interest in running through the game a second time after I had to force myself to finish the first run.
There are plenty of great physics-based puzzle games out there. That makes it hard to recommend one that doesn't do anything unusual except be low-key - and has some flaws, to boot. I'd give it a pass.

I was told the witcher 2 is where the witcher series gets good.  Unfortunately that is not true.  While in most ways it is a massive improvement over the witcher 1, which was one of the worst games I have ever played, minor improvements on a terrible product do not make a good product.
Some of the more glaring issues I have ran into during play.
-Extremely crash prone, particularily when rapidly rotating the camera or moving through doors.
-Terrible boss fights.  Bosses have thus far come in two varieties, terrible god of war ripoffs with illogical ways of resolving the fight (a monster described as having indestructably thick skin is killed by dropping a hand grenade on it for instance) or fights against humans who are more capable than they have any reason to be (superhuman ability needs to be explained in the story!).   The fights all share serious issues as well, such as the bosses starting to attack you while the introductory cutscene fades into gameplay and before you can control, meaning you start most bossfights dead or with large chunks of HP missing.
-Dissapointing story.  As with the witcher 1, there is a good story here, but it is delivered in such a terrible way.  As an example one of your NPC comrades is supposed to be so deep and angsty.  Reason for his angst?  Doesnt like being called names.  Or the time when the guy who has framed you for murdering a king asks you, without a hint of sarcasm, why you are chasing him.  Not quite as offensively badly delivered as the witcher 1 however.
-Terrible character progression.  You can choose between three progression trees, Mage, Swordsman and Alchemist.  There is no point going down the mage tree as the 1 usefull spell is given to you at the start, is not improved by progressing down the tree and you are punished for using it if you do try to build for magic.  The swordman tree is reasonable but overshadowed by the alchemy tree and the alchemy tree is simply overpowered.
-Terrible combat.  The movement is, to put it nicely, janky as all hell.  On top of that attacks have more or less range than they appear to (both Geralt's and the enemies) and you are stuck in animations for obscene times.  This is made worse by wierd enemy behaviour (for example, enemies have set zones where they are active for example, if you move from the zone while trying to fight them they teleport away and then you have to do a little dance on top of thier spawning point to get them to come out.)  And woe be anyone who runs into a ranged unit, they are 100% accurate and if you are within LOS when they decide to begin thier attack animation you will be hit no matter what you put between you and them.
-Generally bad game design in many ways such as quests which are partially broken if you do not complete them in the right way, or having to follow NPCs from point to point in order to progress but those NPCs having incredibly terrible pathfinding, often adding several hundred percent to the time a journey should take (ie a 1:30 journey becomes 8:30), or being given choices of dialogue but only one of those choices being right and the rest being instant gameovers (and instant gameovers which make no sense in the game as well which is the worst part).  And as the icing on the cake they intersperse the game with sections where you play as other characters.  While playing as these characters you have the same base stats as your Geralt, but you lose Geralts abilities.  In some fights the lost abilities are only your magic signs, which is somewhat bearable, but in others you lose your signs, your ability to dodge, your ability to move towards targets while attacking, your ability to use items (etc.), its really goddamn terrible...
It looks nice, a beautiful game no doubt, but that is prettymuch its only good point and it doesnt outweigh the rest.   I recommend avoiding this as well as the witcher 1 and just going straight into 3.  3 is the only good witcher game.

Only half the story, some pretty glaring plot contradictions (which may or may not be corrected if the second half is ever released), and occasionally frustrating controls.
And yet, I liked the game.
Why?
Well, for me (and I am really really bad at platformers of any kind), the gameplay was both challenging and easy enough to make the game progress at a comfortable pace, but not feel too easy or too impossible (and I have muddled through the original version of Abe's Oddysee btw). A tentative thumb up.
First of all, Stellaris is NOT a grand strategy game like other Paradox's titles - it's more Sin of a Solar Empire than CIV or EU. You'll need a dozen or so hours into the game before the realization hits and Paradox is definitely fudging the truth and letting their CK/EU/HoI reputation influence unwary buyers.
You'll definitely enjoy the first dozen hours or so of the game and the sense of wonder as you explore the galaxy is the best I've seen in the genre. However, if you are looking for something deep like Crusader Kings etc, wait for the inevitable DLCs. Currently, diplomacy, empire management are bare boned while trade, culture, espionage are non-existent.
Currently, this is a vanillar CIV V with no DLCs - the potential is there but it's definitely not here yet. This is perhapes one of the weakest, mechanically speaking, or all Paradox's franchises.
On the technical front, game runs without an single issue for 30 hrs or so on a 5 year old machine so that's a big plus in this age of launch day disasters. =)

I really have a love/hate relationship with this game. On the one hand, I love the setup, the character design, and the quirkly portrayal of Red herself.  The game itself... not so much. As others have said, it's like they tried to throw too much into it, and ended up with a bit of a mess.  I didn't have the game killing glitches others have reported, and it's important to note that they may have been patched, but there were a few incredibly annoying issues.  Two stand out:
1. Leaping from pipe to pipe (branch, vine, etc)  is a crapshoot.  I'm seriously unclear over how the game determines you want to grab a pipe or leap/drop past it, but it figured wrong A LOT.  Or maybe my timing had to be perfect, I don't know.
2. Racing. Holy hell in a handbasket, that horse carriage race is unforgiving.  Any mistake at all, and you're screwed, because the camera follows the carriage you're chasing, rather than you, so if you fall slightly behind, you suddenly can't see where you're going.  Not only that, but the camera angle often makes it difficult to see *why* you failed.
Relatively minor issues include:
Keyboard mapping is terrible. Seriously, in this day and age, not using WASD is just being stubborn. And the attack keys seem poorly thought out.  If you couldn't remap, I'd even consider this a major issue.
Limited attack vectors. Basically, if the enemy isn't in one of the 8 major cardinal directions from you, you miss.
Unclear instructions on using magic.  I still can't figure out how to charge up my area attack.
Random rules. Well, not random exactly, but at points, the game will forcibly place Red in a specific spot, even if you're halfway across the screen, and place invisible barriers in place because it wants you to fight the boss battle or solve the puzzle in one specific way.  In one spot, if you merely use an alternate path to a floating island, the game even breaks.
A LOT of platforming, some of it pretty advanced.  My biggest gripe about platforming puzzles in general?  They're not affected by the difficulty level you select, and any mistake results in death.  Fortunately, I had some warning after seeing a speed run, but wow.  Oh, and the aforementioned camera angles make some of the jumps really tough to judge (in some cases, you even have to jump blindly).
Checkpoints. While the death checkpoints are spaced pretty fairly, the game exit checkpoints can be pretty far apart.  You quit the game to do something else, and when you come back, you find you have to replay from the start of the chapter.  Grrr.
Honestly, if I hadn't found a trainer for this game, I doubt I'd have been able to finish it.
Looking back on this review, it looks like I hated the game.  Indeed, one portion had me so frustrated, I uninstalled it.  So why am I not warning everyone away?  Because I can still see the potential in this game.  Red herself is great; she's normally so serious that the occasional Whedoneque joke caught me off guard and made me laugh.   The universe is appealing, and I can see a lot of potential there.  The story isn't as clever as the devs probably thought, but as a seed, it's good.  Woolfe himself was a rather dull villain, but the cliffhanger leaves room to fix that.  I want people to buy this game (on sale, because lord knows it's not worth full price) to encourage Rebellion, its new owners, to make a superior second chapter.

So knew every nuance of the games and their combat systems etc.  They wanted another more modern Might and Magic so...  In a nut shell these players are a lot better at Might and Magic games than I am and so the games difficulty is a really tough ride for a casual player like myself.
I ended up cheating but, it’s a single player game so in the end no one gets hurt by me adjusting the charters so I would have more fun… I gave my characters and few extra points to spend in Attributes and a few for Skills.  I raised some of the skills limits for the classes I played, so instead of maxing out at expert – some of the skills maxed out at master or grand master.  That way I didn’t end up with too many skill points at the end of the game.  The combat never got easy for me, but it was fun and a lot quicker.  I got on with doing quests and following the story – which by the way would do any Might and Magic game I have ever played justice.  I’m going to try it again in an un adjusted way – except I will add primordial magic to all the mage classes so I don’t need an Arch mage in my party every time to Identify and search for hidden magics…   I can really recommend this game if you like good old fashioned RPG’s.

For what it is, NightSky is a nice game. As a rule, I'm generally not very fond of physicsy games, because success ultimately has a tendency to become downright random at the best of times. NightSky does succumb to this problem on occasion, but most of the time it holds together surprisingly well.
You control a sphere of some sort, and sometimes pinball flippers or spinning paddles or some other odd object. The goal is to make it to the end of the three screens which make up each level. The means of accomplishing this vary, and there's what I really enjoy about NightSky. You never know what you're going to get in the next level. Where a game of this type would traditionally feature a couple specific mechanics that you learn and utilize over each world, growing more complex and piling up over time, NightSky just kind of does what it pleases. In one level, you might be using a speed boost key to spin through U-bends and climb higher, and in the next the key you pressed to go faster now reverses gravity. You finish that level, and now maybe you're in some sort of vehicle which could do any sort of thing. You just have to figure out the shifting rules from level to level, and it keeps things nice and fresh the whole way through, while alleviating
NightSky can have a few annoying spots, or entire annoying levels. But overall the game manages to be just challenging enough without being too frustrating. As for visuals... well, I have to admit, I'm growing sick of games copping LIMBO's black foreground motif, but beyond that it does have its own style, and can be downright pretty at times.
There are a series of bonus levels unlocked after completing all of the other levels and finding enough of the secret stars hidden in certain levels, and the higher difficulty mode rearranges levels to trip you up à la Master Quest, if you're into the additional challenge. If you're looking for a physics platformy sphere rolling game with a little problem solving, then boy did you luck out with NightSky.

Alpages: The Five Books is an indie horror arcade title by Nicolas Bernard, the same developer that created Terror Labs. SnipZ, and Showtime 2073. As its genre and store page suggests, you run around killing zombies and other supernatural creatures, all while trying to find 5 books. Each book has a unique enemy that spawns somewhere on the map after you pick it up, the kicker being that they are invincible.
Let it first be said that there are absolutely no worthwhile features to this game. Everything from the poor title screen that has an abundance of spelling and grammatical errors, to the uninspired gameplay itself. Enemies spawn atrociously fast, meaning that if you actually spend your time playing the game the way that the developer intended, you would be doing nothing but fighting zombies, picking up health, and replenishing your ammo supply instead of making any progress toward finding the books. It's best to just keep on running around the needlessly large map instead; it took me about 15 minutes to find 3 of the 5 books.
That being said, I had to turn my attention away from the game and in doing so I instinctively pressed ESC to pause. When I came back to my PC some two minutes later, I found out that the ESC key isn't pause at all, it actually resets the whole game. I have no idea what kind of crap that is, but the developer needs to change that, and fast. It's just the ugly corn-filled turd on the crap cake that is Alpages: The Five Books. Even the HUD is boring, and for some reason when you collect 1 life, you get two, but when you die you lose two lives as well. There are multiple instances of this type of attention to detail missing from this game.
Alpages: The Five Books isn't even worth the $0.54 CAD when it's on a 50% off sale. The world and atmosphere are bland, the gameplay is tried and true but somehow even worse than most indie zombie shooters, and it's set at an unnatural and unfairly high difficulty. To put it bluntly the game just isn't fun in any aspect; unless running around a huge, empty map collecting books, lives, ammo, and health with endlessly, and frequently, spawning zombies that hit too hard is your idea of enjoyment.
