Oh god, how can I start this? First of all I hope you understand my position and dont downvote just because of a fanboy impulse. Thanks for reading. I tried I REALLY REALLY tried to like this game but I just can't (look at my play time, no joking around or justifying over false basis). The story, graphics and music are awesome but the combat mechanics and the insane amount of walking around with a robotic-like animation kills it. I've even tried to play it again with the full combat rebalance mod but... the mechanic itself its soooo broken that I just can't like it. I feel like I have little to no control over Geralt or combat in general for many reasons:
- The awful auto targeting mechanic... Anybody would expect presing a key or pushing the stick towards a specific direction and hit the strike button and see your character attack in that direction but no... Geralt attacks the character that he is auto targetting. I've died SO many times because of that. Trying to cast an Igni sign to the front and seeing Geralt turn around and cast it on another direction is priceless... The same goes with sword attacks. I really felt like I had more control on the witcher 1 and that is saying A LOT.
-Animations are confusing and illogical. Sometimes I hit an enemy and it doesn't count as a hit because the did an evade movement (even though the sword actually FULLY touched them). I thought ok then the same goes for me right? NOPE. On your evade/roll animation, if you get  touched, you are hit... Then sometimes the enemies appear to be stun locked and you think YEAH I can keep hitting them. NOPE. They magically recover from the middle of a "stun" animation in the middle of your next swing and OWN YOU (on higher difficulties). You really can never tell when its safe to keep slashing or back away so the game becomes a slash roll away, slash, roll away, repeat and pray that your next slash doesnt get "magically evaded" and your foe attacks you in a second of invincibility...
-Attack animations are not in your control, sometimes the animation is "cooler" but it takes longer to land a hit and you never know when will what animation appear so you are basically F-ed since you can plan your attacks so well. Theres no pattern the animations are random, no combos.
-You cant block while you walk, yes you read right, YOU CANT.
-Did I mention the walking? You have to walk too much, the backgrounds look nice but will get old and boring once you complete the monster hunt missions and get an empty area.
-Parry+Riposte mechanic is broken. Sometimes you get the symbol to do it and even though the parry animation shows and you block the hit and actually execute the attack, the enemy sometimes keeps attacking you and OWN YOU since you are in the middle of a swing, defenseless.
-You cant drink potions in the middle of a fight and it gets annoying if you sum the time it takes for geralt to sit down, open the menu, make the potion, drink the potion, then stand up.
-At some point you'll find out that you can beat the game spamming Igni signs.
And the cherry on top of the cake of the cake: the game doesn't run so well. Witcher 3 and Gorund Zeroes run much better than this game, and that's a shame :( The game autosaves a lot and dont erase the much older saves. There are so many saves that on one point the load game screen starts to need a considerable amount of seconds to even show up. Sometime it just crashes and brings down Steam too (I have to end the process and restart steam).
Sum up: Personally I think this game its a step in the right direction but it didn't reach the goal as it was supposed to. Thankfully the witcher 3 fixed every detail I'm complaining about. Even though it still shares the auto target function it lets you back away from the middle of a possible suicide attack by letting you cancel it through rolling or evading. The monsters' health bar blinks when they are about to attack, potions during combat and quick navigation through menus are back, etc. That game is what this one was supposed to be, but died trying.
I reapeat: I hope you understand my position and dont downvote just because of a fanboy impulse. Thanks for reading.

Abzû is a beautifully animated exploration game where the main draw is being able to take your time swimming around underwater, interacting with lush aquatic life. It gives you the opportunity to collect shells, release wildlife, and meditate on different statues as part of its trophy/acheivement gathering system. It has a linear plot and there isn't really room to navigate away from that sequence. Though you have the freedom to explore the seascapes provided, the game makes it very obvious when you're straying too far from the intended path and will re-direct you. The plot gradually gets a bit darker, but is presented entirely visually with the assistance of music (no dialogue). Your character never speaks, and you get the most out of the sort of abstractly constructed plot they present when you take your time exploring the places you find.
The soundtrack is beautiful, the animations are lovely, and overall I'm entirely pleased with the $20 I spent on this game. I got 4 hours total playtime out of my first time around, and I'm sure I will play it again in my effort to find all the mystery achievements. If you enjoy a game you can take at your own pace without the pressure of health bars, shooters, etc, I'd most certainly recommend it.

TL;DR: It's worth the price and moreso if it's on sale. Is a good way to get into several kinds of games. Also includes a concept called "FUN".
[Length - average]: This game is too short. Depending on how much of a completionist you are- my playtime would have been 3 hours less if I hadn't gotten lost a couple times while looking in every nook and cranny to get to some of the hidden locations for the lost friends before giving in to frustration and googling it. I also don't think it has a lot of replay value.
[Difficulty - good]: There's not much to say about this, you've got the casual, medium, hard and 1-Hit KO levels. I would say some of the platforming and the 6 Trials are a challenge regardless of which mode you set the game to though.
[Combat - excellent]: Being a sword-wielding-furry-assassin with a cat-like-bat-thing that can shoot lightning and fire, in addition to lightbulbs, who can then do screen-clearing combo attacks is kind of awesome...
[Music/Sound - good]: I couldn't hear the actual music most of the time because of all the exploding enemies and other sound effects but when I did hear it, it matched the surroundings perfectly. The sound effects are also spot on and paired with the music, proceeded to make this 25 year old freak the heck out in Sorrowing Meadow (I would recommend not letting your young children see the spiders or mansions).
[Voice Acting - good]: All the voices were decent which is saying something considering I try to mute that feature most of the time because of how bad it is usually. Fidget's voice actor, especially, nailed it in cutscenes with emotions or humor and her interactions with Dust really made me like the little sidekick.
[Graphics - excellent]: I love the artstyle which is simple yet detailed at the same time and allows for even toasters like mine to run it flawlessly...unless you turn on weather and bloom effects which ruins the art and your framerate simultaneously!
[Story/Characters - excellent]: The story is very short and straightforward for the most part. It's not bad though because it's told well and the characters are what really brings it to life. I would almost describe the game's plot as a prologue or origin story because of...
[The Ending - good]: Other than feeling empty because you have to find something else to play now- It satisfies you by wrapping up the main point of the game while giving you the craving for a sequel it so kindly dangles above you.

Overall, this game isn't exactly the best game I've had from Paradox, it needs a ton of work imo in terms of gameplay.
Although, for the time spent playing this game, i'll say this much. I played one match for a solid 8 hours, and concluded that when you've established a 60k stack fleet and fight other 30k to 40k stack fleets, the game becomes incredibly laggy.
There happens to be no actual limit to the size of the fleet other than what you have access to control, thus late game becomes pretty pointless as its no longer challenging for you, (as the AI already will win), and suppose you are? , you're fighting nations on a capital to capital battle basis for a few slabs of a system (3 to 4 at most)  (Literally, if they have 50 or so systems in their control, I can only take two or three at most) which take a valid 6+ years to take over each time due to the war system. This 6+ year time even on fastest was taking me nearly 2+ hours just to take a couple of cities at a time!
To take say, a 50 system nation on the map, this took me nearly 6 hours to achieve in one play through, which was rediculous considering how nations beside me were much larger and could take way more than I could via war demands.
Ultimately, I'm not exactly impressed in how diplomacy works in this game as it seems pretty pointless considering that finding an allied AI nation isn't really existant except if they are weaker than you are. Based on what I've established on the game, I had half the map vassalized on a 1000 star gameplay, and I've concluded that early game is much more entertaining yet towards the end there isn't really much to do once you've conquered most of the map.
I was expecting to do more things in the tech tree in late game that might have destroyed entire fleets, or had access to more potentially destructive weapons (Like weaponized planets, bigger ships other than a battleship). By the way, fighting in the early game (first 50+ years) isn't even worth it half the time, because the AI will ultimately crush you. They don't have any balancing to make them remotely on par with you, so don't even bother starting a war until you've established yourself economically, technologically, superior to them because if you lose your entire fleet in one go, consider yourself done because the nation beside you will wreck you.
As far as conquering goes, suppose you do take a few planets? Guess what, the population hates your guts, better off purging the entire planet and repopulating it with a colony ship, because slavery is absolutely pointless. Be careful not to lose it to the nation that you just took it from, otherwise troll on you because you have 5 more years to wait to take it back over! Rinse and repeat for six hours and that can get pretty frustrating.
TLDR; Simply put, this game has balancing and lack of complexity that bothers me from previous Paradox games, if you were expecting this to be similar to Hearts of Iron III, EUIV, or CK2, forget it because this is something pretty new. Even though it drops this complexity, it leaves a sour taste in your mouth considering it takes several hours to take over a nation bit for bit, rather than the whole thing. This game isn't terrible, but it needs some more work in terms of diplomacy, military, espionage, which makes up 99.99% of the game.
I'll give it a 6/10, maybe some updates will change my mind, but I'd rather play something else rather than spending several hours trying to take small slabs of a nation at a time when I could just play EUIV and take more over in less time. This is a decent game to play for an hour or two with a small map, but don't think you're going to play this game with 1000 stars for a week or two long without some form of lag, lack of interest, etc.

Abzu is a short, relaxing game that is primarily about exploration and visual stimulation.  It can be summarized as swim around and look at the pretty fishies.  That may not sound like much, but Abzu's execution is superb.  The environments and use of color is excellent, the soundtrack creates a great atmosphere, and overall it is worth experiencing.  It is essentially a walking simulator, with a bit more gameplay, done well.  This is what that whole sub-genre should strive to be.
However, the game is short.  You will beat it in less than 3 hours.  If you like exploring, taking your time, and pausing to look at things you might take 3 hours.  If you are more goal oriented it might only take you 1.5 hours.  This alone isn't a problem, the game is the exact length it needs to be.  Any longer and it would start to drag on.  The problem stems from the $20 price tag, which is very high.  Most people would not feel like they got $20 worth of gaming out of this.
Abzu is probably more realistically worth around $5 or less.  A great experience, but not a whole lot of that experience.  I would recommend wishlisting it and picking it up on a sale.

I've been playing this game for 11 hours now, over the course of 2 play sessions.  TLDR - I love it, buy it, it's amazing and well worth the price!
I'm still very much in the exploration phase of the game, founding new colonies, meeting other empires and exploring with my science ships.  I've been running the game at normal speed with the odd pause to catch up, and there is never a time when nothing is going on and I feel bored.
I know there have been some complaints about the research system.  Basically you get to pick from a small number (never less than 3) projects to research.  These projects are weighted by what you have just unlocked and your progress in the game.  So there is a loose tech tree of sorts, but you aren't limited by a set tech tree like say, Civ V, where you know what is coming and quickly build an optimal path that will be repeated with every play though.  With the Stellaris system there is no obvious path to follow and it more realistically follows real discoveries, where scientist look for funding to work on a project.  More importantly it keeps the game fresh and very repayable.
As to the depth, another complaint.  I keep finding whole new game systems I haven't really encountered yet.  Planetary armies and air forces, multi-species empires, the list goes on.  For espionage, I imagine that is something that will come with DLC.
Oh, the Paradox DLC model.  Sure they really crank out the DLC for their games, but they match that with a low entry price.  $39 in a market where many games cost #60.  Even if you don't buy the DLC it always comes with a free patch with many new systems, expanding the game at no additional cost.
I've been a big Paradox fan since CK2 and this is a great additional to the grand strategy family.

I love this game.  I've played it for well over one hundred hours and I've never actually beaten it.
I think the party generation in this game is excellent.  There are 12 classes (4 races each with 3 unique classes) and 4 party slots.  It's a lot of fun to make different party compositions and try them out, abandoning them and refining your group when the game gets too hard.  I'm not going to pretend to be particularly good at this genre: I've never beaten M&M 6 either and I've played over a hundred hours of that one too.  I did beat the first half of M&M 4&5 World of Xeen, but unfortunately lost my save file.
The graphics in this game are great, although I do have issues with lag.  The frame rate will be smooth at 60+, but when walking through the world it often stutters hard for a second or two occasionally, presumably while loading the world around you.  I tried installing the game on my SSD but it still does it.  Regardless, the artwork of the character portraits is excellent, although the small selection of portraits gets stale very quickly, as do the character barks.  When affected by negative conditions such as Poison, the portraits reflect it in a very satisfactory manner.  My favorite is when a character is hit unconscious (health below zero but not yet below the lethal threshold), the portrait appears very damaged.  Think Doom guy style.
All in all I think this game is well worth a try if you enjoy first-person hack'n'slash dungeon crawlers.
Score: 72%
Would be higher but voices get repetitive quickly and the performance when moving through the world should be better.  There are also some minor bugs that I've encountered like pressing n and m at the same time and having both menus open on top of each other.  If you enjoy the genre or are interested in it, give it a try, otherwise you'll probably want to pass.

This game has pro's greatly outweighing the con's and is worth even the full price (strongly recommend the Deluxe version including the genuinely great Might and Magic VI game). There is considerable depth and rewards from exploration, party play and skillful tactics to make the game enjoyable and (if the first "Con" is solved first) well worth it.
The story diverges from the other MM games and was made to kowtow to the MM Heroes games. It is neither interesting nor fun.
Cons:
Playing, even after purchasing on Steam, requires UPLAY and a Ubisoft account. Players have had numerous problems with this and 90% of the complaints are entirely based on this. Those complaints are valid. I recently read the riot act to one of the Ubisoft developers who viisited the forum for this game, making it clear that players require this to at least be seamless. I recommend opening a Ubisoft and Uplay account first, then, succeeding with that consider purchasing the game on Steam.
Movement is not free flowing like in Might and Magic 6-8 and Wizardry 8, and there is no flying. However there are three things wrong with grid movement, limited visibility, enemies suddenly popping up that were not visible in the distance and fixed time and distance, one grid box at a time. The first two of those limitations are not true for this game, however, because enemies are visible in the distance and vision is only limited by distance and obstructions.
Unlike the other Might and Magic games in the series, it is not possible for your characters to reach their full potential before the end of the game. Players are forced to choose a subset of potential abilities and only develop those. There are only 3 skill points per level-up and a typical ending level of 37 including all DLC and extra quests. Starting at level 1 that gives 108 skill points in the game (versus 160-210 skill points to reach full potential) in addition to what you start with, but each Grandmaster skill costs 25, Master skill costs 15 and expert skill costs 7, to be eligable for a trainer to train you on that Expert, Master or Grandmaster skill. Plus the GM level is much more powerful than Master which is much more powerful than Expert. That is a good thing but if you spread your skill points out too much you will never get there.  The remedy is to carefully play, early on, where those skill points will go and then stick to it. Do not neglect side skills like Endurance (gives hit points) and Mysticism (gives mana points) which are very powerful.
The experience in the game is fixed, mainly coming from quests and there are quests that only parties containing characters of a certain race and class can do. This is not a bad thing in itself, making replays more interesting, but because there are too few quests in the game to reach full potential it is a negative thing. The DLC is cool, but does not provide enough additional experience to make much of a difference.
Pros:
The creatures and situations are widely varying with numerous different environments and difficulty levels. Very difficult foes you might otherwise run into too early generally have a warning... heed those until your party is stronger.
Many of the dungeons contain puzzles to be solved and many of the chests contain riddles. I find those fun and interesting, but there are numerous sites with answers if you become frustrated. Many of the MM games contain riddles and puzzles but this one has quite a bit of that.
The boss fights, of which there are many, are difficult but doable, and careful planning and development of your characters prior to that point is richly rewarded. This is a lot of fun and very well integrated into the story.
The level progression, limited as it is by the scarcity of skill points/levels/experience in the game is still fun and each Expert level is very powerful. When the party characters start becoming Master in various skills and kinds of magic the party as a whole becomes much more powerful. Areas that were inexcessible due to tough foes become doable, opening up much new exploration. The Grandmaster level is so much more powerful than even Master that it is ridiculous (and very fun). Even though skill points are scarce, using them wisely and in a focused manner can make the party capable of facing even the toughest foes in the game. Careful planning is rewarded and mediocre planning is punished. This, more than anything else, makes the game fun and interesting.
There are many different ways to play the game effectively. All of the characters are powerful, but in very different ways. For example a melee character that starts out hitting half the time for 20 damage might eventually wield hits approaching 500 damage. There is plenty of power to win the game using either melee, range, magic or any of various strategic combination. This game shines in these respects.
It really is a lot of fun, including replays
This game is so much more fun than other music games. It combines rhythm with combat, which makes it more challenging than either. The randomly generated dungeons also makes the game more playable.

***WARNING, SPOILERS***
TL;DR: Lifelong fan says buy some of the older games and play them from GoG, not this one.
Long story: I've been a fan of the series since I was born, I've beat MM6 (and loved it), MM7 (and loved it) and MM8 (and loved it), I tried this game hoping for another one of those three (I didn't play 9, but I've heard enough to not want to, I might eventually try it, but as of time of writing, I have not) but too much was changed, the forced grid sucked (angles were a lifesaver in the games I've played, rotate your party right and they have cover, but your enemies are wide open) also, the freedom of the earlier games was destroyed by the forced grid here, the way time passed only when you move from space to space was flowbreaking for me, for lack of a better word.
The last stand approach to combat (Locking you in place if you're in melee range of a hostile) was again, horrible, part of the old fun was being able to run back into town, almost dead, trailing an army of angry monsters, sleep and heal in the inn, then go rejoin the fray alongside the guards.
And (I may be remembering this wrong because I stopped caring) but it was forced turn based combat, DISCLAIMER: I like turn based combat and in fact, love D&D and other turn based games, BUT, that's not Might and Magic, In the other games I mentioned, it was a crutch until you figured out the combat (or got specific endgame weapon & spell combos) and it was useful to take a minute so you can breathe and strategize, I used it almost all game (again, endgame combos shut down TBC) but you could always switch it to whatever worked as you needed, It just feels odd to me.
Finally, (and this is more of a issue with Ubisoft than this game) the universe is new, different, and NOT, Might and Magic, Might and Magic has aliens, blasters, robots, and space ships, the gods are kept vague (I don't remember any ever being named) this new universe has none of that as far as I can tell. The Ironfists are gone, The Kreegans are gone, The Ancients are gone, (and this already happened but...) the planet Enroth is gone. I don't mean that these things are destroyed (Except Enroth...) None of them ever happened, all that rich lore from games 1-9? all that stuff from Heroes 1-4? Never. Happened.
So, to bring an end to my long rant, don't buy this, the older games might not have the best graphics, but they have the heart, soul, and fun this game never will have.
The only positive thing I can say for this is that I got Might and Magic 6 with it, but even then, I should have bought it from GoG for (about) $5 less.

"The audio cuts out, the UI isn't responsive, and the game overall runs very poorly." This is the statement I made in my refund request.
After playing Golf With Your Friends with a couple buddies of mine for 3 hours, the game had grown kind of stale. I was eager to find another mini-golf game to play online with my friends, and after finding Golf It!, I was pretty excited, to say the least. However, this excitement quickly grew into frustration, and within less than an hour of playing the game, I was already ready to request a refund. Here's why:
After booting up the game, the resolution wasn't right and it wasn't fullscreen, so I went into the options to change this. I found my resolution setting and enabled fullscreen, and the home screen looked really good! However, when I started clicking buttons on the home screen, I noticed something was way off; the game wasn't accurately registering where my mouse was, so to click any button (like to host a game or even change other settings) I had to scroll around the button I wanted to click until it showed that I was on it. Another hard night in Steam Town.  I peer into the streets looking for a little fun, but the sight hits me like a Mack Truck full of garbage:  Boss Activision has the city tonight.  A hundred Call of Duty hatchet men; the gunfire's so thick you'd barely be able to see the movie tie-ins pimping their wares if they didn't swarm like the bugs under a June streetlight.  Distinguished old names walk with 'em, but I shake my head in disgust.  I see the bruises and I know old man Activision already bought their souls.
Crows will come to eat Activision's buffet.  But me?  I just pour myself a glass of the hard stuff.  That's when she comes through my door: all black dress and ivory skin like something out of an old movie or a graphic novel.  Looks to kill for.  The whisky burns my guts like a lit molotov and I know I'm going to play this game.  She says she's got a job for me, "survival horror just like the good old days."  I take another drink and think to myself,
I ask for her name and she tells me through a sly smile, "White Night."
Another hard night in Steam Town.
Before you wretch at the prospect of another horror game on Steam, know that White Night is pretty cool.  Okay, so it's got a lot of questionable gameplay elements we knew weren't very good in 1996, a story that's handicapped by its reliance on cliche, and the old cardinal sin of scrapping the visual-interactive medium to tell a story through document collection.  Wait!  Don't leave yet!  You'll notice I still gave this one a thumbs up.  And it's not even a half-hearted "this game is inoffensive but completely mediocre, so my thumb is really dead center but I'm in a good mood today" thumbs up.
White Night opens up with a sequence where you control a period 1930's car driving down an empty New England road in the middle of the night.  Your headlights illuminate billboards along the road with the game's credits while a mournful jazz song plays.  Something like this tells me the developers made something special and they know it.  It sets the tone for a detective horror story with a 1930's noir style with aplomb and lets you really drink in the game's visual aesthetic.
Breathe in.  Exhale.  This game rules atmosphere and it doesn't let up after that strong intro.  The main character peppers his inner monologue with metaphors as colorful as the game is monochrome.  His lines are read with the steady sort of grim determination you'd expect from a noir hero.  The fixed camera angles work artistically, if not necessarily gameplay-wise, with each area having strong framing that lends to the comic-book feel.  The rooms of the mansion the game is set in couldn't do a better job of conveying an increasing feeling of decay and confinement - motifs central to the story - supported by the Depression-era setting.  And the collectible documents bring forth all the history and insanity you need to tie the package together.  It's good.  Damn good.
As a story, though, White Night has some pretty damning weaknesses.  I've already mentioned that it relies on a cliche.  I saw the obligatory twist coming before I was an hour in, less than halfway done exploring the first floor.  And the game did disappoint by doing exactly what I expected.  Seeing where the game was going so early, took a good chunk of the magic out of it for me.  Yeah, the game's tone was strong enough to sock me through the plate-glass window of my imagination, but I didn't tell it to stop!
White Night is a ghost story and the ghosts as antagonists really lack the sort of visceral weight I want from a noir thriller.  Seeing my guy swarmed by flailing ghosts just doesn't have the impact of knowing he could end up with his skull caved in by a blunt object.  In fact, the occult elements of the story really fall flat (not unlike a skull caved in by a blunt object).  There's a lot of metaphysical B.S. involving alchemy that clashes with the very believable letters and diary entries.  A Depression-era noir thriller could definitely make good use of occult motifs, but here I think they mostly serve to disconnect the story from the gritty tone the game set up so well.
Even though story and atmosphere are where it's at for a game like this, let's talk gameplay before you guys turn to hard drinking and fistfighting just to get some action in.  White Night has stolen its clothes from Resident Evil and Silent Hill, if not quite gone so far as to disembowel them and wear their skin.  I don't need to tell you guys about tank controls and fixed camera angles.  This game's got them and has all the gameplay problems associated with them.  You'll experience cheap deaths and confusion from blind angles and getting turned around between screens, make no mistake.
The game doesn't really have combat, unlike its predecessors.  Instead, your main resource is matches, which allow you to explore the dark areas of the house without mysteriously dying.  Interestingly, the matches behave a bit like real matches in that you might randomly get a dud.  Combine this with fixed save points and White Night makes safety an uncertain proposition, which is good for horror.  However, it can quickly get frustrating if you have to redo long sequences between checkpoints or go running back to refill your small supply of matches because you got a bunch of duds in a row.
Match light won't kill or even fend off the ghosts that can instantly kill you, only switching on electric lights will do the job.  Once again this can make things tense, or it can be very frustrating when you have to run a gauntlet of ghosts randomly moving around in the dark.  Yeah, the stakes have been raised, but during these sequences I died so many times trying to navigate them, that I just ended up getting irritated by the futility of it rather than horrified.  It's also worth noting that you can't run past any ghost.  Ghosts meant to block your way until you solve a puzzle will block your way until you solve a puzzle and it's not often clear which ghosts are which.
So the gameplay walks a razor's edge between tension and frustration.  That razor's edge cuts impressively when it works, but when you're juggling it among so many balls, your balls won't feel good when it misses.  And I found it to be pretty hit-or-miss.
Puzzle solving is about what you'd expect from a game with White Night's roots.  There's a lot of find-odd-shaped-key-for-door puzzles, as well as some weird contraption based puzzles that have that contrived "puzzle" feel.  The former have the problem of being too straightforward and the latter tend toward the cryptic, even if there are far fewer of them.  The thing to take away from this is that it isn't a puzzle game.  It's a horror game.
Alright, after all that why do I still recommend White Night?  Can I really sell it to you on the art style alone if it has so many weaknesses?  Damn skippy, I can!  But more importantly, White Night does something great.  Yeah, you'll be brought in by janky, nostalgic controls and those crisp black and white graphics (which could admittedly use better anti-aliasing), but what White Night does best is make you feel like you're an investigator using a hard nose for secrets to fight back the dark.  It does this with its atmosphere and its superlative pacing.  From staggering into a mysterious mansion, to meeting your first ghost with little fanfare, to pressing forward to the darker and more sinister sections of the mansion; from ground floor, to top floor, attic, and basement; White Night keeps getting darker and more dangerous.  It's not a great story, no.  But it's very well told.  It stood out like a muzzle flash in a pitch black room during the Activision Weekend when I picked it up.  I definitely recommend you give it a try if horror is your bag and it's on sale.  For fifteen bucks, though?  Maybe wait.

Then there's the save system...mostly excellent...hell, almost inspired (you rest in an armchair, but first have to ensure you shed enough light on said chair to do so safely!)...but every now and then, you encounter one of those godawful moments of shithouse game design where you go back literally MINUTES of gameplay, having to redo bits you've done a thousand times before, just to get up to that one fateful bit which keeps snuffing you.  An absolute ♥♥♥♥ing pet peeve of mine, I'm not afraid to admit.  But wait, it gets worse...
For me at least, the game fell into a habit of automatically RESTARTING itself straight after I exited it.  This would only be mildly annoying and inconvenient, except...I eventually got so used to skipping through the screens to get to that "exit" button the second time, that I accidentally pressed "new game" and ERASED MY ♥♥♥♥ING SAVE.  My ONLY save.  The only save the game allows you to have at any one ♥♥♥♥ing time.  And I was, best as I can deduce, AT LEAST HALF-WAY THROUGH THE FRIGGING GAME!!  So let's hear it, everybody, for games with a single, solitary autosave.  HALLE-♥♥♥♥ING-LUYAH!!!
In short, an otherwise very, very excellent game marred by some very serious technical shortcomings, and a couple of♥♥♥♥♥♥poor design decisions.  I'm sure I'll get back to it again soon enough, but right now I'm ♥♥♥♥ing livid to be honest.  And this, on the same day on which I had to completely "reset" another one of my computers because it hasn't been able to connect to any internet for weeks now, for, y'know, reasons known only to God and Satan themselves.  Man, I tell ya, if it wasn't for the miracle of VIDEO GAMES, I'd be signing up as a fully-fledged, card-carrying member of the Flat Earth Society right now...

Dark Souls high level of difficulty works well because it allows the player to become familiar with an area and learn how to fight the enemies in that area. The procedural generation of dungeons takes this away.
The slow pace does not work well as a roguelike. I keep having to go through the same, stale first area to get to the interesting parts. Unfortunately, as I am not familiar with the new areas/enemies, I keep dying quickly when I get there. It takes quite a while to get through each area, so I end up trudging through parts of the game I don't want to go through to get to an interesting place in the game.
The procedural generation is mediocre. The levels feel quite similar. And the areas are quite sparse. The environments could stand to be more filled out.
I haven't played multiplayer. I am sure that would be more exciting.

So I've ben playing this game for a while now, and I'm dissapointed the the steam reveiws aren't better than they currently are. I highly recommend at least trying it out and if you do, bring a friend. At the time of writing this, my last run with my friend lasted maybe 3-4 hours and we got to level 7 (our record so far). Now I'll list some of the things I love about it without being too biased XD.
1. Variety - This game has so much variety in weapons, enemies, and environments. In each run me and my friend can always find something new. There are so many types of weapons, and not just like short swords, great swords, and hammers and stuff, many weapons have special attributes such as ice, lightning, grine, and more, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. And as we got further down into the Necropolis, we saw newer and stronger enemies (of whitch eventually brutally murdered us untill we were pretty much nothing more than puddles of blood on the dungeon floor).
2. Visuals - This game is absolutely stunning yet subtle, the lighting is beautiful and assuring, and the environment is alluring yet menacing. The fires are designed in a uniquely appealing way and can give such a feeling of safety and affirmation in the dark menacing dungeon that is the Necropolis. My computer build is decent, i don't have the best parts on the market or anything, and I can play this game with no visual or performance problems.
3. Gameplay - You start off every game with a basic sword and a crappy looking wooden buckler type shield. You have a good variety of attacks (some of whitch you may never use) and some of these may significantly change based on your eqiupment. Different weapons can greatly change how you fight and can often make or break your dungeon run.
4. Story??? - There is some backstory to the Necropolis and its creation, however it isn't just thrown in your face and is in fact easily looked over. Any of this game's story is found only as bits of dialogue from the Brazen Head (the big illuminati guy) or more often from pieces of text on the dungeon walls that can be easily missed, especially while fighting a horde of enemies. However, this subtlety of the lore is just part of the wonder of this game; as we played more and more, my friend and I began to form our own theories and connections as to what was what.
5. Difficulty Scaling - The difficulty scaling in this game is actually a bit strange to describe accurately, but it's unique and refreshing. At first, most enemies likely wont prove very challenging except for in very large goups; as you obtain better equipment, basic enemies often become even easier; depending on your luck you may go for some time with little to no challenge, but sooner or later you will reach a point where even the more basic enemies aren't so easy and instead require actual effort and strategy to kill and approaching a large group without a plan is a death sentence. This sporadic difficulty requires you to stay aware as the game can go from you slaughtering many small insignificant creatures, to you running helplessly from some large powerful creature that you've never seen before.
6. Obscurity - This game is so obscure in every way. I've already described the obscurity of the game's lore, but it goes further, not a single item in this game has a straightforward description. Everything, from weapons to scrolls, potions to codexes, is described only in a small piece of text that may or may not roughly explain what it is and its tier. you start out with tier 0 equipment and slowly obtain higher tier items as you progress (the highest i've personally found was tier 4).  The obscurity of this game may be off-putting to some, but others will find that it adds to the experience of the game, as you won't automatically know what everything is and how you can use it.
7.Humor - Necropolis has a great sense of humor for such a danger filled environment, and as most things are in this game, it is very subtle and can be looked over far too easily. As with the story, the humor is often found in dialogue from the Brazen Head and the pieces of text on the dungeon walls.
Some of these aspects may not be appealing to some, and maybe this game just isn't for them, but this game is no doubt one of my all time favorites and if any of these points did appeal to you, I cannot express how much I reccomend that you at least give this game a try. It pains me to see that this game isn't receiving the support it so rightly deserves, my friend and I have played for hours on end and haven't experienced any issues and would reccomend it in a heartbeat to anyone who has any appreciation for video games.

There are not many games where the sequel stay true to its root and yet produces an outstanding result and The Witcher 2 is on of them. If you haven't played the first Witcher I highly recommend it as the story is closely related and you can even import the save files from the previous game which will have a couple of mentions and some equipment to get you started.
The Witcher 2 has improved vastly; mainly the visuals. In terms of gameplay, they reworked the combat system and spells which result in more solid battles and strategic. There are more gears in this game and also improved crafting, alchemy and smithing where I really had fun dabbling with.
The game picks up where the first left off with choices to make as you proceed throughout the story. Witcher is one of the games I've played where the choices really matter as it changes how the story unfolds and quests dramatically. You get to travel from one place to another in each chapter and unlike the predecessor, you will not be able to return to the previous map. Each map however is not very big but IMHO, are packed with places to explore and each have its unique set of environment all beautifully modelled.
When you feel like taking a break from questings and exploring (and yes there are a handful amount of sub quests in each chapter), you can take part in a couple of mini games. Unlike other mini game, The Witcher 2 actually relates mini games into a sub quest where you can actually have a closure.
Overall this game is great game for any RPG fans and a must have.

Would i recommend this game?
This is not easy to say for me. But now that i have once seen the end i will try top answer this.
If you look at the time i played this game you can see i am clearly of good oppinion towards this game.
I am absolutely in love with the low-poly and pastell coloured visual design a well as the sounddesign of this game and to be perfectly honest this was actually the main reason that drove me back into the Necropolis.
The gameplay is also clearly something i like being a fan off Legend of Zelda and the Dark Souls games with their more deliberate. tactical and slower paced combat.
Necropolis: Brutal Edition made no secret  of the fact that it took these games as example and they mostly did a great job with that.
Fighting the enemys is for the most part thrilling and fun and if you mess up or are to hasty even medium enemys can cost you your progress.
However this game does indeed have problems that need to be mentioned:
1. The game is absolutely awfull at giving the player ANY INFORMATION.
-The game has potions, spells, armors, weapons, bombs and tomes so called Codexes you can buy for tokens of favour from the "Dungeon Master" the Brazen Head.
NONE of these have a clear description of it's attributes and abbilities the designers instead opting only to put flairtext on them that sometimes may vaguely describe what the item does.
This is especially a problem because the tier system means nadda since sometime i opted to use tier 2 weapons over tier 4 weapons because they clearly seemed to make more damage and stun the enemys more.
In a game where any mistake causes you to have to start from the beginning this is not a good idea.
And no, i do not find it a good idea to have to look up information about a game outside of the game.
- It also is confusing because some of the weapons have (neat looking) special effect upon use the charged attacks. However it seems to be different from item to item if the resulting explosion or other area of effect actually has a result on all of the enemys inside of the effect or only the one enemy hit by it.
2.The game builds and fills its levels with enemys, tresures and other characters via an Random Number Generator.
This leads to a few of problems.
- It can happen that you have some (for a new character) of the most obnoxious enemys, the Gemeaters, bipedal hulking Sharkmonsters, directly behind the first door and surrounded by further enemys. If this happens chances are that you will lose imidiately because Gemeaters have some of the worst telegraphed (means the enemys make a certain motion before an attack so the player can predict and counter or evade the attack) attacks that will stun you followwed up by a attack wich can instantly kill you.
- Sometimes i had level areas that were filled with enemys but that i couldn't reach because the RNG design litterally designed an unreachable part of a level. However i never got stuck so that i couldn't progress.
- Even if i absolutely love the Design, Rooms and Designelements overall can repeat too often wich can make progressing trough the game rather repetetive, a problem that i will mention again later.
3. The Roguelike Elements in Necropolis: Brutal Edition are so terribble they might as well not be there.
Roguelike means that if you die you have to start over. But it also usually means that SOMETHING you have foud in your last session will be brought over to change the game up for you or give you a better chance in your next attempt trough something you found in the dungeon.
In Necropolis these are tokens of favour, that you get from the Dungeon Master for completing certain tasks as well as Codexes (books that can give you an bonus) and clothing dyes that you buy with the Tokens of Favour and that stay over from Session to session.
This terribble because:
-The Codexes provide bonuse that for one are as everything else only vaguely described so you have to guess at some. The thing is most of these are so miniscule and without impact they might as well not be there. Most of them don't really changed the way you played the game or gave you much of any usefull benefit. The only Bonuses that i in the end used over and over again was the very first one that lowered the exhaustion (for wich one needs to eat food or specific potions).
- Not only do the dyes nothing but changing the patterns and colours of your clothing (wich are admittedly really nice looking) but you also can only choose which dye to use at the beginning of a session. So if things go well you only can change it once every few or more hours (my last session wich i reched the last floor in taking around 10 hours).
This is a nice thing but again has barely any impact on the gameplay itself.
- And that is it. No seriosly. In my last play trough i had over 10.000 crystals left, a great armor, two tier 4 weapons and most of the reciepts for crafting items. All i got from that were around 10 Tokens of favour and two dyes. None of this you can put back for your next session. That is simply not enough and might keep other people from playing.
4. This game FEELS UNFINISHED:
- First off there are the bugs, enemys FREQUENTLY get stuck in the geography, in walls and level elements like pipes, pillars or altairs and i lost at least one sesion to a bug where even after restarting the game i couldn't progress because after a few meters the game constantly froze and crashed.
- Enemys also get stuck trying to attack the player. Especially bigger enemys get hung up on geography like corners of a door but also smaller enemys can get stuck behind such grand obstacles as a knee high wall. Though i won't moan after to much since...
- MOST ENEMYS DO NOT STAGGER WHEN HIT. This is a massive problem because it means that it becomes nearly impossible to not take damage when fighting more then one enemy. Bigger weapons do actually stagger enemys but that has the result that most light weapons becomes utterly useless since combat becomes a competitions of"who hits the other guy faster". Which feeds into the next problem...
- Enemy mobs (groups of enemys) are either unfair put together by the RNG or rather in a way that is unfitting for the combat system wich is more for a tactical and slower paced approach. It is simply not fun to be constantly stunlocked or to run backwards for halve the level and while wittling down the mass of them bit by bit instead of winning trough tactical talent and being well at using ones weapons.
- There are either effects missing that can tell you if an area of effect attack has had an impact or not
- While you delve into the dungeons deeper levels inscription on the walls as well as the dialogue from the Dungeon Master the Brazen Head (a giant, bronze, one eyed Pyramide) tells you bits and pieces about the world the game takes place in. And what is there is really good and partially funny and serves the atmosphere very well. However, it is simply not enough. After a short while you will have read most of them and then they start repeating quite frequently.
- This is incidentally the biggest of the signs that the game is kind off unfinished. Everything repeeats quite often and if you aren't as into the design as well as into the combat as i personally am it will get repeptitive quite quickly.
5. THE ENDING IS A MASSIVE LET DOWN.
Seriosuly? That is it? After all that hard work?
You don't even get a New Game Plus where you can use the same character to delve into the dungeon once more.
You enter a door and that is it and everything you have earned so far is gone (aside from the Token of Favour of course, bleh).
My positive bias to this kind of game in mind and with these not exactly small problems, wich mostly means that the game needed more, more characters or interesting events or something like that, more Items, more areas, more balance and most of all more polish i can not recommend this game for it's full price of around 27 to 30 Bucks (depending on the currenzy).

After reading all of the negative reviews for this game I was dubious about  playing it.  Thankfully  I was  actually very  pleasantly surprised when I did finally boot up the game.  You really need to keep your wits about you  while playing because   zombies,  and other   animals will spawn  close behind you as well as in front, and  with  several different types of  zombie spawing randomly, some of which are quite challenging to  kill because they are so quick.  You will soon find yourself losing  lives rapidly.
Personally I'd much rather play Alpages in third person,  because  then  I'd be able to  see  zombies and other animals spawning behind me  without having to change my viewpoint constantly; unfortunately  that  isn't an option and consequently  I died regularily  until I developed  a style of play that had me circling  virtually all of the time to keep my sixes in sight.  This did initially  give me  a little  sea sickness and was exhausting, but  once I got used to the style I was able to survive for much longer, and managed to find   three of the books  before   losing all of my lives.
I've played the game  so far for  over three hours and have still to get close to   beating  this  very challenging game, that has  decent  graphics  and sound effects (for the price), with a day and night cycle (when you respwan), and  some very atmospheric and at times  spooky   environments  with the occasional maze like area's that can leave you dazed and confused (I'm now playing  my original copy of  Led Zep's first album  on my old record deck) and for the ridiculoulsy low price of £0.79/$0.99 there are enough game play  elements such as   power ups; for example, other weapons,  ammo and health plants,  and if you  die, the books you are collecting  do spawn in different places, so you never know  where they are going to be  from each play through,  making  Alpages a very replayable  game and IMO  well worth purchasing.
It's not the best survival game I've played, but  really,  for the price, the time and effort I've personally put into the game has been   a very positive experience and does not deserve such a  negative  score that it has so far garnered. At least a couple of hours of game play is needed to really appreciate this game.

I've been playing this game for 11 hours now, over the course of 2 play sessions.  TLDR - I love it, buy it, it's amazing and well worth the price!
I'm still very much in the exploration phase of the game, founding new colonies, meeting other empires and exploring with my science ships.  I've been running the game at normal speed with the odd pause to catch up, and there is never a time when nothing is going on and I feel bored.
I know there have been some complaints about the research system.  Basically you get to pick from a small number (never less than 3) projects to research.  These projects are weighted by what you have just unlocked and your progress in the game.  So there is a loose tech tree of sorts, but you aren't limited by a set tech tree like say, Civ V, where you know what is coming and quickly build an optimal path that will be repeated with every play though.  With the Stellaris system there is no obvious path to follow and it more realistically follows real discoveries, where scientist look for funding to work on a project.  More importantly it keeps the game fresh and very repayable.
As to the depth, another complaint.  I keep finding whole new game systems I haven't really encountered yet.  Planetary armies and air forces, multi-species empires, the list goes on.  For espionage, I imagine that is something that will come with DLC.
Oh, the Paradox DLC model.  Sure they really crank out the DLC for their games, but they match that with a low entry price.  $39 in a market where many games cost #60.  Even if you don't buy the DLC it always comes with a free patch with many new systems, expanding the game at no additional cost.
I've been a big Paradox fan since CK2 and this is a great additional to the grand strategy family.
Recommended.

Keep in mint that this game is a different Genre from their other big hits and the developers would need a bit time to adjust and take care of all issues. The biggest issues for me, are that space battles are not that exciting and some times are lagging. It shouldn't be from my PC. Also, more depth into the diplomacy is necessary - I can't convince a 4th race to join my alliance so I can form a confederacy, even races that I enlightened with my technology, won't join our alliance. I miss the good ol' backstabbing between leaders or maybe my race is too civilized and it's lacking crooks. I also couldn't find a list with surveyed habitable planets or potential sources of resources. The AI needs improvement. Hard to switch between planets when on surface screen.
The music is quite good, but if Paradox add few more music tracks and an optional voice-over for the events - I picture Sir Patrick Stewart, Sir Ian McKellen or Morgan Freeman...  impossible right, or not?. The graphics are nice, however there is still more room for improvements. It makes you think how tiny we are, because I absolutely believe the universe isn't that a lonely place, as right now from our point of view, based on the lack of official mainstream information.
I hope to see how the game will evolve in the future and capitalize on its enormous potential.

Abzû is a beautifully animated exploration game where the main draw is being able to take your time swimming around underwater, interacting with lush aquatic life. It gives you the opportunity to collect shells, release wildlife, and meditate on different statues as part of its trophy/acheivement gathering system. It has a linear plot and there isn't really room to navigate away from that sequence. Though you have the freedom to explore the seascapes provided, the game makes it very obvious when you're straying too far from the intended path and will re-direct you. The plot gradually gets a bit darker, but is presented entirely visually with the assistance of music (no dialogue). Your character never speaks, and you get the most out of the sort of abstractly constructed plot they present when you take your time exploring the places you find.
The soundtrack is beautiful, the animations are lovely, and overall I'm entirely pleased with the $20 I spent on this game. I got 4 hours total playtime out of my first time around, and I'm sure I will play it again in my effort to find all the mystery achievements. If you enjoy a game you can take at your own pace without the pressure of health bars, shooters, etc, I'd most certainly recommend it.

This is a summary of my review video, which I encourage you to watch if you are looking for a more in-depth review.
Woolfe - The Red Hood Diaries is a 2.5D platformer with a hack and slash mentality. The story takes a steam punk twist to the classic Red Riding hood fairy tale. The music and voice acting were done very well, and did a great job of propelling the atmosphere and setting the tone. The environment is well done, and the theme and atmosphere are done perfectly to push the story and embody the tale.
The level design fits mostly with the platforming element. There are a few times when you can't tell if you can or cannot jump over particular railings or boxes. It can be pesky when you come to a boss fight, and due to the camera angle and platforming mechanics you think that you are jumping to safety when in reality you can't jump over said obstacle, or jump into an invisible wall. Overall the character has fluidity and slides along ledges with adequate speed and without looking or feeling clunky. As you progress through the game, the design of the traps that you get through become more demanding and precise in their requirements, and the margin for error becomes greater and greater. Overall I felt that the precision needed to get through the traps became too difficult for the speed with which you had to progress through them. Are they doable yes, but it is just tasking.
The combat is just bad. Yes, the weapon has weight, and there is a fluidity to the fighting, but there is a strong hack and slash feeling to the battles. You are reduced to repetitively pushing the same two buttons, and while it looks impressive, you don't gain any sense of power or control, and your character is so squishy that you are tempted more times than not just to run by the enemies, in avoidance of death. One of the more frustrating aspects of the combat is that you may be able to tell that an enemy is going to hit you, and you try to dodge or counter it, but your character is locked into whatever combo move and won't react until they are finished with it. Which means you die more. The game offers a stealth element, but it felt like it may have been tacked on last minute, as there are very few opportunities to use it, and it just didn't fit into the game very well.
The story started out very promising. I was literally on the edge of my seat for the intro, with a grin on my face. As it progresses forward, it seems to make less and less sense. The mechanics and combat in the game take away from the tension the story creates. To make it worse, this 2-3 hour long game ends with a 'to be continued'!  Just when you think your questions will be answered, more questions and secrets are dumped on you, with none resolved before they leave you hanging.
The sum of this games misgivings and flaws far outweigh any enjoyment I found in this game. I cannot and will not recommend this game, even if it is on sale on steam.

Abzu is a short, relaxing game that is primarily about exploration and visual stimulation.  It can be summarized as swim around and look at the pretty fishies.  That may not sound like much, but Abzu's execution is superb.  The environments and use of color is excellent, the soundtrack creates a great atmosphere, and overall it is worth experiencing.  It is essentially a walking simulator, with a bit more gameplay, done well.  This is what that whole sub-genre should strive to be.
However, the game is short.  You will beat it in less than 3 hours.  If you like exploring, taking your time, and pausing to look at things you might take 3 hours.  If you are more goal oriented it might only take you 1.5 hours.  This alone isn't a problem, the game is the exact length it needs to be.  Any longer and it would start to drag on.  The problem stems from the $20 price tag, which is very high.  Most people would not feel like they got $20 worth of gaming out of this.
Abzu is probably more realistically worth around $5 or less.  A great experience, but not a whole lot of that experience.  I would recommend wishlisting it and picking it up on a sale.

This game is incredible. Although my hours are somewhat low (I play a lot offline) I thoroughly enjoy playing this game. Having beaten Mum's Heart (the boss after Mum) eleven or so times, I am happy to report that every death, every life, every success has been totally different to the last. The extra characters and unlockables give something to stride towards, and it's just one of those games that the better you get, the better it is, not because it becomes easier, rather because it becomes quicker to get to the harder bits. As much as I love it though, there is a certain demographic to whom I cannot recommend it. Yes, all you hard core Christians out there, I am talking to you. If you are easily offended and find the thought of trading parts of your life force to the Devil in order to get stronger mortifying should steer clear and stick to a different game. There are strong references to Satan, and also implications that God is a bit messed up, although an Angel Room is always very welcome as people who have played the game will know. If you are going to get it though, get the Wrath of the Lamb DLC as well. All the extra content makes the game last so much longer, and one that I just can't delete in my quest for more disk space. I have also heard that a lot of people get framerate issues, but even on my crappy♥♥♥♥♥♥computer I have only suffered from them once or twice, and they left as suddenly as they came. All in all, an incredible game, and one of the only ones that will probably never leave my hard drive.

Necropolis, as I think everyone is aware by now, is a mashup between Dark Souls (in terms of its combat) and Binding of Isaac or other rogue-lite games. Sound good, but I am not recommending this game because of 2 dealbreakers:
1. No key rebinding - "V" is sprint, "Ctrl" is dodge; I always set up "Shift" as my dodge key when playing the Dark Souls series or Salt and Sanctuary.
2. No Stagger - enemies do not stagger when hit. This makes combat not fun and difficult to accomplish without taking some damage.
In other games such as Salt and Sanctuary and probably even Dark Souls, enemies that do not stagger do exist, but they are sparse. In Necropolis, even the weakest enemies do not stagger.

It tries to play like Dark Souls, but it fails in the most important aspects.
In combat, there is no feedback to attacks and blocks. You can be hit without even realizing because there is no stagger, no reaction from the character, barely any visual feedback. You have to pay attention to your life to know when you're being hit. It fails in the most important aspects of the combat, that is the heavy and strong feel of it.
The exploration and world are both mediocre. It's really easy to get lost due to the complete lack of any variation in the looks of the world. As a map would solve the issue, I understand why there is no map, but there should be some way to differentiate places, so you can navigate the world. Me and the others that were playing with me got lost for a good half an hour in a level. We barely restarted the whole run. And as all in the world is flat and meaningless, there is no enjoyment in exploring it, at best you can find a slight better gear, but there is never something really exciting.
The final boss. There are no other boss fights, only the final one. It happens in a leve that there is barely anything. And the fight is just a big enemy with a lot of life. We kept hitting it for over one hour to finally kill it, he didn't even had any amazing moves, we just kept moving around a stone until he got stuck into it. And when he died, nothing happened, no drops, no nothing, so we couldn't even finish the game properly.
The bugs, as happened of the final boss not dropping the item to finish the game, are frequent. The terrain causes a lot of issues, and there are multiple reports of these problems over the internet. On the writing of this review, there have been no patches since I last played in December 2016. Without a rework in the navigation and combat aspects, this game is not worth playing.

NightSky, a 2011 indie release by Nicalis, can easily be described as such: it's almost exactly what comes to mind when one hears the word indie games. Picturesque and stylized graphics, simple controls, a short playtime, cerebral yet casual challenge, and an ambient soundtrack by some experimental musician or another.
Personally, I enjoyed it; my play-through took only a meagre 2 hours, but that's well worth the price considering I got it through one of the Humble Bundles. The physics could be a bit frustrating sometimes: sometimes the game just doesn't do what you want it to do, especially if you're playing with poor d-pad, like the good ol' 360 controller. However, such a problem doesn't exist with a keyboard - the only reason I played with a controller is because I lack a QWERTY keyboard, and you can't remap the controls.
Other than that nitpick, the game is a neat, picturesque and ambient little puzzle game, that gives your brain something to chew on without ever becoming frustrating (discounting the control hiccups mentioned above).

If your anything like me, the reason your here right now reading reviews is because this game is on sale. Currently its on sale for 25 cents. And if your anything like me, your thinking of passing up this game due to the mixed reviews. Well I can say that the negative reviews should be ignored, as its clear the writers were expecting to much from this game. Its normally 2 bucks, and right now its 25 cents, what could you expect for that price? Anyways, lets talk about the game.
This is a basic shooter at heart. Its a block based fps involving zombies, so nothing really new there. The gameplay is basic, you have three weapons, a sub machine gun, a shot gun, and a baseball bat. Shooting is smooth, and the performance is solid, no slow downs or hiccups. When you defeat one of the zombies they fall apart in a satisfying way. My only real complaint is the variety of weapons. But its a short game, and I cant really see a use of other guns.
When it comes to the levels, they are typically well designed, starting off small and void of many enemies, and gradually grow in difficulty and length. The actual design is linear, but fun to traverse. The devolper did a good job of keeping the look of the levels varied, as well as the enemies you face. While its true you are fighting simple variations of zombies, they did a good job of keeping them all different looking, and I never knew what to expect from them. This game throws unexpected surprises in several places, that change up how you go about the typical running and gunning.
This game also comes bundled with the soundtrack, which is worth the 25 cents alone. All the tracts fit the gameplay well, and are very good techno style music. The last thing I want to talk about is the games length. Its short, real short. You can finish in about an hour to an hour and a half. But when it comes down to it, I had fun running through this game, and for only 25 cents this is a worthwhile game.

Damn, this game gets a lot of flak.

$30 is a big price--I didn't pay that, and I'm glad. But if this goes on sale, and you don't have anything else you're invested in, at least give it a shot. Clearly you're interested enough to try to enjoy it, if you're reading reviews.
One piece of advice, though, especially later in the game: you don't have to fight every enemy on the floor. This game won't make you do much at all, except progress. I even found places where I could avoid whole groups of enemies if I was clever enough to go around (particularly the swamp). This game has basically no invisible walls and truly wants you to progress--at least, it felt that way to me--and for that reason, I respect it.
EDIT: By the way, I didn't even play this in Co-op, and I've heard that's basically the core enjoyment of the game. So if you have friends to play it with, I certainly recommend.

For some of us, I suppose, it's the near misses that are most memorable.
Bought Necropolis in a sale. I'd had my eye on it for some time, as I've become a fan of games featuring proc gen after playing Spelunky and it seemed like Necropolis was using a dungeon generation methodology I was particualrly interested in at the time.
And the pitch, "Dark Souls meets Splunky" is basically irresistable, let's be honest.
It doesn't take long before the major flaw becomes evident - though the game uses an almost 1:1 layout controller layout to Dark Souls (indeed, making some slight improvements on the layout), only one of the main attacks proves to have any kind of reliable use in combat. In my experience, animation timing, attack and invul windows conspire to bring you down very quickly unless you learn to rely on fast slashes, fast slash combos and some cautious shieldwork.
(Note: I'm not a leet gamer, here! I loved my Dark Souls experience, but I got beat pretty bad...!)
The right weapon and equipment combinations can help a lot - and if RNJesus is smiling on you, you can end up with some nice gear. Unfortunately, you'll most likely find nothing but copies of that gear in different chests for the rest of your run.
I've also been trying to set up a cooperative run with community players for a week and have yet to succeed. Factor that in.
So why the thumbs up?
Because good GOD, this game has personality. Tankers of it. For days.
Necropolis deftly sidesteps the tired art execution of classic fantasy, instead plumming for prog-rock Ralph Bakshi Heavy-Metal 80's-b-movie airbrushed faux-low-poly brutalist goddamn GENIUS. That's the environments. The characters, god, like some eighties, seventies forgotten Saturday morning epic.
But it's when you mix this with procedural generation and a whip-smart premise that things become really magical.
I've played this game for something like 35 hours. I'm still finding new stuff. I'm still seeing old environments mixed together in new and interesting ways - and that still makes sense to me, within the narrative...
You're an adventurer, trapped within the Navel of the World, once a museum capturing biomes and people conquored by the Archmage Abraxis! Now Abraxis has vanished, and the Naval rots, falls apart, and all the custodian (named 'the Brazen Head') can do is lure in thieves and scoundrels (ie. you) and put them to work cleaning up the place (ie. murder anything that moves).
It's a very light setup, but beautifully executed (the Brazen Head is a wonderful piece of design) and it gives the developers licence to create modules of grand, deserted halls, echoing empty throne rooms, decaying plazas, floating highways... And this is only in one of five biomes (that I've counted so far) which come with their own language, traps, creatures...
I've heard people complaining about procedural generation a lot, especially in relation to this game. The phrase "if I saw this in a game without procedural generation, then it'd mean something because a designer placed it there" gets thrown around.
Baloney.
I love my BSP-brush-designed FPSs, my Half-Lifes, my Bioshocks, etc. I love stuff that's custom built. But the entire point of procedural generation in games like these is to try to capture, as if in verse, the very soul of an experience, to encapsulate it in an algorithim and to allow it to propogate in a semi-random, internally consistent system.
When a designer places that altar, it's ultimately an arbitrary once-off artistic choice.
When that altar is selected by the Necropolis' procedural algorithim it's in accordance with a huge, carefully designed and weighted system. It's the opposite of arbitrary. More than a setting glued together by one designer, this MEANS SOMETHING.
That placement is the product of a recipe, one of thousands in a cookbook that defines a cuisine.
Exploring that cuisine is intoxicating, infuriating, fascinating - and always internally consistent and NON-arbitrary.
I LOVE exploring Necropolis.
Suddenly: A canal! Then: Floating platforms. Were these here befo-- a huge spike-laden ziggurat??? What does this mean? How does this fit with what I've seen before? What next? What next?
And it does a good job of capturing some of the essential elements of Rogue too - the importance of scrolls of identification, the desperate use of some kind of mystery potion in a tight spot - submitting your success to the roll of the system's dice. Desperate times call for geninely desperate measures in this game... how rare is that?
A peach, a peach of a shot. If only it had connected.
So despite combat woes, despite Necropolis' weak humour (though occasionally funny, Necropolis uses humour as an eventually annoying crutch for its underdeveloped lore), the lack of engaging bosses, the anemic community...
...you should absolutely experience the Naval of the World. But maybe wait for a sale. The Brazen Head will understand.
--Rev

NightSky is a simple yet engaging physics puzzle platformer using a ball and the various terrain and objects to get through each level. The controls are simple to move the ball which moves quickly, but extra controls are given to move it faster, slower, or upside down depending on the level along with various contraptions and other objects that are required to solve the levels. Each level is crisply and cleanly drawn with black vector objects along with a well textured sky background in nature or non-nature settings. The art style opts for a simple and almost minimal look along with more intricate and articulate designs in other levels. The music and sounds are also ambient to suit the level styles, with natural sounds and small pieces of music to go with each level. Some levels may be really straightforward and easy, while others give a good amount of puzzle thinking or platforming skill to complete. While it looks like just a simplistic game, NightSky gives a good experience with some interesting design and gameplay.
Really good timepasser!!

I went back and forth on whether to give Stellaris a thumbs up or down. I really like Paradox Games: I've played a lot of Crusader Kings 2, which I think is incredible, and I pre-ordered Stellaris wanting it to be really good. Knowing Paradox's history with CK2 and extensive DLC support, I think Stellaris in a couple year's time is going to be amazing. At present, with fanboy goggles off, I think IGN's review has it spot-on. The game has a lot of great ideas mixed up with weak execution. Considering the amount of hype and sales it's already got, I doubt my single bad review is going to tank this game, so I'm putting this here for the devs to hear some of the things that can be worked on.
My experience: The AI was so passive and my empire was so stable in the mid-game, I literally just sat and built battleships for lack of anything to do, and then when the [redacted] came, my 160k death-stack pew-pewed them into oblivion. I then sat and let the game run, and I now have almost every single tech. I'm not sure what's left to do.  I've stopped my playthrough because...I don't really want to go through the chore of conquering every other empire and there isn't really anything else to do.
The biggest problems in my mind are two-fold and related: a lack of mid-game goals, and a lack of meaningful ways to interact with the world at large.
Crusader Kings 2 was fantastic because it tied all its game mechanics together with people with deep traits and interactions you could interact with in multiple ways. It also kept empires from becoming stale because any CK2 player will tell you the biggest challenge with empires isn't conquering people, it's keeping everything together when your leader dies and every single up-start vassal wants to rebel. Stellaris doesn't really have this: leaders lack personality and pops don't have the same impact on gameplay. In all my time as a slaving Penguin Empire, I never saw a rebellion or significant unrest. This makes the mid and late game very static: you don't have reactive goals like 'Murder the upstart Duke of Lombardy' in CK2, and it's made worse by a simple, standard 4x diplomacy and war system, so you rarely feel compelled to interact with the empires around you.
Additionally, Stellaris currently lacks tools to meaningfully solve problems. In CK2, dealing with eg, a useless heir was fun. Do I make him take religious orders? Marry him off to a foreign empire? Straight up murder him? Get him killed in a war? Stellaris comes close with some of the tools to interact with your alien pops, like slavery, gene modification, resettlement and edicts, but the way the game is set up right now alien populations aren't really a challenge: they don't rebel, or make significant demands for independence, or try to change your policies. So...you end up gene-modding them when you're bored, or when you lack things to do. Worse, and this is a big misstep, to deal with actual dissent the game just makes you pay some resources to make a 'Dissatisfaction' bar go down. Considering how well CK2 implemented rebellious vassals, this isn't really a good design decision.
PROs:
- Great empire designer
- Engaging early-game, with exploration and anomalies
- Lots of room to be expanded on
- Genetically modify rebellious citizens
- Meddle with primitive races
- End-game crises
CONs:
- War is really, really tedious
- Lack of interesting ways to interact with other empires
- No real threat of rebellion from leaders/alien pops
- Framerate drops at mid-game makes the game more of a slog
- Creating sectors isn't as fun as having vassals in CK2
EDIT: Welp, the Paradox devs have talked about how their mid-game content was cut last minute before release and they'll be adding it back at the end of June, plus bug fixes and changes to Sector AI so check back then with Stellaris if you're on the fence
