Woolfe - The Red Hood Diaries is side-scrolling platform hack & slash game, developed and published by the Belgian ind(i)ependent studio GriN.
In this game you play as the grown up Red Riding Hood to avenge the one who is responsible for the death of her mom, and dad who died in an work accident in the factory of B.B. Woolfe.
Red doesn't believe it was an work accident and starts her own investigation.
Armed with an axe, a red cape and a total overdose of anger, Red Riding Hood goes lone-wolf on an adventure from the dark Victorian city to the depths of the sewers and further into the woods to grandma's treehouse.
During the game, Red Riding Hood moves through the levels by jumping from one platform to another in order to make it to the end of each level.
During the journey, Red collects grandma's breadbaskets which acts as a checkpoint, demolish crates to collect Woolfe's diaries, fight against foes such as the tin soldiers who occupy the city under the command of B.B Woolfe, rats of the sewers, the pixies from the forest and has to solve puzzles who block her path.
The game has amazing artwork, nice voice casting and great music!
I can't say the same for the combat system which felt quite clunky to me but it didn't bother me that much in the overall picture.
Woolfe - The Red Hood Diaries is a very short game and was supposed to be an episodic game.
Unfortunately the studio GriN went bankrupt at the end of 2015 and canceled the development Woolfe Volume 2.
Not long after that, Rebellion acquired the title and its publisher rights and Woolfe - The Red Hood Diaries is in their hands since then.
If the game is on sale and you are looking for a short fairylike platformer with a dark favlor, then I do recommend this game!
Don't put the bar of expectations too high for this game because it's not a final game but an episode.

I've played plenty of FPS and FPRPGs so to have a genuine turn-based game option is refreshing. It has a more laidback feel than Grimrock and you never end up overly frustrated. The classes have natural limitations so building a resilient party is an interesting challenge. I found the game balance to be good on the harder difficulty level. Individual combats can be a challenge but tactics can be varied to produce substantially different results.
The game sequence is suitably linear and the puzzles are not overly taxing. The essential story is that you're a party out to save the world. There is extra detail presented but it's not engaging. The graphics are reasonable but not impressive and the landscape has an upbeat feel; a contrast to the sombre Grimrock. The mid-to-late game starts to slow down as you end up criss-crossing the landscape to tidy up the loose ends but that's probably because I insist on walking everywhere rather than catching a horse or boat.
In summary, the game's strength is the satisfaction of developing a team that complements each other.
Completions: 5

Might and Magic X is not a bad game - in fact it can be quite entertaining at times, but it's RNG combat, balance issues and poor design choices really hinder the game. I have beaten this game twice and I would say that the final chapter of this game is a good example of all that is wrong with this game.
The third chapter is a long, boring trek through two dungeons that includes silly portal puzzles to pad play time; instead of interesting combat engagements you are instead bombarded by huge number of enemies that can cause a few different status conditions (and good luck finisning the game if you didn't gear towards defending against those); and a final boss with cheap game mechanics that can♥♥♥♥♥♥on you from range while dispelling all your buffs (better have tons of HP).
I get that MMX is trying to go back to the old hardcore way, but having to run all over the place to find trainers for different skills is a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Fast travel is janky and not that great or helpful most of the time either. Also, don't even think about doing a jack-of-all trades kind of build or spend skill points willy nilly because you will get♥♥♥♥♥♥on hard to the point where completing the game will be more difficult that it should.
If you're smart and you take a min/max approach and have a focus build for your party, then the game is quite enjoyable. But if you blindly spend skill points or have no idea what you're doing, they your party is going to be way behind the curve and the game is going to feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥to play. I ended up modding the game and slightly adjusting the buffs to help as I found the difficulty at times to be too frustrating.

Abzu is a game about the ocean. You know, that infinitely beautiful yet terrifying body of water which covers over 70% of the earth's surface? I have to say that personally, I've always found the ocean to be the most fascinating aspect of nature, especially considering how little of it we've explored.
For me, Abzu captured the wonder and dread that I've always wanted from an ocean exploration game. It was a short-lived experience, at around 100 minutes but I enjoyed every second of it. I honestly don't think I've played a game that is this gorgeous. The music is consistently grand, the visuals always stunning. My jaw literally dropped at one point after the discovery of one underwater creature that I recognised from a book I owned as a kid. It's not easy for a game to instill that sense of childlike wonder and joy. As long as you know what you're getting into with this game, a short and non-challenging game, then I think it's near impossible to not love. Just know that there is no fail state, the puzzles are more or less "swim to one device and activate it, swim to another device". If you let yourself get immersed in the world of Abzu, you will not regret it.

I only recommend this if you are a fan or have a lot of patience.
This game succeeds in recreating the Might and Magic "feel" except for the puzzles.  Maybe that's just not possible given how easy it is to Google solutions now.  Or maybe the Might and Magic style just does not age well now that I am older.
Perhaps the biggest flaw in this game is that I just did not care for the story nor the characters.  I blame this on the Ubisoft reboot and the forced integration with the Heroes franchise.
Another flaw is that it requires you to regularly backtrack to do mundane things like train skills (one high level skill requires you to return repeatedly, the last time for an entire in-game month!).  This is made worse by the fact that fast travel is painfully limited.
Do I recommend this?  Only if you are a fan.  And be careful not to let it sink as much of your time as I did.
Note:  I'm a fan.  My favorite M&M games are III (Isles of Terra), and IV + V (Worlds of Xeen).  M&M II introduced me to role playing games as a child back when rocks were soft and computers were made of wood.  I've now played all the main games M&M 1-10.  Not a fan of the Heroes franchise.

Okay, at first this review was very positive. I was a fan of the game at first, and the Brutal update was a prime example of what all companies should try to do. Indeed, this game has potential to be one of my favourite games of all time, but unfortunately I don't think that potential will be realised.
~~TL;DR>>: Wait for a sale, then seriously consider it. DO NOT BUY at full price!~~
Necropolis is a roguelike soulslike with a very solid art direction (with some pretty good semi-hidden lore scattered around to boot, which gives the illusion of scale and left me kind of invested in the world, if only a little) and good design generally. The levels feel open, but not confusing. The progression is not linear but the game does a very good job of guiding you to the next area (not as well as Dark Souls but nothing does that as well as Dark Souls).
The enemies feel fair (MOSTLY) to fight against, and there is an interesting dynamic to weapon types in that certain weapons will affect certain enemy groups more (in a similar fasion to Pokemon, if you will) and you can only carry 2 at a time, creating a choice factor which is completely eliminated because of an issue with two weapons/weapon types which I will discuss later.
The gameplay is, like I said in the overview, a Soulslike mixed with a Roguelike. Especially when playing as the Brute, the game runs on the same control scheme, uses the same basic gameplay signatures (deliberate attacks and dodges, along with the ever present and imperative stamina bar and non-regenerating health which are sustained only by consumables which take time to use and are interrupted in combat) and generally has a massive *I was inspired by the SoulsBourne games* sign on its head. This mingles with the permadeath and procedurally generated elements from Roguelikes to make a very refined experience which actually worked quite well.
Now, the problems.
This game is... not finished. It quite simply does not have the bang for the 30 bucks or 23 pounds or whatever you will be spending on this game.
It took me, an (at the time) inexperienced, casual player who played maybe 2 hours a day on this thing 8 playthroughs to win, at least 2 of which were over in less than an hour. I stand by the principle of justifying purchases with a dollar per hour or thereabouts, and even with substantial leeway, necropolis falls short, giving me only half of my money's worth. You can call that an opinion, or stubbornness, or whatever, but I cannot personally justify spending $30 dollars on the 15 hours it netted me (I have spent about 3 hours doing this game with friends and the admittedly improved netcode stopped that in its tracks however I am confident we could have finished it in another 2 or so). More content is therefore called for, but of course, this is the company that brought us a massive FREE update for this game adding multiple new areas and a new class! In my opinion, another Brutal Edition scale update could very well fix all this game's problems, the largest solvable ones in my opinion I will stick at the bottom of the review.
Alas
Silence
The devs left the game for dead after that update. No more were to follow. They completely ceased all development, as far as I can tell. As I belive they have said, but don't quote me on that, I'm taking it from another review, this game was but an experiment. So why should they finish the game? They got the experience in game design they needed, and after all, most revenue from the game has, statistically, long since come and gone. And so, unless they come back to this game, we will be stuck with half a game which should be sold at half a price.
And so, to summarise, as I explained beforehand, this game is promising and generally well designed but falls short on content. Luckily for us, half price sales for this game come around at leat twice a year so you can just wait it out.
As promised, my opinions on the problems:
The problems are chiefly (in my opinion): Lack of significant replayability once you complete the game once other than, perhaps, a playthrough with friends, fixable by adding some more content, simple as, perhaps including some new bosses, the current one being depressingly easy for reasons I'll go into next (although the game handles replayability very well prior to the completion of the game, with each playthrough unlocking more modules at the procedural generator's disposal and giving you permanent currency based on how far you got which can be used for costumes, books which give you a single certain buff and are kept indefinitely and chests at the start of each new level containing a very competent weapon in case you have fallen behind), problems with the weapon system in that the only thing the final boss can be is a slow, giant clockwork knight which can be beaten incredibly easily using arc weapons and a near endless supply of golden apples which you get for having a cleaver for at least 3 levels, and lastly netcode which I know is tricky and has to their credit been worked on as far as I know, although I didn't play too much multiplayer.
If you read this far, god have mercy on you, for you have lost a good chunk of your life, as have I.
If you skipped to the bottom for some reason: My one question is why? You're on steam, play a game, don't waste your time skimming reviews

Note: It says I've only got an hour on this game, but I played most of it offline so that I didn't get pop-up messages telling me my friends were playing Civ 5 (There's probs a way to turn this off, but I'm lazy. And the reason I didn't want those messages was because I was recording footage for the video you should hopefully be able to see below.
Anyway, onto the important stuff and for that matter the rather straight to the point stuff. For $15, White Night is a very good horror adventure. But before I explain why I'm going to list its downfalls, and it does have many. The game is about 5-6 hours long with practically no replayabilty, has long initial loading times and a frustrating array of adevnture-style puzzles that depend on luck to solve and that progresssion revolves around. Also, the theme of the Great Depression feels tacked on and not given enough focus to be important, the movement animations look clumsy at particular moments, and hovering over and selecting items can be very finnicky.
I think it is important to be aware of all of this before you make a purchase decision, but I'll also stress that you don't dismiss White Night because you read something above that you figure will annoy you. This is because a lot of White Night's problems are irrelevant to White Night's main experience. The game is primarily an atmospheric adventure that runs on your adrenalin and nerves. It strips of you of any power, immerses you in the dark shadows and makes you feel entirely helpless. This makes the player constantly anxious and expecant and I think this state of being the game generates can be likened to the sort in the original Clock Tower. And in this state you don't really care about a lot of this game's imperfections. Well, at least I didn't; I was really too absorbed and on edge to notice or care.
So yeah, I encourage you to buy White Night. Even just to expereince it because I find that not many horror games execute tone and suspense quite as well as White Night. And if you want more of my opinion of White Night I have a full review video below.

So you bought Witcher 3 or you are thinking of buying it, because you have watched others playing it, and now you're pondering whether you should pick up Witcher 2 and maybe 1 up as well. Is it worth it? As someone who has been in this very same situation I can speak out of personal experience.
From a technical point of view Witcher 2 is a
step forward from Witcher 1. Graphics and the characters look much, much better although a bit much blooming. Animations feel a lot better, though personally I'm not a big fan of Geralt's running animation in this game. Combat feels much more engaging than in Witcher 1 and it feels like you have much more control over your fighting. You can actively block attacks, dodge them, alter between quick and strong attacks and Geralt's signs are under an easy quick menu. The few occassions Geralt engages into a match of fistycuffs it's pure QTE though. There are a few cut scenes involving QTE's as well, but not at all that intrusive and annoying. So CD Project Red can be forgiven for this one.
This game also has been published on consoles and therefor it can be played well with controller also. Unlike in Witcher 1 and 3 however, Geralt has to drink potions out of combat and cannot do that in the heat of action. Nice technical detail is the fact that if you have played Witcher 1 you can import the save file and have story line (with its decisions) carry over to Witcher 2 (you can do the same in Witcher 3). Not sure how (much) those decisions affect Witcher 2 though. I personally was unable to notice much of it, other than an "honourable mention".
The story starts pretty much right off at the end of Witcher 1, so having played the predecessor can help you on that terrain. You'll know what happened to Geralt, why he's in the state he's in (still useful for Witcher 3 as well) and how he ended up in the situation you start off in Witcher 2. It all makes more sense, but is not a necessity to play Witcher 2. You get various hints through flashbacks and the logs if you read through them, so you might get a good idea of what's going on.
There's more humour in the dialogues and situations and any romance that happens in the game is given a little more lead towards the
rather than "do or give me something I like and we might go find a quiet spot" and given much more eye-candy than just a "collectible card". Developers also made sure to put some "easter eggs" (little hidden jokes) here and there like winks back to Witcher 1, some sort of insider's jokes. Much like in Witcher 1, the story in Witcher 2 is fairly linear: you move from one area to the next as you "finish" it with no chance to go back to a previously visited area. And each area you work in isn't so much larger than they were in Witcher 1.
Whether you're bothered with the technicallities or not, I'd say it's worth the ride on the road to Witcher 3!

A throwback to the roots of 3D survival horror. Channeling the 1992 Infogrames classic "Alone in the Dark", White Night shares many aspects of the original: Mostly puzzle-driven gameplay with a large, derelict mansion to explore; Crooked, static camera angles Sam Raimi himself would be proud of, and a large part of the story told via books and diary entries. Both games even feature the same Camille Saint-Saëns' composition - A nice little touch.
Not being bound by 90's technology, White Night additionally handles exposition by integrating an ongoing vocal narration. Listening to the somber musings of the protagonist sink in the film noir aesthetic, a goal that is visually even more evident: Everything is presented in black & white, either illuminated by a flickering matchstick or shrouded in ever-unfolding nocturnal shadows.
Finding ways to produce even the tiniest gleam of light to fight back the gloom requires careful observation and thought, since you're otherwise weaponless against the void and its spawn. When cornered, running away is the only option. To make matters even more dire, you're always burning through your stack of matches, a valuable commodity that the game carefully administers to keep up tension.
While White Night is oozing with stylistic charm, in some ways it clings perhaps a bit too closely to twenty-year old design choices; Probably enough so to make most modern gamers squirm in discomfort. You die in one hit. You run out of matches, you're dead. The camera angles sometimes make navigation way harder, especially in high-stress situations.
The worst offender, however, is the obnoxiously bad checkpoint system. Replaying through sizable chunks of puzzles is a common occurrence, since there simply aren't enough savepoints between some scene transitions. I understand that a certain sense of stinginess in saving possibilities is required in a survival horror game, but come the hell on - Don't make me watch story scenes multiple times just because you've set up a murderous wraith around the next corner right after it.
Anyhow, I was brought up on way more vicious stuff so in the end I overcame, but I can easily imagine folks of a less forgiving mental disposition towards games attempting to screw them over to just keel over and capitulate way before the slender lady sings. As the end credits rolled, I walked away from White Night feeling that here's a game that was created exactly for people like me - A fleeting validation that maybe my thirty plus years of gaming haven't been a total waste of time. Some people do still remember.
Next time, also bring back the Cthulhu mythos.

Set during the tail end of the Great Depression, White Night is a stylistic thriller where the contrasts of light and dark are more than just window dressing. Playing very much like Amnesia: The Dark Descent, but with the camera and controls of the early Resident Evil games, White Night begins when you crash your car after swerving to miss a woman in the road while coming home from the bar one night. You follow the woman into a nearby mansion in search help, only to become sucked into a mystery whose secrets are as dark as the night itself.
Say what you will about the Resident Evil style controls, while the've always had their flaws, White Night seems to recognize this and does a decent job of making sure that changing camera angles don't hamper movement too much. Most of the game involves your searching for keys and other items needed to progress through the mansion while reading various diaries and newspaper articles that advance the narrative along the way. The puzzles for the most part are simple enough given either a little bit of thought or a little trial and error and the mechanics of light and shadow that often accompany them never feel gimicky or too out of place. The enemies are usually just another puzzle themselves, living obstacles that can be vanquished by the light. Visually the game's high contrast style is executed perfectly, though I felt the character models were lower poly than they could have been. The anti-aliasing could have been stronger also, as the high contrast really highlights the effect.
The sound is excellent, from the music to the foley, creating a consistent mood thoughout. The voice acting as well is excellent, though the dialog and portions of the writing suffer a bit. This may just be due to English not being the developer's native language however. In addition to the narrative of the protagonist, the woman, and the mansion's owners, there also seems to be some attempt at subtext or metaphor regarding capitalism and the downfall of the American dream, but it gets lost in the mix and regardless of its Gatsby-esque  intentions, feels a little half-formed.
If you're a fan of narrative adventure games like Amnesia, Gone Home, or Among the Sleep and you're looking for something similar with lots of style and a noir setting, then I definitely recommend White Night. It has a few flaws here and there, but its nothing that detracted from my enjoyment of the game.

White Night is good. It plays like a cross between Resident Evil and Outlast set in the 1930's. This is another game that begs to be played at night in the dark with headphones. There's lots of puzzles to solve inside a big spooky haunted mansion and the only defence against the ghosts is light. Most of the rooms in the mansion are really dark and you need to find light switches, breakers, and power outlets to successfully brighten up the mansion and vanquish the ghostly apparations of some broad that died in the house. The story of the game isn't all that great. It's more mystical, depressing nonsense that's been done a hundred times before. The art style of the game is fantastic and mostly really unique. The game is essentially all in black and white with some very minor uses of color every now and then. The game does a good job of setting the spooky atmosphere. Like RE, it uses pre-rendered back grounds, which I liked as not many games go with that style. However, also like RE it's easy to get twisted around when the camera suddenly changes and I died a bunch of times because of it. To navigate the dark areas you get matches. They burn out quickly and you get a limited supply. This mechanic really reminded me of Outlast and the camera batteries. There was only one time when I got down to my final match, but the mechanic does ratchet up the tension as it seems like I was always running low on matches. It was always a nice relief each time I managed to turn on a light. The game is paced mostly well, but about 2/3 of the way through the game it was starting to drag on and sections just seemed like tedious trial and error. Sometimes it seemed like the luck of the draw if I was going to die or not. Ghosts would be blocking the way I needed to go or not for different attempts I made.  The ending sections picked the pace back up again, though. It took me around 7 hours to finish the game. I recommend it.

The quality of the experience is true Paradox fashion, if you've played any of their other games, with enough content and new events popping up to keep you wanting to explore. The game on the whole is intuitive, with informative tutorials in general (assuming you've ever played any kind of strategy game before), and a difficulty system that doesn't hold your hand, but yet doesn't murder you if you play smart.
STATS
OVERALL RATING: 7.5/10
Overall, a good game for the money, that will give any grand strategy, 4x strategy, or sci-fi lover plenty of hours of enjoyment. Just don't be surprised when it takes 5 DLC releases to be bumped up to a 9/10.

Abzu is a game about the ocean. You know, that infinitely beautiful yet terrifying body of water which covers over 70% of the earth's surface? I have to say that personally, I've always found the ocean to be the most fascinating aspect of nature, especially considering how little of it we've explored.
For me, Abzu captured the wonder and dread that I've always wanted from an ocean exploration game. It was a short-lived experience, at around 100 minutes but I enjoyed every second of it. I honestly don't think I've played a game that is this gorgeous. The music is consistently grand, the visuals always stunning. My jaw literally dropped at one point after the discovery of one underwater creature that I recognised from a book I owned as a kid. It's not easy for a game to instill that sense of childlike wonder and joy. As long as you know what you're getting into with this game, a short and non-challenging game, then I think it's near impossible to not love. Just know that there is no fail state, the puzzles are more or less "swim to one device and activate it, swim to another device". If you let yourself get immersed in the world of Abzu, you will not regret it.

The game has many annoyances, the one that I kept running into was your teammates not getting XP if they're stunned when a unit is killed.  WHY!?  I can understand if they're unconscious or dead, but stunned, sleep, paralyzed, etc. ALL prevent your team mates from gaining XP.
My main gripe with the game is how combat is so luck based.  Most units in the game have a 10% chance to poison, stun, paralyze, other status conditions, etc. and a 100% chance to inflict on crit.  This goes back to my previous rant, you're going to lose A LOT of XP and it doesn't carry over to your other heroes that are up.  It just plains disappears into thin air.  You aren't given many opportunities to prevent these and you're limited in ways to remove them.  It's unfun and just plain frustrating.  Also, despite having multiple attacks, boss monsters tend to just keep spamming their AoE attack that can stun your team.  Fun...

TL;DR - If You like old-school cRPGs, buy this on a sale.
As a fan of the series (started with VI, but played pretty much every part), I rejoiced when I've learned that Ubi greenlit a game from a series and genre I've presumed dead. That being said, I acknowledge the fact, that this game is neither the best M&M game nor the best retro-style cRPG. Nevertheless, if you're a fan of the series, or liked Legends of Grimrock, or other similar titles, this one is fun too.
It's rather minimalistic with only three classes and four races, but each race+class combo is treated differently (e.g an Orc warrior is an aggressive Barbarian, whereas a Dwarf is tanky Shieldbearer, and a Human Crusader has some healing abilities) and as the game progresses they get different special skills. Movement is grid based like in M&M I through V, and everything is turn based (enemies won't move, unless your party moved/waited) and the combat, while rather simple, is a snap, once you know what you're doing. The story is quite standard (find four magical thingies to save the world), and is set in the HoMM VI universe, although prior knowledge of that game is not necessary. Nothing special, but it does harken back to an age when cRPGs were simpler, and like I've said, if you liked that kind of games, this one emulates them very nicely, with more contemporary graphics.
Also, I never had any game breaking bugs, that seem to plague other players, although the game is poorly optimized, and after an hour or so the framerate drops significantly.

This game is great. It can be described as a very simple combination of rhythm-based game and roguelike. Does it work, though?
yes.
The entire game revolves around the movement coordination, since you have to follow the beat to move and attack. The controls are effective in this regard, as you only require the arrow keys to do anything. Of course, the monsters also follow the beat to move, most often every other beat while you move on every beat. There is a benefit to keeping your rhythm going, as you will get more money from killing monsters when you do. Money can be spent on a variety of weapons within a play session that change the way you deal with monsters, but you can still beat the entire game with a simple knife if you know how. There are also diamond pickups, which let you buy upgrades outside a match to increase your chances, which you'll want to do if you ever plan to beat the game.
The music itself is composed by Danny Baranowsky and is simply stunning. I love listening to it even outside the game, and if that doesn't work for you, custom soundtrack from your own computer can be used instead. It even has gamepad support- yes, gamepads like the sort you'd see from an old Dance Dance Revolution arcade machine if you're into the game to that degree.
Each monster has a pattern of attack which you will probably need to figure out how to deal with to finish the game. And you will probably die many times trying, since this game has a permadeath system like many roguelikes. But the game is never
. You can look at how you died and see where you went wrong, so there's always room to improve instead of just feeling like the game made you fail. I'm happy to see games that do difficult but fun properly, and Necrodancer is one of them.
If you want an extra degree of challenge (since the game on its own isn't hard enough already), there are unlockable characters, each with their own quirks. No money, no killing monsters, only use one weapon, all beats are twice as fast, die instantly, there's a lot you can do. I won't spoil the story itself, but all the characters do tie in extraordinarily well, so if you feel like they're random, trust me, they're not.
I really wish I could talk more about this game, and
, there is a lot I haven't even touched on. But honestly? Crypt of the Necrodancer gets a glowing review from me. Buy the game, buy the soundtrack, even get a gamemat if you want to actually dance when you play. I haven't done it yet, but I might do it.
If I somehow
haven't sold you, the Collector's Edition (everything) is on sale for under 10$, and the core game for less than 5$. So go buy it! Trust me, you won't regret it.

Basically, this game is a glorified spreadsheet program. Your goal is to take known variables and combine them with hidden variables to get a rating that is as close to 100 as possible. For example: You create a show. In that show you have to create matches and "angles." Angles are basically the story elements. You pretty much have to just use your imagination. Seriously, all angles actually do is tell the program to compare the stats of two or more workers. In it's simplest form, (wrestler A) * (wrestler b) * (product, or fan expectations) = final rating. Now in reality, there are actually hundreds of variables to consider, but that's pretty much it.
The storylines are whatever you say they are. You can do this because you are role playing. You can type whatever you want into the story field and it makes no difference at all. You can even leave it empty. Seriously, all I could think of while trying to create a story was that episode of Family Guy where Peter lets Stewie play with his sock.
So to recap: I paid $20 for a spreadsheet/calculator program where 90% of the gameplay is your imagination. I felt like I was playing D&D by myself.

Woolfe is an interesting game in which some poor decisions were made. For every good thing that can be said about it there is a negative point to counter it. In the end I've decided to upvote it but it's mostly because I, personally, enjoy fairytale-themed games and platformers very much and so playing Woolfe has been a pleasant experience for me overall. However, it might not be everyone's cup of tea.
The game has in my opinion some fantastic level design. No two levels look the same. The environment can go from gloomy to vibrant and colorful and the levels definitely have that fairytale charm to them. The music, too, is incredibly charming. That said there are only a few, level-specific tracks and listening to them over and over throughout the course of the level can get irritatingly repetitive. The fact that there are few other sound effects makes this hard to ignore - especially since Red herself is the only character in the game who ever speaks. (There is another character who gets a line or two but 99% of the game is one long monologue.) I say this so that you can understand me when I say the game lacks atmosphere. The ingredients to make an immersive game are there but they are very poorly managed.
For all the good work that was put into this game, it all falls a bit flat because Woolfe takes itself way more seriously than it can afford in the end. The story tries to be quite dark and full of twists, and I do believe it could have been a pretty good story at that, if only the game were at least three or four times longer than it is and if it dropped the (beautiful, stunning, really) fairytale visuals. It's just hard to see B. B. Woolfe as the monstrous villain he is intended to be when his city looks more like Santa's Christmas village than a den of evil and when you can never see a single person actually suffering because of him and mostly have to take Red's word for it all. The game's beauty ends up being one of it's biggest flaws simply because it clashes so obviously with the dark nature of the plot. Separately the plot and the delivery could both have been very good, but when you put it together it just does not work. It doesn't work and it makes me sad because Woolfe could have been a very good game.
As for the technical side of it - the game controls nicely, the combo system is a sweet touch, but again it's not perfect. The other big problem I have with this game is the HP system, which I just don't understand at all. When you die in combat, you respawn basically right where you died, making death absolutely inconsequential. It's also a good thing, though, because when it comes to environmental hazards, the game is utterly merciless and any contact with any spikes or saws or, heck, even a log that stands in your way, is an instant one-hit K.O. Sometimes even a slightly misjudged jump will have Red dying with a blood-curdling scream of pain when really all she did was trip on a twig, making some of the deaths in the game terribly annoying and hilarious at the same time (did I mention you can get killed by poop?). Items that increase your HP are scattered across the levels but I never once needed them because when I did actually find myself low on health I would soon die and respawn with full health on the spot once more. The whole thing just doesn't make sense.
The difficulty levels are well balanced, at least. That is to say, playing the game on easy will not take much effort, beating the game on normal actually gave me a sense of accomplishment because I did struggle several times, especially with the bosses, who I feel are actually reasonably challenging without taking /too/ long to beat. And playing the game on hard really feels like you have to focus on your combat strategy a little if you want to make progress. Collecting the diary entries for the achievements can be a pain, though. It took me longer than I'd like to admit to realize that even though the game says certain entries are in certain levels, they are in fact found in the preceding levels. That's just a btw tip from one achievement hunter to others.
Like I said, this game has a lot of charm that would have definitely paid off had the devs only spent much, much more time working on it. It should take way more than 2 hours to go through this story - a story that does not fit the environment it's set in at all and a story that ends with an annoying cliffhanger on top of it. As it is Woolfe is just a not bad, not great platformer for a lazy afternoon (or if you're fast enough, possibly just a free lunch break).

I'll be honest, I only bought this because the Humblr Store had it on sale and it was a pretty looking game with furries that took itself seriously instead of being a mascot title. That's a rarity, especially in the kind of mainstream stuff you buy on Steam or XBLA.
That was the reason I bought it at first, but I finally got around to playing and it wound up being the best $2.99 I ever spent and a game that might actually break the top 10 on my list of all time favorite games.
The first thing you'll notice going in is that the graphics are BEAUTAFUL and there's some real nice fine detail in the animations like the fabric of Dust's clothes rippling as he moves. The effects like explosions, projectale attacks, and lighting are also really pretty and can result in some great atmosphere and awesome moments during combat. It feels almost like an interactive cartoon at times.
It also ran maxed out flawlessly on my 750ti/FX-8320 at a solid 60FPS that only dropped to 51 during loading and cutscenes, but I think that's more an issue with how the game load assets than something that more horse-power or optimization is going to fix
The second thing is the story is great and will more than likely bring you close to tears on far more than one occasion, I can only describe the emotional rollercoaster than ensues from the ending of the second chapter onwards as something that wants to break you one way or the other. The story has some fantasy cliches, but it uses them well to paint a world that world that likable because it would be unashamably idealistic if it wasn't at war. I'd almost say it remained that way in spite of itself because all the drama and heartache makes it feel very much like you're earning a happy ending for all the people you help along the way.
The game also has a welcome sense of humor in it's lighter movemets that comes from hanging a lampshade on common RPG tropes like stuffing huge items in your pockets or random fetch-quests.
The gameplay is a simple side-scrolling RPG with Castlevania exploration and some pretty hefty rewards for putting the effort to cheack everywhere and uncover every secrect in the gameworld. The combat is very much a button-mashing that relies on timing and keeping up with on-screen action to rack-up combos and avoid getting hit instead of complicated combos or a huge arsenal of moves.
So yeah, I'd say this is worth a buy and a place in anyone's libraiy.

Pros:
-Colorful, twisted, fairytale world a la "Alice: Madness Returns"
Cons:
-Episodic releases (with no indication that this is not a full game)
-Devolper is bankrupt (no future episodes in sight)
-Disorienting platforming camera and controls
-Uni-dimensional, voiceless characters (aside from protagonist)
-No combat feedback
-Pointlessly talkative protagonist
-Nearly useless combat abilities
-General lack of substance and polish
Woolfe certainly showed a level of potential, with appealing artwork and promise of an intriguing plot. Unfortunately, once past the trailers an opening segment, the player isn't given much in the way of an experience. Though, the environments are generally attractive, close inspection uncovers disconnected placement of objects (lamp posts not actually touching the ground, breakable boxes looking identical to indestructible ones, etc) as well as a lack of interactivity that makes the "world" feel flat.
As far as story, there is little inspiration. Red starts out a vendetta against B. B. Woolfe for her father's death with little more than suspicion of the entrepreneur's involvement. Although Woolfe's guilt is blatantly oblivious to the player, Red initially has no clear reason to back her desire to kill him. She does find evidence (from a predictable twist about her father's career), and a potential conspirator, but she kills him before making any attempt at interrogation. From there it is rinse and repeat. Find a little evidence of guilt, expose some more predictable plot points, and kill someone in your way without sufficient cause.
Adding to the lack of personality in the game is that no one speaks outside of Red, and Granny. Bosses don't even get dialogue to introduce themselves, antagonize Red, or even grunt in battle. From a story telling standpoint this is a major shortcoming, as the player has no investment their supposed enemy, thus there is little motivation to fight, let alone care about or even remember the experience. Interestingly enough, Red has the opposite problem. Simply put, she speaks too much. Making pointless quips every five steps, her voice is soon tuned out, or worse yet becomes a disruptive frustration, considering she is meant to be sneaking for an extended period. The girl also speaks in lack-luster, half rhymes. The concept itself could have been rather whimsical, but it feels forced due to poor word play, and how the gimmick was often abandoned for several lines.
Moving on to game play, the terms lacking and frustrating once again come to mind. While the camera is set in a relatively fixed position, Red can traverse levels in full 3d motion. Often when platforming the fixed perspective makes judging jumps difficult. Red also, lacks a permanent shadow to provide feedback regarding her position relative to platforms. This makes it aggravatingly easy to over/under shoot platforms on the z-plane (toward or away from the screen).
In addition to platforming, there are basic puzzle mechanics and combat. The former is presented as expected in any game of the genre, and deserves no real comment. Fights on the other hand are like jumping, as in easily misjudged, leading to repeated death. Enemies have little reaction to taking damage so it is difficult to fend off multiple targets. Special abilities provide some help with crowd control but it is  easy to become stun-locked when trying to use them.
A point should be made that combat seems to be discouraged initially. Based on Red being portrayed as "sneaking" through the city, and enemy deaths prompting a certain comment box ( indicating that killing them may be a negative karma event), one might gravitate toward avoiding combat. At a certain point however, progress can only be made by killing opponents in front of a door. This dynamic was never used until that point and not even hinted at, leaving the player to wonder if they had missed a switch.
Finally, and most importantly, total game play takes less than two hours even when collecting all secrets. The reason for this is that Woolfe appears to be released as episodes, and ten dollars gets you chapter one. This is possibly the most frustrating aspect, as there is no clear indication on the store page that the software is only a partial game, amounting to little more than a demo or tutorial level. Combining this with poor gameplay, forgettable characters, and the very important (and not publicized) fact that the devolper is out of business makes the experience a complete disappointment.

Let me start by saying that I am a huge fan of twisted retellings of classic fairytales, so the moment I noticed that a twisted version of Red Riding Hood was being created as a videogame, I was very excited. That aside, this game is quite tricky for me to review, so I will do my best.
For starters, the story is quite interesting. It takes place in an industial city called Ulrica, which has heavy steampunk elements, and it follows Red Riding Hood as she tries to solve the mystery of her father's death. Industrial tycoon B.B. Woolfe is ruling over the city using his mechanized soldiers, and it is Red's mission to infiltrate his archives and find out if her father's death, who was working for Woolfe at the time, was really an accident, or if foul play was involved. It will probably maintain your interest, and I found Red's delivery of hers and her family's backstory through rhymes really amusing. There are also a lot of collectibles that add more depth to the lore of the city and many of the characters.
Moving on, the art style is amazing and goes a long way in creating a wonderful, eerie but enchanting atmosphere. The empty city of Ulrica is a marvel to behold: the lonely houses covered in snow, the worn out boats and the cold lake water that runs through the town, everything adds to the feeling of isolation and constant danger that Red is experiencing. The dim candle lights that glow from the house windows, the posters of children that went missing, all these details come together to create a threatening, but at the same time strangely alluring atmosphere of mystery.
Music-wise, I believe the composers did an amazing job in making the players feel as if they are playing in a dark fairytale. They dressed up the game quite nicely, with slow, low melodies when Red is moving through the town, undetected, and more intense pieces when she is hunted by enemies, or is in a dire situation.
Now for the bad stuff.
At times, the controls are unresponsive, specificaly when it comes to jumping. There were several times when I lost my life simply because Red did not jump over a gap, although I had pressed "space". I have seen that this is a common point of complaint from other players as well. Keep in mind that I played the game using a keyboard, so maybe this is not a problem when playing with a controller.
Another problem is the camera. The developers themselves have said that, originaly, the game was to be a 2D platformer before they decided to move it to complete 3D. However, it seems as if the 3D part was added after they had developed a major part of the game with a 2D mentality, and this has created depth perception problems. There will be times when Red will need to jump to a platform that is in the backround, but the camera will remain in 2D mode, making it extremelly difficult to understand if your jump will be succesful or not.
A third problem was the second half of the game. Although, visually, it is one of the most beautiful things I have ever seen, there is a sudden spike in platforming difficulty that feels a bit cheap. The depth perception problem and jumping issue mentioned above make it extremelly hard to traverse the various, deadly platforming set pieces. I found myself dying endlessly in that part, and I have had a lot of experience with platformers. I kind of felt as if they made it like that on purpose, just to add a bit more time to the game.
Speaking of time, the game is extremely short. It took me two hours to finish it, and that is with all the dying I experienced in the second part.
Finally, I did not particularly like the ending. I know the game was supposed to be released in two volumes, but I still wanted to have at least a bit more information before its end, since it created more questions than gave answers.
To conclude, yes, I do recommend this game. It has its problems, but it also has an undeniable charm, especialy if you are into twisted retellings of fairytales, like I am. As a platformer, you will find better games out there, but it is decent in that department, and the setting makes it even more appealing, despite its flaws. I was saddened to hear that the developers went bankrupt, and I wish them the best in whatever they do next. However, good news is that the game was bought by Rebelion, a well known company, so there is still hope for a continuation of this tale.
Hopefully, Red will eventually live happily ever after. :)

Game seems to be going a bit under the radar so thought I'd shed some light. White Night is a horrorish adventure game with a minimalist art style, almost all in black and white. Everything in the game is pure darkness unless illuminated by a light source, and so it often creates scenes oozing with style, especially when couples with the fixes camera angles.
While the game has some obvious survival horror roots, it is mainly an adventure game, never really involving any sort of combat. The game is set in a decrepit mansion evoking the likes of Resident Evil and Alone in the Dark, but playing out a bit more like Silent Hill. Lighting is one of the main puzzle mechanics. You need light to explore and interact with the house, so you need to manage matches so you don't run out. Spending too much time in the dark or running into one of the residents will not end well. The puzzles often involve either lighting up areas to force enemies away (they can't stand electric light) so you can progress or lighting area so you can perform an action that would be too hard in the dark. There are also some traditional "mansion owned by loonies" types of esoteric puzzles to solve, though they are probably a bit on the easy side.
The game's story is a bit bare bones. The main character is driving and swerves his car to avoid hitting a ghostly woman and from there enters the creepy mansion of the Verner family and is stuck investigating their secrets. From there there's not a ton of meat, with the vast majority of the story being fleshed out with journals to read that are dropped like every 10 feet. Some of these have some questionable translation. Even still, the game has some pretty obvious plot turns and twists that everyone will guess an hour in, which can be frustrating to watch the game treat as big deals later.
Where the game excels in is atmosphere. The enemies you face are consistently creepy and rarely get to be a chore like in a like of similar games. Some great sound design. Not reliant on jump scares, though there's a couple good ones, and the way it treats the enemies with never really being in focus is unsettling. When you take back an area of the house by turning on the lights it feels like a real accomplishment. The game does have a few cheap deaths from the fixed camera angles if you're unlucky. If you get stuck on a puzzle too it can be easy to run out of matches and really screw yourself, though I only came close to this once so I imagine it won't be an issue for many.
Game lasted me 5-6 hours and should be roughly the same for most. It's not a game I'd shout from the rooftops about but it's a good little entry if you're looking for something creepy. Good first outing, will look forward to seeing what they can do with a bigger budget and maybe better translators.

A really great but flawed game. The contrast of the white and black really makes things more tense than most spooky games. I feel like these devs are really big Silent Hill fans, as they take a lot of cues from the series: the helplessness, the atmosphere, and also the technical issues.
This has a weird control issue; when you move from one camera angle to another, the direction you are pressing sends you into wherever that direction is as opposed to the direction you are going (I hope that makes sense). This is INFURIATING when I'm trying to run away from a ghost and the camera angle changes and I run right back into the ghost.
Honestly, that's the only really bad thing about this game so far. I love the Depression-era setting (which no one does and I appreciate), the spooky mansion, and the use of light and darkness as a gameplay mechanic.
ADDENDUM (after actually beating it): the controls are goddamn frustrating. So. Goddamn. Frustrating. It's like tank controls but without the precision.
The game's puzzles are pretty subtle throughout the game; you just have to get this thing to put in that thing to unlock that door. The last 2 chapters just go straight up Silent Hill puzzles, with matching pictograms and♥♥♥♥♥♥ I think it's a weird progression.
Overall, I'm disappointed. I could see the ending coming a mile away. There's a lot of design choices that just bug me (especially with how you play the ending, you'll see). I would compare this to Murdered: Soul Suspect, in that it's a great idea with a lot of gameplay design decisions that bring it down. I still recommend it, but only if you have a high tolerance for stupid controls.

White Night is a suspenseful adventure game. Everything that it does from the graphics, to the voiceovers builds on that suspenseful feeling. It's a good game.
Video Review:
What is it?
White Night is a Noir-horror adventure game. The game plays similarly to a Telltale game, where the player wanders around a place looking at things and trying to solve various puzzles. The main difference between this and a Telltale game is that White Night uses only the keyboard to play (no point and click) and there are no quick-time events (as far as I've seen. Noir and horror are not two genres that expected to see put together. After this game it seems like a no brainer, but beforehand I wouldn't have thought that the level-headed nature of Noir would mix with the superstitions of a horror game. I'm glad I was wrong.
The graphics are the first thing that will come to most peoples mind when they see this. The game is entirely black and white except for the few sources of light that you will find throughout the game. This adds significantly to the tension of the game. Most of the time, you will move around using match-light. When that goes out, there is definitely a feeling of dread. You know that there is something, somewhere that is after you. What if it's right behind you and you just don't know it yet? Beyond that, I never find myself wishing it was in color. I do sometimes dread the lack of color, because perhaps if there was a speck of color outside of my tiny match flame, then the world might not seem so sinister.
The story of the game is conveyed mostly through memoire entries and newspaper clippings. This means that the game will be reading intensive. I don't mind that so much, but I know that there are some people who play games to get away from that sort of thing.
Is the game scary? It is, but it won't try to scare you by throwing things in your face. This game has so far been brilliant at building suspense. Take one moment, for instance. I was plugging in a lamp, because I felt so inclined. As I plugged it in, there was a knock on the door next to me. I knew that there would be something behind it. Beyond that, I knew that I would have to open it. The dread I felt beforehand helped to heighten the fear that I felt as I fled from the wraith (I mean, I had to open the door, I needed to know for sure).
With all this being said, this game (so far) has not proven to be terribly difficult. The puzzles have been fairly straight forward. That being said, I've only played a little over an hour of the game.
Pros:
-An amazing suspenseful atmosphere.
-A go-at-your-own-pace feel. You are limited by the number of matches you can find in the house, but there are a lot of them.
-Vivid and simple graphics that help to create the games suffocating atmosphere.
-So far, the story has been interesting. I want to know what happened to the people who lived in this manner, and that's a good start for a game.
-Simple, non-stressful mechanics. The stress of the game is more situational then mechanics based (like quick-time events).
Cons:
-The game can be frightening. That's not a con for everyone, but if you can't take scary games then you should think long and hard about this one.
-If you play on a keyboard you will get the distinct feeling that the game was meant to be played with a controller. I'm pretty sure that that is the case. It doesn't detract much from the game, aside from putting the run button on the awkward U key.
Overall, this game has an amazing atmosphere and an engaging narrative. I'll be playing a lot of this game in the future. I would definitely recommend it at the price of $15.

I rarely write reviews, but I just completed Little Inferno and feel...overwhelmed and excited! I first saw this game played on YouTube and I bought it thinking it would be a neat little time-consumer. Was I ever wrong! Little Inferno is much more than just burning stuff and watching the flames flicker out. There is a depth here you wouldn't expect at first glance. It's a short game (I completed it in just over 7 hours, but I also spent a lot of time distracted, and making sure I got all 99 combos, some of which are a little...vague), and yet it ends on a high note that made my heart swell at 5 in the morning.
The graphics are a little bit Tim Burton; unique, peculiar, and that sort of creepy-cute; the fire effect is realistic and oddly comforting. The music is fantastic and
, when it picks up you really
it; it's not just background noise. Gameplay is pretty standard and easy to grasp (click-and-drag, mostly), and the only thing really holding you back are the combos, which are mostly obvious - the more vague ones feel rather satisfying to complete.
If you want a rather quick game that's fun to play, easy to understand, and surprisingly multi-faceted and emotional - buy Little Inferno.

Little Inferno is a quirky and fun game. The main plot takes place in a modern time with a twist. The entire world has frozen over. Cities of people thrive indoors and never step foot outside. A company called Tomorrow Coorporation makes a fireplace for kids to burn their toys in. Yay! We can be warm! But what happens when you run out of toys? You buy more, of course! By buying toys, you can unlock new magazines to buy toys from. During the game, you will recieve letters from different people. Without these, the story would have no plot whatsoever. Miss Nancy, the CEO of Tomorrow Coorporation, your neighbor Sugar Plumps, and the weatherman will all send you letters. These letters may include quests that you MUST do in order for the game's story to continue. They are all simple and the hardest they get is sending a toy to Sugar Plumps.
Overall, this game is absolutley brilliant. Burning toys and getting more to burn? Who would have thought of it!

Don't be afraid to explore, but dangerous caves are what they tell you, dangerous. Come back to them later!

Even though I had fun with this game, overall I can't really recommend it.
If you are a huge fan of the Might and Magic series, you might give it a try, because it will tickle your nostalgia with countless references to the old games and will at some points even feel like them too. But sadly it's nowhere near the level of the old Might and Magic games. This game feels more like a below average RPG trying to be a Might & Magic game instead of a genuine Might & Magic successor.
I don't wanna throw around "bad game design" as a buzzword, but a lot of moments in this game certainly feel like that. Overall the game lacks a lot of polish. There are a lot of moment which make you question what the developers were thinking and it really needs several patches imo. But sadly the development for this game stopped, so it kinda has to stay in this current state. Let's not even talk about all the bugs this game still has.
Contrary to most RPGs I played, the battle system in this game just feels really frustrating and not fun at all. Especially if you don't have a proper party setup the fights can get ridiculously punishing and force a lot of restarts (which take pretty long in this game and are always annoying on principle). On that note, I think the recommended default party is utterly ill-equipped to deal with what the game throws at you in the last third of the game and the DLC. Which is already a really questionable design decision in itself. Before you attempt to play this game, definitely look up a decent party build or the game can actually become extremely frustrating (on normal difficulty) and even impossible to beat (on hard difficulty).

I'll say right off the bat that I enjoy Necropolis, but I have to give it a negative recommendation.  The short version of my reasoning is that it's just not worth $30.  The $15 sale price that I got it for would be a perfectly fair regular price, in my estimation.  In terms of the game itself, there's not any one big thing that brings it down.  Rather, there are a lot of small but significant irritations that make the game difficult to like, the kind of things that should have been caught and corrected in QA.  It feels like a beta.  A well-polished beta, mind you, but it just doesn't feel like a finished product.
One of the bigger problems with the game is an over-reliance on random chance.  The level of randomization involved in the types and density of enemies that spawn in a given area means that the early-game difficulty curve is all over the map.  Virtually all of my runs have lasted either less than 20 minutes, or more than 2 hours, depending entirely on whether or not the game spawns a gank squad of strong enemies on the first couple levels.
Many ranged enemies mix poorly with the blocking mechanics.  Knockback from ranged attacks pushes your character back far enough that by the time you've closed the gap, the enemy will have charged up its next volley, and the cycle repeats.  This problem can be avoided by dodging in the case of beam attacks, but homing projectiles track well enough that blocking is your only real option.
Certain enemies feel weirdly unbalanced.  Notably, large crystal Hoardmen seem to absorb four or five times as much damage as smaller crystal enemies, but tend to spawn in large numbers as though they were trash mobs.  The giant skeleton spiders encountered in the later levels have a ridiculous damage output, capable of effectively one-shotting a Blackguard class player character with maximized HP and max-tier armor.  They spawn far more frequently than I would expect, given how dangerous they are.  When one enemy is resposible for virtually every late-game death a player experiences, it should indicate that the enemy in question is a bit overpowered.
I've tried to avoid making direct comparisons to Dark Souls thus far, but here I just can't help it.  In Dark Souls, using a healing item during combat is risky, but doable if you pick your moment well.  The animations for using healing items in Necropolis are similarly slow, but compared to Dark Souls, Necropolis' enemies move more quickly.  If you attempt to heal in combat, you are effectively guaranteed to get hit.
Necropolis is close to being a very good game, but it's held back by a mound of small annoyances.  Unfortunately, everything I've heard indicates that the developers have ceased support for the game, ensuring that Necropolis' audience will forever consist only of people with an unreasonably high tolerance for getting screwed over by random chance.  If the devs were continuing support, this review would be a tentative thumbs-up.

Summary: An Alice: Madness Returns-esque game that's visually stunning but rough around the remaining edges
It's unfortunate that the development studio had to declare bankruptcy as there was potential for Woolfe to come closer to Alice: Madness Returns standards which is where I think it was going if it wasn't for money troubles. A Kickstarter/Indiegogo campaign could recover this game.
The bad bits for me were:
- Voice-overs: above average, but would've liked to hear more emotion in the narrator's voice as I didn't quite feel like I was being captured by RRH with the relatively fixed and tense tone the narrator used. Lack of voice-overs for other characters within the first couple of hours of playing it didn't help. Granny was the first one outside of RRH to actually speak any words
- Music: During tense/key moments the music just stays the same and doesn't really fit what's happening at the time so the story being told isn't coming across as it should
- Combat: Expect to take hits as dodging is nearly impossible and there's no method of blocking (certainly not in the first couple of  hours of gameplay) and it doesn't appear to scale well on different difficulty settings.
- Cutscenes: Some of the more dramatic cutscenes such as the introduction to the Pied Piper and the entrance of Woofle's carriage lacked any sort of tension and were not accompanied by the right music or camera effects to help instill that tension/drama
- Dialogue: Minor point, but some of the text dialogue doesn't match up to what's being narrated at the time
- Environment: Found it very difficult identifying whether or not some easter eggs (Woofle emblems) would be accessible at a later stage in the game or at that very point. If they were accessible at the point you find them, I found it impossible in a few cases to figure out how to reach them, especially as up to that point most Woofle emblems have either been in your direct path or otherwise intuitively hidden behind boxes or a relatively easy to identify path (although it might be challenging to walk it)
The good bits were:
- Visually stunning; Easily ramped it up to high settings and embraced the beauty of it. They didn't spare much expense on the terrain and props and for the most part the characters themselves were excellent. Animations were good but needed a little polish.
- Musical dialogue; if they invested a little more time in getting emotion across in the narration this would've been very captivating but I did like the musical/rhyming dialogue, it was a nice touch.
- Gameplay variety; enough for me not to feel like I'm grinding away doing the same old thing. Environment interaction to learn about the story, elements of third person, side-scrolling and platformer gameplay, combat that includes special weapons and combo's and a light-weight tutorial that doesn't feel like it get's in the way of you playing the game.
Overall, it showed promise, but I get the feeling that the money was funnelled predominantly into the visual effects when in actual fact they could've easily spared enough to get the weaker aspects up to scratch which would've make it a well rounded game.
For now, if you see it cheap, get it; as it's worth a few hours of your time.

The game was developed by Humble Hearts and published by Microsoft Studios.
The game was released August 15, 2012 for the Xbox live arcade after winning Microsoft's 2009 Dream.Build.Play competition. It can currently be purchased on PlayStation 4, Steam, Xbox 360, GNU/Linux, and Mac OS.
The world of Elysian Tail is vast and spans multiple media. Currently, Humble Hearts is working on a 2d animated feature film, at least, according to the game’s official website.
Gameplay:

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a 2d action rpg platform game, meaning that although the base gameplay involves jumping from one platform to another there is a whole lot of combat.
It seems like Dust is competing with Dynasty Warriors to see who can put more enemies on the screen at once.  This is ok though, because combat is fluid and easy to pick up.
Dust has numerous combat abilities and even a couple magic attacks thanks to Fidget, his magical, flying, fox-cat-dragon companion. She also provides moral support for him throughout the story.
There are RPG elements, but this is an RPG light game. When you level you go up in power but you don’t distribute attribute points or choose new abilities.
Just when you think to yourself, “So, I run, jump, and slash. That’s about it, right?” NOPE! Dust has many puzzles and secrets hidden throughout the game. You’ll even find major characters from other games hidden in chests. When you rescue another games’ mascot they give Dust a permanent buff to his stats. Needless to say, it is always worth while to search for these captive characters.
Graphics and Music:
The game features strong 2d graphics with rich backgrounds. Though in some cut scenes when they zoom in on the characters the gradients they used can look a bit off. Other than that, I found the graphics to perfectly fit the atmosphere of the game.
The music in Dust: An Elysian Tail does a great job of setting the mood of the gameplay and even tugged my heartstrings during a few of the pivotal story moments.
Controls:

I played the game on the PC with an Xbox controller. The controls were developed with that specific controller in mind and are very fluid. I never found myself getting frustrated by the controls during my playthrough.
Story:

Story is where Dust: An Elysian Tail shines. This game is heavy on story and cutscenes. At one point during my playthrough, I had a whole room full of people watching me play the game. During one of the longer cut scenes, a friend said it felt like the scene was reaching Metal Gear length. This was not entirely true but it made his point. This game is trying to tell you a gripping story and it succeeds. No wonder it won the Dream.Build.Play competition in 2009.
Voice Acting:
I find very few indie games want to include voice acting because it can be hard to find the right actors and is a very costly process. Dust does an amazing job in this area and the actors do a great job breathing life into their characters.
Overall:
As a whole, I found Dust to be a worthy use of my time. If you’re looking for a great side scrolling platformer with RPG elements and puzzles, or just looking for a gripping story outside of the JRPG and SHOOTER heavy world, this game is for you.
FINAL VERDICT:
I had a lot of fun with Dust and I think you will too, My final verdict for this game is PLAY IT! You won’t regret it, unless you hate fun. Then you might. I, for one, hope to see more games like it in the future.

As someone who has played countless hours of soulsborne games, I really enjoyed this game. The combat, items, graphics, and lore is what made the game fun and enjoyable. The lore is centered around items and jokes, which is fun at first, but when you really start wanting to know more about the necropolis these jokes really get in the way.
The maps are all randomly generated minus the hubs. You will get lost in the necropolis and enjoy it the whole time. The difficulty has a weird curve. The first level can be pretty challenging, but if you can survive the first level, high chance you will make it to level 3-4. If you can get a strongish weapon early on you will be fine. Level 5-7 can be conquered with decent gear, maybe a couple good potions, and a slightly better weapon than the first. Level 8-10 is where it gets difficult. You will find yourself using a lot of valuable items just to survive and get past a group of monsters.
This game is really fun with a friend. You can play with up 3 friends and it really is a whole new experience. You can either all go in as a pack, each seperate and find your own path, or split and hope you guys find eachother again. There is team damage, so beware.
Biggest issue with this game is the price. $30 is way too much for such a simplistic game like this. They should have done what Salt and Sanctuary did and just sell it for 10 bucks or less. This game has so many negative reviews do to the price, but I don't think the price should be what determines if a game is good or not.
All in all, fun game solo or with friends. Price is too expensive so get it on sale. Game is good

This will be the first game review I am doing.
I will be rating this game based on these 5 elements:
-Gameplay
-Level Design
-Art
-Sound
-Reply Value
Disclaimer: I don't really care about the story when I play platformers (actually pretty much all games in general) as I tend to focus more on the players gameplay experience.
Introduction; Dust: An Elysian Tail is a 2D platformer which mainly features face-paced battle action that keeps your adrenaline pumped and fingers constantly pressing buttons when you play the game. The player controls the main character of the game, Dust, and goes on an adventure to recover his memories.
-Gameplay [9/10]
Dust: An Elysian Tail has pretty good combat mechanics. The same button that makes Dust hack and slash is also the same button that makes the character blocks. This will trigger a more predicting playstyle from the player instead of having an extra button for the player to cancel the attacking animation to block, it forces the player to be patient and be aware of what he/she is doing even when the combat is so fast paced. The different projectiles that are available for Fidget that can be unlocked after playing the game for awhile will make the player study his/her enemies, different projectiles will have an advantage/disadvantage in situations. I really enjoyed fighting those bigger enemies, good fighting patterns that makes me feel like im fighting a miniboss.
[-1] -Not much combos so that combat will feel repetitive and boring after fighting grunts for awhile.
-Level Design [9/10]

White Night story’s unfolds in a manor which appears to be completely cut off. Your character finds himself there without really understanding how. It’s the 30’s, times appear to be very troubled and unsure, somehow it feels like cities and civilization are collapsing in the distance. After first lines of voice-over, you can already understand how tainted you are, the fatality, the alcohol…
The atmosphere at the very beginning of the game is Noire (obviously), warm vocal jazz, deep voice of narrator speaking… Horror part comes far later and to speak the truth White Night events call to my mind a Noire mixed with supranatural plot rather than a classical survival horror.
Adventure deeply reminds me of the original Resident Evil, one unique location (the manor), levels and rooms feel like a maze, previous scene wasd’s subjective control, the static camera which automatically switch point of view also does a great job. You have only one save game and you don’t get to control it.
Beside of staying enlightened, you walk from room to room trying to find keys, useful items, or any clue that could explain what’s going on in the manor, you have one ally, the gost of a singer who used to live there.

An imperfect gem of a game.
The Good:
- Great art design, and excellent atmosphere
- Well-crafted level design
- Interesting gameplay mechanics and puzzles
- Good integration of light/dark mechanics
- Excellent pacing for the majority of the experience
- Plenty of "game" (~5 to 6 hours for a first playthrough without getting all achievements)
- Above-average writing and voice work
- Nice-yet-predictable storyline
- Genuinely creepy, with a few jump scares for good measure
- Puzzles avoid "moon logic"
- Actually fairly challenging. This is not a walking simulator
- The "noir" look works, most of the time
- Bug-free, for the most part
The Bad:
- Lots of aliasing.
- Low poly models, and some poor animation work here and there
- Save system is a good idea horribly executed. You will lose some progress here and there.
- AI is unpredictable in a bad way. Plenty of cheap deaths waiting for you
- Fixed camera angles make for hit-and-miss
- Predictable ending
- Limited resources can be aggrivating if you're stuck
- One or two lame puzzles
- Sluggish opening act throws the pacing off a bit.
- Unskipabble cutscenes
Overall, if you're a fan of Resident Evil 1, it's hard not to recommend this game. It has a lot of great ideas, is pretty scary at times, and moves the player along at a nice pace. The price is great for the content that is here. Not a ton of replayability, but plenty of achievements for those who care. This could have been a lot better visually if there had been a decent anti-aliasing solution in place, but it doesn't really hold the game back that much.
Be prepared to experience a few cheap deaths, and lose a little progress (it's only really annoying when it happens too long after a save, or after a longer cutscene). Other than that, this is an excellent peice of entertainment for fans of the genre, who want to see it with a noir bent. Dark, brooding, creepy and very fun.
I don't really want to cover the story here, because that's part of the fun of playing the game. I will say I didn't find it to be the main attraction of the game; the game runs quite well on inertia -- exploring the environment, opening up new areas, solving puzzles and of course dealing with all the creepy things sprinkled about gives more than enough reason to spend time in this world. Mise en scene is high, and while I found the written material (books, letters, etc) to be written very well, the core storyline is not hugely intruiging. Your mileage may vary. Short version: You go into a house. Bad stuff happens.
Score: Buy it.

Pros:
This game is magic. Absolute gold. (And I don't even like FF games.)
Fun to play (I literally spent 200+ hours on this. I think I might be a bit biased)

Analysis:
Upon first glance of Final Fantasy VII, I almost blew it off. Steam Christmas sales changed my mind quickly.
I picked it up and started it. The beginning was slow. Not slow enough to deter me from the glory that I would experience later on though.
You start off as Cloud, an edgy, roided up, Ex-SOLDIER mercenary. You are hired by AVALANCHE to rig one of the mako reactors to explode. You do this. Easy stuff.
Story continues (I'm not going to spoil anything. Just look at this review and determine if you want to buy it.)
You will find enemies that you will absolutely hate. I'm quite sure my least favorites were the parasites and Master Tonberry. The story will tug a few heartstrings. I choked up a bit when a couple things happened. There'll be some twists and turns that you might not expect (Unless you were played the original. Then enjoy this masterpiece again, friend.)
There'll be some goofs and gaffs. The characters are unique and their dialogue is entertaining.
Still not going to spoil anything... but when you get to the ending, Be prepared to have some of your soul ripped out of you because it's so gosh darn good.
Conclusion:
The game is almost perfect. It's flaws will and have been pointed out, but I'm not here for that. I like the game for what it is and I highly recommend buying it. It's been worth the 200+ hours and I definitely got my money's worth.

This game has plenty of flaws and you'll need hardware way above the listed requirements to enjoy it at decent framerates, but man, is exploring its wide, grid-based world and fighting using its turn-based combat system enjoyable!
This is an old-school RPG where you create a party from scratch or using pre-made characters and go adventuring. While initially linear, the game opens up more and more to exploration as you progress. Not everything is at your level either, which is a breath of fresh air if you're used to Skyrim and the like: make sure to save often, because taking the wrong turn or entering the wrong cave can put you in a lot of trouble!
Flaws:
- Uplay
- Sometimes bland graphics with high system requirements (some dungeons do look great though)
- Long intro cutscene and a story you won't care about
- If you're like me you'll find the beginning town and first combat encounters boring
- Repetitive voice acting of your characters (fixable by digging in the game files)
- RPG system is not the deepest or most interesting I've seen
You also need to be aware that this is not really like the old World of Xeen games, and it is not like M&M 7-8-9 either. It's pretty much its own beast, mixing elements from both and adding or modernizing others.
I'm still recommending the game despite all its flaws, which goes to show how good it is. And it's pretty much the only recent game available for this particular blend of turn-based, grid-based exploration.
