This game is a strange creature. The interpretation many players would have upon hearing "randomly generated permadeath with dark souls style combat" would be "Binding of Isaac and Dark souls are both niche titles that garnered a lot of respect, if we mash them together we can market to that specific niche." But that's not what's going on with this game. Harebrained Schemes isn't a gaming powerhouse, which might lend some artistic integrity to their work if they weren't working for a publisher. I didn't see the name on the game, but if the trailer is to be believed, this game was published by Bandai-Namco. Rest in Peace. Having a publisher isn't the end-all-be-all of video games, though, so you'd be within the realm of reason to check out this cool looking, bizarre mashup.
Unfortunately, this game is not the experience it should be. If I had to use one word to describe it, it would be "Contrived".
To be clear, the game isn't a nauseating garbage fire like most of what BN has put out recently. The art style would be the biggest draw. The angular graphics, cosmetically pleasing character design, and sense of archaic beauty are what attracted me in the first place. In addition, the recent patch has added a variety of enemy types that all feel unique and have good character design.
Unfortunately, anything good that could make this game a worthy use of time is a stone house built on sand. Fighting, the primary mechanic, is unsatisfying and borders on broken for two main reasons: animation time and stamina. The stamina irredeemably contrived and make no sense in terms of balancing. Basically you have 5 types of attack: fast, heavy, charged fast and heavy, and a jumping attack. Every single one except the basic fast will put a cap on your stamina. This is true for each and every weapon. To understand how game-breaking this is, a bit of context is required. Every single action in the game requires a chunk of stamina, whether it's dodging, attacking, blocking, or even running faster than enemies, and you need to have your stamina as full as possible all the time because if you don't have the stamina to block or dodge, damage is unavoidable. A cap on your stamina makes combat virtually impossible, so right off the bat, you lose access to 4 out of the 5 moves available to you with any weapon and will have to play the whole game using only the fast light attack.
You may be thinking "There's plenty of moves in dark souls I never use, and I feel like that's fine. Why is it such a big deal?" Well, even if you decide to use only the fast attack, combat is still an unfair, clunky, barely playable mess. This is where animation time becomes a problem. The time and stamina required to even attack an enemy dooms the player if they are trying to fight more than one enemy. Even against a single enemy, the cracks in the design show through. If the player attacks a single enemy and hits them, there's a chance to knock it down. Rinse and repeat, the player wins. If the player loses that chance, the enemy's stagger animation will can BEFORE the attack animation of the player does, and you won't have a chance to even put up your shield before the enemy gets a good whack at you. However, cheesing your way through single enemies is unintentionally easy. While blocking, you are invulnerable, and anything that attacks you gets staggered. The enemies have no problem taking swings at you anyways. Block, smack, block, smack, win. It's not engaging or fun in the slightest.
But in combat with groups of enemies, the cracks run all the way through and the game breaks.
Your attacks my hit all of the enemies coming at you, but you won't knock them all over. Any enemy you miss will land a cheap shot, staggering you just long enough to get hit by another enemy, which has a better chance of knocking you on your♥♥♥♥♥since you were staggered an opening you up to a ton of unavoidable damage. Blocking is useless since you can only block an attack from a single enemy. What really separates this game from dark souls is the players ability to fight multiple enemies in a variety of ways. In DS, there was an element of challenge in making sure you managed enemy positions so you weren't getting hit by one monster while focusing on another, or equipping the right weapon for killing multiple enemies at once. That doesn't exist in this game. Weapons are all basically the same and all enemies are the same speed and they all run directly towards the player, leading them to cluster into an undodgable death ball. You will be left with only frustrated contempt as you drain several healing potions after every fight.
This game is smeared with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t in other regions as well. There's only two playable characters, the questing system is cringeworthy, the crafting feels like it was shoehorned in because it would make the game more marketable, the map generation ensures that exploration can be randomly lethal and some crafting impossible because the wrong ingredients spawn, and most glaring of all, your model only has 8 points of motion with no animation between them and it looks AWFUL.
As much as I like the idea for this game, it's not worth the money, even if it's on sale. I'm afraid it won't be an enjoyable experience without some fundamental changes, even if it gets continued support. But with steam and Bandai-Namco taking critical cuts of the profit I don't think the devs will be able to. Harebrained schemes, I'm rooting for you.

Dust: An elysian Tail is a a 2d hack and slash platformer.
Plot
You play as a swordsman called 'Dust' who has amnesia and finds himself in a forest. Along with a couple of entertaining companions, Dust will explore the land of Falana through mountains, forests, volcanos and tunnels solving quests, stopping genocidal monsters and finding the truth about his dark past...
Gameplay
Dust plays similar to metroid and castlevania games. The game is seperated into areas  which can be reached by moving from one end of the screen to the other (left to right and vice versa). There are platforming elements incorporporated, with you needing to use a few moves to reach certain places, though it's not as difficult unlike guacamalee. Combat is a great. You start of with limited moves with your one and only weapon, the Blade of Ahrah. As you defeat enemies you gain experience points which you can use to upgrade health, stamina and unlock new moves. You also find money which is used to buy items (like health recovery etc) at stores in the few towns you visit. Along your travels you will encounter a variety of foes including mines, melee guys, zombies, gjosts and gunships. There are also some boss battles in the game as well. Besides followuing the main quest, there are a few side quests you can partake in which offer a variety of rewards in return.  I played this game with a controller and I highly recommend you do the same as it feels more fluid and natural than keyboard and mouse.
Graphics
Most of the graphics are great. The 2D animations are colourful and attractive to look at. However, the 3D models aren't well detailed and doesn't fit well with the 2D sprites. Overall howeevr, the game looks vibrant to look at.
Audio
Excellent. The character voice acting for the main charcters are great and humorous (in a good way).   Other voice acting is decent. The music is great to listen to and fits well with the game.
An excellent and entertaining game that will surprise and satisfy fans of metrodvania and new comers alike.
A relaxing experience, it is worth a playthrough. Too bad it's so short.

I really wanted to like this game, because it seemed to have a number of concepts that I'm really interested in. However, it fell flat in enjoyment level for me simply because there were way too many problems that I had with it and not enough areas that I found good. I started out being really into it, but quickly started wishing for the game to be finished already (especially considering that I was already aware of how short it is). Overall, I think the game could have been really amazing but I don't recommend it as it is, and as it will remain because of the series being dropped.
PROS
- The visuals were great and most definitely the best part of the game, particularly the world design. I think that this part of the game was what was worked on the most and I can obviously appreciate how beautiful it is because, hey, who doesn't want the game they're playing to look nice? The forest area with the gravity defiance was really pretty and I almost wish that that could have been explored more (with better platforming, at least).
- I liked Red's character design a lot for the most part, truthfully I like concept art of her more than her in-game model but that's mentioned more in the cons section.
- Interesting use of rhyming dialogue that fit the fairy tale genre.
- Red's voice acting was satisfactory, I mostly just liked the way her voice sounded rather than how it was in general.
CONS
- Regarding Red's design, I feel as if she would have looked a whole lot better without the scarily big eyes that didn't feel like they were shaded properly (the whites of her eyes were rather freaky, it felt like her eyes were designed normally and then just blown up way too much for the final product).
- The rhyming dialogue was sometimes forced and felt off, definitely wasn't very immersive after a while of playing the game.
- The landscape depth or view and perspective was really disorienting for me. Often times it felt hard to tell what was an area I could interact with and what wasn't, and there were several instances where I believed I was landing on a platform but apparently wasn't simply from the camera angle being off. This fact could be rather frustrating especially alongside the fact that there were many instant death interactions that you had no warning of whatsoever. Needless to say, I died a lot simply from the platforming itself.
- The combat was clunky and at times felt unfair. There were a number of attacks from enemies that killed me in one hit out of the blue, but even aside from that it could be hard to manage attacking and dodging safely because your weapon accuracy and the hitboxes of your attacks and the bodies of your enemies seem to bug out a lot. The special attacks you get throughout the game are highly unreliable as they miss more often than not, and you're not given much direction as to their usage being limited by whatever "mana/energy" concept was used in the game.
- The story was interesting, but felt so rushed. It really feels like the game could have been a whole lot longer simply from having the story drawn out so that players could experience more of it. I understand that this was only the first part of the game that was planned out to be a series, but regardless I think there could have been more added for the aspects of the plot that were developed.
Very enjoyable experience overall. Gameplay and visuals are superb. Big thumbs up for voice acting, really made the characters feel alive.

The Witcher 2 was a wonderful game in all aspects and a major improvement over the first game in the series. Geralt isn't only dealing with Temeria anymore. The fate of all the Northern Kingdoms is at stake.
The story and narration lives up to the hype of the first, and in fact, has Geralt making many more decisions with varying consequences. Characters are much more fleshed out. Be prepared to face situations where you're wedged between two characters that you like, only being able to help one of them. Many times, decisions simply don't have a right answer, and other times it can be good vs bad mystery that you have to decipher by paying attention to clues given to you. You get to shape Geralt to become the character you want. My main complaint, is that the game eventually forces you to a fork in the road. This decision essentially takes over a full chapter in the story, and I although you get to visit places from both paths in one playthrough, you can end up missing a lot of important story elements if you aren't careful. I ended up glossing over the sidequest for an important character in the Witcher 3 because I was so invested in finishing the main quest. It's also totally neat to see decisions carry over from the previous game, and don't forget, the decisions you make also carry over to the Witcher 3!
Combat has been completely overhauled. Say goodbye to the timed clicks, because the new combat system is entirely momentum based. The new perk tree allows Geralt to fight as a swordsman, a mage, a hunter, or any combination. Sword swings are dictated with the left and right mouse buttons, alllowing Geralt to alternate between fast or strong slashes. Enemies will flinch when attacked, giving your offenses a sense of weight. Spells and sidearms can be conveniently selected and used via a quickbar, and Geralt can roll around dodging attacks like a madman. There's still much room for improvement, however. Fighting still feels a bit clunky at times, and ragdolls (or the lack of) can make killing enemies really awkward because they just topple over. Attacks from bosses can also have extended hitboxes, as I have died many times over after getting clipped by an attack that was seemingly out of my range. Rolling may become your primary means of mobility, and it can be troublesome to use. Enemies will tend to swarm you, and blocking/reposting leaves you vulnerable from other angles while rolling may tumble you into other enemies. It's all about tactically positioning yourself, which can be seen as a welcome challenge, or an eventual annoyance. I will definitely say that there is a high learning curve to this new combat style. Unlike the first Witcher, which has Geralt acquire each of his Witcher signs throughout the game, the Witcher 2 throws all of the signs at you at once, along with a load of projectiles and potions which aren't explained very well at all. I totally failed the tutorial, which suggested for me to play on easy. I was still able to complete the game on hard, but it was far from easy. Aside from the main gameplay, you can also participate in dice poker, arm wrestling, and brawls (QTE simulator). They weren't that fun, but hey, they're not nothing.
Graphically, the game is beautifully designed. The forest outside Flotsam was densely packed with greenery and looked totally sinister at night time. It was dissapointing that there were no major cities to explore, but each settlement Geralt visits has a unique rugged atmosphere. I do think that the world is a bit oversaturated, though. Colors tend to be very sharp. Characters also have great face textures, and unique characters have great memorable designs. Unfortunately, a lot of models are reused throughout the game for minor characters. The music, although my least favorite of the three Witcher games, still isn't bad at all. There was a wide array of scores that fit both emotional and intense scenes from the game. To me, the soundtrack just sounded more like stereotypical fantasy music as opposed to The Witcher or The WItcher 3 (hands down my favorite!). Still, try listening to the song Sorceresses. It's quite enchanting.
In the end despite some flaws, The Witcher 2 was a true fantasy RPG mixed with exceedingly challenging yet rewarding combat. I highly recommend playing the original Witcher to get a better sense of the massive story/world and a basic handling for Geralts abilities. It is defintely an exciting experience to learn about the world of the WItcher.

ABZU, while being relatively short but incredible and unique experience, proves once again that size doesn't always matter. Vibrant and colorful surroundings pull you into this incredible sea world that many may consider a 'work of art'. ABZU is a masterpiece in its own adventure genre leaving experience that'll be very hard to forget.
Every once in a while, in our industry pops up a game that serves as a perfect example on how to leave right impression on the player, offering a unique and fascinating experience that's often very hard to forget. ABZU is that kind of a game. While exploring depths and swimming through the sole heart of the ocean, you'll immerse yourself in this world overloaded with life. This beautiful underwater adventure takes you on an unforgettable journey, progressing without any clear goal. ABZU is all about the observation and exploration of this vibrant and populated ocean.
Taking shark for a ride, jumping out of the oceans like a dolphin, or just simply wandering in this massive area, ABZU has it all, and even though a story doesn't have a lot that it can hold onto, the game's interesting and innovative gameplay will certainly intrigue some of you.

At a deeper discount, and at a price of a movie ticket, this game holds something valuable and unique that's definitely worth experiencing. Beautiful and charming world lays out solid base for exploration.

While San Francisco may be better known for its private clubs such as U.S. Open venue Olympic Club or San Francisco and Lake Merced golf clubs, there are a few public gems in the immediate area and a wealth of daily fee courses in the metropolitan area. Within San Francisco, the famous TPC at Harding Park, where the late Ken Venturi developed his game, is probably the best known. Renovated a few years ago, the course has played host to several high profile events recently, including the President's Cup and the Champions Tour's Schwab Cup. But there are some less expensive options inside the city (although certainly not cheap), such as The Presidio -- a former military course turned public, with terrific views of the Bay – Golden Gate Park and historic Sharp Park, a 1932 Alistair Mackenzie design. But because San Francisco is landlocked and quite congested, the vast majority of great public golf lies in the surrounding areas, from Oakland to the wine country north and south. For example, just across the Golden Gate Bridge, there's Bodega Harbor Golf Club, a Robert Trent Jones Jr. design overlooking the ocean. About 45 minutes down the coast from San Francisco is the 36-hole Ritz-Carlton Half Moon Bay, which rivals Pebble Beach, when it comes to ocean views. Or head toward San Jose to check out the impeccable CordeValle Golf Club, the former home of the PGA Tour's
Open. Of course, if you're in San Francisco, it would be a shame not to carve out a couple of days to head south to the Monterey Peninsula, where you’ll find the famous Pebble Beach Golf Links, Spanish Bay and Spyglass Hill, just to name a few.

ABZU has me extremely conflicted -- I was actually so close to selecting "Not Recommended"
The world, story, and music is what makes ABZU great. It's no secret that ABZU looks visually stunning and the music seamlessly transports you through the oceans.  There is a deep story involved here, however I would have liked to see more as the ending sort of ends abruptly and you think  "Oh.  That's it?".
The problem I have with ABZU, which will draw some ire from many reading this, is that it is not a game.  It's actually difficult to describe exactly what ABZU is. An experience, maybe? Your goal is essentially going from point A to point B and pressing the X button occasionally. There are no enemies, and you cannot die. Yes, there are entities that you should probably stay away from, but even if you don't you get a bit of a shock, then you just keep going.  I also found the controls to be extremely clunky.  Often times I was fighting with the controls to try to change the direction of which way I wanted to swim.
I greatly enjoyed the world, don't get me wrong.  Visually stunning with a grand orchestra. An experience that should definitely be recommended. But At $19.99 for essentially 1 and-a-half hour to 2 hours? ABZU honestly does not have any replay value unless you reeeeeaaaallllyyyy want those achievements.   It's one of those titles that make you go  "Wow that was neat", then you essentially play something else and ABZU sits in your library.
Make no mistake, I did "Recommend" ABZU, but personally it's around a 5/10.   It's just a very hard sell for what is basically $20 for 2 hours. It leaves with so much more to be desired.  I, and I'm sure a ton more, would love to see more from this. More story, more locations, just more everything.
Maybe an ABZU 2?

A horrible smear on the history of dungeon crawlers.
I love dungeon crawlers. But M&MXL is so lazily implemented, there isn't a simple moment where you could find any polish. UI's look like they're made for a mobile game, sound is simply everlooping stock effects, map design doesn't support tile-based movement a single bit and graphics look like it's randomly lifted from Google Sketchup Warehouse free models. Oh, and don't get me started on balance.
Take the very early lighthouse quest for example. With each building level, difficulty scales up *rather* nicely, so you have to work to clear it. But when you get to the boss, you realize that you're 10 hero levels behind requirements and get splatted like a fly.
Same goes for other areas. You can work hard and kill two spectres in front of the crypt, but dare you step inside; the very first mob you encounter will turn your entire party into fine paste. Long story short, what the hell is this?? This isn't balance. This isn't "hard game". This is - describing it the best I could using English - crap. Poorly designed, heavily unpolished, insanely stupid crap.
This game could have been with very simple design improvements, such as making sure there's trainers for all skills in the "starting town", better scalability of skills and stats, more logical difficulty progression for enemies, making secret finding optional instead of mandatory and so on. Nothing of such exists. So look elsewhere. Legend of Grimrock series does all that much, much better.
Wouldn't recommend to anyone.

Necropolis: Brutal Edition offers a diverse, action packed, procedurally generated, roguelike 3-D experience.
*Note: I got this game 50% off. At the time of this writing the developer is still listing this game at $30 bucks. My thumbs up is for the $15 version, so to speak. I do not believe this game is worth the full price they are asking*
Looking over the shoulder of your character, selected from one of two character classes (Blackguard or Brute) and drawn from one of two genders (conveniently, male or female), but available in a wide variety of unlockable colors, a new complex of dungeon rooms, elevated walkways, snowy mountains, moist swamps, complete with monuments, loot and smashable this-and-that, is generated for each play through.
A mere two character classes seems weak to me, especially given the multiplayer component that beg for a diversity of abilities to make the experience different from playing solo.
Furthermore, though the game includes some unlocks, the previously mentioned character colors and the Codexes (described below), there is very little to make your particular adventurer feel unique. However, given the snarky dialogue, that generic samey-samey feel seems intentional.
A wide variety of weapons, some with special abiltites, such as additional damage types or an unusual buff and debuff, are stashed about the Necropolis for your baddie smashing pleasure. Even after nearly seventy hours of play and one completion (as of this writing), I still occassionally come across a weapon that I don't recall encountering before.
The game also provides a smaller variety of armors and shields that allow for some really interesting combinations, both strategically and aesthetically. Just like with the weapons, there are specific enemies and situations in which a particular piece of equipment might shine, while in other encounters that piece of gear might actually be detrimental.
Additonally, there are Codexes, special unlockable books that give your character an extra ability or change a rule of the game. Everything from extra stamina regeneration, vampirism, leaping ability and even books of recipes for the craftable food and potions are available in the starting library, as well as is in the end room of each level.
Once a Codex (or a color scheme, for that matter) is unlocked, it remains available for all future playthroughs, allowing for some measure of progression that transcends any particular character's death.
The whole place is strung together with bits of readable graffiti lore on walls, as well as occassional narration from the Necropolois's host, the Brazen Head (a large pyramid encountered at the beginning of the game and at the start of each new level). Many of the quotes and comments are often sarcastic and attempt to make light of the doom.
The Brazen Head also provides quests (you can have three at a time) that are randomly generated kill X or fetch Y missions that provide Tokens for unlocking Codexes and color schemes. The Brazen Head is appropriately dismissive of your petty quest completions, continuing the darkly humorous tone.
The art style is slightly polygonal, but charming and effective. The colors are somewhat muted, reminding me of playing ancient IBM games with a 4-color CGA adapter (I'm old). The environments are varied, mixing and matching together in enough different ways to keep the experience fresh for several hours. There are a great many secret areas, difficult-to-get-to places and unusual situations to be discovered, keeping me coming back to make sure I saw it all.
The combat is highly reminiscent of Dark Souls, with strong and light attacks with a weapon in one hand or a shield/crossbow in the other, with either being chargable. Blocking, leaping and dodging round out the combat abilities, along with a variety of potions and scrolls which can be found or crafted. I found combat to be both challenging and rewarding, though there comes a repetition to the enemies, the deeper one travels into the Necropolis (more on that below).
Compellingly, I found Necroplis quite different from one play-through could be from the next. The beginning room and chambers at the end and beginning of each level are essentially always the same. In between, though, there is enough terrain, and ways of mixing and matching the areas together, along with enough different monsters and loot to create very different play experiences.
The monsters themselves are generally well rendered in the same slightly-polygonal simple style as your character. Most can be quite challenging on first (or even second, third and fourth) encounter. Since the monsters themselves are of different factions, some hating one another more than they despise adventurers, it isn't uncommon to walk into the middle of a melee or come across a pile of weapons and money (bodies disappear on death) marking some massacre that played out while you were in a different part of the level.
My major complaint with the monsters is the limited number of scripts available, so that many monsters are re-skinned versions of an earlier, simpler creature, moving and attacking just the same as the weaker version, simply requiring more hits to kill or potentially one-shotting your adventurer.
All-in-all, I've really enjoyed Necropolis, playing it only occassionally since getting a finish, going back again and again to see what strange collection of monsters, terrain and gear it might spit out, creating a unique little story on each play through.

Now, I played Demon's Souls all those years ago and when I heard there was a third spiritual successor "Dark Souls the Third", I knew I had to check it out.
In this game you play as the titular "Dark Soul the Third", an unspoken hero who must make their way through the dungeons of (I had to look this up online because the lore is so rich and deep) Sen's Fortress. As you make your way deeper into the Fortress, you come across harder and harder enemies, there is sometimes some platforming, and the game ultimately ends with an unbeatable boss, just like Demon's Souls. Now that might sound like a very simple game, but thats just the skinny of it.
In Dark Souls the Third, you can summon friends to help you through Sen's Fortress. This can both make the game easier and harder. Easier because when the Red Crystal Phantoms invade you (classic Demon's Souls) there are more of you to spread around. Harder when everyone wants loot and you can hit each other when you're all flailing around in combat. The multiplayer adds a lot of fun to the game, especially because it can take quite a long time to trek through the fortress, as you don't get a map and I forget how the layout goes evey time I play it.
The Pyramid of Londor is there evey time you go down a floor, offering a chest if you so choose to spend Humanity Tokens on it, which you get for succeeding quests given to you on the previous floor by the Pyramid of Londor. These Tokens are permenent, so you can save up a bunch over several play throughs to spend.
In classic Demon's Souls style, there are no set classes. You can choose your gender, color, and if you want to be a big guy or a small guy, and then just use whatever gear you want. Sure, some armors give you buffs which makes you better with certain weapons, but we all play Fashion Souls here, armor is for looks, not for numbers. There are many different weapon types all with pros and cons, as well as a stamina system (CLASSIC Demon's Souls) which requires you to eat to keep up good maximum stamina if you have been using a lot of strong attacks. The crafting in the game is good too, especially when you can craft a ton of Estus Flasks and never die, like a champion.
Dark Souls the Third is a fun game, especially if you have someone to play with, you get to go on a dungeoneering adventure for hours and hours until you either get shafted hard in the factory area or get good enough gear to become not unlike gods.

I'm going to open up this review by being straight up honest: I'm not a big platform game fan.  I don't hate them, but they really aren't my favorite genre. This is why it's taken me so long to get around to playing Dust. That being said, Dust has two major pluses going for it over other platformers for me. One is that the actual platforming elements are fairly simple and straightforward, and even the 'tricky' portions are not the type to be super frustrating. The other is that it is a Metroidvania type game, which I am much more tolerant of anyway.
To be blunt, this game is really good. It has a generally good pacing, with some minor but not game-ruining exceptions, and on top of that the story is actually engaging and interesting, which is an unusual thing for any platforming game I've played before. The combat is fast-paced without being overwhelming, and the difficulty is easily adjusted to the player's level of skill, though hardcore action gamers may find the game a little easy for them. It is one of those games you look forward to playing when you get home, eager to see what the next level or revelation brings, and it's a breath of fresh air amongst the first person shooter crowd. While hardly the only side-scroller these days, it's a testament to how high-quality indie games can be.
This isn't to say it's perfect. The game's RPG elements, while interesting, are not particularly deep. The crafting system requires either a lot of grinding to utilize fully, or can be ignored entirely, which means that it either needs work or should be removed entirely. Finally, some of the sidequests require some real snooping around even above and beyond what is expected, making them a little frustrating.
On the whole, these complaints are exceedingly minor though. It boils down to this being a very fun game worth 15-20 hours, and at the current price it's a steal.

An amazing RPG experience that builds upon the lore of both The Witcher books and the first game. It does not require you to either read the books or play the first game to greatly enjoy the game, but is full of tidbits for those who have.
It's difficult to tell what choices have what repercussions, whether immediate or delayed, and so the game sucessfully pushes you to role play your character rather then choose options due to obvious gameplay benefits. There is no clear good or evil path, but to paraphrase the game some point, only choices and their consequences.
Combat is interesting and can vary greatly depending on how you build your character. Its very different from how the combat in the first game plays, and in my opinion, much improved. Your character will be effective no matter whether you focus on Swords, Magic, Potions, Traps, Throwing Knives, Mutations, etc, but each options requires a specific style of play. This, along with multiple paths to take during the course of the game and multiple endings adds immense replayability. Combat can be difficult, especially at first, but various difficulty settings allows the user to tailor the difficulty to their own taste. Dark mode is exclusive to the enhanced edition and besides its almost realistic level of difficulty, it contains item sets specific to it, which helps the player meet the challenge. Insane difficulty makes the game into a rogue-like. Once the main character dies, the journey ends and your saves are deleted.
The graphics are beautiful even for 2015 standards and make playing through this adventure visually pleasing for the most part. A few visual glitches detract from the experience, but overall can be forgiven considering the rest. The music matches the tone of the game at all times and is masterfully composed.

Alright.  Now, I really want to like this game.  I have tried.  I have played hours of it, but the game simply does not do it for me.  Overall, the game mechanics, the content, the tech-tree, ships, etc. on offer is plenty and varied.  However, the game, for me is too much of a reskin of GC II, which is not to say that is a bad thing, but it would seem the developers did not aim to improve upon the old game with the new.
My biggest gripe with GC III is the mundane, haphazard, and back-seated approach to combat.  There is virtually (if any at all) player interaction during combat.  The player assembles a fleet of ships, sends them against an enemy fleet and simply watches the combat unfold.  Of course, the player upgrades one's ships and develops military techology as a way to enhance the fighitng capacity and abilities, but in no way can one direct anything during combat in real time or in turn based.  This is a lost opportunity.  The devs could have really gone out and made combat interactive, and improved the old game systems with new mechanics in the new game.
A general criticism, completely shrouded in my own subjective leanings, is that the game is not immersive at all.  The music, the environment, the galaxy, the races, and so on just feels bland.  I do not get any sense that the galaxy is a living and breathing arena filled with races, wars, trade, and diplomacy.  Of course, all of these things do happen, but there is no real sense of signicance from these interactions that gives me a sense of immersion.
I would personally not recommend this game to those players wishing for a more interactive combat system.  However, the game overall offers enough content, graphical fidelity, and overall competence for me to give it a very, very lukewarm recommendation.

These days I think people only really play it for nostalgia's sake.
Though much of the game's mechanics are modernly outdated, like most of the mini-games and some of the UI that are a little odd & time consuming to get around, it's got an extremely engaging story and non-linear exploration with satisfying rewards to back it up. As you progress your ways of exploration vastly improve and it's a rewarding experience when those points are reached.
During a battle the camera is set by default to cinematically move around. When you're choosing a target after selecting an attack, item, or whatever to use on and the camera's still moving it can be a little bit of a nuisance to try and set the cursor to your desired target. It can be a bit time consuming on making sure you've selected the right target in this case especially if the camera's still moving around because an attack is in progress. It doesn't help that the game functions on an active time battle mechanic so if you take too long deciding a target the enemy may make a move before you make a selection. The cinematic camera viewing can be toggled to sit still to look like previous Final Fantasy games.
Some of the maps can be a little confusing to get around where the blame is on the map design. You and other 3D NPCs are basically walking in front of either a still image or a looping video. When trying to go through doorways, roads that curve oddly, or whatever the like it can be extremely confusing to get around and find out where exactly you can set foot on the map.
The graphics are blatantly outdated, maybe even for 1997, but I think there's a real big charm to that.
The most in-depth part about this game regarding the actual main gameplay is the Materia system where each piece of Materia either casts a spell, summons, support other Materia, etc. which almost all will take the biggest roles in battles.
For better or worse the story, characters, music, and the world of FF7 is really what makes this entire game highly unique which got me hooked up until it's kind of lame ending.

Sketch! Run! is very nice casual and a bit educational game. Controls are very easy and you only need your mouse. Yes you read it correctly, you don't need keyboard to play it, mouse is everything you need. Game is very simple as you draw springs to jump with left mouse button and shoots small fireballs to destroy blocking squares. In all levels there are various photos in background with title from same country or smaller scale location. Game contains 4 seasons at this moment with 5th coming out soon. Each season have 20 levels with first one very short introduction of new obstacles. In each season  levels gradually increases in size and gets bigger and bigger. Every level has it's own theme based on country or other location.
I found my country level and was dissapointed how short it was. So i decided to write suggestion with links to more information about Lithuania and guess what.. 2 days later they updated that level with more content!!! how awesome it is when developer responds and updates so fast (if you feel something is missing from your country go to forums and make a suggestion). . It was hard to decide whether gameplay is good or not but after few minutes debating with myself i can say that it is good. On first play 2h went really fast and i enjoyed despite few minor things. If you need to do few jumps upwards just spam your springs and it will be easy.

I can't justify graphics for this game. Everything is simple and nice. It doesn't feel that game is lacking something in graphics but at the same time there is nothing achieving or impressive.
I can't put controls in pros just because there are minor issues in camera movement i found frustrating. Apart from that everything is fine and the fact that you need only mouse gives out an idea how simple everything is in Sketch! Run!.
Pictures are nice and levels itself are good enough but there comes a bad part. Lots of levels are very similar to each other what makes game a bit repetetive but since game is that easy and casual you don't think about that too much and play along. One more flaw in level design is some obstacles placement. There are few Erasers (obstacle which deletes you instantly and you have to start over) placed in very bad places and it feels like you need luck to get past them. Amount of different obstacles type is very small. There is no variations in visuals of same obstacle and all of them looks same.
Even after some flaws i can recommend this game because of it's easy nature. It is so casual that you don't feel doing much while playing and just enjoy. Sountrack makes it more enjoyable and in full view makes it easy to play.

Might and Magic X doesn't try to reinvent the fantasy RPG, it sticks pretty close to the roots and the tried and true tropes of the genre.  And that's precisely why it's fun.
You will create a party of heroes, and you've got a decent variety of options to choose from, enough that I wanted to play again after finishing to try out some different party makeups with different skills.
The game plays out on a grid, viewed from a first person perspective, which gives it a classic dungeon crawler feel, but you've also got some convenient modern concessions such as the ability to look around freely, and an automap.  This gives you just enough of those old-school tingles to warm your aging nerd heart, without the frustration of trying to map the entire world yourself on graph paper or figure out which direction you are facing. (I know there are those who prefer that level of masochism in their gaming, I'm not among them, these are dealbreakers for me these days.)
You'll get a decent level of challenge on the default setting -- you will have to think about your own party's skills and spells, and how they will work against different monsters attacks and defenses.  It's not coddling you but it's not so "hardcore" as to be unfun.   There is no level scaling here, so you will need to explore around the world a bit at times looking for encounters that are appropriate to your squad's level.  Personally i enjoy this part of the game, but if you're looking for an open-world experience where you can go anywhere you wish and always find beasties who aren't quite good enough to kill you, this isn't it.
This game scratches some of my chronic itches that big budget games just won't touch anymore, much as I love them.  Namely:
It's turn-based
It's party-based
there's no level-scaling
it lets itself have fun with charming little gimmicks like riddle chests and open-ended questions.
It's not driven by a cinematic narrative
It doesn't try to reinvent the genre.
These last two points are the key to why I have enjoyed playing the game so much.  There's something mentally taxing about playing a game that tries to introduce a lot of new elements, especially when it's a heavily story driven experience.  I have to invest time and energy learning a whole new world, yes sometimes that's great.  But sometimes the story or gameplay doesn't hold up and I end up abandoning the game.  Sometimes I just want to kill monsters and loot treasure in a world that goes back to the familiar well of orcs, elves and dragons.
So, give me simple, give me palatable, give me something that feels old-fashioned, but looks nice and bows reasonably to modern game conventions like automaps and quest journals.  Give me something that fits like an old shoe, without the stink.  give me more games like M&MX.

Few games take a journey below the blanket of shimmering ocean waters and even fewer provide an experience that is memorable. Most notably, their unintentionally weak attempts at incorporating controls that are as smooth on land as they are underwater. ABZU is not only an exception to those games, it is a shining example that, when done right, deep sea adventures can make for an incredibly enjoyable experience.
ABZU drops you off in the middle of a shallow and calm body of crystal clear water that looks like something out of a postcard. The character you take control of is fitted with what can only be described as an advanced diving suit with a headlamp and sonar-like ability, used for communicating or interacting with the world around you. Hundreds of colorful and vibrant fish swim around you in a nature that displays curiosity and wonder, which will likely be reciprocated by your own amazement. Swimming further and diving deeper you’ll find yourself surrounded by waving plants that reach for the sky above, schools of fish that swirl around in bustling habitats, rocky trenches and sunken ruins. As you dive deeper, the sun’s strength wears thin and leaves only a faint glow on the environment, where the dangers nestled far out of light’s reach reside.
As you descend deeper into the unknown, along the way their are hidden collectible shells, and large shark statues that can be found and meditated on. During meditation you can sit back and watch in closer detail the life swimming around you. It’s not necessarily something you’re required to do nor is it something that adds much depth to the gameplay itself, but it’s still aesthetically pleasing.
There are two major aspects to the game that stand out as it’s greatest strengths within the first five minutes of play. The first being the controls. (Though like the Store Page notes, a gamepad is strongly recommended. I had had a very hard time trying to play it with keyboard and mouse.) They are as smooth and well-rounded as the atmosphere around you, and incredibly simple. While their depth could be viewed as a downside, the journey in itself is not something that aims to be challenging. You cut through the water as elegantly as the fish around you and can maneuver through tight spaces with ease. I attribute half its success to the technical workings of the game, and the other half to the third person camera that drifts almost freely behind you, as if it’s another diver watching from a distance.
ABZU’s second greatest strength is its visuals and sounds. In rare circumstances, extremely dense schools of fish would drop the framerate significantly, but because of ABZU’s slow and casual gameplay, 30 frames per second doesn’t break its pace. As you progress the environments grow in variety and tone, from bright suntouched surroundings teeming with life and character, to somber open stretches that are made even more peaceful by ABZU’s wonderful score. Sunken structures have become playgrounds for the creatures of the deep, like some massive decoration for an industrial size aquarium. Textures are rather simple, but the abundance of foliage and life adds a great deal of eye candy to distract. The animation behind every moving thing is fluid and serene, and the excellent lighting / visual effects make for a stunning and memorable experience.
Despite all it’s wonderfully designed gameplay, there simply is not enough of it. Now I will say that what content is provided is thoroughly enjoyable, every minute I spent in the game was fantastic, however, the journey itself took a little over an hour to complete. I received this via Humble Bundle’s $12 monthly subscription so basically it would equal out to almost $2, though it’s retail price is $20. Take from this what you will, and please, if aquatic games are your interest then you’re in luck, but there is simply not enough replayable content to justify its asking price. I’d even go as far to say that you can view all there is to see in under three hours. A sale or discount of some sort would be your best option.
ABZU provides a masterfully designed experience with smooth controls and fluid camera work. Visually stunning and aurally satisfying gameplay that reminds of Disney’s Fantasia but on a player controlled medium. It’s asking price is a questionable one for how limited the content is, so I strongly advise purchasing during a sale. The games features a campaign mode with connected scenarios on randomly generated maps, but none of the researched upgrades or ship designs carry over from mission to mission, so it’s really just a series of skirmishes. There is cross-platform play where you can save and continue on another device, which is a nice feature. Before each mission, the crew composition can be set, which determines research rates, population caps, and build speeds. The interface is clearly designed for a mobile device, with inconsistent tool-tips and a lack of useful information: for example, the game should indicate when units have all weapon slots filled when in building mode, and it should more clearly display how often a component has been upgraded. Each map is covered with plentiful capture points that provide cash (to purchase things) and upgrade points (for upgrades), but scouting is tedious because ships move very, very slowly. Ships and defenses can be purchased, and all must be customized with weapons and other items like drones and defenses; designs can be saved for use later in the same scenario. In addition, there are researched upgrades that are applied to all ships, and specific upgrades for each component that can be added to a ship. Having both of these options is confusing and unnecessary, as choosing one or the other (I prefer the research route) would have sufficed. Units will auto-attack nearby enemies, but can be instructed to focus on specific subsystems. Enemy ships can also be boarded. Every mission lasts too long due to the slow speed of the ships and the high number of enemy units. Because of the pacing issues, interface shortcomings, perplexing research options, and lack of campaign continuity, Battlevoid: Sector Siege is not a successful adaptation of the series to the real-time strategy genre.

It seems like there is a polished fleet game here, the visuals are nice and clean, it seems well programmed, etc but the interface is far too unintuitive, and there are literally parts missing that don't tell you unit limits, turret limits, etc.
Here's what you can expect :
I struggled with this game's lack of conveyance, mixing "too much" with "too little".
E.G.
you have ships that your main station can spawn to create your fleet, but aparently there is a limit, because when you hit it, you are told you can no longer make any. What's the limit ? where is it on screen, or what menu, because it's not there that i could find. You are only told when you hit the limit, it's an invisible number that only shows when it's too late.
E.G.2
You have turrents and bays, turrets for weapon mounts and bays that spawn fighters/repair drones. bays can be on ships as well as stations, and guess what? There are limits as you first load-up your your initial captured station with it's available 4 defence areas, loaded with turrets and fighter bays, then next when you capture a station you are told you can no longer buy any more bays ???
What's the point in having 4 defence areas pers station if you max out the game's limits on a single stastion, maybe even sooner if you equipped your fleet with bays? what are you supposed to use to defend the other stations ?
The same "bays" limit applies to ships you spawn from your motherstation, you can equip bays to the motherstation HQ, and even your ships spawned form *that*, and BAM ! you've blown your bays and turret limits.
Similarly the "upgrades" function is odd, because you are supposed to know that you need to click on the weapons, then see the vasrious upgradable functions like "range", "recharge speed", etc and it shows boxes above each function, but instead of clicking those boxes to perform the upgrade, you need to look for the button all the way to the side of the entire menue area and click that. Worse, those upgrade functions and their boxes apear in the normal weapon desription menue items and are NOT upgrade releavnt.
You literally have duplication where you have the SAME visual descriptions of weapons, with the "range", "recharge speed", etc graphs boxes...but that is not the place to upgrade them ! yopu have to go to the UPGRADE section WHICH LOOKS EXACTLY THE SAME !!
Even something as simple as the "PAUSE" and "GAME SPEED" is unintuitive. If i told you that it uses the simple, universally understood paradigm of "PLAY" and "PAUSE" icons, you might guess "oh that's easy enough, just hit the play/pause toggle anad that does exactly what it should right ?
Nope, you hit pause, and "GAME PAUSED" apears in words next to that icon. Where does the "PLAY" button come in? It's right there, underneath, it's the *speed* button, you click it multiple times to alter the multiplier, but it also UN-PAUSES the game,a nd when it does it resets the game back to 1x speed, regardless if you had it on 4x speed, etc.....how is this intuitive ?
If they can't get simple things liek that right, it's no wonder the rest fo the interface is a mess.
I had flashbacks to when Windows 8.0 initially released, and you were somehow supposed to know invisible things like how to invoke the "charm" bar, and how to float down to the corner to invoke the start menue, etc.
Too frustrating to plough on and figure out what these invisible limits are, so i'm going to be unibstalling this. Which is a shame, because the gameplay looks really good, but if the interface and mechanics are borked like this, what's the point in suffering trying to have fun with it ?

NightSky is a very short, but neat, physics-based puzzle platformer. You control a ball which must be rolled through a series of levels, solving various puzzles along the way. The game does a good job of easing you into the various different techniques required to progress. It starts off easy, with simple things like speeding up and slowing down to control momentum, then advances to more complex tasks such as changing the spin of the ball on walls and slopes to fling yourself to otherwise unattainable heights. Along the way, you'll also have to solve a number of puzzles involving objects such as balls, cannons, rotating platforms, wagons, blocks, an assortment of different ball-powered vehicles, and more.
Complementing NightSky's solid physics gameplay is its unique graphic-style. The levels are rendered in a dream-like palette of rich hues in the background and stark black terrain and objects in the foreground. It really is quite impressive and soothing to look at. Add in some subtle music that plays from time to time, and it all comes together nicely. If you're like me, you'll also find yourself wanting to take a screenshot of nearly every screen, because there's always something neat to look at. That said, one major downside to the graphics (and the game in general), is that it only runs at an extremely low resolution. This is a seriously unfortunate issue for a game like this that depends so much on its visuals to stand out. Additionally, the game doesn't even run full-screen properly. In order for it to run full screen (albeit with "blown up" visuals), you should make sure to download the "unofficial" 1.1 patch from the developer's web site (more info below).
That one major issue aside, this is still a game that is worth checking out. Between the solid gameplay and the beautiful visuals, there's a lot of variety packed in such a small package. And small, it is - the game can be fully completed in around 3-4 hours. Once finished, there is an extra bonus level that can be unlocked by finding a series of hidden "stars" throughout the main quest (don't worry, the game tells you which specific sub-levels the stars are hidden on, so it's fairly easy to find them all). But aside from that, there's not much else here. There is supposedly an HD version in the works (which will in theory fix the one major issue noted above regarding graphics resolution), so it may even be worth waiting in case that ever materializes. Regardless, whether you get the current version or hold out for a true HD update, this is a game that is worth experiencing if you're a fan of physics puzzlers or games with unique styles and gameplay.
*** Note about updating the game: The default download that comes from Steam runs in a very low resolution that can't be changed. However, there is a post in the developer's forums (and also in the official Steam discussions) which links to an updated executable (NightSky11.exe). I recommend downloading this. Rename the original "NightSky.exe" in your SteamApps folder and replace it with the 1.1 version (rename it "NightSky.exe". This version allows the game to run full-screen, though unfortunately not at a higher resolution (so the graphics will be slightly blurry). Still, it's much better than nothing.

Woolfe is a very short 3D platformer and hack & slash hybrid with an enjoyable art style, a good main character, and a bunch of apparent design flaws, including boring combat and bad collision detection.
Woolfe – The Red Hood Diaries is a partly crowdfunded action platformer that tries to create a modern rendition of the old and familiar fairy tale.
As the sub-title states, the game is not really fair, albeit this stems from an apparent lack of design.
For a 3D platformer, it has bad camera angles and terrible collision detection: you can get stuck inside objects, hover in mid-air, or die from something that isn’t even in your vicinity.
For a hack & slash, the combat is repetitive two-button mashing with only a few, mostly useless combos.
And on top of all things, the eight levels barely offer any length; each can be finished in 10-15 minutes if you don’t bother to search for all the secrets.
The story fares slightly better: Red Hood is a great character, and she has a compelling backstory, just like the world she lives in. Too bad this story is told in collectible diary pages, because the game itself lacks any kind of plot. It just feels half-finished with things like an unexplained magic system or a main antagonist who doesn’t even have a spoken line.
Woolfe is not a good game. But it is very far from being a bad game. It is full of passion– you really can feel that in every pixel. It was just too far too big of an undertaking for the small development team, and they couldn’t live up to their dreams.
Still… It deserved better. They deserved better. In the end, the story behind the game, just like the tale, is a bittersweet one, with maybe more morals in there than we would want to accept.

I have only played the game for a few hours, but i have gotten a pretty good grasp of the game in that time. If you played Battlevoid: Harbinger then you will like this game as this takes place in the same universe and has a few similar features from the previous game.
The games main drive is its basically a skirmish gamemode. Where you have 2 spacestations you and the enemy and your objective is to destroy the enemy station using ships which your station produces and once you kill the enemy spacestation or vice versa the match ends and you then go into another match and repeat the process.
The campaign comes in 4 difficulties Easy, Normal, Hard and legend which take play on a 30 sector map with 5 enemy factions and your faction each with 5 sectors. Each faction hate you and there is no diplomacy system in the game. so to complete the campaign you must capture every enemy sector. When you start a game you'll be given 2 choices of which will put you in a match against a certain faction the choice the game makes cant be changed.
There is a skirmish mode that you can do which has 1V1 or 2V2 for the gamemode domination which is your typical match and it has a undersiege gamemode which is what you play when your defending your sectors in the campaign. Before you start your match you can choose if you want to start with low, medium or high cash what difficulty you want to play on, for which you can only choose easy, normal or hard, what events will appear during the match and for domination what map you want for undersiege the last choice is how big you want the enemy waves to be low, medium or endless.
Each faction have their own ship designs and weapons so you can tell what you'll be up against when you face a certian faction or when they jump into your current match.
1.After completing a match you'll earn a certain amount of tokens which can be used to buy more powerful ships, defence stations or research trees on the sector map under the unlockable tab to use in matchs from that point on.
2. In this game you play as a commander in charge of a spacestation defending against the enemy commander's spacestation. You can add turrets to the station or build ships using the ingame currency.
3. Mines randomly scattered across the maps increase the rate at which you gain currency and upgrade points, which once captured will have 4 slots to place defence stations to help defend the mines from enemy units.
4. Upgrade points are used to upgrade turrets, fighters or used to speed up research.
5. Research is used to give in match bonuses to your ships, production or to unlock high powered turrets which can then be used on your ships or stations.
6. During matchs the game may trigger events on the map such as a blackhole has formed which you must then avoid or it may spawn ships of another faction to attack both you and the other commander. ( I have not played this game for to long yet so there may be other events, these are just the ones i have seen so far. )

Be warned, this is not a game for everyone.
Those looking for a rogue-lite Dark Souls will be disappointed. Dark Souls this is not.
Those looking for a more hardcore Zelda clone, there are no puzzles, you will be disappointed.
Those looking for depth, stay away. This is a bit of a pond.
This game is challenging, yes, but more so in the beginning. Everything is randomly generated and if you cannot secure enough food or the resources to craft it, you can be pretty screwed. When you are hit you are stunlocked like 95% of the time, which can lead to more hits and thus the end of your life on that run. Dying is brutal in this game since you lose all "progress" (how deep you got into the levels) that you made. Ah, but the real progress comes from the tokens that persist between characters which can be exchanged for Codexes at the ends of every level, dyes from the old man merchant found at the beginning of the game and at the ends of every level, or opening gold chests (the items for these do not persist, so it's a waste imo) found at the starts of every level starting with floors 2 and below. I use plural because there are many branching paths between each level, some can be dead ends or even lead back up to an unexplored section on a previous floor (which can then also lead to a dead end). There can be lots of backtracking if you get unlucky or want to explore every last corner as there can be "illusory walls" and little red-tipped pyramid scavengers that might contain a better weapon that what have currently.
Enemies may appear different, but they only fall into about 5 or 6 categories who all have the same AI: if they're alone, they'll run to find another, which is usually a group. Fights are rarely 1 on 1. There are no bosses amongst the randomly generated floors, so nearly every encounter is the same, only in a slightly different location.
The look of Necropolis like a mix between Wind Waker and Dark Souls: bleak dark shades of grey over cel-shaded (untextured) surfaces. Although this minimalist style really struck me when I first saw it and has grown on me more since. I enjoy the character designs quite a bit, so finding a new armor set is pretty rewarding. The environment, however in the first half is what you'll be seeing most- large grey boxes with barrels or crates every now and then. Sometimes you'll come across a trapped statue. Oh boy.
The deeper levels start to include (but not limited to) swamps, snowy forests with cabins strewn about rarely, a sewer system, more industrialized areas with a slight steampunk feel. But due to the randomized nature of the game, you may never see these on the same character.
Animations are generally good when it's just the player character. Every weapon has its own attack speed to try to add variety, but each attack feels clunky. As for the sound, I miss the weighted shlinks of swords against chain and flesh, the smashing of hammers against bone and the cold floor, the burning hiss of acid as it eats away your stamina and health. However, the ambient sound is decent, with crackling torches, pitterpatter of feet as you move around and backtrack, the synths in the background egging you on for more exploration. The music is very light, non-intrusive, reminds me of a sort of fantasy Tron.
There is no story as one would expect from a rogue-lite, but there are many scratches and scribbles on the wall conveying legends and myths of the world. You also have obfuscated item descriptions that will leave you scratching your head, resorting to trial and error until you memorize them or consult a wiki, even AFTER you identify them with a scroll (colors of items are unhelpful since they're randomized as well). The omniscient  Brazen Head is your "guide" similar to GLaDOS, but nowhere near as funny or memorable. Actually that description fits any of the "lore" you find. The attempt at humor can be rather immersion breaking your first time around on a solo playthrough as it doesn't exactly fit with the rest of the feel of the game. Although after playing it more times, perhaps your perception of the game will change.
What usually redeems this game for most people is the co-op. Yes survival in these bleak boxes is rather addicting, as you can plan out attacks on hordes or enemies and the loot. Friendly fire is there, of course, because why not, so caution is needed. Unless thrown to the wind for a bit of pvp, you murderer. If one does die however, a teammate can revive you with exhaustion which can be circumvented with food or potions, but that defeats the whole purpose of permadeath for a bit more fun in mind. Yes I'm convinced this game was designed with co-op as the priority, and it shows. This game is a good way to kill an afternoon with a few friends.
There are things I haven't touched upon here, but you can expect to see what I've said. This game reminds me of an arcade game back in the day, a quarter-eater like Castlevania but without bosses (except for one).
There are many faults, and A LOT of missed potential, but I do enjoy it. It is a real shame it wasnt more popular, and as a result, the devs may no longer work on it.
Pick this up on sale when it's around $10-15.

Woolfe, The Red Hood Diaries is a short adventure and 3D platformer in the theme of Steampunk and Little Red Riding Hood with a hint of Batman. It has okay music and an okay story that is elevated by the lore that is provided on the side. The theme gains the game two imaginary points and made me play the game in the first place.

Hint 2 - about speedrunning:
+ Quite a pretty game
+ Little Red Riding Hood theme
+ Okay story, rhymed
+ Okay music
+ "Diary" collecting lore, in-game and meta
+ Skippable cutscenes
0 Possibly the first episode of a series

- Pretty short game

The game is no Pixar movie but comes with respectable graphics. Cutscenes are presented in rhymes. The music is not outstanding but far from irritating.
The game features collectibles that each provide more insight into the story or the development of the game. They are collected in a  "Diary" which is available from the main or in-game menu.
The controls are usable but fighting took some time to figure out. If you ever had a fencing lesson where you weren't allowed to block or if you read about Johann Liechtenauer's school of sword fighting you are probably set.
The life-bar is pretty short, so basically, don't get hit. Life regenerates when outside of battle.
There are no upgrades but you "learn" a number of special moves which are, well, of no use to me. Their higher damage is accompanied by a too long recovery time, and the base attack, although a bit weaker, gives good control over a fight.
I put "learn" in quotes because: 1. You can only execute specials in the in-game chronology after the game tells you about them; and 2. the game makes you invariably re-learn the special whenever you pass the corresponding point in a level, complete with game pause and the requirement to execute the "new" skill in order to make the tutorial screen go away.
At times I fell through the map.
Once while running with wolves, I tried to roll out from under a tree, dropped through the pass and died - guess which achievement I was going for at the time.
The other occurrence is repeatable and in the sewers. To the right of the mirrored time challenge there is a tunnel where you can see the tip of a boat's bow. When jumping into the tunnel and then double-jumping as far right as possible I fell through the top water plane without dying (but usually taking fall damage). I could, then underwater, walk around the pillars carrying the elements of the room above the surface. I'd die when getting too close to those crushers or burners, or when getting under the next water plane to the left.
The game is a short, just around three hours for a simple playthrough and about twice that for completion.
When the 3D platforming had to stand the trial of repetition it became slightly infuriating. Basically you have to jump from one irregularly shaped object to another irregularly shaped object without another plane of correspondence. So there is a good chance you'll misjudge jumps. For the speedrun you just have to learn.
I recommend Woolfe, The Red Hood Diaries because after all it was interesting, fun and satisfying. If you are are worried about length of the game, I suggest buying it at a discount.

A simple 15-20 hr side-scrolling action game. A Metroidvania with anthros.
tl;dr review:
Play it but mute the voice. Longer full review below.
I initially bought it mostly because I heard it was made by one guy, and the fact I love metroid games. Well technically, this game is made by one guy + a bunch of voice actors, but it really should have been made by one guy and no voice actors. More on that later. I was rather curious seeing how a single guy could write, programme, draw/animate a game all by himself.
In terms of combat and enemy variety and overall gameplay, I say this game is pretty great in that department. Dust: An Elysian tail gives you basic sword attacks like a simple side-scrolling action game, but it includes some Devil May Cry-like combos including the ability to launch enemies a helm breaker style attack an a parry system similar to like in Metal Gear Rising using holding the light attack while facing your enemy at the correct timing. The defining characteristic of the combat system is the dust storm, where dust spins his sword wildly that when combined by his little friend Fidget's elemental attacks results in a giant storm of elemental fury, projectiles flying everywhere, chain lightning, pillars of flame. My only complain is that there are only three elements, not a lot of variety there.
The difficulty of the game is weird though. RPGs always come in three forms, either they start really easy and become insanely difficult in the end, forcing you to grind, or, you start hard and end the game steam rolling everything even the boss (Oh Skyrim is the biggest culprit of this). This game contains RPG levelling and one that makes the difficulty that goes easy>hard>easy. The final boss was more of an endurance run rather than an actual challenge with 4 phases which is... too long. You might say he's the final boss, it should be long, yes, but it also wasn't challenging, so I was basically waiting to win and wasn't anywhere near death or in need to use a healing item (which the game generously drops a bunch). With the large amount of enemies you fight leading up to the final boss, you're gonna overlevel, and that certainly did not help. Still, besides the final boss, the first three bosses, when you aren't actually overleveled, did in fact gave me a challenge. Thus so this is another one of those games where the final boss ends up being easier than the first. But no matter, the other bosses had clever patterns and were a decent enough challenge so I'll let that easy final boss part go and give this gameplay a 9.
Combat and Gameplay 9/10
Story is.... ehhh. Of course it's not Lord of the Rings, I'm not expecting an epic story, but well, forget it. The gameplay alone is good, just don't bother with the story, it's not important nor a deciding factor of buying this game.
Story - whatever/10
Level Design is an important thing in a metroidvania game, and overall I did not feel that this game had a very good level design. It's really straightforward, so much so it's kinda boring. The world is put together with an overworld map connecting everything, and if you ever played Castlevania: Order of Ecclessia and found how straightforward and boring the levels are, well there you go. There's not a lot of branching paths and most of the secrets are just so obvious I wouldn't even call it a secret anyway. Remember that feeling when you first broke the glass with a power bomb in super metroid? or when you discovered the area where the rain mysteriously stopping in mid air is actually an invisible floating platform? Of course, I'm not saying the game is just a straight line every level, neither was Castlevania: OoE. All I'm saying is, this game didn't give me any real sense of discovery like when I'm walking through Dracula's castle in SotN. Many of the collectibles are just in too obvious locations.
On the other hand, the game does have some interesting platforming sections. Some good some bad. They're not the Tower of death level of difficulty or cleverness with moving platforms, spinning blades, spikes and medusa heads of course, but it is a good enough challenge in their own right.
Level design - 7/10
Sound, music is good, lots of catchy tunes but the problem is.... the voice acting... oh no... Nooo.. Just nooo............ This is why this one man game... should have remained a one man game. The voice acting is anywhere from acceptable to just plain awful. And I'm not talking about Fidget which many other reviewers seem to hate. For me, Fidget (and Dust actually) sound okay. But Ginger is bad. She's suppose to be sad and depressed as the story claims, except every time she talks, she sounds indifferent, like a robot, not giving a damn, even when a certain character supposedly died at the end, she was like "oh no what do I do....??". Like I said, the music, is pretty good. The voice acting? NOPE, NOPE, NOPE.
Overall 8/10. A solid side scrolling action game. The Combat is awesome, the enemies and bosses are really clever. The dust storm mechanics just makes fighting in this game fun as hell. The only real downside of this game is the voice acting, and that's it.

Might and Magic is a cult Dungeon Crawler series, which got its up and down. The down mostly came after the 7th episode (which was already seriously less good than the 6th).
Unlike Dungeon Master (DM) and Legend of Grimrock (LoG), it’s not real-time but turn based. The good point is that it lets you play at your own pace. The down point is that it creates less tension than real time fight and it feels less dynamic. Both can also be seen as advantageous when you just want to relax (although even in turn based game you still can feel pressurized from time to time ! ;-) ).
But there’s also another major difference : M&MX, just like its ancestors, doesn’t feature an unique deep dungeon ; instead, it offers you an open world with numerous small dungeons and a few medium ones.
From these 2 characteristics, it means there’s no dungeon offering any memorable nor challenging exploration. Once in a dungeon, you’ll never feel lost, and except for a very few exceptions, you won’t even feel confused about what to do or where to go, especially as there’s no puzzle (with a couple of exceptions) and the secrets appear depending of your party abilities and not of your own observation skills. And all that without taking account of the automap.
On another hand, exploring the outside world is more engaging. And the where-to-go challenge comes up when you have to decide what is the next dungeon you want to go. As there’s no level indicator, it means you can end up in a too hard dungeon. This raises another issue:  you can’t play without quick save & load, as it’s impossible to escape a started combat, which is for me a mood killer.
But it’s not that bad, because of another bad point : the game is quickly too easy, which means you’ll rarely have to worry about getting in a too hard fight (if you play in the normal difficulty).
This brings us to the combat system. So it’s turn based. You need 1 or 1 and half healers (because often 1 healer can be paralyzed/asleep/stoned/etc…), and although there’s tank build, there’s no tanking in the way of World of Warcraft (and Dungeon Guardians ;-) ) : there’s no aggro building. You still have a few “attack me during this turn” spells, but most bosses are immune to them, so actually the tank doesn’t need to have much more HP and armor than other party members.
The combats themselves, once you have digested & understood the numerous abilities, are actually simple, easy and mostly straightforward. No, in M&MX, the difficulty comes from the resource management. This means that the difficulty comes from the choice of using or not HP & Mana potions during the fights. Almost no fight can be fatal as long as you have enough potions to go through it. This is even more true as it’s a turn based game, so you have all the time in the world to analyse the current situation and choose the most pertinent ability correctly. So to sail through the game, you just have to understand how much potions you can use in each fight. The number of potions is limited ; you can buy some from shops, but it seems they don’t reappear afterward. But you can also buy limitless rations, that allows you to sleep after the fights to recover all your HP & Mana.
As 1st, you’re short on gold, but after a while, you’ll get a ton of it. So the difficulty comes from resource management, but you get more or less limitless of them after a while ? So yup, there’s not much difficulty anymore after 25% of the game done.
There’s an hard mode, but this one is just too hard to newcomers ; you’re expected to already know the game to pick it (although you aren’t told so in the selection screen), but once you know the game, it is also too easy as you just know how much potions & rations you need to go through the dungeons & world. Plus, still, after a while you just get a ton of money again.
The combats aren’t really boring nor too repetitive, though. There are enough abilities, effect variations, kind of mobs, and special events to keep things interesting. It’s just that without time pressure, there’s not much doubt about what to do, nor doing it quickly enough.
So that’s a bit a pity as the game itself is pretty nice. Discovering & exploring the world and its dungeons is captivating. The character leveling is nicely done (but not great). There’s a ton to do and see, even though the story holds very little interest, which is a bit annoying in a game with such a big world : it builds very little implication in the player, roaming all around, jumping from dungeon to dungeon without caring much about the goals. Ending is nice enough though, as the background of the story is well exploited.
There also are a bunch of riddles in the world, and a few dungeons made of only 1 puzzle to solve and nothing else, plus 1 dungeon made of several puzzles but without any mobs nor real exploration. Puzzles were mostly annoying for me, and I guess riddles are decent if you’re into that kind of thing.
Visually, it’s shockingly ugly at 1st ; the 1st city is painfully horrible and technically it feels like we’re back in the early 2000’s. Following cities aren’t much better, but the world and the dungeons are usually well done with a good artistic direction.
Interesting combat system plagued by its easiness after a while, simplistic dungeon exploration partly compensated by open world exploration, average puzzles, unequal visuals & atmosphere.
So all in all, this is a game that is bigger than the sums of its parts and offers a nice adventure, despite all its shortcomings.
