Be warned, this is not a game for everyone.
Those looking for a rogue-lite Dark Souls will be disappointed. Dark Souls this is not.
Those looking for a more hardcore Zelda clone, there are no puzzles, you will be disappointed.
Those looking for depth, stay away. This is a bit of a pond.
This game is challenging, yes, but more so in the beginning. Everything is randomly generated and if you cannot secure enough food or the resources to craft it, you can be pretty screwed. When you are hit you are stunlocked like 95% of the time, which can lead to more hits and thus the end of your life on that run. Dying is brutal in this game since you lose all "progress" (how deep you got into the levels) that you made. Ah, but the real progress comes from the tokens that persist between characters which can be exchanged for Codexes at the ends of every level, dyes from the old man merchant found at the beginning of the game and at the ends of every level, or opening gold chests (the items for these do not persist, so it's a waste imo) found at the starts of every level starting with floors 2 and below. I use plural because there are many branching paths between each level, some can be dead ends or even lead back up to an unexplored section on a previous floor (which can then also lead to a dead end). There can be lots of backtracking if you get unlucky or want to explore every last corner as there can be "illusory walls" and little red-tipped pyramid scavengers that might contain a better weapon that what have currently.
Enemies may appear different, but they only fall into about 5 or 6 categories who all have the same AI: if they're alone, they'll run to find another, which is usually a group. Fights are rarely 1 on 1. There are no bosses amongst the randomly generated floors, so nearly every encounter is the same, only in a slightly different location.
The look of Necropolis like a mix between Wind Waker and Dark Souls: bleak dark shades of grey over cel-shaded (untextured) surfaces. Although this minimalist style really struck me when I first saw it and has grown on me more since. I enjoy the character designs quite a bit, so finding a new armor set is pretty rewarding. The environment, however in the first half is what you'll be seeing most- large grey boxes with barrels or crates every now and then. Sometimes you'll come across a trapped statue. Oh boy.
The deeper levels start to include (but not limited to) swamps, snowy forests with cabins strewn about rarely, a sewer system, more industrialized areas with a slight steampunk feel. But due to the randomized nature of the game, you may never see these on the same character.
Animations are generally good when it's just the player character. Every weapon has its own attack speed to try to add variety, but each attack feels clunky. As for the sound, I miss the weighted shlinks of swords against chain and flesh, the smashing of hammers against bone and the cold floor, the burning hiss of acid as it eats away your stamina and health. However, the ambient sound is decent, with crackling torches, pitterpatter of feet as you move around and backtrack, the synths in the background egging you on for more exploration. The music is very light, non-intrusive, reminds me of a sort of fantasy Tron.
There is no story as one would expect from a rogue-lite, but there are many scratches and scribbles on the wall conveying legends and myths of the world. You also have obfuscated item descriptions that will leave you scratching your head, resorting to trial and error until you memorize them or consult a wiki, even AFTER you identify them with a scroll (colors of items are unhelpful since they're randomized as well). The omniscient  Brazen Head is your "guide" similar to GLaDOS, but nowhere near as funny or memorable. Actually that description fits any of the "lore" you find. The attempt at humor can be rather immersion breaking your first time around on a solo playthrough as it doesn't exactly fit with the rest of the feel of the game. Although after playing it more times, perhaps your perception of the game will change.
What usually redeems this game for most people is the co-op. Yes survival in these bleak boxes is rather addicting, as you can plan out attacks on hordes or enemies and the loot. Friendly fire is there, of course, because why not, so caution is needed. Unless thrown to the wind for a bit of pvp, you murderer. If one does die however, a teammate can revive you with exhaustion which can be circumvented with food or potions, but that defeats the whole purpose of permadeath for a bit more fun in mind. Yes I'm convinced this game was designed with co-op as the priority, and it shows. This game is a good way to kill an afternoon with a few friends.
There are things I haven't touched upon here, but you can expect to see what I've said. This game reminds me of an arcade game back in the day, a quarter-eater like Castlevania but without bosses (except for one).
There are many faults, and A LOT of missed potential, but I do enjoy it. It is a real shame it wasnt more popular, and as a result, the devs may no longer work on it.

So, I completely understand that my positive reaction to this game is incredibly personal, and, while I'm in no way blind to the obvious flaws in the game's design or execution, I still personally consider it my Game of the Year, 2014. I've been a fan of the Might & Magic franchise, both the RPG's and the strategy games, from childhood. When 3DO went bankrupt and dragged New World Computing down with them, I was saddened, and initially excited when Ubisoft bought the license and started working on it again. Then they released their games, and, apart from the Clash of Heroes spinoff, which became one of my favourite games ever partly due to its tongue in cheek nature, I've been sorely unimpressed by them, especially by Ubisoft's behaviour as a publisher.
But then this game happened, and it is such a genuine piece of work that I couldn't help but love it despite the obvious flaws. I could go on for a feature length article about why this game is so personally important to me, but I'll limit myself to the technical aspects: this game has a great story and a great atmosphere, and it plays like a modern version of those old school, grid based, first person RPGs like Lands of Lore or, well, Might & Magic 1 through 5. Of course, this cuts both ways, in that Might & Magic X carries over some of the flaws of those old games we moved past, most noteably incosiderately placing two mobs of wildly different power levels within close proximity to each other, combined with an inability to actually escape from a fight once it's engaged. Also, like others have mentioned, it's not optimally balanced, and it's got the occasional, sometimes crippling glitch.
Then again, a lot of old school RPG's weren't balanced, and had their bugs that made things annoying, and while we certainly should have moved passed this in the two decades, if you're already used to dealing with them, Legacy isn't egregious about it. And, for a Ubisoft game, the bugs and glitches are remarkably inoffensive.
Like I said, great story, great atmosphere, and, you know what, some very solid puzzles that you don't see much of in modern RPGs. Like, legit puzzles, riddles, gimmick dungeon levels that are mostly intuitive, not easy enough to be insulting, or so obtuse to be frustrating. Also, if you're, like me, a huge fan of the original Might & Magic franchise, there's this moment at the end of one of these game spanning quests that made me giddy.
So, yeah, recognizing that this is a flawed game, it's still incredibly important to me, and I still highly recommend it to traditional RPG lovers.

tl;dr review:
Play it but mute the voice. Longer full review below.
I initially bought it mostly because I heard it was made by one guy, and the fact I love metroid games. Well technically, this game is made by one guy + a bunch of voice actors, but it really should have been made by one guy and no voice actors. More on that later. I was rather curious seeing how a single guy could write, programme, draw/animate a game all by himself.
In terms of combat and enemy variety and overall gameplay, I say this game is pretty great in that department. Dust: An Elysian tail gives you basic sword attacks like a simple side-scrolling action game, but it includes some Devil May Cry-like combos including the ability to launch enemies a helm breaker style attack an a parry system similar to like in Metal Gear Rising using holding the light attack while facing your enemy at the correct timing. The defining characteristic of the combat system is the dust storm, where dust spins his sword wildly that when combined by his little friend Fidget's elemental attacks results in a giant storm of elemental fury, projectiles flying everywhere, chain lightning, pillars of flame. My only complain is that there are only three elements, not a lot of variety there.
The difficulty of the game is weird though. RPGs always come in three forms, either they start really easy and become insanely difficult in the end, forcing you to grind, or, you start hard and end the game steam rolling everything even the boss (Oh Skyrim is the biggest culprit of this). This game contains RPG levelling and one that makes the difficulty that goes easy>hard>easy. The final boss was more of an endurance run rather than an actual challenge with 4 phases which is... too long. You might say he's the final boss, it should be long, yes, but it also wasn't challenging, so I was basically waiting to win and wasn't anywhere near death or in need to use a healing item (which the game generously drops a bunch). With the large amount of enemies you fight leading up to the final boss, you're gonna overlevel, and that certainly did not help. Still, besides the final boss, the first three bosses, when you aren't actually overleveled, did in fact gave me a challenge. Thus so this is another one of those games where the final boss ends up being easier than the first. But no matter, the other bosses had clever patterns and were a decent enough challenge so I'll let that easy final boss part go and give this gameplay a 9.
Combat and Gameplay 9/10
Story is.... ehhh. Of course it's not Lord of the Rings, I'm not expecting an epic story, but well, forget it. The gameplay alone is good, just don't bother with the story, it's not important nor a deciding factor of buying this game.
Story - whatever/10
Level Design is an important thing in a metroidvania game, and overall I did not feel that this game had a very good level design. It's really straightforward, so much so it's kinda boring. The world is put together with an overworld map connecting everything, and if you ever played Castlevania: Order of Ecclessia and found how straightforward and boring the levels are, well there you go. There's not a lot of branching paths and most of the secrets are just so obvious I wouldn't even call it a secret anyway. Remember that feeling when you first broke the glass with a power bomb in super metroid? or when you discovered the area where the rain mysteriously stopping in mid air is actually an invisible floating platform? Of course, I'm not saying the game is just a straight line every level, neither was Castlevania: OoE. All I'm saying is, this game didn't give me any real sense of discovery like when I'm walking through Dracula's castle in SotN. Many of the collectibles are just in too obvious locations.
On the other hand, the game does have some interesting platforming sections. Some good some bad. They're not the Tower of death level of difficulty or cleverness with moving platforms, spinning blades, spikes and medusa heads of course, but it is a good enough challenge in their own right.
Level design - 7/10
Sound, music is good, lots of catchy tunes but the problem is.... the voice acting... oh no... Nooo.. Just nooo............ This is why this one man game... should have remained a one man game. The voice acting is anywhere from acceptable to just plain awful. And I'm not talking about Fidget which many other reviewers seem to hate. For me, Fidget (and Dust actually) sound okay. But Ginger is bad. She's suppose to be sad and depressed as the story claims, except every time she talks, she sounds indifferent, like a robot, not giving a damn, even when a certain character supposedly died at the end, she was like "oh no what do I do....??". Like I said, the music, is pretty good. The voice acting? NOPE, NOPE, NOPE.
Overall 8/10. A solid side scrolling action game. The Combat is awesome, the enemies and bosses are really clever. The dust storm mechanics just makes fighting in this game fun as hell. The only real downside of this game is the voice acting, and that's it.

Wow, where to start.  I think Dust is one of my top 10 favorite platformers ever.  The art, animations, and visual effects remind me of Don Bluth films from my childhood.  The in-game music and effects are immersive, and the final theme during the credits is perfect for the way it ends.  Things on the screen are constantly exploding or being blown around.  Controlling Dust is a joy in itself, especially once you start using the aerial dust storm in combination with other moves (I'm playing with a controller).  The story likely isn't anything you haven't heard in some form before, but it's told well with voice acting that I actually didn't always skip through.
Then there is the gameplay itself.  It's an RPG full of hack/slash action and platform jumping.  No puzzles or tactics.  You keep the same weapon the entire game, upgrading only armor and other items.  Soooo many side quests and easter egg characters to find.  The world map is simple enough to jump around so you can get those 100 percents after gaining new moves.  The level design encourages complete exploration and constant fiddling to try to get to new places just in case there is a chest or a key, which there almost always is.  The size of the maps and placement of save points feels just right.  New items are most often crafted from found materials, and are easy to manage for maximum effect.  Toward the end of the game, you likely won't even need consumables and can just go grab up any treasures you missed along the way without worrying about your health, even against the final boss (which might be a turn-off for some).
I could have completed the game in less than 20 hours, but I wanted to get everything, and it rarely felt like a chore, even when I had to spend a good chunk of time failing at something, only to discover later that there's an additional ability that makes it easier.  I rarely gift games to anyone, but I think anyone who likes action platformers should play Dust.  I would buy it again at full price.

My first impression about the game was how it looks so promising. I really loved the theme and story. Having a badass female protagonist in a dystopic fairy-tale is simply my thing.
What I really liked about this game is:
+ Voice acting - it was sooo good.
+ Narration - unlike many other people, I enjoyed the rhyming sentences really really much. <3
+ Character and environment design.
+ Art style.
+ Music.
Now let's get to the things that I didn't like.
There were quite a few bugs and game parts left unpolished here and there. It was obvious that the developers didn't spend enough time for usability/playability testing and QA. Even though it was still playable, controlling a character in a 2.5D world was a major distress when you cannot move the camera to see the positions of the platforms. Jumping on the wrong place because I couldn't see where exactly the other moving platform on the XZ plane, dying and spawing from the last checkpoint which is literally on the other side of the world has made me lose lots of time. And also, it made me want to ragequit maybe a 4328732 times.
Another big problem was that enemies not having a health bar in combat, unless they're a boss. It doesn't affect playability that much, though.
I am actually surprised that this game got that many negative reviews. Indie games usually have myriad drawbacks mostly because of the lack of experience and resources. Still, the game is very short, and you are the one to decide if it's worth paying for a game having many issues. However, I found the good sides of this game strong and I would recommend it.  Definitely, worth giving it a try.
Note: I did not play the game that long. I left it running while I was AFK.

This game encompasses everything I love about video games. The graphics are beautiful, the story is engaging, and the music draws you right in. This is, however, an action RPG/Metroidvania, so none of that would matter if the gameplay and level design wasn't up to snuff. Luckily, that's not the case. The controls are tight and snappy. Dust does exactly what you want him to do, when you want him to do it. Although more simplistic, I almost felt a Devil May Cry influence in the combat. It's action packed and relentless. The level design is varied and entertaining. I eagerly looked forward to what I was going to find on the next screen. The enemy designs were also quite good. The headless zombie things in the third section made me smile every time I saw them. The one complaint I have with this game is the same one everyone else has. The boss fights. While not bad, they just don't measure up to the rest of the game and they're definitely a bit on the easy side. But you should absolutely not let that one small thing stop you from experiencing this game.
Dust: An Elysian Tail is just plain fun, no matter how you look at it. I can't wait to play it again on a harder difficulty once I get through some of my backlog and I'll eagerly await a sequel.

I definitely recommend collecting all of the journal entries and reading them because they add a lot to the story that isn't necessarily told during the traditional gameplay and are also pretty well written. The Witcher 2 continues the epic story of professional monster slayer for hire; Geralt of Rivia. If you have played the first game you will probably already have an idea of what you can expect. The Witcher 2 begins a few months after the events of the first game. If you haven't played the first you may be a bit at a loss with regards to some elements in the story.
Without spoiling the story you proceed through the game searching for the 'kingslayer' and the choices you make will ultimately decide the ending of the story you get. (This ending can then be transferred to Witcher 3.) You follow one of two main story paths. You either can side with blue stripes commander Vernon Roche or with Scoitatel renegade and guerilla fighter Lor'veth.
The combat in Witcher 2 has been refined considerably from the first game. whereas the first game relied on a timing mechanic; The Witcher 2 adds in things like parry's to the mix.
I strongly recommend playing the first game prior as it will give greater context to the events that occur in this follow up. I also strongly recommend playing this game prior to Witcher 3 for the same reason. However the Witcher 3 does a decent job of providing additional information about the world and characters. You can find these in in-game character profiles as well as books you can find during your playthrough.
As you can see it took me about 40 or so hours to play through the game. But this is a game where your investment will pay off with a satisfying conclusion that you can then build on in the Witcher 3. If you are looking for a deep story driven RPG where there is no 'right' choice; and for those choices to matter? Witcher 2 is a fantastic choice.

Let's be honest here: Stellaris isn't stellar, it's good but not mindblowing.
The premise is great: being able to define who your race is is great and how that evolves throught the game is realy enjoyable.
Starting off as xenophobe colectevist (bonus to slave tollerance) and decadent (penalty for not having slaves)  and weak (penalty to army damage) realy defined my race's playstile in the early game,
1. find race
2. invade race
3. enslave race
4. army of slaves
5. Win!
However it didn't go like that, more like:
1. Find primative race
2. infiltrate race's government
3. control entire race
4. uplift and greet race then
5. Enslavement! bwahahaha
Then somewhere along the line i lost the xenophobe trait and gene spliced myself to lose the decadent trait so now xenos are equal citizens (they may still be a bit bitter about the enslavement... and purges... but w/e).
That to me is the real hook of Stellaris. The story of how your starting race is changed by the game and how your own actions change it.
On to other things:
The situation log/quest system certainly fleshes out the character of the game: Collecting specimens for your local xenomuseum and the flavour text just from finding an abandoned solar sailer makes the universe intoxicatingly real. Though the rewards lost the attraction after a while(+xamount of tech is can only be so interesting to a point...) but often the continuation of the chain of events was reward enough. I had an event chain about some kind of narcotic plant that distracted the population of one of my planets and over the course of the chain all kind of Modifiers happened to that planet and after everything i'm pretty sure the planet ended up with nothing special and I'm ok with that as I realy enjoyed seeing what would happen.
The soundtrack is enjoyable (I found myself humming some of the tracks now and then) but it get a bit repetative after the 20th time round. Also it is inconsistent with the ethos of the race (the soundtrack to my Xenophobe race's first steps amongst the stars should have been trepidation not wonder. Something the (fantastic) writing gets right but not the soundtrack).
Combat is... your number vs my number. There is a game of Rock-paper-scisors going on behind the scenes but there are no tooltips that actively tell you about it(had I not immersed myself in devdiaries and the Blorg streams I would have had no idea about the rock-paper-scisors.).
The UI is a characterless clickfest. Having to hit either M or E to switch between glactic and solarsystem view is cumbersome and it requires far too many clicks to do something as simple as building a ship. Select/hover over Solarsystem -> hit E/M to enter it -> Select spaceport(or select planet -> spaceport tab) -> Build -> Select ship. Then after all that there is no ♥♥♥♥ing rally point system, aaaarrrrrg! (atleast not that I have found) this makes it insufferable to try and build up and collect your fleet(Sellaris desprately needs EU4s army builder).
Tech! Not having a tech tree infront of your face it realy interesting. Sure initialy kinda daunting but it meant that quite often I was honestly curious to see what would pop up next and being able to gain the ability to research techs from enemy debris after battle alows some fantastic tech skipping and battlefield equalising.
I was going to wrap this up by saying that Stellaris lacked depth but I don't think thats true anymore, sure it's not oceanic deep but but there is certainly some there it is just amazingly badly signposted (to those who have played did you know you can augment your ground troops after they are created, no? Well I'm not surprised, I only found it after a couple of accidental clicks). Maybe after a paid dlc or two (grumble) these annoyances will be adressed but I feel Stellaris is till worth a thumbs up even so, sure wait for a few more patches and bugfixes if you're unsure.

It's a spiritual successor to the previous Might and Magic games - you know, before they tried going 3D (MM6), then went 3D (MM9) and generally went the way most old-school RPGs at the time did and tried to modernize their worlds when 3D was a bit too new, and screwing everything up.
Looking at you, Wizardry 8, Ultima 9 and Might and Magic 9.
As a turn-based grid-based dungeon crawler, it's pretty good if a bit simplistic. It follows the lore established by other Might and Magic games, with maximums for skills based on class and only having a handful of those. It's also a bit easy to bone yourself early on, so go read an FAQ or two before tackling. You know, like the old days (where it was on BBSes, or picking up the game guide).
Definitely recommended for its quality, and doing a ton with a little and for keeping the flame alive. Would buy MM11 in a heartbeat.

Might & Magic X is an okay turn-based, retro crpg that do have some interesting ideas, but poorly executed.
You play as a group of adventurers whose task is to deliver the ashes of their master in the Agyn peninsula, only to be greeted with brigands and monsters and political intrigue that plot to shatter the Empire from afar.
The game start with a character creation that lets either pick pre-determined adventurers, make up your own or let everything choosed randomly. You will find 4 generic playable races being Humans, Elfs, Dwarves and Orcs, each race featuring 3 unique classes each, even though each one can be summed up as Warrior, Ranger and Mage.
Each class have its own set of special abilities, along with a late game 'promotion' that will let you unlock Grand-master skills and new traits, although it's kind of blurry which one seems to be the most effective in what situations. Some classes are very late game based where others are early game efficient, so i recommend check a wiki before throwing yourself blindly into the game, especially if you want to play in Hard.
Character progression will grant you attribute points and skill points to allocate in different capacity. You can raise the level of your skills up to a certain stage where you will need to find a trainer to unlock the next matery step, while granting you with additionnal traits. Each classes can only unlock certain skills up to a certain level of mastery, but every classes feature almost the same skills.
Although, playing in hard, i started by allocating points in Vitality, especially for my 'tanks' so that they soak up more damage, until i realise that it was more a waste than anything since the Skill trait "endurance" end up giving a stronger health pool than what you can get from the few points the attribute will grant. So i'd recommend spending most of your points in dps or critical, eventually Spirit so that your caster can keep up firing spells.
It is a fairly simple system, though one of the major complaint i'd have is that one of the skill tree that will give your melee caracter more combat skills will only grant you with more Mana, where you actually need them to control and add more strategy to your actions in combat. The main weapons traits will let you carry better weapon indeed, but never give you any actual skill to use in battle so, you end up wanting more dps rather than more mana for skills you don't have anyway.
The "seek a trainer" system is also pretty sweet on paper, but they happen to be a bit randomly scattered through out the game, and so you'll find out that a lot of 'expert' trainers for early game skills you'd be tempted to spend points in will be located in later game zones you can hardly reach with a lower level. So you find youserlf specialising in skills you will be able to actually train rather than taking the ones that feels interesting for your build but can't make anything out of it because you can't properly train them.
A good thing though is that the peninsula is somewhat open world with dungeon scattered around so, you rarely feel claustrophobic about your environment, compared to other dungeon crawler. You will find yourself exploring the world with care, trying to find every small cave or dungeon, hidden secrets and chests, which is probably the best part of the game. Most of the zones will be level capped so you'll know when you enter somewhere you don't have the level required for, mainly because most of the mobs will destroy you. But if you are determined and have a good team composition you can sometimes wander always a little further, which feels really rewarding to overcome enemies that gave you a beating a few hours ago.
Although... you don't have that much to do in the exploration in the end. The peninsula feels really small after a few hours in, even if populated with a lot of little things and npcs all around, it always feels like once you've killed everything and clicked everywhere the zone become empty, with rarely any reason for you to come back. Unfortunatly, the game features a lot of backtracking, and an old chool fast travel system that, even if i liked it, can be a bit dull to use just to bring an early game npc a quest item you found in the other side of the map.
Also, you can't interract with much of the walls or what is around you by yourself, so there would be no hidden switchs or moving objects around. It is fairly restrictive for most of the secrets will be overly obvious, highlighted 3D details you can only interract pressing [spacebar]. So in a way, it is very contextual.
You'll speak to npcs and use different items like chest or barrel that will let you raise certain stats the same way, which is a shame because the game do present you with a lot of puzzle that are sometimes clever, but never escape the "mash everything and press every floor switch until you find a solution" problem.
Combats are turn based, you have to take an action, either walking or attacking with your whole groupe, before the enemy move and so on. Each group will only be able to attack adjacent to their position so you will have to use the landscape and diagonales to prevent from being flanked by too many monsters at once. It's also important to know that once you're engaged with a group, aka next to their square, you can't move anymore or leave the battle. Enemies will also follow you to death once you aggro them so, once a combat start there is no turning back. Which can become really frustrating at time, especially since the devs use a lot of that fact to put you in really hard, unfair embushes you can't really prevent.
The level design and placement of a lot of monster group will also be in favor of the monsters themselve rather than the player. Rarely you will have the line of sight to hit and lure monsters from afar, which makes ranged based classes or character build less powerfull than the regular melee ones. The only reason you'd max out a "perception" based character would be to detect traps and secret or eventually aggro at long distance just so you can lure enemy into a corridor, which is a shame.
So is the game any good ? Well...
I've never played a Might and magic before so i'm kind of unaware of its lore or what the former games were. The only one i almost got into was the 6th, but when i discovered it, Morrowind was released and so i was put off by the graphics.
I approached that game thinking why not try the latest one so maybe i can get into the others, but the least i can say is that the game deliver its lore in a very unwelcome fashion for a newcomer. Most of the things that is narrated refer to a lot of details out of the peninsula, giving a sense of never really concerning you in any way except for the ancient war and a few other, quest related notes scattered here and there. Same goes for the npc that will usually tells you about themselves or about the empire but, never in an engaging way. So naturally, i left the background behind, only to realise that certain quests and puzzle needed you to answer things related to the informations you'll learn everywhere.
Also, it may be because i have a Radeon but during my playthrough, i encountered a hell lot of visual glitches too like, background elements clipping and disapearing, reapiring when you face them. Some mobs were stuck in their animation making the game broken.
But somehow, i liked the game. I liked the exploration and that feeling of completion you get from going back to early levels and finding solutions to encounter you couldn't beat.
It's just really sad that the game feels like Ubisoft taking the oportunity and success of indy games like Grimmrock to grab some cash with a really low budget game. Because it feels rushed in many aspect.
In the end, i'd recommend that game if you ran out of retro crpg or if you love Might and Magic. But if you're new to the genre i'd recommend to look for something else.

All in all, I can think of no reason not to give
anything below 95/100. If I had known how much I would enjoy this game, I would have bought it myself ages ago.

Most puzzling part about this puzzle game is apparent... lack of puzzles. Or well, it's just very easy and rather short, even if you take into account the extra stuff for finding hidden stars.
But I found the journey pretty enjoyable, akin to exploring some interactive artsy picture. Nice downtempo game. It's indeed all about the journey.
In essence it's a 2D platformer where your goal is to cause a ball to roll past exit. For the most part you control the ball directly, the direction and speed it is rolling about. Some levels give you extra powers like reversing gravity or breaks that improve precision of rolling and make the ball stick to given surface better (sometimes such extra stopping power is forced to be active at all times). A few levels put the ball in role of an engine to some kind of Da-Vinci-nesque machinery. And there are also levels where you control parts of the scenery instead of the ball.
No real challenge here, but still it's a piece of sweet escapism, if short.

tl;dr: 5/10; beginning of the game was enjoyable, but the end of the game had MASSIVE amounts of issues. Would not recommend buying at full price.
EDIT: After finishing the game, I have to say, it did get a lot better. The flaws are still present, but the last Test is much better than the ones preceding.
Okay, so I have a lot to say about this game.
For starters, I really enjoyed this game. I really did. Keep that in mind. Now, for the rest:
My first problem with this game was the movement in the air. Well, the lack of it. When you were running around, having to jump from platform to platform, you really just can't do anything. Missed at the beginning just barely? Too bad! You died. You have to restart the level from the very beginning. THE VERY BEGINNING. I'll address that problem later though. The second issue lies in the same area as the first: Why put platformer-esque bits in a first person shooter? I really don't understand this. It's... not well-done, in my opinion. The movement is too choppy for this to be a part of the game.
Okay, so back to the part that I talked about earlier. Going back to the very beginning whenever you die. I really don't understand this part. The levels are long and tedious occasionally, especially starting on Test #6. #6 is entirely a platforming stage, and there aren't checkpoints. Not a single one. This stage frustrated me very, very thoroughly.  I really didn't have the urge to beat it, but I did simply because I wanted to beat the game.
Then came Test #7.
Test #7 is taking the platforming aspect, adding a terrible gun and a time limit. It was atrocious. It was, honestly, what made me quit the game.
Well, I guess you can't ask for everything.
And then the balancing issues: The guns, when you have both, are RIDICULOUSLY overpowered. You don't have ammo. You don't have to reload. Constant shots. There's a way to spam both pretty much at the same time that kills everything practically instantly.
Okay, so now that I've gotten out the rant, this game is still fundamentally enjoyable. At least for the first half or so of the game. I made it through to Test #5 and was thoroughly enjoying it. Test #6 was where the developers just tried to make it a genre it's not supposed to be. First person shooters are supposed to be shooters, not a mix between Mario and a Roblox obstacle course.
For the rating:
I'd give this game a 5 out of 10. I so, so wanted to like the whole game as much as I did the very beginning. It felt so good, but then it was just painfully annoying closer to the end. I couldn't even beat the entire game because Test #7 was just so annoying. I would not recommend spending money on this game; at least not at full price. lf it's on sale, I may recommend buying it. Basically, just not worth spending too much money on it.

I was actually having a pretty decent time playing Dead Bits, for a bit. While amateurish, the developer clearly had at least a basic grasp of game design, and there was a lot of variety in the challenges. It wasn't a straight-up FPS, it was sometimes a platformer, sometimes an FPS, and sometimes a "hit-things-with-a-bat game". It combined all of them at certain points too, which I think is where it really shined.
Unfortunately, I couldn't finish it. The game is rather difficult, in spite of the simplistic AI, mostly due to the challenges being laid out like an endurance gauntlet. Now, I like gauntles, they're fun, but the stages are pretty long and there's a distinct lack of checkpoints. After retrying the sixth stage around four times, I just couldn't be bothered to run through again. The amateurish game design and intentionally harrowing first person platforming are tolerable and even enjoyable at first, but on repeat runs they become annoyances. It's a real shame, too, because with even a semi-generous checkpoint system, I would've had a pretty good time.

TL:DR
I reccomend this game under the condition that you buy it while it's on sale.
I do enjoy the game, and find myself easily consumed by it when I actually have time to play it, but I have to agree with a lot of the other reviewers. The game feels empty and unfinished, and I really hope to see more added to it to make it feel a little more alive. I love the art, combat, and the ominous dungeon crawler vibe, and that keeps me playing the game, but I dont think I'd be willing to pay full price for perhaps 2/3 of a game.
The weapons all pretty well feel the same only really varying in speed of the swing , and I'm ok with that. I don't need stupid and crazy different animations and gimmicky variety to have fun; I'm a simple man. I do love the weapon and armor designs, and their unique effects, but they don't always seem to have that much of an effect. What I mean by that is the flaming weapons don't seem to do any more damage than say, an ice weapon might. There are weapons with knock back and increased chance to knock down an enemy, but other than that, the enchantments on weapons just make a tier 1 weapon into like... A 1.1 tier weapon.
I've found that the enemies vary nicely, you've got maybe 5 or 6 different styles of enemy, and a small amount of random others so that doesn't bother me at all, and I find that the combat, again, is satisfying and fun. You have your basic enemies that run at you, there's little robot guys, and floaty orb things, and there are unique boss-ish enemies, some enemies are a little more cautious and might try to run and hide; I don't feel that variety is an issue. I don't see a problem with what we've got with respect to varying enemies.
The sense of humour is silly and enjoyable. It's not the funniest but of comedy I've ever read, but it was a welcome and unexpected aspect of this game. There are ancient writings and script on the walls that are just silly, some potion and scroll descriptions are silly, and I think it works
The level designs and the fact that the game is procedurely generated is great! I love that! Every dungeon crawl is different, and even if the combat is sort of always the same, at least it's still fun, and my exploration needs get fulfilled! This game makes me feel incentivized to explore in hopes of finding new armour, new weapons, and of course, a new floor, but where it falls flat is that it also feels very empty. You fight, grab your crap and go. I don't even have a reccomendation for a fix on making it feel less empty.
The art style is loveable and fun and I feel really suits the mood of the game. The game is very dark and is lit primarily with magical crystals and I think it looks fantastic and different.
Another thing that brings me back to this game is that I know there will always be something new and different for me to explore, but I really do want to see more things added and fixed. I don't know if it's my set up, or the game, but I find it to randomly be unresponsive to my x or a button when trying to jump or use an item, and upon using an item, I may become stuck in place unable to move until the game realizes that I still want to play it
As it is, I'd give this game around a 6.5 to 7/10 because it's fun to play but does need a little bit of work and love to make it greater. Maybe another new character select, perhaps an assassin class and some work on making the game feel a little less empty. The art is great, and simplistic and I love that, the game play feels good as long as it doesn't freeze up on me, and I love exploring the new places every play though gives me

Stellaris is easily the most fun I've had in a strategy game since playing Civ 5 with all of the expansions.
+ Intuitive controls
+ BEAUTIFUL space scapes
+ Immersive (let me do this "one more thing" before saving for the night)
+ Thematic (enslave, watch robots rebel)
+ Minimized micromanagement
+ Incredibly detailed alien race customization. Be who you want to be
+ Space combat is strategic, not player controlled (strategy games with player controlled ships annoy me because strategy and space flight are two entirely different skill sets. I don't want to fly and manage 500 ships. Let the AI do that part)
+ Expansive and lots to discover
+ Well written events and unique procedurally generated stories that you ultimately determine and get to tell (Want to genetically modify a race of aliens so they hate their planet and move to a neighboring empire, go for it)
- Mediocre in game tutorial (YouTube is pretty much required)
- Huge learning curve
- Interface could be better
- Automation could be better

How to describe The Binding of Isaac.... Well, it's got all the right ingredients for an awesome and addicting game. The premise (loosley based upon the biblical story of Abraham and Isaac, and I do mean loosely) is fairly straightforward, but leaves the creators a lot of wiggle room to tweak and alter things as they please. The art style is a strange mix of charming and horribly gruesome that allows the game to throw in some truly dark elements without the risk of offending or disturbing any players too much. The game itself runs on the "quirky" troll engine, which ensures that if you're doing too well, the game will almost certainly knock you down a couple of notches very soon. Thankfully, the troll engine is not entirely unforgiving, and when you mix it with the procedurally generated maps and gameplay, you have an insanely addictive game with just enough challenge to frustrate you and compel you to play more at the same time. 8/10.

The Witcher 2 continues the epic story of professional monster slayer for hire; Geralt of Rivia. If you have played the first game you will probably already have an idea of what you can expect. The Witcher 2 begins a few months after the events of the first game. If you haven't played the first you may be a bit at a loss with regards to some elements in the story.
Without spoiling the story you proceed through the game searching for the 'kingslayer' and the choices you make will ultimately decide the ending of the story you get. (This ending can then be transferred to Witcher 3.) You follow one of two main story paths. You either can side with blue stripes commander Vernon Roche or with Scoitatel renegade and guerilla fighter Lor'veth.
The combat in Witcher 2 has been refined considerably from the first game. whereas the first game relied on a timing mechanic; The Witcher 2 adds in things like parry's to the mix.
I strongly recommend playing the first game prior as it will give greater context to the events that occur in this follow up. I also strongly recommend playing this game prior to Witcher 3 for the same reason. However the Witcher 3 does a decent job of providing additional information about the world and characters. You can find these in in-game character profiles as well as books you can find during your playthrough.
As you can see it took me about 40 or so hours to play through the game. But this is a game where your investment will pay off with a satisfying conclusion that you can then build on in the Witcher 3. If you are looking for a deep story driven RPG where there is no 'right' choice; and for those choices to matter? Witcher 2 is a fantastic choice.

Staple genres tend to exist because one game broke the gameplay mold, forged ahead into the wide open frontier and established itself as a new experience. After that bold experiment comes the endless iterative development - new takes on the old recipe - that tend to be defined more by how they differ from the original genre establishing title than any way else.
For the 4X game in space it has always been Master of Orion. Since it's release there have been many attempts to take the crown and yet we tend to compare all newcomers to MOO when we consider the key question "Is this alright, then, or what?"
After almost 15 hours of gameplay I can now say, confidently, that I have a new gold standard for 4x space games. Stellaris. When even a faithful rerelease of the venerable Master of Orion left me wanting a little something more, Stellaris has delivered all of my "It needs to be..."s and all of my "It would be nice if..."s and come up with a few touches beyond.
There's a lot to be said for creating a new genre, but sometimes taking an existing genre and making it completely yours is even more impressive!

Final Fantasy VII isn't my favorite in the series - that honor goes to IX - but it is without a doubt one of the best JRPGs ever made. The story is pretty deep and tackles a variety of issues such as humans polluting the planet, self-doubt and identity, and rebirth. There are times where it can be confusing but I associate this to the translation which is something they should address in the remake - a new script will be a warm welcome.
The gameplay itself is a weird mix of traditional and innovative. It's turn-based and the materia system isn't really all new if you've played Final Fantasy VI before but the way the game blends these mechanics together make for a very fun and quick-paced system.
My main gripe with the game mostly revolves around the fact that it is showing its age. I love the graphics as they are so that isn't where my problems lie; instead, I find small issues with some dated mechanics. Yuffie and Vincent are optional characters when in fact it would have benefited the game if they were integrated party members. Some of the side quests are way too obscure for some gamers to figure out, such as the Fort Condor sequences - try completing it without a guide telling you when you should keep coming back! - and the Enemy Skill list might have been improved if there was an in-game list or chart. Missable enemy skills and materia shouldn't be an issue anymore since gamers should have an opportunity to complete everything even when they're at the last save point of the game. Grinding isn't too bad but it is still there; the system in Bravely Default, where you can adjust the difficulty, random encounters, and more would have worked wonders here.
But those are all small issues. I'm sure if they made this game today none of those problems would be there... and hey, they're making a remake so let's hope they fix the problems and improve on what already works well.
If you've never played this game then you owe it to yourself to give it a try. It has a great story with amazing characters, a fun battle system, iconic music, and a dozen mini games to keep you distracted for hours. It shows its age but then again in some ways that's not a bad thing.

‘Tis here game. I like it. Steampunk subgenre on Steam is certainly not as visible as cyberpunk. Being a fan of both, I knew it was only a matter of time until a dev team shall show proper attention to detail and affection for faux Victorian Age machinery. And I was right. That time has come and Steamroll is unlike any puzzle game I played in recent memory. Anticto impressed me. This is their first Steam project.
Unity Engine shows versatility once again, provided it reaches capable hands. Steamroll is hard to pin down to the puzzle genre alone since besides physics-based puzzles (minigolf-like, if you will) it strives to be a story-driven experience and for the majority of its gameplay it succeds this. A well written plot that’s sprinkled with comic relief and constant engineering jokes. Let no one claim ever again that engineers are humorless. You roleplay as a rookie operator of a SCARABEUS Mining Mod.18 which is to put it in simplified terms, a mechanical sphere used by miners to work in Steamroll’s hazardous environments. Dev team really made an extra effort in drawing up all those diagrams detailing  the exact measurements, effects and mechanical aspects of your new job, as if you were handed over a user’s manual for your new Sphere.
It wouldn’t be called “Steampunk” without proper use of steam power, right? The game’s User Interface is straightforward but nicely simulated with a pressure dial on the left side of the screen and another dial on the right, with a steamball selector for ammo or walls and ramps. What’s that all about? Well you didn’t thought you would mine by smashing your state-of-the-art metal scarab head-on into whatever’s standing between you and the end of each level, did you? Our trusty steampunk sphere has two operating modes. One involves rolling along while in transit and the other mode, is an anchored position from which you can shift into a steamball launcher. These balls serve as the main puzzle solver since you’ll have to make clever use of them, by bouncing walls and other structures, in order to hit a switch or remove debris. Varies by situation and you are fortunate enough that these steamballs are quite versatile. They can be equipped with anything from mobile walls and ramps and even good ol’ explosives. Because nothing spells “mining” more than blowing rocks up! And other things, including yourself if you’re not careful.
Plenty of ways to fail a level since deathtraps are at every miscalculated turn. You see, the SCARABEUS being a steam-powered huge rolling sphere and all, you can’t really dash in a straight line by your heart’s desires. You will have to bounce off walls and ledges if you are to move from point A to B. Takes some time getting used to this, but I call it part of the experience. The game is never unforgivingly difficult and you always have a prediction line, clearly estimating the path of your launched steamballs. As with most video games, the key to success is a mix of patience and quick reflexes perhaps if you’re into speedruns. I like to take my sweet time and explore the surroundings, collecting screenshots and all that jazz. You know, the regular stuff.
Steamroll isn’t overpriced at all, given the state in which it presents itself along with the inclusion of both Cards and “Cheevos”. In fact, it was bundled recently and it shall be found in such offers in the future as well. Quality titles such as Steamroll tend to appear every now and then in well-priced deals, just to draw attention to it while you neglect the run-of-the-mill titles bundled along. Surprisingly few cons to this title. I had to be nitpicky just to choose two weak points. Only 18 (relatively short, once you get the hang of it) levels so far. More would really be welcome, Anticto. Full Steam Ahead!

Little Inferno is a game about setting fire to different objects. That's all there is to it...Except it's not. Little Inferno is indeed a game about setting fire to things but a game that simplistic also pulls of something unique. This game is very emotional. It makes you happy and joyful that you have fun and nobody gets hurt, it makes you feel guilty when some objects cry and scream, it makes you sad along the way of the story and most of all it makes you question what you're doing with your life. IF YOU READ ON CERTAIN PARTS OF LITTLE INFERNO MAY BE SPOILED. SPOILER ALERT. Throughout Little Inferno I've had a blast. This game is a gem. A bit rough around the edges, but a beautiful treasure to adore. Let me get in on it a bit deeper, okay?
First off, I love the concept. After the "Hoodwinked" movie, is this the best attempt to retell the story of Little Red Riding Hood. In a completely new way, I might add. Instead of being a little girl, who gets swallowed whole by a big bad wolf, you're a young woman (quite an attractive one, I'd say) out for revenge on BB Woolfe. Clever, right?
Then, the visuals. This game has a bit of a grimy, yet magical fairytale like look to it. The cold of winter makes the whole scene even darker and just.. plain cold... BB Woolfe is a human, but man, does he look awesome! They really made him a man who represents a wolf, with the facial hair and the fur coat. Wonderful! The red of Red's hood sticks out pretty nicely against the environment. You're clearly the protaganist of this story, which is not a fairytale. After all, there is nothing fair about it.
Then there is the combat. It is kinda choppy (not just because you use an axe as your primary weapon). To me, it all boiled down to tapping the attack buttons multiple times to hit hard and swift, with minimum damage to myself. It works, kinda, but even the smallest of rats manage to sneak in a hit before I can kill them. That's a slight oversight, but really all I can complain about.
The characters are lovely. Well, there are only four, not counting the robotic soldiers. Red is clever, cunning and pretty witty. She can make lovely snide comments, even to the game designers at some point. I really loved that :)
Woolfe is dark. You can tell he is a man of power who does everything to stay in control. You don't get to see him often, but you can just feel his prescense everywhere.
Granny is.. well.. granny. She is the only family Red has left and is not the fragile old lady the books make her out to be. She is pretty strong, almost capable of holding her own in these troubling times.
And there is the Pied Piper. He is just a coward that serves as a mid-way boss... He has a backstory, of luring in little girls and such, but I think he could've been expended upon better.
Anyway, if you're in doubt of buying this game, or not, just do it. The game does end in a cliffhanger (SPOILER) and there probably won't be a second game any time soon, since the company who made it, sadly, had to file bankrupcy...

If you don't care about the steam achievement, you can play through the normal enemies on casual and temporarily switch to higher difficulties for the bosses. I'd recommend a look if you like metroidvanias and are okay with the setting.

So after several hours of playing abit of VB! I feel its time to review it.
My initial thoughts was this game is going to be OK, but i was actually quite impressed once i got in the swing of things.
It doesnt have spectacular graphics but it does have a modern retro feel to it if that makes sense, which is good! its straight forward and simple to understand, no silly controls just the basics which is all you need, you can actually play with 1 hand if ever you feel like doing that lol.
They do say its best played with a controller but myself prefer k/b mouse, it just feels more responsive to me, but you do have alot more control with a controller so its really what you feel comfortable with.
The gameplay itself, well its like a retro dogfighting space shooter thats super fast paced, it offers a nice selection of game modes such as survival where you fight waves of different types of enemies and last as long as you can, to challenge mode where you need to hit the checkpoints within the time limit, then theres the arcade mode which is more like your story mode where you have to follow a mission, which is actually my favourite mode, theres also an online mode which im yet to try out but im sure i will.
(Be aware some modes not mentioned are still locked and are not currently playable right now)
The ships are not bad, a small variety to choose from and unlock through gaining points, they all have there own specs to suit your style but no customisation im afraid, that would be a cool feature to add tho.
The sound fx and soundtrack are pretty cool too and fits nicely with the games style, i did find the music abit glitchy at times or out of sync but not enough to annoy or put you off the game.
So overall I will say its not for the hardcore gamer but one of those games youl go back to every now and again, and if your an achievement hunter this will test your skills abit, and as im the type that gets frustrated quite easily i didnt find playing this that bad at all, infact i dont recall raging to this once so far, its actually quite relaxing to play.
Im not gonna rate it but i will say its worth buying for those casual days! So go get it and enjoy! i did!

One of the best action plateformers I played to date.
Responsive gameplay, relatively few moves, but most of them requiring you to think before pressing buttons in order to be able to hit enemies without taking damage yourself.
The graphics are really nice, with good animations. The only detail that might bother some people is the use of animal people, because it seems that a lot of people forgot that it was a big thing in the 90's kid programs we were watching, and somehow assimilate it to dirty pornography (no clue why personally).
On the sound department, the music is great, and the voice acting correct, if a bit "anime" style (I happen to like it).
Difficulty-wise, it should hit home for most people, the easier modes being doable without too much skill required, for those that want the story, or to familiarize themselves with the controls.
The harder difficulties are not your basic "more HP, hit harder", the enemies will more actively try to hit you, and the fact that most screen feature quite a few enemies in groups, it makes the whole thing way more challenging.
The only passable part about this is the last boss, that is way too easy, compared to the rest of the game.
The controls are responsive, and it is possible to completely play with either a gamepad or the keyboard + mouse combo, and the two control schemes were done differently, so that each takes full advantage of the strengths it offers.
All in all, a great game for anyone having even a passing interest in the action plateform.
To top it off, the whole game was made and ported by a single person, with only the music and the voice acting not being from him, which should put to shame every single one of the shoddy ports that we get.

Overall this is an enjoyable puzzle game with an interesting steampunk theme. If you're a fan of physics based puzzle games then this is well worth a look, particuarly if you enjoy the steampunk theme.
The gameplay has an interesting mix of turret based "pinball" shooting combined with a movement mechanic (I'd call it light platforming without jumping if that makes sense). While the sections focused on movement are not the most enjoyable parts of the games they are integrated into the puzzles in a manner that's more integrated into the puzzle than the simple "clear a path to the exit" that you get in a lot of puzzle games.
My primary complaint with this is probably the length. I was able to complete the entire game (including achievements) in just 7 hours the first time through. I'm not opposed to short games in general but the problem with short puzzle games  (including steamroll) is that a short game means that you don't really get a chance to build up a repetoire of tactics that you can use in future puzzles. That's particuarly noticeable here, each level feels completly different and for the most part strategys and tactics that work on one have very little impact on another.
Now saying "each level feels different" does sound like an odd complaint but for a puzzle game I like it when later levels build upon skills and tactics that have been taught and used in earlier levels because it generally means that the puzzles have a greater level of depth to them. Steamroll doesn't really have that, each level and to some degree even each turret spot has a single, relatively unique solution to it that probably won't come up again.
Overall though this is still a solid game. The gameplay is fun, the plot is decent and the artwork is solid.

Preordered game and have been playing paradox titles since EU2.
The game isn't bad, but unfortunately there is no "maybe" button on steam so..
It has a promising structure, but at present it's pretty shallow and boring.
- Diplomacy is pretty bad: barebones options, AI doesn't react to deals they should accept with their eyes closed. War system is terrible (no cb to declare; autosurrender..don't even gert me started)
- AI is very weak. Acts passively, never really a challenge. Allied AI will blob and follow your main fleet regardless of actual strategic situation.
- Planet development is basic at best (seen better systems in 10 year old games), espionage non existent, trade (trade routes-commerce) is absent.
- Battles are very underwhelming. It's a paradox game I know, but really: weapons come with different ranges, but all battles invariably end up in a chaotic melee. No orders, no behaviour, just blob and pray. Very weak. Land battles were better in Moo2, a 20 year old game.
- The resource gathering and starbase construction is very similar to galciv, it's ok but it gets repetitive. And it's not original.
- Paradox has a strong tradition of "historical" games (real world-historic events). Without this context, I feel this game looses a LOT of appeal and originality.
I mean this would be an ok game in its present state if it wasn't by Paradox.
If I think that this game has VIctoria 2 as a mommy and CK2 as daddy, it's really a letdown and it doesn't live up to the hype.
Of course, there will be (many) DLCs. I personally dislike this marketing strategy (DLC spam) and I think in the long run it will be more negative than positive for gaming in general.
TL;DR: would be ok if I wasn't expecting Victoria-Hoi-Ck2 in SPACE. As it is, it's a step back.

Stellaris is easily the most fun I've had in a strategy game since playing Civ 5 with all of the expansions.

+ BEAUTIFUL space scapes
+ Immersive (let me do this "one more thing" before saving for the night)

+ Minimized micromanagement
+ Incredibly detailed alien race customization. Be who you want to be
+ Space combat is strategic, not player controlled (strategy games with player controlled ships annoy me because strategy and space flight are two entirely different skill sets. I don't want to fly and manage 500 ships. Let the AI do that part)
+ Expansive and lots to discover
+ Well written events and unique procedurally generated stories that you ultimately determine and get to tell (Want to genetically modify a race of aliens so they hate their planet and move to a neighboring empire, go for it)
- Mediocre in game tutorial (YouTube is pretty much required)
- Huge learning curve
- Interface could be better
- Automation could be better

Steamroll is a unique puzzle game with echoes of Marble Madness and various contraption type strategy games. The game has a steampunk theme which ties in nicely with the mechanics of the entire experience. Above is a short video of gameplay, and below are my initial thoughts on the game and purchasing recommendations.
was provided a preview copy of Steamroll by Antico and for that we thank them.
There is a sense of humor to this game that had me laughing within ten minutes of rolling my ball around. I blew up an entire mineshaft and the operator of my ball reacted appropriately, which I found hilarious and genuine. The gameplay reminds me of a childhood classic in Marble Madness with a slight twist. There are a few hiccups with audio and video that I found, but beyond that this is a solid title with real potential for replay especially if it becomes steam workshop capable after release.
I had to stop and really consider a couple of the puzzles and as you can see in the video, I make mistakes like blocking a follow up shot with a piece of my solution. I found that aspect to be satisfying, and the puzzle completions felt like an accomplishment. There are new mechanics added in as you progress and they really are unique. You can change your steamball to be a wall or bomb early on, and those options in conjunction with one another make up your potential solutions.
The only downside I could find is there are a few graphic and audio stutters here and there, and certain aspects need some finishing touches. That is to be expected from an early access game so I can't see any reason not to pick this one up if you enjoy puzzle games, or were ever a fan of the old Nintendo game "Marble Madness". I personally enjoy this type of game mechanic and motif so this once hit a home run for me.

At one time I thought GC3 might be able to offer a bit of competition to them.  I no longer do.  Therefore it might be better if instead of paying US$50 for this to wait for one of the other games to come out.  Though maybe just keep an eye on GC3 for the standalone expansion due for 2017.  Maybe it can bring the magic back to the franchise.

Staple genres tend to exist because one game broke the gameplay mold, forged ahead into the wide open frontier and established itself as a new experience. After that bold experiment comes the endless iterative development - new takes on the old recipe - that tend to be defined more by how they differ from the original genre establishing title than any way else.
For the 4X game in space it has always been Master of Orion. Since it's release there have been many attempts to take the crown and yet we tend to compare all newcomers to MOO when we consider the key question "Is this alright, then, or what?"
After almost 15 hours of gameplay I can now say, confidently, that I have a new gold standard for 4x space games. Stellaris. When even a faithful rerelease of the venerable Master of Orion left me wanting a little something more, Stellaris has delivered all of my "It needs to be..."s and all of my "It would be nice if..."s and come up with a few touches beyond.
There's a lot to be said for creating a new genre, but sometimes taking an existing genre and making it completely yours is even more impressive!

I was set on not recommending this during my first few hours of gameplay. It didn't feel like a bad game, but also didn't feel like a good one either. After Legend of Grimrock it just felt so much more shallow and silly and ... just.. not as good.
I still don't think it can compare to Legend of Grimrock, but after having put many more hours into it - it grew on me enough to give it a good review.
Why is it not as good? Well, the story is not as enticing, the puzzles are less interesting, the upgrades are less exciting, too much clutter loot, and overall not as well-designed. It's designed well enough, but there are plenty of large areas that are there just to waste your time moving through them, while they actually bring no benefit to the game (no monsters to fight, no secrets to find).
But despite all that the game still offers plenty of enjoyment. Combat system is turn based, so you have time to control every character without rushing.
Leveling up is rewarding, it is possible to make a badass character who can take regular-enemy life bars out in 3-4 hits.
There are plenty of spells to cast, weapons to use, armors to put on.
There are rings, amulets, potions, buffs, debuffs.
Level up system is decent, with both attribute and skill increases.
Not every class/race has access to the same tiers of skills, but a lot of them have access to most skills in general, which is nice. For example a mage may not start with a dodge or crossbow skill or be able to advance to a grandmaster level of those, but he can still get to an Expert level.
Towns are pretty large with many NPCs, (if you're into that. I'm not, but i appreciate the effort developers put into this.)
All in all it's not an amazing game, but it still deserves a positive review because it is well made, and it is actually kind of fun (the battles anyway. i'm all about the battles.) And after you've played through Legend of Grimrock three times and unlocked all the achievements and just don't want to play it anymore but still want something like it - Might and Magic X one is an acceptable substitute.
This game is VERY Early access.  This game is headed in the right direction, and will definitely be a great game.

One of the best action plateformers I played to date.
Responsive gameplay, relatively few moves, but most of them requiring you to think before pressing buttons in order to be able to hit enemies without taking damage yourself.
The graphics are really nice, with good animations. The only detail that might bother some people is the use of animal people, because it seems that a lot of people forgot that it was a big thing in the 90's kid programs we were watching, and somehow assimilate it to dirty pornography (no clue why personally).
On the sound department, the music is great, and the voice acting correct, if a bit "anime" style (I happen to like it).
Difficulty-wise, it should hit home for most people, the easier modes being doable without too much skill required, for those that want the story, or to familiarize themselves with the controls.
The harder difficulties are not your basic "more HP, hit harder", the enemies will more actively try to hit you, and the fact that most screen feature quite a few enemies in groups, it makes the whole thing way more challenging.
The only passable part about this is the last boss, that is way too easy, compared to the rest of the game.
The controls are responsive, and it is possible to completely play with either a gamepad or the keyboard + mouse combo, and the two control schemes were done differently, so that each takes full advantage of the strengths it offers.
All in all, a great game for anyone having even a passing interest in the action plateform.
To top it off, the whole game was made and ported by a single person, with only the music and the voice acting not being from him, which should put to shame every single one of the shoddy ports that we get.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a fantastic mix of action adventure and Metroidvania with beautiful graphics, a good story and okay voice-acting. Also fun to play.
+ Beautiful character, level and combat art; organic looks
+ Okay voice-acting
+ Good story
+ Metroidvania
+ Fading out overlay where obfuscating avatar except for really important stuff
0 Dynamic zoom sometimes make battle harder than necessary
- No Inn (100% hp)
- Scenes need multi-skips because animation cannot be skipped
- No restart for challenges!
- Digital analogue stick, either no movement or full speed
- Auto-equipping food to quick-use slot; vanishing items/loot; automatic item-consumption
- Slipping of edges after jumps
Hint: There is are two decision-based achievements. In order to get them manually save before entering  Ivydale Glen or on the first save point you encounter there.
I was immediately enamoured with the game when only a minute or so into the gameplay breaking a wall gave me an insight into the developers humour
. When seeing others play the game I was already impressed with the game's design but doubted gameplay would be tight and fun. Fortunately my doubts proved baseless.
Controls are basically very tight and fluid except for one major flaw and a few more or less seldom occurring situations. Overall playing with a controller is pretty much the same as playing with keyboard and mouse, i.e. one didn't feel better than the other.
The major controls thing is that movement speed is controlled digitally as opposed to analogue, i.e. when using a controller and moving with the analogue stick the avatar is either not moving or moving full speed (which is also not very fast).
When platforming you need to stand for some time on a platform in order to be able to jump from it, i.e. having one platform above another and to its side you cannot swiftly jump from the lower platform to the close edge of the higher platform and, changing direction, jump again right away - that will always be considered a drop.
Blocking is an essential part of combat and you are told you need to face the enemy but it's not always possible to change the character's direction in time. Furthermore, it seems the enemy also has to face you. There are some bigger enemies that may be distracted and attack away from you thus backhanding you without the chance to block.
The character will gain a dash ability which allows for quick evasive manoeuvres. Unfortunately, this cannot effectively be used to pursue an enemy which drew back since immediately following with an attack will have the avatar automatically attack in the direction opposing the dash direction as opposed to attacking in the direction the player indicates with the analogue stick.
A few times battle was made harder than necessary when graphical foreground elements obfuscated avatar and enemies or when the dynamic zoom goes in so far that the tells for incoming attacks cannot be seen, the latter being a problem with the final boss.
I demand total control over use of items so I feel somewhat angry at the game for effectively not letting me disable consumables. You can deselect the current consumable but as soon as you collect another it will automatically be assigned to the quick-use slot. Additionally, the game automatically uses Revival Stones when dying and automatically gives away crafting supplies when that can advance a current quest. In theory, I'd like to save up Revival Stones for boss fights but since the game has some enemies being able to one-shot you the stones are often wasted on underlings. With enemies like that I deemed consumables useless and never healed except for testing at the beginning of the game, the occasional bump of controller against my desk and save points that heal up to a certain percentage of total HP (depending on your difficulty level). Later on, you will receive equipment with regenerative attributes. The game indicates when it deems the avatar close to death which is basically nice but irritating over longer periods, read the whole beginning of the games. That's why I think the threshold for "is dying" should always be lower than what the save points heal you to.
I feel like changing regions in the game should fill up your HP or there should be some kind of Inn that lets you sleep and heal up.
I like games that let you skip sequences. This game  has that to a degree. You can skip dialogue but only dialogue. You still have to wait through any intro, outro or intermediate animation. This also may require you to skip more than one dialogue per sequence. When dying in quick succession I felt like the death animation was sort of celebrated too much and I wanted to be able to just skip to loading.
Somewhat related, the challenges could use a reset button bringing you back to the start of the challenge for when you know you can't achieve the wanted ranking in the current run.
Some more minor bickering:
Sometimes loot gets stuck inside walls even rewards from destroying static objects.
I don't see a reason loot should ever vanish as long as you don't leave the "room", i.e. the area shown as one location in the minimap. Here, loot is gone after something like 10 or 15 seconds.
I think it adds to the flow of the game that loot jumps around a bit. Then again, I was aggravated by loot often jumping over my head. And why doesn't Dust Storm simply collect loot instead of randomly flipping it around?
The player cannot leave a room if enemies are close, that's okay. However it's not okay that enemies can leave the players attack range by leaving the edge of the room.
Why would you have more than one blueprint of anything or be able to sell more than one? It seems blueprints are acting as high-value loot which doesn't really compute.
Some more praise:
If for some reason the avatar is where HUD elements go the HUD becomes see-through except for essential information like low HP - very well done.
Again, design feels like it has received some love. Regions have different designs and apart from where you expect otherwise, i.e. with built-up structures, the levels look very organic, i.e. they do not feel lazily pieced together from some palette. And there are atmospheric elements that show effort over simply making a playable game, e.g. wild life or footsteps in the snow.
The Ugly pendant is a really nice fix. It allows to get that one achievement even in late game. Thanks for that.
Dust: An Elysian Tail is one more very easily recommendable game, even if you are already somewhat tired of platformers.
