I have to admit this review is viewed through Distant Worlds colored glasses and I've only played 10 hours of Stellaris at time of writing. Currently Stellaris is a very buggy and very thin Distant Worlds clone with multiplayer capabilities.  Granted - to date Distant Worlds has had 7 years of updates and expansions, but so many mechanics are so similar and my love of Distant Worlds so emphatic it's difficult not to compare them.
The multiplayer certainly adds to the fun if you have friends willing to play 20+ hours with you.  Of course it takes an extra hour to figure out how to get them to join your lobby since that's really buggy - though patch notes suggest that was addressed today (I haven't had a chance to test).  I've only played with one friend, in discord, with a predetermined alliance (after communicating where we were on the galaxy map and prioritizing researching each other's race) and that's been fantastic.
Stellaris has some odd ideas about micromanagement and automation.  You can only manually manage 5 worlds until the game mechanics lower the efficiency of your worlds and you are forced to create sectors for automation.  Sectors just pump out resources, skewed to your desires, and take the planets off your outliner making it difficult to select them.  Though I find it really strange you can't automate your research ships for exploration or put your fleets on a patrol path.
Domination and Conquest are currently the only victory conditions.  I hope diplomacy / economic / research / race specific conditions follow fairly soon.
My experience with war spoils has been pretty poor.  When initiating a war from an alliance you get to request how spoils are divided between the members of your alliance.  Through the course of winning a war the AI constantly spams you with peace agreements that only give resources to the alliance member who initiated the war vote.
Distant Worlds is by and far my favorite space 4x game and Stellaris really scratches that same itch while providing multiplayer capabilities.  I've take the chance to introduce a friend to the genre and the multiplayer has made that really fun.  If you're planning to play Stellaris solo - just play Distant Worlds until Stellaris has a couple expansions or really stellar workshop content.  Admittedly I'm not too familiar with Paradox's other titles to know how fast the necessary content will become available.

What I like:
- It has a nice difficulty level.
- Nostalgia successfully evoked for people who played classics such as Lands of Lore or Eye of the Beholder.
- Fights and character builds require some strategy.
- You can make notes on the ingame map. For example, you can write there "spells" next to a shop where you can do that, or "axe" at a spot where you can level up a characters axe skill.
- Some replayability possible. The puzzles and enemies will be the same, but you can build a different party of different classes and thus attempt to beat the game with a different setup, using the higher of the two available difficulty modes.
- Some of the puzzles and riddles are fun.
What I dislike:
- Ubisoft. That means you have to deal with Ubisofts Uplay nonsense, bad support, DRM and whatnot.
- The game is sometimes a bit sparse in matters of telling you where to do what. Without researching sometimes on the internet where to do what, you might get frustrated.
- I had one annoying bug so far.
- Sometimes, every couple of hours, it crashes. Since it saves automatically ever now and then and has a quicksave option, this is bearable though.
- The graphics are mixed. They're not good, but some models and parts of the dungeons look nice. Other parts, especially outdoor textures, look very bad if you get closed.
Neutral:
- Some of the game mechanics make sense gameplaywise but are highly illogical. For example, the buffs on your party (like one that protects you from damage) last a certain number of turns (during combat) or moves. But you can, for example, rest for 8 hours to regenerate your party, and those buffs are all still up. Sometimes you can also rest for 8 hours before a boss fight, and the boss will just wait until you're done.
- In some of those old RPGs I liked that the positioning of the party mattered (melee fighters in the front, ranged fighters and spell casters in the back). In this game, the positioning is irrelevant.
- The difficulty is not increasing in an entirely linear way. You will encounter enemies you can't beat at that point. On the other hand, the game saves automatically all the time, so you just reload and ignore that part for the time being.
So, all in all, if you like those retro-RPGs, this one is ok. It's not great, but is entertaining enough. 25 Euro is a bit expensive in my opinion, but for 15 Euro or less, like during a Steam Sale, I can easily recommend it, as far as you don't buy it randomly but realized that you get a retro style RPG instead of a new Witcher or Elder Scrolls. Well, and you have to be aware that there are still a couple of bugs in the game.

Woolfe: The Red Hood Diaries feels confused. It wants to reimagine the Red Riding Hood fairy tale into a darker, Victorian gothic tale (bearing no small resemblance to the similar idea applied to Alice: Madness Returns) but it doesn’t know how. Ideas bubble around on the surface but always seem to pop before they’ve been explored, and looking deeper only exposes a bigger jumble of incompatible objectives that refuse to settle down as they pull the game in different directions. Pull hard enough, and pretty soon it’s all collapsed at your feet.
Take for instance Woolfe’s world. Grime drips off the walls, buildings cast ominous shadows as they attempt to pierce the skyline; rats bite at your feet as you hide from the giant mechanical toy soldiers patrolling the streets, as the city’s drudge trickles into the river. It’s all wonderfully moody and full of character, something Woolfe lacks in every other area but seemed to at least nail in its setting and tone.
But then it hesitates and starts questioning itself. Soon the dim streets of the city are replaced with surreal canyons and floating pathways. No justification is given as to why or how the world has suddenly changed so drastically, it’s simply presented to you as if its inclusion in the game is context enough. It was at this point about halfway through the game that everything began to fall apart around me. The world lost its personality and consistency, and without that to hold onto I began to drift in and out of various states of disappointment, no longer able to deny the problems that had been present from the start.
By forcing me out of the one thing I had started to love, I was left looking at a shell of a game that had taken off its masked and didn’t know where to go from here. The clunky platforming took on new levels of annoyance as I slipped off of ledges or improperly judged a distance as the fixed camera panned away. Combat continued to be dull and flimsy, lacking a sense of impact and killing me at the drop of a hat, as if the numerous bottomless pits and one hit kills throughout the levels weren’t enough.
And finally I was confronted with Red herself. At first, like her city, she felt cold and calculating. Her sense of motivation wasn’t extensively explained, but her determination provided enough of an explanation. She was a simple character, but one that felt inseparable to her game, and her small bits of dialogue helped sell the idea that this was someone with a history and a goal, not just a model of a familiar protagonist.
The more she said though, the harder I was able to buy into the illusion. Her comments began to unsuccessfully break the fourth wall, crack jokes about things that wouldn’t exist in this world, and continue to fail to stick with the game’s attempts to rhyme each line. The oddly written verses are maybe the most distracting thing out of the lot, dropping in and out of rhyme at random, making me question if it was even intentional half the time.
Woolfe doesn’t feel like a game that suffers from an undeveloped vision, it’s one that started with a great idea but had no understanding of how to bring it into existence. That makes it an even bigger disappointment though because I feel that it could be great, if only developer Grin had had more time, or a bigger budget, or more experience. There’s a game somewhere in here that I’m dying to experience, and maybe there’s still some hope that it will appear in part two, but as of now it’s all bark and no bite.

Seeing that quite some of the bad reviews missed some central points, I kinda felt the need to drop one myself! Sorry ´bout that.
Actually, the mere fact that, while having lots of arguably good "big" games, I keep coming back to this one should say it all.
The "Rogue-like"-Tag on a game is tantalizing to me. And the more down-to-the-core-Rogue-like it is, the more I like the game. Only regrettable feature would be ASCII-graphics ;)
And these games tend to be hard. Very hard. The kind of hard that the majority of younger people can´t cope with, maybe? The Generation WoW: clicky, blingy , levelup..! I don´t know. I know, that back as a kid in the former GDR, I "played" Bards Tale on a C64, hundreds of hours, without even knowing what an RPG is. No Internet, Nobody to ask...
I believe that this is the reason for the success of, say, Dark Souls. It´s so hard, that winning something is actually rewarding again! And that feels good.
And I like Rogue´s Tale! You have to know that it´s hard and random. But that also means the very next item can be that difference-making blessed Ring of Something... You do die, and sometimes cheaper by the Dozen, but hey, it´s hard! But over time, you learn various ways of shaping chances in your favour. If you play it like an generic japanese RPG, then you are bound to fail early and often. It´s a turn-based game, every turn you can make the best decision based on stats and inventory. Most of my (hundreds of) deaths were avoidable in hindsight.
In short, if you like the concept of rogue-likes, maybe played NetHack and the like, or if you like challenging games, then this one´s well worth a try.
For people who enjoy games that splash you with levelup from the start, you might find this game, ahm, ...unrewarding, which is great irony in itself!

NAH-AH mothafacka. Those who think it's 'easy' obviously haven't played it.  It's not repetitive in any way, which I value in an indie/rogue-like games and it's incredibly satisfying to beat the game. Especially for the very first time. Just. Trust me.
There is just so much in this game, secrets, treasures, that it's a bit over-whelming. It's like: you think you know a lot about the game (leave alone 'know everything about the game'), but I can almost guarantee that you don't.
Oh and it's based mostly around religious stuff and God and Satan and a bit more Satan. Did I mention there's a lot of satanic  things? And Devil + Satan <3
All in all, it's one of the funniest, weirdest rogue-like games I have ever played, hands down.
Definitely worth every hour I have poured into it.
Can't wait what 'Binding of Isaac: Rebirth' has to offer with the whole Co-Op function added to it :3
Lastly: There are rare golden piles of crap in the game. Just how awesome is that??!

NightSky is an interesting physics based puzzle platformer. You control which you can move left and right, and depending on the situtation you have certain powers such as the ability to go fast or invert gravity. These powers make for some interesting puzzles.
I never found myself stuck for more than a couple of minutes at a time in the game because most of the puzzles were logical (as logical as a physics platformer can get).
Later on in the game, there's certain parts where you'll control a vechile, these add some variety, but very rarley were they interesting enough.
The game has an interesting graphic style and soundtrack that create a great atmospheric mood.
As a whole, I enjoyed NightSky but it's hard to recommend it for more than 3 or so dollars.

tl;dr: Get one of the games listed below instead, unless you know what you do when you buy a "real Rogue" game - endless frustration.
Positive:
This game is for hardcore gamers, those who like getting their teeth pulled without anesthetics, because it is badass. :)
Still, if you want to have fun playing games, I suggest to play any of these games instead - from casual to more hardcore:
Why do I suggest these games, instead of Rogue's Tale? Any of these games will give you a feeling that you survived the last encounter (or did not) because of choices you made. In Rogue's Tale you realize each time something happens that you won or lost because of the random number generator - your decisions do not matter. Toss a coin instead - on tails you lose.
It felt to me like playing an old buggy version of Rogue where the end boss can spawn one step from you when you enter the dungeon. Monsters, loot and interactable objects seem to be generated completely randomly. You do not survive or die because you made the right decisions, you do so because you had a lucky or unlucky roll. As Rogue's Tale's environment is mostly open areas (not narrow tunnels or small interconnected rooms), you can rarely use the environment to your advantage.
Using other monsters to your advantage is sometimes possible. Creatures who are usually docile may attack your opponent if you lead him to them. Unfortunately some of your opponents will be of the invincible kind, so that they decimate the complete level, including you, without losing one hitpoint.
This is how my playthrough for the first ten adventurers went:
In my eyes, the game's major flaw is that it is Rogue. You will die because of the flip of a coin, after a few seconds or minutes.

The Binding of Isaac,
I picked up this game in a sale and I regret not getting it sooner. Considering even at full price it's own a few bucks. The best way I think I can explain the game is that it's a Rogue-Lite. In that it's got Rogue-Like elements but isn't anything like the game Rogue. The game consists of exploring different levels. When you die you have to start again and the levels are always randomised as well as the items you'll pick up along the way, so you'll always have a reason to go back and keep playing. The game is always changing.
You walk around using the WASD keys and shoot your tears (which are projectiles that do damage) using the Arrow Keys. It's very challenging but is just so much fun. I've played 32 hours of it so far and I'm loving it. Just want to keep going back.

Game was updated 27/01/2016. I'm using this space to update my review based on those changes. Original review is down below.
They have implemented WASD controls and have now made wall jumping a tad easier. This makes playing the game more comfortable and with the improvements to wall jumping less frustrating.
Fixed the music abruptly stopping after death. You can now finally hear the chill music track and I dig it.

Original review:
Pros:
Price is on point - For such a simple game I feel they nailed the price point perfectly. If you enjoy challenging platformers, I feel you can get your £0.79 worth.
It's challenging - Not a surprise there! If you're like me and like a quick challenge there's something in here for you.
Simplicity - You're a square avoiding death, it doesn't over complicate things, it knows what it is and sticks to it.
25 levels - 25 doesn't seem like a lot but having spent an hour on just 6 levels I feel there's easily enough content.
Devs listen - They're very open to feedback and have proven to change the game based on said feedback. Fantastic to see!
Cons:
(Fixed as of 27/01/2016) - 1 Music track - Swiftly fails hard on the music front. I would like to say I've heard the whole track however when you die (And you will die a lot) the music instantly stops and starts from the beginning. Within just 9 minutes I hate to mute the game entirely and put on my own music! Extremely frustrating to listen to.
(Improved as of 27/01/2016) - Controls - For the most part the controls are fine, so why is this in the cons section? Wall jumping. Yup. Wall jumping. Wall jumping is the most infuriating part of this game, it's not challenging, it's not fun, it's a wrestle with the controls and it sucks!
Improvements:
(Fixed as of 27/01/2016) - Don't restart music upon death, let that little sucker continue playing! The addition of 2 or 3 more music tracks would be extremely welcome.
(Improved as of 27/01/2016) - Re-work wall jumping! I can't even put down in words how frustrating it is to mash up & left then quickly let go to mash up and right in the hopes it's timed correctly to achieve a wall jump. Make is so your square can stick to the walls for easier jumping or rework the whole wall jumping together!
Achievements don't pop at the end of levels - They only pop once you go back to the menu.
(Implemented as of 27/01/2016) - Add a level notification, I had no idea I had completed 5 levels till I exited to the menu. Once the player has moved to a new level and quick flash of level [number] would be welcomed.
Simple leaderboads - Just to add a tiny bit of competitiveness to the game. Add a simple leaderboard of the top 10 fastest finishes. It's simple and could spur somebody on to beat that No.1 - adding a small amount of replay-ability.
Conlusion:
If you like quick, fun, challening levels I see no reason why you shouldn't pick this up. The game needs improvements there's no doubt about that. However, what we have now is still an enjoyable game despite some flaws. Overall I give Swiftly 6/10.
Two words: Checkpoints Needed

This game is amazing, and highly recommended for people who enjoy 4x or grand strategy games such as Civ V or Europa Universalis IV. In this game you take control of a civilization, each with its own strenths and weaknesses, and explore the universe, colonize worlds, and conquer your enemies. The game has some unique strengths compared to something like Civ V, in that all of the civs have their own unique tech tree with all sorts of unique flavor for the civ you are playing as. Also unique to the game are frequent moral decisions you have to make, like the planet you just colonized has plants with psychoactive properties that are dangerous but enhance the intelligence of the user. Do you ban them for the safety of your citizens or do you embrace them and gain a research bonus?
Another thing I like compard to Civ is that the games seem to have more of a dynamic rise and fall of empires dynamic, where if a civ is losing, they will sometimes surrender their planets to a civ they were allied with. This civ may have been a minor player, but they are now elevated to great power status. There are interesting little things like that that happen sometimes.
The game is outstanding, and really has infinite replay value. Stardock has done a great job of supporting the game so far, and has indicated that they have plans to refine and expand the game for years to come. ( I saw a post where the lead developer talked about having plans all the way until 2019!). If you are remotely a fan of strategy games, this game is well worth the purchase.

Maddening, frustrating, and hard to put down, Rogue's Tale is a punishing roguelike in every sense of the word.
"Unfair" might get thrown around. It might feel like it is, at first, when you basically start with nothing but a stick. But as you slowly (very slowly) gain progression: a potion here, a starting piece of armor here, and you start to learn the extreme subtleties of the game, it begins to really shine.
I never beat the game. I only even challenged the final boss once (and wasn't even remotely prepared). I haven't played it in months, but I still think about it. I think about runs I got cocky in, thinking I was overpowered, and paid for the sin of it. I think about one run where I started and died within 2 steps from a boulder. I think about runs where... so many runs. So many deaths.
I understand the mixed reviews. This is a game you really have to play a lot (and I mean a lot) to get why it's actually pretty good.
This game pulls no punches. Be prepared for that.

I have about 30 hours in now and have restarted a couple times.  As such, I have really only experienced the exploration and early expansion phase of the game.  Yep I play slow and enjoy the ride.  But so far so great!
As opposed to commenting on every little bit here, I think the key element that has really caught my attention is the feeling that I really am a fledgling race enountering and dealing with all the things a fledgling race exapanding out to the stars might experience.  I play pretty much every 4x space genre game out there and Stellaris has provided a different feel to be sure.  It has been quite immersive for me as I encounter and investigate all the different 'stuff' you run into whilst trying deal with events, new races, pirates, etc...
This really has kind of a unique feel so far.  Instead of just rushing colony ships and colonizing so you can build more colony ships, colonize more, rinse repeat, there are many things that need your attention.  Paying attention to your resources, prioritizing spends, and dealing effectively with the many things that 'popup' can really make a big difference in terms of empire growth.  While still important of course, its not just about colony spam and I like that.
I read many of the pundits saying Phase 1 fantastic, Phase 2 slows down and feels grindy, and the Phase 3 again looks great by ramping up the action with end game events.  So I dunno about Phase 2, but what I have experienced so far is great and I think Paradox has scored pretty well for the opening offering of a game that is really fun now, and has incredible potential for the future.

26 hours. Maybe I've rushed through it a little. I've skipped plenty of side quests. I
skip side quests, not even when you need to probe-mine the entire galaxy to outfit Normandy mk2, but this...was something else. It failed to engage. And the worst part of it is, the game isn't even actively
, it's just...poor. So I'm going to rip the game apart, not because I think it's bad, but because it was just such a massive letdown. Still, gotta play through it to avoid all those clever folks telling me I don't get it because I didn't play it, right? TL;DR at the end.
I was told this is some sort of distilled perfection (or close to it), with a grand story, great characters, memorable, one that would keep me on edge, yadda yadda. What I got was the world in which every guy only has "plouguing" and murder on his mind, and every woman is a harlot that gets violated eventually. This isn't cynical and realistic, it's exaggerated and cartoony. When everyone is such an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that the main character doesn't stand out even when being a complete and irredeemable ponce himself, I simply have to wonder how come the world looks medieval, as in, how they ever made it out of prehistoric.
And now, Geralt, a witcher, one of those guys who are both infertile and immune to most diseases, and seeing what the first scene when you start the game is, it's pretty obviously he's just pretty much an adolescent fantasy, especially when we bring in the fact that half the world is out for his head, but that's just a minor inconvenience to him while he can go around, kick♥♥♥♥♥ take names, bang wenches, like he doesn't have a worry in the world. If that's not a Mary Sue, I don't know what is. The only thing that saves Triss from being one of those as well is that she doesn't get much screen time. Assuming she'd get no futher character development at least. As for the other plot-important characters? Well, as much of a stick-up-his-proverbial-hindquarters jerk as Roche can be, he's one of the rare people who display any integrity. Zoltan I could relate to, if only because of the "Gods, I'm just so bloody sick of everything" disposition. As far as anyone else goes, it's the eight deadly words: "I don't care what happens to these people." A world that makes me utter those has, thoroughly and utterly, failed its purpose and made its entire existance meaningless.
The story of conspiracy upon conspiracy upon conspiracy loses steam soon, and everything becomes utterly unsurprising and while not entirely expected, the reaction is more like "Oh. Right, naturally there was something else." rather than "HOLY HELL!? You serious!? THIS IS BIG!" I'm sorry, but after a couple of 'big twists' the player somehow starts to expect one around every corner, and they utterly fall flat when they come. It doesn't matter what the twist
, if you know it exists it's already failed its purpose. And again, it could have ended like Enter the Dominatrix from SR4, and I wouldn't feel a thing because I lost any kind of real interest way, way before that.
The combat consists mostly of rolling around and waiting for an opening to slash at every now and then a little, and even the music or occasional pompus cutscene could do little to make the fights any more interesting. Roll, roll, slash, roll, wait for the enemies to unclump, roll, slash, slash, rinse and repeat. I ended up just setting it on easy and spam them down eventurally, and even
was a bother rather than something I'd look forward to doing, and I
killing some pixellated miscreants now and then as stress relief.
The world isn't very open, since nothing you can do outside the quests (and there aren't many of those) carries any meaning. Sure, I
farm cash and get all the recipes and try all potions for no reason other than cathcin'-'em-all, but I can do that in a game that's
that kind of stuff, say, Skyrim. And the progression of story quests? Mostly my stubbornness and hope "it gets better" is to thank. Plus, the fact that Dandelion wrote the journal can't be an excuse that the writing there is so poor as if Dandelion wrote it. It seems as a flimsy justification for shoving all mediocre fanfic-level writing with saying that an in-universe character wrote it. Come. The. Hell. On.
When it comes to graphics and sound, at least they tried hard with the music that could actually be pretty neat to listen to once I manage to mentally detach it from the word "Witcher", but the engine just seems inefficient and real power-hungry. Nothing my PC couldn't handle even on highest settings, but still, if Alice: Madness Returns can optimize hair physics as it does without hogging all the system resources(TM), I'm sure the engine could have used some optimization as well.
TL;DR: All in all, W2 is a relatively solid game that can stand on its own feet, but there's simply nothing else it can do, and merely being able to exist without drawing negative attention to yourself is not exceptional, it's mediocre. While it's not actively bad, it's failed to live up to the hype and promises, and been a complete letdown, thus the thumbs down. I tried to like it. I tried to care about what's going on. I've given it so many chances only to run into "People acting like brainless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s scene #32" and "Implied♥♥♥♥♥♥scene #75". Eventually, the suspension of disbelief is smashed for good, and the game became a chore, to be completed first and foremost to get it out of the way and be rid of it - leaving things unfinished is just poor form.
Witcher 3 can wait. For a decade or two because I sure as blue blazes ain't subjecting myself to a risk of this fiasco again anytime soon and especially not at full price. I don't regret playing Witcher 2, but I'll file it under "failed experiments I learned from" rather than "positive experiences".

Now, Stellaris is one of those games where you can just tell that the dev team cared a lot about their game and worked really hard to make it as great as they possibly could. As soon as you get into the game you realize just how large this games potential could be, from you being able to create your own species all the way down to it's ideals and beliefs, to being able to bring the entire galaxy under your control and all the other races in it. Unfortunately for all it's polish and care, the game has quite a few bugs, especially for one that has never been in early access, but the majority of them that I encountered were mostly minor (graphical glitches and UI problems). So I'm going to list all the good and the bad about the game and make my judgement from there.
Pros:
(+) Game's art style is astounding and obviously a lot of care went into every detail.
(+) Gameplay is solid and entertaining, even hours later.
(+) The amount of technologies, weapons, and designs means that even though there are very few ship designs, it still feels like you're fighting something new.
(+) Subtle references to other space related movies and games, like having a Xenomorph army from the Alien movies or one of the fungal races being like a virus taking over a host's body like in the Last of Us.
Cons:
(-)  Quite a few bugs. Even though they were minor ones, they were in just the right place to make them more noticable (and more annoying). Things like the portrait of a planet's background showing up black, or a large green box covering the top 25% of the screen when you open a menu.
(-) The ships don't default to your flag's colors, and there is no ship painter. This can be disappointing when you're engaging a race that uses the same ships as you do, and that they look exactly like you do.
(-) Little room for expansion. This game suffers from what most other 4X games do, in that, it places your neighbors extremely close together. I understand that it's for action's sake but sometimes when you are surrounded by neighbors who hate you, there really isn't much you can do.
Overall, I have to give the game an 8/10. It's really fun and looks and sounds nice in places, but there are a few glaring issues that could and hopfully can be fixed. Maybe with a patch, maybe with future DLC, but fixed either way. I'd definitely recommend Stellaris to anyone who likes space games, 4X games, or the sort.

The mixed reviews put me off this game for a long while, but I finally picked it up and was pleasantly suprised. I'm a die-hard fan of Might and Magic VI, which I've gone back and played several times over the years. This installment lacks the scope of VI, but captures the spirit of it.
Planning and developing your party is the main highlight, despite a few minor issues with how skills are distributed across classes. Although there are party combinations that are clearly "better" if you are optimizing, there are lots of possibilities that are doable and fun, even by just using different skill distributions amongst the same classes.
You have to accept that you can't get everything you want on every character or every party, since there is an effective limit on the experience you can gain in the game. This can be frustrating, but forces you build more intelligently and make sacrifices to get the skills you want. The game itself is somewhat linear and lacking in the open-world feel of other Might and Magic games. The story isn't very deep or compelling, similar to Heroes VI.
The grid movement and turn-based combat are off-putting at first, but they ultimately created interesting opportunities for tactical gameplay. Combats are often repetitive although there are some variations in tactics based on the specific enemies. After beating it on the normal difficulty, I immediately played through again with a new party on the "Warrior" difficulty, which provided a fun challenge that felt like a different game, at least in the early going. Even after beating it again, I still find myself brainstorming different party combinations I want to try.
Overall, not an "amazing" game, but quite enjoyable, with good replayability. Certainly better than the average review indicates. Now I'm primed to go back and play VI again.

Best RPG I've played in years, and has quickly become my single favorite game. After playing this I just HAD to play the rest of the M&M series, and I played from 3 to 9 and loved every second of it. This is how RPGs are supposed to be!
Pros:
- awesomely fun RPG game in pretty much every way.
Cons:
- support was unfortunately pulled by Ubisoft before a host of audio problems could be patched out, so we're stuck with them forever now. Battle music gets stuck on all the time, sounds constantly don't play or have wrong volumes. With a long enough play session you can end up with 3+ battle songs all playing at the same time all out of synch, which is pretty irritating to hear. these problems are extremely disappointing since the game itself is otherwise so amazing. exiting and running the game again does fix it though (temporarily).
- After having played the rest of the series, there are a few things in comparison that I miss, but these are not strictly good or bad:
- most M&M games have an accelerating levelling scale. progression is slow in the beginning, but by the end you're gaining like 10 levels per trainer visit. in this one, progression does start slow, and does accelerate at first, but at the end it slows to a crawl, and you end up basically frozen and will never be good at everything you could have been good at. this is pretty strongly different than the other M&Ms where you could master everything about your class and still have tons of points left over. depending on your point of view this could be a good or bad thing.
- this game actually has *better* tactical combat than any of the other M&M games, and depending on which classes you choose, you can still become very powerful. though the classes are actually very imbalanced as well, some being extremely powerful and some being very weak. again, this may or may not be a bad thing.

A very guarded thumbs-up: nothing awesomely innovative, but it can hit that just-one-more-turn like a good TBS.
The developers have improved AI balance from early reviews: Easy really isn't hard once you learn the game systems, but on higher difficulty levels I've been out-teched, I've been zerged, I've seen one AI militarily dominate two others while I'm playing a turtley game and then become economically unbeatable.
Downsides, to me:
* the midgame twist can get a bit samey, or be a little too highly random - sometimes I have to absorb 80% of the impact, other times I never see a single infestation.
* it seems like it invites just a little more micromanagement than I'm interested in doing; if I'm rebalancing population allocations every time a city grows it slows down enough to lose my interest. Civ has the same kind of friction in high-level play, though, so this shouldn't be too surprising.
* the technology *order* is random, but you get access to every technology every game, and I haven't seen a time after the first 50-100 turns where changing the depth of a tech in the tree made a huge difference. Perhaps this becomes more of an issue with high-difficulty slow-game-speed play? At standard speed and low to mid tech, I've never been able to have a default technology build order, but I've been able to find a standard preferred set of troop types and usually deploy the same kinds for most of the game.

If you were a fan of the first game then this one is more of that, just another amazing game.
The gameplay is very similar to the first, and i found that mean difficulty actually provided more of a challenge this time round. They took the different modes(hangmans gambit, nonstop debate, etc) and "improved" them, some changes i liked while others not so much. they also added new styles like logic dive which was fun and different from the other modes.
The story follows a similar path of the first game, while throwing more curve balls and false leads at you. The only difference from the first game story telling wise is that it takes much longer for the story to take the nose dive into the meat of the story.

Island mode(this games version of school mode) i fell was handled a lot better then the first game, making it more streamlined and faster to complete.
The negatives of this game would have to be some of the "improvements" and some new modes added to the trials. The Rebuttal showdown and panic talk action modes just dont feel right at all. with the former just not making much sense at times and button masher in essence, and the later just not working timing wise at all. hangmans gambit takes a lot to get used to aswell. I am not a fan at all of the new 2d movement system the game uses in its overworld. I encountered numerous minor graphical annoyances like the background images having floating pixels(as if the artists didnt fully clean the canvas of isolated pixels) and some images going negative when infront of another colour or image, or just outright disappearing. there is also a still of chiaki that has a solid black square on her that is obviously not supposed to be there. I also dont understand why the decided to add monomis island game mode, its just not fun at all and by far the worst part of the game. Pandora is great 4X game in sci-fi setting, greatly inspired by Alpha Centaury but different enough to give it it's own flavour. It offers true sci-fi feeling thanks to powerful but balanced abilities like orbital scanning/bombardment early game and nukes/black-holes/massive orbital deployment mid-late game. You can't achieve this by modding CIV as the mechanics are not there. It is not as complex as CIV, but thanks to this it has faster pace so the average game will not take that long (but you can play huge marathon if you want it slow). Last but far from least, it actually has challenging AI, so you can get interesting game even against AI without bonuses, which is very rare these days. You should definitely get the Eclipse of Nashira expansion which includes the improved AI and also adds new interesting event to the game.
GOOD
- operations (new concept which is done very well)
- challenging AI
- dynamic interesting games (much less likely than CIV to end up in constant "End turn" clicks)
- definite "one more turn" feel
- music, but could use more tracks
- graphics is OK even if not stellar
- story/lore/background information for each faction is rich and interesting
- factions are unique with quite powerful abilities or penalties to offer different approach (but seem to be balanced quite well)
BAD
- victory progress is not communicated well, e.g. you have no clue what to do to achieve scientific or economic victory from the in-game information
- one late game ability (EMP-blackout) possibly doesn't work (not sure though)
Note about AI
AI doesn't role-play and even the most pacifist faction will back-stab and eliminate you if it feels it is strong enough for it. If you are too weak or too strong, the AI's might all pick you as target. This is intended and expected from competitive play (good players would do the same). But it somewhat dilutes the great back-stories invented for each faction. It would be nice if there were 2 modes, one competitive (current one) and one role-play (were factions follow their agendas, e.g. ecologist would be pacifist, growing forests and preserving fungus, despite it being non-optimal approach).

After having spent 5 hours playing this game, I'm not sure I'll go back, I feel as though I did literally everything in one playthrough. The first two hours were great, exploring, avoiding traps, appreciating how the world felt handbuilt even though it was procedural. But that soon faded, and it became a mindless trudge.
Yes, the levels were varied and the loot was abundant, but it didn't mean anything, there was nothing to do in the levels but fight and try to figure out where the hell to go. The loot didn't matter past what moveset it had and what tier it was. sure there were advantages and drawbacks, but those "unique" effects had very little real influence on gameplay, which became mindless attacking. Trying to use a charged attack in the midst of a brawl meant you definitely got hit and also lost a sizeable chunk of stamina, not just stamina, IT REDUCES YOUR STAMINA CAP. Now the fight takes that much longer as I walk backwards to allow my stamina to recharge, because (as I will explain) you cannot use food or potions during a fight without getting hit and stunlocked. Then after the fight you don't get to play the game, you get to craft food, which will take about a minute from crafting to consumption, which will really add up.
Not once did I find the charge attack to be useful as enemies just walked towards you and attacked, they might as well have all been zombies. Where were the ranged enemies? Where were the timid enemies that would avoid you? Sadly, they aren't found here, only increasingly tanky enemies that soaked up damage and time.
The "challenges" given out by the triangular dungeon master left a lot to be desired, and if you advanced too quickly you may be stuck with the same "quest" for multiple floors, creating a severe lack of tokens.
But did tokens even matter? Like many answers to the questions this game has forced me to ask, the answer is no. The skill books (codexes?) never seemed important to me, it felt like quite a bit of work for almost no payoff, I always chose the gold chest. Tokens were too difficult/boring/tedious to earn (break pottery? Funny at first but absolutely mind numbing) and the payoff for earning them was entirely too mediocre. When these challenges involved killing X amount of a certain enemy, I was at a loss, because there are no clear introductions to the enemies, and no journal in which to read about these targets. It took me probably 2 hours to realize that the Inugami I was hunting were, in fact, the dog/wolf creatures. If you hear "Inugami" and "hound enemy" doesn't immediately come to mind, message me, we can start a club.
The levels are one thing I really enjoyed about Necropolis, until they became too large to easily traverse. The chalk didn't solve the navigation issues I ran into, why stop the player from playing your game? In the 5 hours I put into this game, atleast 1.5 were spent wandering to find I had gone the wrong way and slowly walking back to the beginning to try a new route. I understand the intended effect of true exploration, but this is a game, I want to play, not commute between seemingly endless areas. A map, even just a compass that points north would have made my experience much less frustrating and slow.
But I also found that I would have been enjoying myself if there was something in these interesting environments to do other than fight monsters and open chests. Multiple times I found myself having fought past tough enemies to find myself in front of what appeared to be a shrine or large statue, and yet they served no purpose but as eye candy. In the first few levels I lit glowing gems after making it through a variety of traps, where were these throughout the rest of the world? and furthermore, what in the hell did these crystals even do? You have chosen vaguely worded phrases over clear cut descriptions, which means I don't know what's going on in a world I'm desperately trying to immerse myself in.
What was worse was how easy the game became as I got deeper and deeper, my brute, with all his tier 4 gear, was not challenged by any of the monster within. I never had to think about health items as they were so easy to come by, especially later on as producing arcane food became trivial, which also solved my stamina issues. I believe this game becomes infinitely more fleshed out with the addition of stats. Give my character strength, constitution, dexterity, even something as simple as attack or defense. My brute shouldn't be smart enough to use the crossbows, he's a walking tank. You say the game is in the same vein as many other rogue-likes or rogue-lites, yet there was almost no difficulty to be found past being able to block/roll from attacks and avoid being surrounded by empty-headed monsters. The hardest part of the game for me was avoiding accidentally striking other players or being hit by an enemy while behind them (fix those hitboxes).
And the weapons themselves were simple to choose between, if it was below your current tier you ignored it, if it was above you swapped to that weapon, vague advantages/drawbacks meant nothing when you knew the raw damage was higher. If each weapon, shield, armor set just had a few randomized stats, I become that much more involved in how I equip my character.
The uniqueness of the weapons did make them fun, until you realized that there were essentially four weapons that came with different random effects. And some of those effects were gamebreaking, upon finding the greatsword that makes money and items fall from enemies you hit, I was getting a blessing on every floor, but without anything close to character stats I don't even know if the blessings were worth it past making my health bar bigger.
The consumption and creation of items was also incredibly slow, I get that the player shouldn't be able to heal instantly in the heat of battle by gorging her/himself with food (looking at you Elder Scrolls), but potions should be quickly consumed so I can stand a chance in battle. How do you expect a player to make use of a stone-skin potion when it only lasts about 15-30 seconds but consuming it in battle is not an option? Why does crafting take any time at all? Why do I have to wait for an animation to play before I can craft again? Design choices like these keep me from playing the game, and make many potions other than health useless, along with throwing items.
Did anyone use throwing items? Did any playtesters enjoy the 2 second delay between pressing the use button and throwing the item? Play your game, get a throwable, and honestly try to use it. Of course I can "sneak" up on the enemy and throw it before they see me, but in an actual fight where I see many enemies grouped up I don't think about using the throwable because they'd already be hacking away at me before I was halfway through the animation. This is both a mistake made in the design of throwable items and in the enemy AI.
What I see when I try to visualize the essence of this game is that it is fighting against itself. You want interesting descriptions that players will have to read and analyze to understand, but you also throw mountains of unimportant loot at them, so instead of reading your humourous descriptions, they look at the type and tier, ignoring your hard work.
You've designed a wonderful variety of enemies with clear hierarchies of difficulty, but every single one of them behaves in the same way, I'm not fighting a spider/gemeater/skeleton, I'm fighting a healthbar with X moveset.
You've created a fantastic set of environments, but nothing is in them. The first few floors and the castle tileset were the most interesting be

I think the best word to summarise ABZU is 'cool'.
Now, let's clear one thing up; this game is short. I completed it 100% in a little under an hour and a half. But I think what a lot of people miss is that the length of a game doesn't determine its standing. Wouldn't you rather play an awesome game for two hours instead of a crap one that lasts six?
ABZU is the perfect example of this. For what it offers, an hour of gameplay is well worth the time. The sound-staging and beautiful art design are a joy to experience, and (certainly for the latter half of the game) they emmerse you into the underwater paradise created by GiantSquid.
My only issue with the game is the complete lack of challenge. The game is not 'rewarding' in the same way as, say, Pac Man is. It requires absolutely zero effort on behlaf of the player, putting it in the same vein as a walking simulator, I'd say. But, again, that doesn't mean it isn't good!
I think ABZU is a game worth playing, but not at the full price. I was fortunate enough to get ABZU in the February Humble Monthly Bundle, so I wasn't at all concerned about getting the 'value for money' one usually hopes for when purchasing a game at £15+.
ABZU is worth playing if you enjoy creative and cinematic gameplay. Just don't expect to come away feeling that you've achieved anything for yourself.

- the 2 boss fights are a total nightmare even at easy difficulty (yeah i started with normal and since the combat was meaningless I set it to easy just to make it faster)
- health system is a joke. You insta-die touching\hitting (broken) hit-boxes or you die in combat while still having some health (guess health calculation is not accurate)
- checkpoint system is annoying as hell (many of them just in front of cutscenes or "tutorials" that each time you have to skip IF you can. And yes: you will die a lot and thus you'll hate those cutscenes\pauses)
- ending is
- your abilities are a joke as well. You even learn a new one during the fight with the last boss. And I didn't even use it because it's bad.
- invisible walls where you expect to be able to jump (oh..guess what? you probably will die)
So... is this game a total disaster? Nope.
The game is actually a pretty short platform with a unique style. I would have preferred an adventure direction instead of the combat.
Is the game finished? Nope.
- the game is also very unpolished
Dlc with a decent endig or expansion may be coming; at least I hope they make it free.
Is it worth the price of 9,99?
this is very personal.
For me it is not; I played much better games at that price.
Luckily for me i got this for 2,50 VAT included from a reseller site.
That's  a very small amount, but compared to other games it offers much more less as value: but the game is from a new indie company so I'm happy to have purchased it and I hope GRIN will deliver more games.
Still, when it is on sale, buy it if you are interested. It's an OK game after all.

NightSky is a really interesting puzzle/platforming game where you control a ball and try to get it to the right edge of the screen. The game is executed well on many levels, and it makes for a great overall experience. Also, the ball is often placed in odd vehicles, which are pretty fun to mess around with.
The game isn't terribly hard. Not sure why it was in the Indie Royal "Difficult" bundle.
The game's engine works very well, and the physics work as they should. The game controls well, except that it sometimes switches what some of the buttons do... it's more of an annoyance than a hindrance. The environments are really cool, but the music is a little grating.
It took me forever to get JoyToKey configured, since it doesn't tell you which keys are important at first. Feel free to ask me for my XB360 controller config.
The game's too short to recommend at $10. Get it if you can find it under $5.

NightSky is a pretty nice physics-based puzzle-platformer with simple and intuitive controls, small but cool puzzles and a fairly interesting graphical style.
There is a minimalistic story about why this is happening and what it is about, but it's really not worth mentioning. Basically, you steer a ball through 11 different levels while making use of your 'brake' and 'turbo' function and very basic physics.
The game features some really cool gameplay elements such as inverted gravity, catapults, vehicles and stuff which add quite a bit of nice variety into the gameplay.
Playtime for one complete playthrough (including collecting all hidden stars to unlock the bonus level) is around 2,5-3 hours, so it's not really a game to spend days with, however, the game also features an advanced mode where the (same) puzzles are slightly harder to master due to missing level parts, ramps etc., so this might add another 2-3 hours of gameplay to the total counter.

The aesthetics are simple with its mostly silhouette layout and the music appropriately adds to the ambience when it actually plays.
The gameplay is actually more skill-based than puzzle as physics play the biggest part of the gameplay though there are some legitimate puzzles in game but they're far in between.
There are 2 difficulty modes, Normal and Alternative, and 11 worlds that consist of 13 levels each save for the very first one.
Normal mode is for a casual playthrough while Alternative significantly increases the difficulty with slightly & very cleverly altered levels that can suddenly demand more timing, patience, and just overall skill in general.
There are also some hidden stars that are spread throughout the game's Worlds. Their sole purpose is to unlock the rest of the last World's levels. Finding hidden stars is basically like finding an alternate path to a level they're hidden in so long as you know what level they're in and where exactly they're supposed to be at, which you can just look up. That said it can often be a challenge itself just to reach them.
It doesn't take very long to finish the game but with its decent level design, very functionable physics, and neat aesthetics & sounds it's not a bad game.

My first impression of this game was very good. It has some very interesting concepts and is a mixture of Europa Universalis 4 and traditional 4X space strategy games.
However, after playing for 15 hours, I now have the feeling that I am playing an unfinished version of Europa Universalis 4.
For example, in EU4, you are told by the game why an ally is refusing to go to war with you, i.e. because he has good relations with your enemy or because he currently cannot afford another war because he is still recovering from a previous war. In Stellaris, however, you simply are told that your ally is saying no, without providing any hint on the reasons why he is doing so.
I have also encountered several serious bugs in the game.
I assume that Paradox (the publisher and developer) will continue to develop the game and improve it significantly, as it has done with EU4. Quite a few of these improvements for EU4 were free. However, many were very expensive. Currently, if you buy all DLC for EU4, it will cost you over 220 Euros, which is equivalent to 250 US-Dollars. I'm afraid that Stellaris will suffer the same fate.
If Paradox improves the game as it has done with EU4, and if it changes its DLC policy to a more reasonable one, I will gladly change my rating to a positive one.

At first glance it doesn't look like much more than a GC2 remake.  In depth play, however, will demonstrate 2 important things:
#1 It is much more than simple graphical improvements....the AI "Under the hood" is VASTLY improved.  I try not to load saved games after a mistake (unless it was something I did unintentionally) and while I've had some 'close calls' on normal difficulty (i.e. the game plays as smart as it can, but doesn't *cheat* via extra recources etc..) but I have never been actually been beaten by the a.i. of any 4X game on normal diffiulty.....until now.
To be fair, after a game or two, you will learn each of the races tactics, and be able to adapt to them.  I won't spoil it, but the Drengi on your first game can be horribly ruthless, until you figure out their strategy (1st game...it might be too late), but once you learn it they become easy to defend against....though they are still a &*^% annoying pain to counter invade.
side note:  I've heard rumors that each game the AI will adapt to YOUR playstyle.  I cannot confirm or deny that because I tend to try something different each game so I don't think I've developed a pattern.  I also make custom races most of the time.
#2:  Seemingly 'minor' improvements DRASTICALLY change the game.   As an example....gone are the 'incremental' improvements in the tech tree (particullarily for the weapons and defenses).  Each step requires some significant investment, but also provides significant advantage to its particular speciality.    Ensuring investments in tech are aligned with both your strategy, your galactic map situation, and the threats against you are more important than ever across the entire tech tree.  That is one of MANY examples.
Overall def. worth the buy, especially if you pick it up on sale, like I did.

I'm going to write this review assuming you already played the first game.
The plot of this game is that you and 15 of your classmates from Hopes Peak Academy are taken to a tropical island to get closer with each other and bond. However, the murderous Monokuma returns to host yet another killing game. This time, the stakes are that you're only allowed off the island if you murder a classmate and get away with it. The execution of this plot is done extremely well.
The game is broken up into 3 different gameplay styles. These are known as Daily Life, Deadly Life, and the Class Trial. Daily Life and Deadly Life are the same as the first game, giving you time to bond with your classmates and exploring the island and giving you time to investigate the murder of your classmates respectively.
The Class Trial is broken up in the same way as well, with there being novel sections that show revelations in the plot and in the murder case, and numerous mini games that lead into these novel sections. The minigames, however, are very different from the first game. The only minigames that retained its format from the first game are Bullet Time Battle (renamed to Panic Talk Action) Nonstop Debate. (Improved) Hangmans Gambit has been altered from a point and click spelling game into a matching puzzle game where you actually have to think about what you're doing. Rebuttal Showdown and Logic Dive are the new minigames introduced in Danganronpa 2. Rebuttal Showdown is a lot like nonstop debate, but instead of sitting through a series of statements from numerous different people, you slice through statements made by a single person with the WASD keys, and then you use Truth Blades to cut through contradictions within their arguments. Logic Dive is the other new minigame and is played as a runner style game where you jump over pits, and dodge blockades while answering questions to get further in the case.
TL;DR
Story: 9.5/10 No obvious plotholes, but some minor pacing issues
Gameplay: 9/10 Gameplay is extremely fun for almost the entire game, but it has its dull moments.
Music: 9.5/10 Soundtrack is superb
Overall Rating: 9.5/10

If what you crave is oldschool grid-based 3D movement combined with turn-based combat, don't look any further - it won't get any better than this. But if you do not like these two basic features of the game (or even just one of them), you really should keep away. You've been warned.
"Legacy" harkens back to the Might & Magic games of old - and with this I don't mean Might & Magic 6/7, but rather M&M 3 "Isles of Terra" and M&M 4/5 "World of Xeen". You can still buy those from GoG, but the once stunning VGA graphics are real hard to endure nowadays, so it's a blessing that Might & Magic X exists. While the graphics here aren't exactly top notch, they are still very beautiful and atmospheric. (Almost) everything else is like it was in those old games: A deep turnbased combat system at its core, a big upper world to roam freely with your party of four (plus two hirelings), towns, dungeons, inns, merchants, quests, riddles - the whole shebang. In this, "Legacy" has much much more to offer than, say, "Legends of Grimrock II".
Given all the above, there are only two real downsides to the game: The first is that it is unfortunately technically unoptimized. This becomes noticeable to the user in the wide upper world, where there's sometimes hitching while you move your party a tile - even with the most advanced GPUs in town. This is strange as the game really shouldn't be very demanding at all (the only reason that could explain this is that the engine seems to rely more on your CPU power than on your GPU). This does detract from the oldschool RPG fun only slightly, however.
Well, and the second downside is of course Uplay. I once swore I would never buy another Ubisoft game from steam again until they got rid of this utterly useless and annoying additional DRM-scheme, but when I broke my vow and reinstalled it  (just for this game), I noticed that it at least became much more unobtrusive compared to how I rember it from a few years ago (when I played "Farcry 3" for a while). Also retrieval of the long forgotten password for my account was no problem.
If I had to give "Might & Magic X - Legacy"  a score, it would be 8/10 for fans of grid-based RPGs with turn-based combat. I would have given 9/10 if the game were optimized. The last missing point is because I really miss some features from the old games, namely: sorcerer guilds and banks that give interest on deposited money. Also, while the story always played second fiddle in M&M games and the narrative we are presented here is ok, I liked some of the storylines of earlier installments better. A nice touch, though, is that (if you are perceptive) the great "sci-fi setting" twist of "Might & Magic 3, Isles of Terra" is at least alluded to in "Legacy" too.

I think the best word to summarise ABZU is 'cool'.
Now, let's clear one thing up; this game is short. I completed it 100% in a little under an hour and a half. But I think what a lot of people miss is that the length of a game doesn't determine its standing. Wouldn't you rather play an awesome game for two hours instead of a crap one that lasts six?
ABZU is the perfect example of this. For what it offers, an hour of gameplay is well worth the time. The sound-staging and beautiful art design are a joy to experience, and (certainly for the latter half of the game) they emmerse you into the underwater paradise created by GiantSquid.
My only issue with the game is the complete lack of challenge. The game is not 'rewarding' in the same way as, say, Pac Man is. It requires absolutely zero effort on behlaf of the player, putting it in the same vein as a walking simulator, I'd say. But, again, that doesn't mean it isn't good!
I think ABZU is a game worth playing, but not at the full price. I was fortunate enough to get ABZU in the February Humble Monthly Bundle, so I wasn't at all concerned about getting the 'value for money' one usually hopes for when purchasing a game at £15+.
ABZU is worth playing if you enjoy creative and cinematic gameplay. Just don't expect to come away feeling that you've achieved anything for yourself.

ABZU was abzulutely fantastic on the eyeballs. Beautifully rendered environments with a real lifelike feel to all the fish swimming around. The music really set the mood while the gameplay was simple and smooth. The devs told a very simple story, but oddly enough I felt for some of the characters. The menus were really easy to navigate. The added meditation mode for each stage is pretty cool.
The only real downside for this game that I experienced was the terrible static noise. It must have something to do with the quality of audio they recorded in and my cheaper headphones. This problem is pretty consistent with other people as well. It wasn't game breaking for me, but I can see how some people would go crazy over hearing that noise all the time.
Pros:
- Incredibly beautiful environments to explore
- Relaxing music
- Collectables
- Smooth controls
Cons:
- Awful static noise playing all the time. (I think it has something to do with the bass in the music.)
I wouldn't spend full price ($20) because there is about 2 hours of actual gameplay, but if you're really into the undwater scene, ABZU is a wonderful game to play if you want to relax. There's no overwhelming enemies or hair pulling puzzles.

I'm giving this a thumbs up, but I really mean to give it a thumbs sideways.
If you wish Civ5's beyond-earth-mod was a bit better, this is the game for you. The biggest downside is that even with the developer assuring people that the AI is much better now, it's still incredibly braindead. It will declare war on you for no reason, it will offer peace for even less reason. It may decide to never attack you, or it may blitskreig your cities. You can never rely on the AI to do anything but stab you in the back the moment you're not paying attention. And the AIs will always cooperate very strongly with eachother. So it never really feels like a free for all, it feels like a vaguely structured 1v7 beatdown.
It was fun for a short little game, and had a reasonably interesting story, but it definitely could use some more content or replayability. Overall still fun though.

It's a better-than-average 4X game, with some niggling problems that prevent it from really being great. The tech tree is varied and interesting each game, which is definitely a plus, and the economy has some novel wrinkles which make it a bit different to the typical 4X without being excessively micromanage-y, although it does start getting that way in the late game. The AI is the biggest problem, really; if you get too far ahead technologically / economically, every AI player will suddenly turn on you and mercilessly dogpile you into the dust. For this reason, I recommend playing on medium difficulty and small maps, where the balance is actually quite playable. For larger maps, and "easier" difficulty levels, you're much too likely to trigger the dogpile scenario and have your game suddenly and unexpectedly cut short. Not a bad game... but not really enough here to recommend it over (say) Civ V or AoW3, unless you really love the Sci-Fi setting. Speaking of the setting, this is pretty clearly a homage to SM:AC, and it does a fair job of evoking the atmosphere of that game without slavishly copying every element of it.

I didn't dislike Little Inferno, but I do feel that it was way too expensive for the length and theme of the game. About 98% of the game is just burning things, a task that I found to be a waste of time since what generally draws me to games are good plots and well developed characters. I got the game because I was told that its storyline was really good, but it's less of a storyline and more of an ironic message you get at the end. Certainly, I can see how Little Inferno could be fun, but for those expecting an engaging plot or characters, this is not the right game. If you enjoy puzzle games or games that don't focus on story, you may like Little Inferno. I enjoyed receiving messages from my neighbor and finding combos was occasionally amusing, but overall it seemed to me that the majority of this short game was just fluff to fill the time. While that is kind of the point, that doesn't do anything to justify the cost and time spent up.

But not all is bad with this game, and here's the list of the things that hold this game up:

But I cannot give this game a thumbs up... because I feel like there is so much missing from the game!  There is so much promise here, so much potential, but the game feels like it was cut in half.  the Story is unended Red Riding Hood has gained a very supernatural power through her grandmother, and that's it.
I do think this game is worth more than $10.00 due to it's amazing visuals and wonderful writing and a glorious gameplay system.  And I do think you should buy it at its' current state!  The developers should be supported to the best of our capabilities by buying this game and playing through it and letting them know how much we love it. At a glance, this game it's a straight remake of Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri. You can easily recognize the feeling of a Sid's game, the hexagons, the landscape, and the mechanics.
And furthermore, you can discover some little things here and there... not real bugs or issues, but little flaws. Thanks to these flaws you can say "ok, this is not a game from Sid".
A lot of people said these things before me... and I guess that are all true, but I like this game. It's truth. I enjoyed it. Since the first time I played it.
The first time I played, everything was fresh and new. The other factions were far from my cities, no one declared war to me immediately, I was able to take my time and clear out some alien nest. The events were real surprises, the research gave me real new things, new weapons, new capabilities. BUT my faction was distroyed by sudden war escalation against me.
Playing a second time, the game was quite similar: aliens eat me, I'm at war with everyone and I don't know why... The entire game takes about 100 turns.
Ok... third shot. I drop the difficulty level to easy. Just few turns in, I'm at war with everyone again, aliens eat me. My faction is canceled from the world.
In my opinion, the real problem with this game is only this too wobbly game-balance. You can win a game in hard mode because other factions help you to reach your goals or you can lost your capital city in a stupid way during an easy-mode game.
I like the graphic, I like the soundtrack, I like the mood... So yes, I recommend the game.
Yes, I recommend the game for those that like this genre.

It's been a long time since I've played it but this game was such a standout experience for me I decided to review it.
I'd consider it the definition of a "Modern" Rougelike. It plays just like Angband but everything has fully detailed sprites and the game uses a classless perk based progression system.
The game has really short 2-3 floor dungeons which make you feel like you're really making progress as you almost always end up "Clearing" a dungeon.
The difficulty isn't that high and it's felt like the most accessible Rougelike I've ever played. It's coolest feature though is a Heirloom meta game, you unlock items for new characters by performing certain tasks ingame, e.g: Slay the Frost Wolf boss and you can start the game with a pet dog or start the game with a single cleric spell if you manage to learn every cleric spell on a single character.
The game is alot of fun and I'd recommend it to anyone who hasn't really gotten into rougelikes before.

I've mastered roguelike games like The Binding of Isaac, FTL, and Dungeons of Dredmore, going all the way back to roguelikes from the 1980s like Temple of Apshai. When I bought Rogue's Tale I was pretty excited - the first few playthroughs were brutally hard and I was very excited to learn how to conquer the dungeons.
Hours passed, and more hours of gameplay passed, and eventually I found that while I could learn some new tactics, ultimately I would be defeated by any random monster that landed a few lucky hits, no matter how conservatively I played. This trend continued, and continued, and no matter what items I got or strategies I used, I basically could not figure out how to get very far in this game.
My conclusion is that the game just isn't developed enough to provide adequate strategies for the player, and instead leaves most of it up to chance. It's too bad because the game had good potential, but ultimately I'd recommend staying away from this game as it needs a lot of work before it is actually "playable".

Finished the story in 30 minutes. Then I unlocked practice mode. A bit backwards, don't you think?
So here's how it works:
You are the cosmonaut, basically a herodude out to kill hordes of machine enemies who share your colour scheme. You move your mouse to move around like it was the mouse pointer, left button is a standard attack, right charges your super attack when you hit/kill things with it, both buttons at the same time unleashes your super attack. You gather points and unlock in-game achievements in the 5 different stages.
There are things I like - the infinite continues, the mouse moving the character (as a concept), but I really don't care about hunting points and trophies when the story and gameplay is this anemic, the soundtrack just alright and the design sort of bland (with some additional issues keeping track of the hero and shots). The stage variations are of the early arcade model - they're a different background with a different set of enemies, there's no terrain features that do anything (to my recollection).
In short and my humble opinion: cool controller idea, needed some more work before being worth 7.99 Euro.

Legacy of the Elder Star is a simple SHMUP with a very pretty art and twist in the control scheme.
The beautiful art, nice effects and good music unfortunately masks a game devoid of any character in any area. It's telling that the only characteristics of the protagonist are his name and his tacked on grin, without which he would sit right at home amongst the enemy drones. The pattern continues with art which lacks most of world building background detail and most enemies have a theme of mechanical and gray. I'd really like to see more beautiful high-resolution 2d art in games, but the resolution must be filled with detail - otherwise low-res pixel art is better when I can use my imagination subconciously to fill gaps of pixels with detail. The Music is great and fits the game very well.
Nothing above would really matter if the game had an interesting gameplay that challenged and surprised the player. There's a serious lack of bullet patterns in this game. Fighting becomes so predictable and boring way too fast. Unfortunately bosses know only a few tricks, different phases only having more difficulty or speed added. Same applies to basic enemies. First level of most other shmups has more to see that this game. Most shmup pattern staples are just missing like bullet barrages that move at different speeds or mazes. Currently once I find where the bullets come from and find a safe spot I rarely have to move.
The replayability is really nice touch with challenges and different weapon loadouts. Unfortunately replayability won't fix these problems.

First off I've been a fan of Paradox games for a long time, I enjoy the depth they have and the whole "making up your own stories" thing that happens as you play.
Stellaris being a blend of the 4x and Grand Strategy genre had me excited.
PROS
+ Great race creator, lots of options for traits and governement types, unique portraits and comeplete freedom in naming everything and selecting a homeworld type
+ Interesting research system, one of the things I hate about tech trees is in multiplayer people would min max and beeline techs so you'd have to play super competitively all the time. The research being semi "random" in this with certain techs being weighted to appear more often depending on other techs you have really feels like an organic research system and stops people beelining the "best" tech build
+ A lot of tech variety, from weapons to passive techs, there's a lot of variety and the best late game techs have some cool stuff associated with them
+ Great flavour text and a semi "quest" system, you scan anomalies and discover ancient civs or shrines to gods etc which starts a mini chain of objectives leading to sizeable rewards.
+ Different Government types actually feel fairly different.
Definitely not the only good parts but I don't want this to drag on too much.
CONS
- Mid to Late game when there's lots to calculate even better rigs can experience a bit of slowdown (Devs are working on this)
- Few bugs here and there, e.g. When an Empire sends an embassy to you, they say they're creating it on THEIR homeworld not yours. A few placeholder personalities seem to have been missed.
- AI can be a bit lackluster, some people have reported problems with singeplayer games being boring as the AI empires dont start wars etc. I haven't found that and it could be because they have peaceful empires around. I've found the Empire AI to be not bad, the Ally AI is shocking however, they rarely defend their own space and their fleets just follow you around.
- A lot of confusion about how the mechanics work together, I've seen lots of complaints about the influence system about people not having the amount of influence income to play how they want, personally I've never had a shortage of influence even in larger Empires, the problem I think is the game rarely teaches you how to manage your influence based on whatever Gov type you choose.
- UI, I find the UI incredibly frustrating at times. It's clean and functional, but at times information you expect to be displayed is just missing comepletely, stuff is often hidden layers deep into menus.
Niggling problems that I assume are going to be fixed soon:
The ability to name some things and not others, I can rename Admirals and Generals, but not my Empire leader (not that I've found)
I can rename fleets, ships, and ship class but I can't rename individual ground armies?
Text errors, trading and exchanging embassies sometimes an AI Empire will say it's doing those things to itself, or appear to talk to themselves instead of you.
That's about it, right now I love the game, it certainly needs some polish but its a great game. My singleplayer capaign hasn't gotten boring at all and I'd say I'm well into the midgame of it, up to battleships, needing sectors to manage planets.
The combat is both simple but also has some depth to it.
Right now I would definitely reccomend the game and it's likely to only get better as Paradox have a good track record of supporting their games with patches and DLC for years.

I love Gal Civ, am a huge fan.  I have played these games since the first.  I am also an adamant 4X player.  This game was released over a year ago and has had several DLC.  I chose to wait to buy this game later in hopes to snag all the DLC and get a game patched and ready to rock.  For the most part, this is a classic Gal Civ game with all the latest bells and wistles in 4x graphics.  However, it's just that, a graphical improvement on that same old game.  There are a couple of interesting features like ship roles and support ships, but don't expect much else to be new.  It's still a solid 4x game, and I am glad I waited to pick it up for a bargain deal.  I definitely like Gal Civ, and this is definitely that.
Now the bad:
Bugs.  Namely crash to desktop.  Multiplayer is still near unplayable.  My friend and I experienced crash to desktop and host disconnects about once every hour or two.  We learned to save every turn because we didn't know when we were going to get booted, or the AI would get stuck on a turn indefinitely.  I am surprised the multiplayer experience is so bugged out after over a year of support.  Single player is more stable, but the game crashes to desktop every once and a while, so save often.
Overall, if you like Gal Civ, you will like this game.  If you are kicking the tires, wait for a steam sale before you pull the trigger on a purchase.

Back before Final Fantasy was little more than walking down a corridor and watching the next overblown cutscene, Final Fantasy VII was THE GAME TO GET. I can remember when my friend first brought his Playstation to my house. As a kid, I♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants at how far the games had come since the NES and Super Nintendo. My friend showed me Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. He showed me Resident Evil. He showed me Quake II. Then he showed me what would become my go-to favorite game of my lifetime. That, my dear friends, is Final Fantasy VII.
This is the game I've been keeping my Playstation around to play annually, like I have every year since it's release in 1997.  This is the game that I have put an eye-wateringly stupid amount of hours into. I can't even think...1000? 2000? Everytime you play this game, there is something new to find, there is some new thing that you missed on a previous playthrough. There is something new to appreciate and a new fond memory to be made.
Final Fantasy VII is living legend.
Call me a fanboy if you will, but understand my position. The new FF's are for the birds. Final Fantasy 3(6), 5, 7, 8, and dare I say 9, are all considered classics for a reason. It isn't about being a fanboy, it's about your childhood. It's about my childhood. It's about all us twenty-somethings having to live in the wastelands we call modern mainstream gaming. What  you have to understand is, Final Fantasy VII is THE reason why RPG games are now mainstream.
Does anyone else miss Squaresoft?
