After getting this game, it was quite apparent that some of the reviews need updating. It is also worth stating that many Let's Plays on YouTube are dated. That said, this game is more than a bit quirky with some features that I have not seen in any other 4X space game, and some standard features omitted. I suspect that for most players, those who appreciate it for what it is will get a great deal more satisfaction from it than those that feel compelled to compare it to most 4X games.
The first thing that stands out as an amazing but unexpected bonus is the ability to export your designs to a 3D printer, either your own or you can have it shipped from a site (file provided to the website automatically by the client). While Space Engineers I have heard also has this feature, I have not heard of such a feature for 4X games generally. I decided to test the feature, though I didn't go through with the purchase, and found the cost to be about $13, depending on features (e.g. material used, $13 was for a plastic model).
It is worth mention, however, that this game has no intrigue (as in spying, plenty of diplomacy) or planetary bombardment. It does have planetary bombardment, but not as an exclusive way to eliminate a colony. It only makes invasions easier. You are required to invade planets to take them, which is nice in that for many games it is just easier to bombard a planet then recolonize it, but at the same time obviously you lose the fun of bombarding a planet to oblivion.
The game has some pretty high requirements for a 4X game, due to the ability to generate maps that might not be so large for an RTS, but for a TBS are absolutely gargantuan!
The ship design system is pretty awesome. As one might imagine from the fact that you can 3D print your vessels, you can also design your vessels in 3D rather than the usual 2D placement on tiles. It really feels like a Legos set, the pieces just snap together at various points. If they don't fit quite right, the game allows you to adjust the rotation, offset, and so forth to make the design more visually appealing. Speaking of which, you can add a number of stylistic parts that have no cost or benefit to the design except to provide more space, or to make it more visually appealing. An important note, however: some parts will be symmetrically doubled cosmetically, but it only has the benefit of one part.
You cannot control your ships in combat, though you can view the combat if you so desire. It is visually appealing.
The tutorial goes over very little, and what you are looking for might not pop up right away on google. The best way to learn the game is from observation. That said, the UI is pretty intuitive, and far less micromanagement is required than your typical 4X game. That doesn't mean that micromanagement won't help, but it isn't absolutely necessary for planets and so forth.
As for the learning curve, I started my first game on "Beginner," having skipped through a good portion of the tutorial. I have completed a handful of games of Civilization, RTW2, AoW3, and have started a handful of other 4X games. At this difficulty, I am finding myself holding on well enough, but not doing particularly well. Guessing that I am at the midpoint of the game, I have a good shot at victory but by no means is it a guarantee.
I got this game on sale at $13, and it feels like a steal. At full price it is still less than the standard AAA game at $60, and $60 I would say is a fair price. Full price is a pretty decent deal, on sale this game seems like a steal, but only if you can appreciate it for what it is.
edit: so after playing a while, I found something else worth mention: modding in new races is actually quite easy, though for the sake of simplicity I prefer to just go with a full sized foreground such that you can't add a background and take the leader profile directly from the foreground picture.
One other thing that is worth mention: while it can be seen in Let's Plays, it is easy enough to miss the fact that the ship range system is highly unusual in this game, in a manner which leads to less micromanagement but also is less realistic. Ships have no supply limit. Instead, the distance which they can travel away from the nearest refueling point is capped. It is possible, if you have a refueling point far away from the others, that you will not be able to reach one planet from the others if a ship's range does not overlap. However, fortunately you can influence ship range individually by adding life support systems (instead of supply systems, but same idea. Both increase range in their respective games).
edit: I have come across a new downside: Support is cumbersome. In regards to how effective it is, I have just begun the process of working through some technical issues, so when and if everything is sorted out I will describe the process.
No real technical support is available via the Steam forums, you are redirected to their website, where they will send you an email regarding known fixes and downloadable programs that might fix the problem. Be wary of the fact that though the game seems to work initially, it can fail later.
Well, they have an application that you can download to automatically acquire all the necessary information for the bug report, which is a very nice feature. We'll see how useful this all is after everything is over with.
edit: I am changing my review to a negative review, since their customer support is substantially sub-par. They will close the ticket if you don't respond within 24 hours. Vacations aside, technical issues can arise with people's computers. No quality information is provided on Steam, you have to go through the website. With the number of people having technical difficulties, I can no longer bring myself to reccomend this game.

Witcher 2 is my favorite game. It is a solid RPG with a lot of action and a brilliant story. It is very mature in a lot of its themes and situations. This game is based on novels written by a Polish authornamed Andrzej Sapkowski. You play as Geralt, a Witcher, or a genetically enhanced monster hunter. They have been described as a kind of warrior monk. Geralt drinks special potions that let him far exceed the abilities of normal humans. These potions are needed to battle the various beasts of the realms. Witchers also have a very limited understanding of magical energy called Witcher's Signs. Basically the Signs are spells, like a fireball and a paralysis trap spell and a few others. Geralt is an interesting character because he is not quite human but hes not a monster either. Due to their methods and abilities, however, many in the world see Witchers as freaks and monsters. Which is really what the game's ideology is all about; the greyness in everyone, not the clear cut black and white. Which to me, is a welcome change from the usual: 1) "hey I'm a good guy I will help you" 2) "Not my problem Kachinsky" 3) F*** YOU F*** FACE," that many other game are notorious for. Geralt is often put in positions of just making a choice, not good or evil, just difficult decisions that have a lot of positives and negatives to them. The story is top notch, and eerily real in many of the stuggles of the world.
Geralt has a set of skill trees (sword, magic, alchemy) that the player can advance in any way. All into one or spliced between the three. Sword fighting is a core mechanic though, so no matter how you play, Geralt will always have two swords. A silver sword for monsters, and a normal sword for humans. There are a few other weapons too but mostly its swords. Depending on the player preference combat can be a bit like the Batman games, or the Assassins Creed games. In some ways it can be like Chivalry: Medieval Warfare. Weapons and armor play a big part as well and can effect all of the skill trees. Making the game very balanced between gear and character tree choices. Not to the crazy levels of a Diablo game but enough to make for a very quality rpg.
Mostly though, Witcher 2 is a lot like skyrim. I do not want to bash on skyrim here, it is also a great game that a lot of people absolutely love. I feel, however, that Witcher is far better than skyrim and think the people that love skyrim should try the Witcher. Both games have the northern lore and feel. Witcher 2 is no where near as large or open as skyrim. Witcher is much more linear but the story and combat and the world just feel so much better in every way to me. The enemies and the different races were better portrayed during the game. When I came to a new town in skyrim I did not get that feeling of truly new. Just another town and another barbarian guy leading it. Witcher was totally different, you get the feeling of racial tensions and social tensions in every part. The powers that be are very different and each very developed and very human. As it plays out you really see how the choices alter the world, instead of it coming down to "OK I'm a good guy so I will save good guy town." A lot of games try to get that feeling across of the characters true M.O. and demeanor but fail. Witcher acomplishes this very well. Triple AAA quality. Superb graphics, superb voice acting. I enjoyed every character. There were a few times, of course, where some tones were a bit off but that happens in every game. Overall amazing game. When I learned that this game was made by a small studio in Poland I was shocked.
As someone who never read any of the books and did not play the first game, I found that after a second playthrough the story and everyhting started to click and I realised how well done everything really was. The way the game is, one would want to play it at least twice to see both sides of what is going on.
It seems as though more than a few people found the game to be really difficult. It can be, but now there are plenty of guides and discussions about it. The game has a kind of reverse curve for the difficulty. It is much harder in the beginning due to a lack of points in the skill tree and low grade weapons and armor. By the end though, Geralt is pretty much on par with jezuz. I like games of this nature, because being really stong at the end makes it feel like you really acomplished something.
This game also has subtitles in many languages so I found it made a great gift for steam friends who are not natural to the english language.
I would reccommend this game to anyone. Especially anyone who likes Skyrim, Assassin's Creed, Batman, Chivalry, or even the imfamous Darksouls 1 & 2

The casual setting auto-levels Dust, but the more difficult settings allow players to allocate 'gems' into which particular stats you favour. Wow what a horrible game... The graphics are extremely dated, and not in a charming way (this game came out in 2014? srsly? Oblivion came out in 2006 and its graphics blow this away!). I have seen indy titles with better graphics and effects, I expect more from an AAA studio. The interface is clunky, wtf is up with the weird "tile based" movement system? You are stuck on a grid?!? What is this? Might and Magic II? MM6, 7, 8 and 9 had no problem letting the party freely move and look around, you toggled "turn based mode" on and off when needed. This game locks it on runs the world every time you step into the next grid tile (you know the way the old DOS 1-Xeen Might and Magic games did...). The character races, classes and skills are pretty basic and lack the options and depth of the games predicessors. It's like they decided to try to capture the look and feel of old titles but managed to capture all the negative things about them with none of the positive.
I haven't played much but I already noticed several assets are recycled from previous games... Mostly sound effects that are from MM6, 7, 8. Several of the jingles, the sound of the quest log opening and closing, the sound of drinking potions are all from the old games. It is laughable and only makes me wish I was replaying one of the old titles.
I mean... Might and Magic VIII Day of the Destroyer, a game that came out in the year 2000 had 7 base classes, plus 7 promotion classes, plus the dragons. MMX basically has 3... a "warrior" a "hybrid" or a "caster" and the class is a bit different depending on race. VIII had 35 unique skills, X has 25 and they aren't very creative. Your wizard can't even grand master all of the magic spells. VIII had very distinct magic skills, the 4 elemental magics were for wizards, the three "self" magics were for healers and the light\dark were shared (there was also class specific magic...) This game, I am not sure exactly how to distinguish between a healer and a caster, you don't seem to start with any healing spells. The previous few games were cool because you could explore the world freely in real time and then press "enter" to go into turn based mode when needed; you didn't feel like you were locked to a rigid grid.
Also, dare I say, the graphics are almost better in 6\7\8. I mean sure they are low res pixelated sprite based images mostly but at least the characters wander around in real time, with a walk cycle. Your characters move their lips when they talk (yeah, no one moves their lips at all in X... it is sometimes hard to tell who is talking). It was a bit primative but at least it was easy on the eyes. Even MM3 through Xeen looked good, in a cartoony oldschool DOS way (and in Xeen the characters moved their lips when they spoke.) MM1 and MM2 had crap graphics, grid based game play and you had to draw your own maps (sort of) but they came on 5 1\4 floppies so they get a pass.
Plus, no game since 6\7\8 has had the awesome inventory and equipment equip screens that 6\7\8 had. You could actually see what the thing in your inventory looked like and when you put it on your character they actually looked like they were wearing or using that item. MM9 and X went back to the oldschool "list of items" method and little squares to put the items in to equip them.
6\7\8 had a few animated cutscenes, and they were animated well for their time. This game has an extremely long intro, plus another 10 minutes of naration as soon as the game starts and it is all told with still images and voice overs with characters that can't move their lips.
The only thing that X seems to have taken from 6\7\8 is some ripped off audio assets.
Add to all of this the "wonderful" experience of having to use UPlay... F-ck UPlay. It took quite an effort just to get this game to launch on my PC (among other things I had to sign up for a 3rd UPlay account because for some reason they can't find my old credentials) and - it wasn't worth it.
The Might and Magic series peaked with 6, 7 and 8. 9 was OK. X is pretty bad.
Go back to remaking "Heroes" clones Ubisoft! If this was an Indy title I would cut it some slack but... come on, this is Ubisoft, the guys who brought us Assasins Creed and Far Cry. Ubisoft and Limbic Entertainment are way above "Indy" level developers. I haven't been this disapointed with a game with the title Might and Magic since Dark Messiah. These guys are making me start to consider MM9 as one of the "good" Might and Magic games... (and I used to hate that game! Well, hate is a strong word. Strongly dislike is more like it.) I miss 3DO and New World Computing. They would have never let this happen.

TL;DR: The game lacks enough variety still, but it's getting there. It could be really excellent with another update or two. I'd totally change this review to recommended if improvements are made. Devs pls! Suggested improvements are listed in
+ Good artstyle, with decent jokes throughout
+ Pretty good crafting system that compliments the small carrying capacity of your character
+ Fun and challenging dungeon-crawling gameplay, that gets much more difficult the further in you go
+ Currency system really makes you weigh your options between items and blessings (i.e. leveling up)
+ Currency is shared between players (when collected, not when spent)
+ Fairly unique and useful items that can temporarily make a difficult enemy much easier
+ Some dud items and traps that really are deceptive at first glance
+ Environmental hazards and enemy rivalries make for some very tactical gameplay; this subtle detail is a very excellent choice
+ Biomes are very intricate, if a little pointless at times
+ Fun sidetasks that require decent work to complete
+ Co-op is always addictive
= People complain about the lack of item descriptions, but honestly this doesn't bother me; It's a creative choice and forces players to focus more on their observations of item effects
= Tokens of favor, codexes, and dyes are the only things that carry over between playthroughs; this is a satisfactory choice for a rogue-like that has different classes
= There is no map to go off of for each floor
- Drops are too common and have little variety
- Mobs get boring after the 5th time and have very little variety until later floors
- The DARK SOULS ROGUE-LIKE has ONLY ONE BOSS FIGHT at the end; mobs are basically the only tpe of encounter you'll face
- Crafting resources are not shared, making them difficult to collect in multiplayer
- Biomes and mobs appear in a very similar order in each playthrough, causing drops to follow the same pattern
- Biomes are also sometimes very open but sparse; tilesets are usually just hallways; few interactable objects to speak of
- Classes have little variety except for stat differences
- AoEs are often very weak and useless even if they are nice-looking
- No real magic weilding aside from single-use scrolls and very sparse magic wands
- Only other long-range combat is crossbows. No regular bows to speak of, and both long-range weapons are surprisingly rare
- You will most likely be forced to sword-and-board style gameplay in each run; makes combat very repetitive
- Sidetasks encourage boring grinding which clashes with the typical quick-playthroughs of rogue-likes
- Co-op is a little wonky, as progress is saved on the host's file, and friends may lose progress if accidentally disconnected; Additionally, jumping in later in the host's game will make it difficult for guests
- Although it is challenging, it won't be so much for Dark Souls veterans
- At times you will notice the game takes its mechanics almost too much verbatim from Dark Souls
- Textures for drops are sometimes bland, and the top right part of the hud is also a little boring
Still not quite there yet. Perhaps the biggest issue in the game is variety. If there are so many weapons, enemies, biomes, and two (hopefully eventually more) classes, then why don't they feel different? Swords and axes are all too similar, and tiers only affect stats and maybe an elemental difference. Staves don't actually have any magical attributes even though they drop from mages, meaning they're basically like greatswords, which are basically like hammers. This goes on ad nauseam. More than half of the mob types are melee-based (although there are the few real gems like the floating laser-shooting orbs, the mole-like enemies, and the floating monk-like enemies with extendable arms that hit HARD), and the only two classes are also strictly melee-based with the only variety being in stats. No special skills to speak of.
(outside of the very few wands and single-use scrolls)
The game really restricts itself to sword-and-board builds most of the time, but there's plenty of variety that can easily be added and I really hope the devs notice this untapped potential.
Effective rogue-likes like Enter the Gungeon have a few classes that have unique special attributes and a plethora of different items that can be obtained, each of which have different unique effects and capabilities. A similar approach can be used for Necropolis weapons.
There really are ways to make this game work to its strengths and even add new strengths.
For basing itself off of Dark Souls as well as other rogue-likes, Necropolis chooses to leave out the few aspects that really define those good games.
In Necropolis, you're almost guaranteed for an enemy to drop its weapon if it has one. While scrolls, potions, and food are a little more rare, they're still quite common. In one run on Enter the Gungeon, there's no way you're going to see even half of the item pool the game has to offer, but that's more than likely in Necropolis. Note that enemies don't drop as good of items as chests, and chests are much more rare, but the extent to which enemies drop items is a little too much. Additionally, both Dark Souls and rogue-likes pride themselves on their boss fights.
While these are more intensive changes, they're still very good ideas to add to the game in the long-term.
I know Necropolis can get there, they just have to push content that can address these issues with variety. Perhaps the most blatant issue is that the mobs and biomes are so unvaried that you're guaranteed to get howlers and pyramid men in the beginning before it really opens up in the later floors, and this also means that you're guaranteed to get the same weapons in the beginning in each run. Additionally, many of the biomes have some cell designs that are very large and open for exploration, but there is often very little to discover in these areas.
The game still feels unfinished as is, and I wish they had spent more time to make sure the amount of content matched the hefty price tag, but they still could. I hope they realize they still have a chance.

A few noteworthy things first: yes, this is only episode 1, so naturally it ends on a cliffhanger and overall isn't very long.
All Kickstarter backers of course will receive episode 2 in addition. For all others I think 10€ are a fair price. Also consider that sales now ensure the quality of episode 2.
I really wanted to like the game - I was a backer since Gamescom. And I mostly liked it.
The art design is very beautiful, the sounds (which have come a long way since the Gamescom demo) are good, the collectibles/backstory thingies are nice, the setting is cool, Red Hood's remarks are often witty, and so on.
I didn't have any crashes. Followers of the campaign on Kickstarter, Facebook and/or Twitter will see the game and understand how much effort this small independent team from Belgium put into this game and how that mostly paid off.
But: Don't get me wrong, I'm fine with a hard game. But the checkpoints are often ridicolously far away from each other. When dying close to the end of a section means having to re-do the whole long section the frustration potential is plainly high. Also, checkpoints do not really save the game, if you quit it and restart later you often end up a while before your last "basket" (checkpoint). Not cool.
Also, standard controls on keyboard sometimes seem fiddly and non-optimal.
Yes, I would still recommend the game. But I do hope for a patch for the checkpoint/saving system - or at least a better one in episode 2.
(I played on "normal" difficulty. There also are "easy" and "hard".)

The problem was always the sea of information you inevitably start drowning in without getting your feet wet with fan tutorials (looking at you CK2, and EU4) or some such.
Stellaris breaks this trend.
This game serves as the perfect gateway game into these, and it doesn't even have to be that way--Stellaris itself has enouch charm and depth to keep you around, especially knowing that it will be supported in the time to come.  If space isn't your thing, then sure this is an excellent way to be introduced to the genre, but otherwise you can do away with your hesitation from intimidation.
The in game tutorial is integrated into the main game and helps you understand how to look at a star system and decide what's important and what you need to do.  It's not step by step, however: your helpful AI gives you a list of tasks that are recommended to be finished for a fledgling galactic civilization, and within this list it tells you how to do it and why it's important.  It's up to you when and where you want to do each thing, or if you want to at all, but in general it points you in the right direction.
It isn't flawless, however, as the deeper you dive, the more options you'll encounter, and the more options you encounter the more likely you'll feel like you're drowning.  I've personally never had that feeling and I honestly do think the game does a good job of easing you in, but it's definitely probable that some players will become overwhelmed.
There's something else that isn't talked about too much, but can clearly be seen from reading other reviews.  Stellaris and other games by PDS showcase their grand strategy by the expanse of their setting.  In this case, you're another civilization among other aliens across the galaxy.  The game truly shines if you're seeking a narrative or if you wish to roleplay.  The game offers plenty for both those who want to efficiently dominate (through peace OR war), or those who want to create a story.
I haven't played it long enough to find out how it holds up in the mid/late to late stages of the game, but I imagine the management across star systems is terrifying.  Not everything is explained very thoroughly, either, and either trial and error or the community will have to pull through for you (for now at least).  I've heard complaints that the UI isn't very good, but I found it delightful both aesthetically and functionally.  There are truthfully some bugs to be ironed out, but it's only the third day or so and many major ones have already been dealt with, proving PDS's support.
Stellaris offers plenty for everyone, and its accessibility is seriously impressive considering its scope.  This is all from single player experience, by the way, I can't wait to see how exciting multiplayer is.  The strategic management from planetary troops, to space stations, resources across solar systems, and fleets across galaxies is both intimidating and amazing.  The experiences you come across from this is something other games can't touch.
I recommend without a doubt.  If you're on the fence because you're afraid you won't be able to grasp it, I'd say give it a try.  If you don't spend two hours creating your own alien empire you can still refund it during the tutorial.

I've finally played enough that I think I owe this a review.
Pandora's very clearly inspired by Alpha Centauri, but the underlying mechanics are quite innovative and different. At core this game is about super specializing your cities, micromanaging the population in your cities, and fighting the other factions. Unfortunately, the game doesn't really *tell* you how to manage your population or make the interface intuitive to focus around it.  At best, it offers 'lock buttons' on population types.  The combat is so-called multiple unit per tile, which removes some of the problems of Civ's one unit per tile.
The game falls down badly in diplomacy, where the AI seems to essentially perform a force count comparison to decide whether to attack.  Get behind in military force and you'll suddenly find yourself under attack.  Lose or even have a few units weakened in the skirmish and suddenly the other AI will all decide to join the fray and you might as well restart.  The tension, of course, is if you're building tons of military to avoid the AI pile-on, you aren't shotgunning ahead in science.
In combat, the AI seems to be decently competent, although late in the game they build tons of lower-tech units as opposed to higher tech ones.  They will brutally shell your cities with artillery and destroy modifier tiles.  The guy who rewrote the AI deserves a pat on the back for the challenge they offer in combat.
As for personality, Pandora doesn't have any wonders or memorable personalities like Civ's Montezuma and Ghandi, just the brutal optimization game of managing your population and keeping up your military.  The game's systems are too brittle to allow for casual play.  If you're not carefully optimizing everything from the beginning, then you're not going to have fun. This game was a missed opportunity. Civ needed some competition or at least someone doing something new and different.  This isn't it.

I frankly wasn't expecting anything more than a bland generic Civilization or a bland generic Alpha Centauri...
And indeed, the game is pretty much a generic Alpha Centauri. But it's much more well made than I imagined it would be. The presentation is pretty good, the interface might not be the most beautiful one in the world but it is polished and functional, the tooltips are truly helpful, ingame information is easy to find, etc.
The semi-random tech tree is pretty big, with each research unlocking one specific item (a building, operation, project, unit part or such). Research seems to be quick overall, so are you constantly getting new stuff in small increments.
I tend to dislike unit customization in 4x games; more often than not that's just busywork. I enjoy the way customization works here, though, some of the pieces you unlock give you interesting specialized units.
But more importantly, I think, is that ultimately what bores from other 4x games and make me go back to Civilization (or to Grand Strategy games) is the AI. There are a number of 4x games out there that are extremely polished and sleek, with interesting and well designed system... but ultimately I grow bored of them rather quickly because the AI doesn't seem to have any clue whatsoever about the game. It's like I'm playing alone in a sandbox, no matter the difficulty. As much as the AI of CivV is criticized, it at least tries to win and to interact with the player.
From what I could gather, Pandora is now being patched by a person from the community, who has been focusing on AI improvements. Obviously I haven't played a lot of it yet, but from the matches I've played, I really enjoyed the AI behavior I saw (except perhaps by how quickly they changed their mind regarding diplomatic agreements) - it seemed to react really well to what was happening around it, I felt like I was having an actual impact in the game world instead of playing by myself while the AIs played by themselves.
Bottom line is: Pandora is giving me the "one more turn" vibe that non-Civilization 4Xs almost never manage to give me. The fact that there are decisions to be made almost every couple of turns (instead of long dull periods) and the fact that the AI seems to be really trying to compete with me are what collaborate to this, I think.

Once again, another  game with unlimited potential was spoiled. By now you'd think that video game manufacturers (Specifically Electronic Arts) would know better.
Here are the reasons why I say, no, this game should not be bought:
1. There are too few nations in this game. Giving the game more nations would make it much better, since there is more competition for the world.
2. Get rid of the damned growth! The game forces you to grow and colonize new areas, even there is nothing else to colonnize. When you colonize the world and have nothing elser to colonize, you still get kicked around by your own cities eventually. You lose minerals, food, science, and credits, losing your military and formers. Why must you lose formers when they are required for making your nation stand back up?
3. Too few unit types. There are only 3 vehicles of each kind, walkers, tanks, boats, troops, and strike craft. This seems a little limited.
Here are the reasons why I would recommend this game:
1. The unit customization in the workshop offers a whole new way to play 4x games. You can customize your foot soldiers with missile launchers, machine guns, snipers, and more. This isn't limited to just foot soldiers though, strike craft, tanks, and boats all use this as well.
But that's probably it.
Do NOT buy this game, it is a waste of time, space, and money.

Going into this year I didn’t expect the horror game genre to impress me as much as it has. It is notorious for producing a lot of poorly made and cheap thrill caliber cash grabs. The Steam catalog is literally full of them. Anyone who has had a Steam account for any reasonable length of time can rattle off several of them without even thinking about it. But to be honest I’ve enjoyed quite a few horror games this year. Many of the ones that I have reviewed have impressed me. For example, in the past couple of weeks I featured Downfall and a few days later followed that with Shadows Peak which I believe is the best horror game that I have played since last year’s Until Dawn on the PS4.
That brings me to today’s feature on Hush Hush: Unlimited Survival Horror. It was released – remembering I use the Australian Steam store – on March 26 which is a week as I write this. Sadly, the game already appears to be heavily hidden in the Steam library as the game possesses just the single solitary review which is also a private one. I assume that it is the hefty $19.99 ($17.99 when it was on its debut discount) price that have scared the punters away.
And then when I try to open the game I realize why nobody has reviewed the game and there is already a documented case of it in the Steam discussion forum. The game doesn’t download anything whatsoever when you attempt to download the game from Steam. Of course the report that it feeds back is missing executable. I’ve reported the issue and will return to the game at a later date.
Returning to the game the next day the issue that I had has been repaired and the depots have been repaired enabling me to play the game. Anticipating fun I load the game. Getting the value proposition out of the way early, unfortunately, I can tell you that in my opinion – the missing executable aside – the game is in no way worth the current $19.99 asking price. The content in the game just isn’t engrossing enough to be anything more than your mid-tier indie game.
First of all the character that you control’s moves are quite clunky. Clunky actually does a very good job of describing the game in its totality. The camera – although there are at least three camera options (left, right and centre) are not the best. Field of vision is mediocre. The graphics are okay at best. The gameplay is mediocre as you wander around caves destroying crystals and hiding and moving away from ghosts and other horrors. It shows some potential but it misses the mark because of the clumsy play and certainly at this price point.
Pricing your game appropriately is a tough challenge. You don’t want to mark it too high because people wont buy it and you definitely don’t want to put it at a too low a point and miss out on important revenue. This one is in the too high zone because of its downsides. I could possibly overlook it if they weren’t asking you to pay this much and would consider half the asking price to be a much more reasonable expectation.
I do hope that the development team keep working at creating games even if I would give this one a miss.

Witcher 2 is my favorite game. It is a solid RPG with a lot of action and a brilliant story. It is very mature in a lot of its themes and situations. This game is based on novels written by a Polish authornamed Andrzej Sapkowski. You play as Geralt, a Witcher, or a genetically enhanced monster hunter. They have been described as a kind of warrior monk. Geralt drinks special potions that let him far exceed the abilities of normal humans. These potions are needed to battle the various beasts of the realms. Witchers also have a very limited understanding of magical energy called Witcher's Signs. Basically the Signs are spells, like a fireball and a paralysis trap spell and a few others. Geralt is an interesting character because he is not quite human but hes not a monster either. Due to their methods and abilities, however, many in the world see Witchers as freaks and monsters. Which is really what the game's ideology is all about; the greyness in everyone, not the clear cut black and white. Which to me, is a welcome change from the usual: 1) "hey I'm a good guy I will help you" 2) "Not my problem Kachinsky" 3) F*** YOU F*** FACE," that many other game are notorious for. Geralt is often put in positions of just making a choice, not good or evil, just difficult decisions that have a lot of positives and negatives to them. The story is top notch, and eerily real in many of the stuggles of the world.
Geralt has a set of skill trees (sword, magic, alchemy) that the player can advance in any way. All into one or spliced between the three. Sword fighting is a core mechanic though, so no matter how you play, Geralt will always have two swords. A silver sword for monsters, and a normal sword for humans. There are a few other weapons too but mostly its swords. Depending on the player preference combat can be a bit like the Batman games, or the Assassins Creed games. In some ways it can be like Chivalry: Medieval Warfare. Weapons and armor play a big part as well and can effect all of the skill trees. Making the game very balanced between gear and character tree choices. Not to the crazy levels of a Diablo game but enough to make for a very quality rpg.
Mostly though, Witcher 2 is a lot like skyrim. I do not want to bash on skyrim here, it is also a great game that a lot of people absolutely love. I feel, however, that Witcher is far better than skyrim and think the people that love skyrim should try the Witcher. Both games have the northern lore and feel. Witcher 2 is no where near as large or open as skyrim. Witcher is much more linear but the story and combat and the world just feel so much better in every way to me. The enemies and the different races were better portrayed during the game. When I came to a new town in skyrim I did not get that feeling of truly new. Just another town and another barbarian guy leading it. Witcher was totally different, you get the feeling of racial tensions and social tensions in every part. The powers that be are very different and each very developed and very human. As it plays out you really see how the choices alter the world, instead of it coming down to "OK I'm a good guy so I will save good guy town." A lot of games try to get that feeling across of the characters true M.O. and demeanor but fail. Witcher acomplishes this very well. Triple AAA quality. Superb graphics, superb voice acting. I enjoyed every character. There were a few times, of course, where some tones were a bit off but that happens in every game. Overall amazing game. When I learned that this game was made by a small studio in Poland I was shocked.
As someone who never read any of the books and did not play the first game, I found that after a second playthrough the story and everyhting started to click and I realised how well done everything really was. The way the game is, one would want to play it at least twice to see both sides of what is going on.
It seems as though more than a few people found the game to be really difficult. It can be, but now there are plenty of guides and discussions about it. The game has a kind of reverse curve for the difficulty. It is much harder in the beginning due to a lack of points in the skill tree and low grade weapons and armor. By the end though, Geralt is pretty much on par with jezuz. I like games of this nature, because being really stong at the end makes it feel like you really acomplished something.
This game also has subtitles in many languages so I found it made a great gift for steam friends who are not natural to the english language.
I would reccommend this game to anyone. Especially anyone who likes Skyrim, Assassin's Creed, Batman, Chivalry, or even the imfamous Darksouls 1 & 2

Background: Picked up in a bundle, played with my 8 year old nephew.
Impressions: Enchanting. Absolutely charming and lovingly crafted. I've had few gaming experiences quite as rewarding and intriguing. The simple, talkative exposition via letters is pitch perfect and the holds together perfectly with the gentle score and cute visuals. The story does take some oddly dark turns and some of the visuals are mildly creepy (not for young kids, without being anything bad.. just not all sweetness) which I actually enjoyed as it made the plot all the more interesting.
I can see this is not a game for everyone. It's short, simple and lots of text to read. But if you take the time to enjoy it it's a fine experience.
The Good:
*Simple mechanics, fire looks and works great
*Charming visuals, music and characters
*Each item burns differently.
*Builds a world though letters and descriptive writing
*Dark plot twists and creepy toys add interest
*Combo system is rewarding to puzzle out
*Superb, rewarding and unexpected finale
The Bad:
*Could be longer, all over in a 4-6 hours
*Some combos are really hard to figure out
*The darker elements of the toys and story can be off-putting
Recommended for: anyone with a love of simple, elegant puzzle games with beautifully crafted stories.
Conclusion.
8/10. Not for everyone but there's a lot here if you give it time.

First off, I'd give this game 6/10, but still I don't necessarily recommend it. It has enough good things going for it that some people might like it, but the bad qualities almost outweight them. Most importantly, the interface is one of the worst I've seen in a long time. For example, you can't see your armour rating from the inventory, but have to go to character screen (and even in there it's not on the first page). The inventory system is garbage anyway, you can't see how much you are carrying, and there are WAY too many categories, potions, formulae, crafting materials etc. Other annoyances about the interface include having to stop to use the medallion (and you will have to use it very often), trying to open a door but instead lighting a torch next to it, not being able to sprint, et cetera.
I've not progressed far in the main story yet, but so far I'm not particularly impressed. There are way too many characters which pop up in conversations, and you can't look them up during the chat. One guy approached me and told me some guy had sent me a message and a package, but I couldn't find him from the journal. Looking him up on the internet, I found out he was from the first game. Even had I played the first one, I'm pretty sure I couldn't have remembered some random name from an earlier game. Also, having escaped to a remote location via the river, I was found by bounty-hunters the following afternoon. There is no way they could have found me that fast, and that immediately broke the immersion. Most of the conversations so far have been okay, but I've yet to see anything special which would explain the high praise this game has had for its story. I'm not sure what people meant this is "mature storytelling", maybe it means that you see naked women (no men though so far, which is sad), most of the character are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, drunk or violent. These may qualify as mature themes for adolescents, but probably not for most adults.
I hope to continue playing this, because there are good things about this game, but the irritation from a thousand minor design flaws is really getting to me. There's a chance this might turn out to be an okay game, just badly made, but I'm not holding my breath. This is what happens when the design focuses too much on graphics (which run very poorly, even though they are rather pretty even on lowest settings). Oh, and the stealth mechanics are so bad I can hardly believe it. And don't get me started on the meditate-to-drink-potions rubbish. All it does is it makes you need to quick save all the time, and when a combat starts, you'll probably want to reload and meditate-to-drink-potions and face the same enemies again. A game which relies on loading a save is not doing everything right.
Thankfully I only paid less than 3 euros for this.

I loved it and had a great time playing it, but you may not.  So, let's discuss it's progency, for a moment.
The game owes it's existence to the joyful Legend of Grimrock, which did a great job updating the games of my youth.  MMX is an even more direct throwback to the original Bard's Tale in 1985.  The Bard's Tale took Wizardry and added outdoor areas.  Sure, they weren't that different -- they were basically dungeons with sky blue tiles as opposed to underground grey and brown tiles, but the effect worked on me.
If you have some nostalgia for the early days of RPG gaming, this will likely hit a home run.  It reminds me of playing games on my Apple II, even including watching the graphics render.  What I really enjoyed most was developing my characters and watching them become increasingly powerful.  I wanted them well prepared for the final battle, and there are many opportunities to improve their skills and their loot.
Pros:
- RPG nostalgia
- Good skills and character development options
- Good magic system
- The individual quests and dungeon were mostly fun
- Combat is well done
- To me, at least, the game is almost perfectly balanced (with the stock party).  Only toward the end did I begin to feel overpowered.  Most of the game, the battles were close and tense, but rarely did my entire party die.
- Great opportunities for exploration -- there is always something new to find
- No monster respawns!!  Once you clear an area, it stays clear.  I like that.
Cons:
- Graphics look good, but take a long time to render.  At one point, the landscape renders well before the castle sitting on the landscape renders.  That's just weird.
- Members have your party have comments about everything going on around them.  I love that.  Except that they repeat the same things over and over and over again.  We get it... human cities are as dangerous as the jungle.  Let's move on.  When characters finish a major battle, they cheer an entirely disingenuous "Yay!"  It sounds exactly like a bunch of poorly paid actors sitting around their home microphones trying to appear enthusiastic.
-  With some exceptions, most of the battles use pretty much the same tactics.  I had the same criticism of Dragon Age.  So this game is not unique, in this regard.
I've invested about 55 hours into this game.  And I had a lot of fun doing it.  If you have  a soft spot in your heart for the RPG dungeon-crawling heyday of the 80s, I think you'll really enjoy this.  I sure did.

TL:DR - This is not a faithful recreation at all. The clostest thing you get is the freedom to make your own party of characters and even this is very limited. Besides that, you are moving along with a grid-based world, permentally stuck in turn-based combat. In a world that punishes exploration.
===Combat===
Combat is all turn-based. If you and an enemy are right next to each other, you cannot move. This means that once you engage in combat, You're stuck. No leaving. No retreating. And this becomes a serious problem when you start to explore. You will go to areas that you are not prepared for. And You will get into combat with things you cannot fight. And You can't run. You will die... For exploring... In an open world RPG that encourages you to explore. The previous might and magic games have made it possible. But the problem is the addition of this grid based combat/exploration. In previous games, you could go to an impossible difficulty area, and the first attack kills a party member. You turn, and run away. Maybe lose another party member to a stray shot. But you can still run away and escape. Nothing bound you, like a grid does here. If an enemy engages you in melee combat, you're stuck exchanging blows. No smart manuvering or tactical fighting like in previous games or in legend of grimmock.... No, make your attacks, take your blows, repeat until you or the enemy is dead.
===Exploration===
As mentioned previously, you are punished for exploring if you happen to end up in an area you cannot fight in. You have to use that quick save... Alot. Its not even fun to explore. Everything is grid based. So you will find boundaries, and areas that look like you can go through but you can't because the grid says you can't go here. It's a massive step down from the previous games where you could scale mountions, fly above and look at the whole world, or jump into the water and risk drowning to discover cool treasures. Heck, it was rewarding to go exploring in areas, that your party wasn't prepared for, to grab some of the loot there. None of that in this game.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a fantastyic beat'em all that draws inspiration from the great Muramasa.  This game has everything that a player looks for in a video game:  poetry, wonder, quality gameplay, smart ideas and fantastic implementation, powerful sensations and great pleasure/satisfaction.  I strongly recommend this game for the following reasons:
Pros:
+ Both an enchanting and brutal environment/story.
+ A magnificient artistic direction.
+ A speedy and nervous gameplay.
+ Over 10 hours to finish the game.
+ A good soundtrack
+ A low price for the quality of the game.  Seriously, there are some garbage games out there for $49+.
Cons or Tips:
+ Start with higher difficulty if you want a serious challenge.
+ Combos could have been made more complex.

This is a pretty fun rogue-like. It has a pretty comfortable combat system and the overall mechanics are familiar. The minimalist models and textures actually work really well for this game.
I really like the overall feel of Necropolis. It's got a sense of humor. It's got a nice design aesthetic. The game is strongly influenced by the Souls series, but it is uniquely it's own thing.
My brother and I beat this in co-op in a little under 20 hours. That being said, I am still seeing new items every game. I feel like there is plenty of replay value, and have yet to see 4 player co-op mayhem.
Combat reminds me a lot of Prepare to Die Edition, and I feel like that is at least in part a design choice. I think this is one of the more prominent influences of Dark Souls on this game. Some of the weapons are slow or have funny arcs to their attacks. You can injure and kill other players in co-op mode. You can accidentally queue up attacks at inconvenient times.  This game is not a beat em up. You die if you are careless in your methods. I like that.
You don't completely start over from scratch every time you die. There is a persistent currency that you can use for upgrades or to unlock new color schemes for your character. You can also craft food and potions from materials you find.
This is a very fun and replayable game for the price tag. If you like rogue-likes or the Souls series, or both, you'll have plenty of fun.

This game is modeled after Might and Magic 1-5, in the sense that it takes place on a grid and is entirely turn-based.  It has a lot of what made the old might and magic games good to great, but you'll definitely notice some streamlining and trimming of features.  All character skills have shifted towards combat, and you won't reach a point where you get a forester or mountaineer perk that lets you pass through impassible terrain.  Regardless, fans of the series will enjoy a bit tighter of a Might and Magic experience.. and those unfamiliar with the series will be in for some new challenges and possible frustration.  Playing on Warrior difficulty, there were some definitely challenging moments, but I managed to make it through despite picking sub-optimal character classes.
At the end of the day, it was a good solid dungeon crawl with an old-school feel.  Recommended for someone who wants a dungeon crawl with the occasional puzzle.

The Binding Of Issac is a game I would reccomend,
TL;DR 7/10 fun to play  for a couple of hours, shallow game mechanics leave you wanting more and rely to heavily on the "random" aspect of the game, artsyle's nice yet gory, sound assets and music is pretty good if a little repetitive and the story is forgettable at the very least.
First of all lets go over the game mechanics.
You play as Issac, a scared little boy who is hiding from his mother in a basement after god tells her to sacrifice him to prove her faith. You start in an area which teaches you the basic controls, WASD to move around, space bar to use an item, shift to throw a bomb and either the mouse or arrow keys to fire projectiles. Tears being the stock projectile you start with each round. The levels are a mixture of randomly generated rooms that contain various enemies that will try to kill Issac, some rooms contain a passive upgrade that will boost Issacs abilities in some way (damage, attack speed, attack pattern etc.), some rooms contain an item shop (coins are found throughout the levels) and finally the final type of rooms contain a boss battle. The bosses themselves are fun if a little bit easy all it talkes is to beat them is to move away from them and keep shooting, as is the same with every encounter in the game, there's barely any strategy to it and this is where my biggest gripe with the game is. it becomes boring very quickly. for the first couple of hours I had fun blasting my way through enemies and trying tostack as many passives as I can but it gets old after an hour or so. the main motivation (for me anyway) was the sense of accomplishment when you beat that boss you tried so hard to kill before but were too ill equipped which brings me onto my next point. Whether you win or lose relies on the random aspect of the game. This means that you can either have a godly run where eveything is going your way or a run that is doomed to fail. personally I feel games should not be this way because however good you are at this game means nothing if you dont get good drops.
On to the artsyle.
There isnt really much to say besides that the cartoony yet dark and gory art direction works to give The Binding Of Issac a certain charm and compliments the story perfectly. its innocent yet visually disturbing at the same time and I LOVE IT!!
The Sound design is also top notch, the ememies all sound creepy and alien, the music is good and matches the settings perfectly, I feel they should have included more songs though as along with the gameplay it gets repetitive after the first two hours or so.
overall, the game is good if a little repetitive and is perfectly worth it for $5 or less and I expect more great things from the sequel.

Alright, so I bought this game when it became available for Pre-purchase and this is my "first" review of a game.
After a 24 hours of total playtime, I can tell these:
-Gameplay will slow down and sometimes game starts to lag when lots of things happen.
(However I believe that Paradox will fix this problem with patches.)
-Time-consuming. I mean, literally, last night I wasn't able to sleep at all! "One more research, one more battle!"
-No "micromanagemant" for battles. You can equip your ships with aggressive or defensive computer chips and that's that. You can't order a certain ship to attack another ship. They're all automated.
-Planets/Moons become repetitive. After a lot of surveying, you realize that the planets look like each other a lot.
(Someone made a video review for this game said they could use some kind of "random planet generator".)
+Satisfying visuals. They actually done a great job with the stars, blackholes and etc.
+Also satisfying micromanagement of your empire. If you have played Civilizations before, you'll get used to it in no time.
+Sleek/Simple UI. If you prefer, your robot guide will notify and give you info every time something happens. Very good for learning the basics.
+HUGE map. I mean, literally, it so HUGE that you can't keep an eye on everything. LOTS of Empires, LOTS of stuff going on.
+Primitive/Superior Civs. You invent FTL and go to space bla bla... When you do that, you may get b*tchslapped right in your face by another empire that was in space WAY LONGER than you do.  Also, you may b*tchslap another civs which may be in Industrial Age, or maybe Bronz Age even.
+Detailed race/perks creating. Really, it gives you a lot of options to create your own race.
+Very easy and accessible gameplay. What I mean is, you can select a constructor/science ship and order them around by right clicking the ststem/planet/moon etc. Right click, opens up a menu. "I was like-wuuuuuut".  Mouse hover info and simple screens make it easier to make "strategies".
+OST's are really AMAZING. I really care about sounds in a game and Stellaris doesn't disappoint me with that. "Thank youuu"
CONCLUSION: You should buy this game. There are a lot of rooms for modding&DLC's so I guess Paradox will provide gameplay improvements with patches&expansions.

For anyone who thought that MM6 and MM7 were the best games in the series, this game is a huge let down. The developers took the best part of the game series, the sandbox element, and replaced it with a linear piece of junk.
There were three aspects of the game that I enjoyed, the riddles and/or puzzles, being able to gather most quest objects without having the quest active yet (it saved me a lot of running around and back-tracking), and the fallout-style epilogue for some of the completed quests, that I got after beating the game. It could have given me a little extra time to read them, but whatever.
That said, those are the only three elements of the game that I enjoyed and if I had to rate the game on a scale of one to ten, I'd say it'd rate a three with their inclusion.
The rest is just full of dross, I beat the game and started today on the Falcon and the Unicorn DLC. Got fed up when it just transported me to the dungeon and dumped all the stuff I had. Even if I would have gotten my things back by getting to the second level of said dungeon, the approach and how it handled the interaction does not make sense to me.
Having said all of this, I can forgive a lot if there is a good story included in a game.
The story given is a piece of crap. The more I think about diffent elements in it, the less it makes sense to me.
It is presented in such a way as to celebrate how humans can do anything, while slandering the names of two real-life angels according to the bible, and presenting the policy of the separation of church and state as something that is needed because the angels are the corrupt element in the government. This just doesn't make sense to me in a fictional world, where as far as I know every other supernatural being is given a made up name. Why go to the trouble of offending people who believe the two named angels are real beings in the real world, and one of which is described in the book of Daniel as the Great Prince who protects the Jews? The writer could have just as easily made up another name for these mortal non-angels as they are presented in the world.
There are other issues I have with the game, lots of them, but you don't need to hear general griping from me. Just suffice to say that my personal tastes find this game to be extremely lacking on several levels, despite looking forward to playing it since I heard that it was being made.
Some may claim that I'm setting the bar too high, but I think it's high enough for an expectation of what to expect from a game calling itself 'Might+Magic x:Legacy' when the Wizardry series ended on an awesome note with Wizardry 8. I can play Wizardry 8 to this day and have an awesome time, but I can tell you all that I'm never touching this piece of crap again. Later! Time to play Wizardry 7, I want to see what I can do with a party starting W8 as allies of the other races...

TL;DR: Get the game. You wouldn't even be here reading reviews if you don't like space 4x games, and this is a great 4x game
First of all you start in a galaxy of a maximum of 1000 stars(there are mods to play even more stars). planets/asteroids,etc are in orbit around stars, which adds a nice immersion, Factions are randomly generated every game, instead of the same old prebuilt factions that you have in other 4x games, although you can build your own factions to spawn in the galaxy if you wish do to so. and there's lots and lots of different variable options so that you basically will never meet the same faction twice, huge number of government types, ideas, culture, races, ship types, FTL types, etc. Faction customization is great, It's like every possible faction personality is available to create. you can even customize the random names the factions give to their people, ships, fleets, armies, planets, stars, etc.
Tons of events are happening in the galaxy as well, giving it more personality and flavor, sometimes the game gives you quest-like missions where you have to study this wreckage, then it will lead to another points of interests, leading to new techs, bonuses, etc.
Empire management is awesome, you can actually select your type of government(and change it in-game) resulting in different types of bonuses and government systems. You can have a democracy where there's an election every 5 years, 50 years, or a dictatorship, empire, religion-based faction, science-lead faction, etc, etc. Each elected leader has different personalities as well, with different aims, platforms, etc. Some ruler will want to bring back slavery to your empire when elected for example. Rulers are picked from a pool of leaders, basically your admirals, generals, researchers, and governors in your empire, and they have different agendas if they get elected as leader, Support the one you like the most. Factions can also form up inside your empire if your population's culture and beliefs become more and more varied. Some people may like the current government, some people may want changes or reforms.
The population system is also well-made. You can actually play as a non-genocidal xenophilic type, where every race(or certain races only, it's up to you) is welcome to your empire. again, unlike other 4x games where it's you or them. You can have an empire composing of many different races, a pan-species empire. and they can have different privileges, like giving them rights to vote, to move freely, etc. You can be as racist as you like or as welcoming as you like. or both! welcome them, and then exterminate them! Your choice. You can even genetically manipulate your own species, or other races, or create robots, androids, or genetically enhanced soldiers, some races might be better soldiers than others, use them as such.
Some would say the diplomacy is lacking compared to other games, but I beg to differ. There's lots of things to do in the diplomacy side. First of all, FEDERATIONS, you can actually form federations with different factions, not just alliances, but federations, you elect a federation president every few years and rotate around the different members, the federation also has their own shared federation fleet, comprising of technology taken from all the members. It's similar to GalCiv's United Planets but you aren't forced to join and it's not automatically created for everyone, even enemy factions. Lots of different treaties like star chart sharing, non-aggression treaties, embassies, research ventures, and good ol' resource trading. There's no traditional 'trade lines' trading like in galciv though. You can make a faction your vassal, and there are multiple types, you can even play as vassal to another empire and eventually liberate yourself from it if you want to. you can also integrate them into your empire.
One more awesome thing is you can actually see primitive civilizations in game!, and they all vary and you can see them in different states, whether they are in the early space age, bronze age, industrial, etc. or you might even see a dead world where a past civilization blew themselves up due to nuclear war. If you are playing as non-humans, you might even see our own Solar System!, maybe we blew ourselves up? maybe you just arrived in time before we do? or you arrived during our cavemen days and chose to observe us instead? You can observe them, advance their technology, abduct them for experiments or even uplift them, or invade and exterminate them.
Resources system is well made, you mine minerals from planets, asteroids, either from orbit, or if you have the planet colonized, on the ground. You need minerals basically for everything that you construct. You can construct power plants, in lots of different ways in order to get Energy Credits, which is the main currency of the game. You also have three research resources: Society, Engineering and Physics, and different celestial bodies give bonuses to them when an orbital station or facility is constructed. You also gain influence points to use on diplomacy or actions related to your empire/faction/government.
You also can have three researches going on in parallel, which is Society, Engineering and Physics, which is much more immersive as well. no more having to decide whether to research for your colony infrastructure first or for your military strength, etc. Technology is smartly randomized every time you finish a research, meaning, there is no fixed research tree, you get the immersion of really researching stuff, as you won't know what technology lies far ahead.
Space Warfare is similar to your usual Space RTS games, with the good addition of Turn Based like status reports, where you can see statistics of the battle while it is going on, there is also land warfare in which you can create and recruit armies and invade planets to finally colonize them, you can also get air support from your ships in orbit and bombard the planet however way you want.
Great game, huge great potential to become one of the best space 4x games ever made after more content is made(DLCs, expansions) I'm not saying it's lacking content though, it's got more than enough to keep you playing. My expectations on this game was not that high considering all other recent 4X games have been 'meh' for me, and I haven't really played any Paradox Interactive games that much. It's already better than most if not all other 4x games out there, and it's only going to get better with time.

The Devine Ascension is too weak in its Southern outpost to sustain the invasion, so the aliens quickly move on to attack us in our mainland. We regroup multiple times, playing it safe and concentrating most of our army on the Southern border, just a few hundred miles South of our capital.
Year 13: The alien invasion was repelled. Yet, with the religious fanactis in the North-East, there is no time to celebrate our brave troops.
Year 15: The religious fanatics have been wiped of the planet. Unfortunately, we were too worried about the life of our noble service men and thusly, attacked too cautiously. Also, we had significant forces concentrated on our Southern border, to defend against an alien invasion. Now, most of the former "divine" empire has been taken by the Terra Salvum faction - what we took with fast, mobile units to get a piece of the cake, is far too little. Man, what a shot in the foot!
Year 15-27: Our army goes through a major restructuring and we have difficulty keeping it up to date with current technology. We dont really know how to catch up with Terra Salvum, as the diplomatic affiliations make it difficult to atttack anyone who is a major player in this game. Meanwhile, our cities disappear in smog and our people die of lung cancer.
Year 28: We have poluted this planet 400x times worse than we ever poluted earth. We have massive production facilities though now we lack the minerals to produce at maximu capacities.
Year 29: Terra Salvum developes a new super weapon, mini black holes, to annihilate whole cities and armies. Our most current super weapon is still called "nuclear missiles". We have to do something!
Year 30: We do the only rational thing: Declare war on the Solar Dynasty, the second weakest empire with only 4 cities. Their out-dated and weak military is no match for us. Year 32: We regroup our forces, and develop further nuclear capabilities. New weapons and new wars will make our people forget that they are hungry and unhealthy, and that we are out of living space and minerals. We plan an invasion of the Noxium Corporations territory. Year 33: We ll see. I am not there yet!

I love games like this. Well, I love games like this when they don't have massive problems. Pandora: First Contact is marred by two things as far as I'm concerned, though both of them are kinda the same thing - the enemy AI. I say enemy AI because that's what it is. Unless you jump through a mass of hoops and play in an incredibly specific way and don't let population get higher or lower than that little gap between X and Y and don't let your cash reserves do the same, or your armed forces power level, or the amount of land you have, or the improvements, or the... you get the idea, right? Long story short, it's next to impossible to keep the AI controlling the other factions happy, and when it isn't happy it becomes schitzophrenic. One turn it hates you but wants an alliance, the next turn it loves you but is denouncing you and cancelling all your treaties. It must have been incredibly hard to code an AI worse than the one in Civ 5, but they did it.
The second problem with the AI is just how utterly it cheats. I'm honestly not sure that they didn't tag the difficulty levels backwards. To test just how bad it is I started a game on the lowest, easiest difficulty level and a couple hundred turns in I'd colonised and developed the continent I was on and the the enemy factions in their two or three tiny little cities were still totally, utterly eclipsing me in reasearch to the point where they were fielding units two or three tech levels above what I had available. This is with the entire research output of about ten massive cities crammed with scientists and it was being completely outmatched by two or three crappy little cities with maybe one or two tiles upgraded around them. I literally had more scientists than any two factions had population and they were still outresearching me!
If these are ever fixed, this will be a nice little game. Right now though, it's just too frustrating to play.
Edit: Okay, a tiny bit late adding this but not too long ago a big patch was released that was the dev's basically going 'yeah, we made the AI a cheating pack of superpowered madmen/women and we got tired of the complaints so here's us fixing it'. I haven't gotten around to trying it yet, but it does claim to solve a fair few of the complaints I have.

Well, it's been a while since I got Stellaris and Paradox as well as modders are working hard to improve it.
All in all, I think it is wonderful, but there are two things that really get to me once I've played a while (don't know why Steam only shows 60 hours, I've played way more than that):
1) Planets. If I colonize a new planet, shift around population, build something here and there... well, it feels like a colony, like a tiny settlement somewhere on a huge planet.
... And when I switch to that fully-colonized size 20 planet that has a citizen and some powerplant or mine or government building on every tile? It feels exactly the same.
For me, the game lacks something here, something that makes planets, particularly the handful you build up to be the commercial, industrial and (one would assume) administrative/cultural hubs of your empire feel like they are actually densely-populated capitals, not just a village with 20 inhabitants. And I'm not talking about changing a texture in game that adds some lights all over the planet.
2) Battles. Space battles and ground combat are, if we're being honest about it, fairly dull. Now, that's true for most paradox games - nobody's playing EU4 and CK2 for those sexy battles - but I feel like there should be a more noticeable difference between sending stacks of 1.000 soldiers each into battle, in an age where you really didn't have much control over your troops once the armies had clashed, and singular high-tech ships (and futuristic infantry) fighting in space (or on the ground), presumably while constantly communicating with the brass.
My point is: There's room for improvement. It's a grand strategy game, not Homeworld, and that is fine, but it seems to me like there ought to be a little more to it than that - more customization, more control or maybe more noticeable differences between the weapon types.
As it stands, it's functional, but it could be so much more.
I heartily recommend this game, no question there, but as good as it is: It's certainly not the 4X space game to end all 4X games.
If anything, it makes me wish all the more for something like a lovechild of this and Aurora4X.

The short version.
Although a clone of Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, Pandora is *not* Alpha Centauri. It is not even close. The art assets are far inferior, the diplomatic dialogs display the wit of a high-school student, and the factions, although almost identical to those of Alpha Centauri, are not motivated by their ideology, rather they display no obvious motivation at all. Indeed, they are often completely erratic, and will go to war for no reason, offer peace after losing a few units and then declare war again a few turns later. Over and over, and regardless of faction. They will also erratically make and break treaties over and over, and will throw snide comments at you in an attempt to sway the other factions against you. Independently of faction as well as over and over and over. Lastly, the quotes associated with the research lack the cultural sophistication of those from Alpha Centauri, and are often uninteresting or even annoying. In other words, the interest in the technologies and in the interaction between factions has been tossed out, and replaced with snide and ham-handed commentary.
Pandora changes the game situation a bit. Rather than mind-worms and a nascent god consciousness, Pandora has varied and aggressive indigenous lifeforms that have a significant role in player development as they will harass your early colonies and inhibit expansion. There is also another alien race that will pop in with superior technology and try to terraform the place as well as wipe everyone out more directly.
There are some improvements to the interface, the management system doesn't lock you in a modal update sequence after each turn, and you actually get incident reports that you can click on to find out what happened. So, to the author's credit, some improvement has been made, although you will still get multiple dialogs overlaying combat so they have failed to fully understand the concept of 'communication' and the difference between noise and information. On top of that there is the stack of making or breaking treaty dialogs and the personal carping communications after each turn ... well, maybe after every *second* turn.
Nevertheless, Pandora is a playable and a technically competent game on the Alpha Centauri model. If you thought that Alpha Centauri took itself too seriously and needed to lighten up, Pandora might work for you.

Galactic Civilizations III is in a word, good.  It is an improvement upon Galciv II in many ways (which is what you always want from a sequel), however this experience is still sometimes marred with the occasional bug, or lack of polish
For those that have never played a Galciv game before, let me give a brief overview.
For starters it is a 4X game (Explore, Expand, Exploit and Exterminate).  This means that like many 4X games you will be creating an empire from, the ground up, researching new technology, making alliances and enemies and eventually destroying those enemies some times.
In many ways, this game resembles the popular Civilization franchise, however there are several key differences.
1) this game is in space.  there are no hills, rivers, lakes or "ideal" city spots.  you cannot just create a colony where ever.  it has to be on several randomly generated (and varing in quality and appearance) planets.
2) the colonies can specialise further than any city ever could.  There are planet wide bonuses to certain things, and due to limited space on a single planet, you have to choose carefully what you place down.  New to the series is the idea of "adjacancy bonuses" which work similar to Xcom, in which there more buildings of a similar type you put down, they all give each other bonuses
3) you can create, design and upgrade your own personal ships.  Unlike in Civilization where you have stock units, and Endless Legend where you can "upgrade" units, in Galciv you literally design and build your own units from the ground up.
4) Also unlike other 4X games, there is very little combat early on.  infact, rushing to combat usually means you lose.  Galciv takes the approach of "we just got into space, we are not going to immediatly start strapping guns on things"
as such, races are much more likely to develop alliances with you, and trade, which leads to an overall more peaceful and relaxing game.  Also, when war does come, it comes in force.
5) Finally, the Ideology system works a bit like beyond earth, but more subtle while at the same time granting greater benifits.  You choose between Good, neutral and Evil essentially, and each tree has amazing benifits.  not only that, but you are not confined to one like in Civ:BE, as you can take perks from all 3 trees at any time
So to wrap up this little intro for people new to the Galciv franchise, think of this game like Sid Meiers "Starships" if that game was actually good and interesting
Now, for those who have played Galciv before, but are unsure about getting Galciv III.
It is more than just the graphics that have been improved.  The ship creation kit is more in depth and advanced than ever before.  The Ideologies are actually quite interesting, and while not game changing they certeinly make it more fun.  Tech specialization, which is where you can choose 1/3 benifits for each tech (e.g. longer range laser or faster laser, less expensive components or less mass etc) adds a great deal of tactical thinking to the game, as it forces you to specalise your empire, although the other 2/3 techs can always be traded for.  The addition of strategic resources adds a bit of a resource grab in the beginning, and can allow for some really powerful ships (which is always fun)
However, the Ai cheats like always at higher difficulties to dont expect any groundbreaking innovation there.
There are also dozens of smaller changes, like rally point management or the ability to go to an empire screen and tell all ships empire wide of type a to upgrade to type b, or stop what they are doing and travel to point c is really handy.
all in all, if you like 4X games, or the Galciv series, I suggest you pick up this game.  It may not be a 10/10 ign, but it is definetly one of my favourite games of the year

Going from the start there was a very long boring prologue. Then as we arrived at Flotsam I was stunned. The first few quests were so cool and everywhere was eye-wateringly brilliantly graphically realised. I was truly staggered for about six hours. Then bang-smash down to earth with Kayran, a horrible hard boss. Followed by lots of googling to work out the next quests. (There is no marker and no hint.)
